docs.title: ABS and EPB — circuits and DTC codes
docs.text: Tags: #abs · #esp · #wiring-diagram

docs.title: DTC codes (code → meaning, verbatim)
docs.text:
DTC Meaning (verbatim, Russian) English C131000 Цепь датчика скорости заднего колеса открыта Rear wheel speed sensor circuit open

C131000 was read on a Bestune X80 from the ABS/EPS module of a FAW diagnostic app (V2.00.027, vehicle software V13.70) at 44,328.10 km on 2024-11-05, before repair. The extracted report does not show the status column, so it is unknown whether the fault was active or stored. An open circuit means the sensor wiring or connector is broken or disconnected and the signal is lost, so check the rear wheel speed sensor, its wiring and connector before replacing the sensor; the report gives no repair procedure.1 For wheel-speed-sensor damage stories see ABS sensor damage from a pothole and the ABS tone ring identification.

docs.title: ABS/ESP circuit (wiring diagram page 1107)
docs.text: From the X80 wiring diagram page 1107, "Brake Electronic Stability Program" (ESP, electronic stability program).2 - Fuses: ABS\ESP 5A (Si57), ABS\ESP2 40A (Si12), ABS\ESP1 25A (Si8). - ABS/ESP control unit: F33. - Wheel speed sensors: F18 front left, F40 front right, ABL1 rear left, ABR1 rear right. - Steering angle sensor: I35. - The control unit is fed from the relay block I25/I26 (IGN1 Relay 1, IGN2 Relay 2 and ACC feed) with ignition switch I34 positions. The ESP/Start-stop Off switch is cross-referenced to page 1125, the BCM to 1117 and the gateway control unit to 1113. - Connector pins 1-38 are printed but the extracted text does not map them, so use this for fuse and component identification, not pin tracing.

docs.title: Electric parking brake circuit (wiring diagram page 1108)
docs.text:
From page 1108, "Electric Parking Brake System".3 - Fuses as printed: BNT 40A (Si1), EPB 30A (Si34), PKE EPB 5A (Si58), Room Light 10A (Si54). A "2.0L&MT" note appears near the EPB fuse; its association is unclear. - EPB control unit R29; EPB switch R34; left EPB motor ABL2 and right EPB motor ABR2 (connector pins 1 and 2, + and -). - Cross-references: clutch switch FS1 (manual transmission) page 1101; reverse switch 1104; brake light switch 1117; gateway control unit 1113; PKE controller 1119; small light dimmer 1125. The backlight operating indication is on the same circuit.

Procedures for releasing the EPB and changing rear pads are in electronic parking brake and rear pad replacement with EPB.

docs.title: Brake caliper repair kits
docs.text:
Tags: #front-axle · #rear-axle · #part-number

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

docs.title: Front caliper repair kits
docs.text:
Two main options reported for a front caliper rebuild: - B5CA0339KIT — full FAW-direct kit with piston, seals/rubbers, sold by Kitzapchasti and similar resellers.12 - FC01-3501010-1 — cross-fit kit from the Besturn B50 parts family, reported as usable on X80 front calipers.1 - Generic repair kit combined with a separate MASUMA MBC-0008 piston is also reported as a working combination.1 - Guide-pins-only kit: B5CA0339NAP (no piston/seals, just the pin hardware) — useful if only the guide pins need replacing.32 - Separately, a front caliper guide (lower mount) repair kit is sold via Kitparts for 1,390 RUB (RU market, May 2025); addresses squeaking and misalignment caused by worn lower-guide bushings specifically (narrower scope than the full B5CA0339KIT above).45

Sourcing note: КитЗапчасти (Kitzapchasti) sources parts from the Chinese factory supplier GiKong, the same factory that supplies FAW itself for many parts — pricing runs roughly 30% below official dealer rates, but quality is reported as variable batch-to-batch.67

Right front caliper bracket (restyle) is not sold as a separate part on the market as of this reporting. Workarounds: (1) source a used/salvage caliper assembly; (2) buy a complete new caliper assembly instead of just the bracket; (3) try a Mazda caliper as a possible cross-fit — compatibility is unconfirmed, so verify before committing; (4) use the guide-pins-only kit above if the bracket itself is intact and only the pins are worn.891032

docs.title: Rear caliper repair kits and sourcing
docs.text:
• B5CA02646Z — rear caliper repair kit (seals, springs, piston components), sold by Kitzapchasti for ~2,000–2,080 RUB (RU market, late 2024/April 2025 pricing); this is the standard rebuild option for a serviceable caliper.11121314
  • If the caliper body itself is damaged beyond a rebuild, owners source used complete calipers via marketplaces like Avito (regional availability, e.g. Magnitogorsk in one case), or buy new complete calipers at higher cost.15161718
  • General guidance from owners: don't economize on brake components — prefer a proper rebuild kit or known-quality parts over the cheapest Chinese alternative, given the safety-critical nature of the part.12

docs.title: Guide pins (both axles)
docs.text:
Rear caliper guide pins ("направляющие"/slide pins) are steel rods with rubber sleeve bushings, distinct from the piston/seal kit above. FAW Besturn B50 rear caliper guide pin kit, part FC01-3502036, includes the rubber sleeves and steel rods and is reported as cross-fitting X80; similar guide-pin kits are also listed directly for X80 on Ozon.1920

Maintenance rule: guide pins should move freely. If a pin is seized (common after water exposure/corrosion), it must be extracted, cleaned, and re-lubricated — some owners do this without replacing the pin/kit at all, since the pin itself is often fine once de-rusted.21

Cleaning/rust-treatment procedure (applies to both axles): remove the pads, extract both guide pins (note: the two pins on one caliper often have different construction/length — track which goes where), wire-brush off rust, then apply fresh brake-system-safe (PAG) grease and an anti-corrosion grease (MS1600 specifically recommended) to the working surfaces before reinstalling. Inspect the rubber dust boot for tears — a torn boot is what let water/grit in and caused the rust in the first place. When reinstalling pads, the ground/contact-end rivets can be filed smooth to avoid damaging the dust boot on reassembly. If a disc is seized/rust-stuck to the hub during this work, use a proper mechanical brake-disc puller tool, not a hammer.2223242526

docs.title: Rear caliper piston: screw-in design, not push-back
docs.text:
Unlike many hydraulic calipers where the piston simply pushes back into the bore, the X80's rear caliper piston screws in (rotates clockwise into the caliper body) as it retracts — pushing on it directly does nothing.272829 Correct retraction requires a dedicated screw-in tool: a T-shaped wrench with perpendicular handles and a calibrated depth stop, used to rotate the piston in to the correct depth for the new (thicker) pads.3031 (See the electronic-parking-brake card for how this piston retraction fits into the overall rear-pad-replacement sequence, including the debate over whether a plain scan-tool "release" is enough on its own.)

After retracting/reinstalling, the brake shoe/pad wear sensor should be reset through the vehicle's diagnostic menu if the car has one, rather than left unreset.32

docs.title: Rear disc overheating — guide-pin/boot diagnosis
docs.text: Intermittent overheating of a rear disc (one side noticeably hotter than the other after driving) is typically caused by one of: (1) a stuck guide pin or torn dust boot on that caliper (most common — water exposure can corrode/seize a pin, as in a documented case at ~40,000 km); (2) contaminated brake fluid or a sticking cylinder; or (3) a collapsed brake hose restricting fluid return. Because guide-pin seizure is the most common cause, owners recommend servicing the guide pins and dust boots every time the pads are replaced, as routine preventive maintenance.333435363738

docs.title: Rear piston retraction — additional tools and methods
docs.text: Beyond the dedicated screw-in tool described above: a specialized tool costing ~600 RUB (RU market, June 2025), or a bolt wrench from a grinder/angle grinder used manually (rotate clockwise one full turn while pushing inward), both work for the rear piston retraction. Total job time typically 30 minutes to 1 hour.3940414243 A separate, non-screw-in method reported for the rear piston: connect two wires to the battery with reversed polarity on the rear caliper to drive the piston back; alternatively, use the electric parking brake system itself (press the brake pedal and the parking-brake button simultaneously) to retract it. A third method involves a specific button-press sequence. The reversed-polarity wire method is reported as the most reliable for manual control (see the electronic-parking-brake card for the button-sequence release procedures in full).44454647

docs.title: Front caliper cross-fit from Mazda 6 GH, rear seals from Suzuki (community shop report)
docs.text:
• Front caliper pins and seals from Mazda 6 GH (2008–2013, 2.0L) fit the X80 front calipers — confirmed by an owner who also notes the pins themselves weren't purchased separately, only the rubber seals, which fit and "means it should work."48495051525354 One owner initially received an incorrectly-labeled "Lynx" branded part at a market stall claimed to be for Mazda CX-5 that turned out not to be the right part — verify the actual cross-reference rather than trusting a seller's verbal claim.55
  • Rear caliper seals from Suzuki Grand Vitara reportedly used in some repair shops as an alternative, per an invoice/accumulation record seen by a community member — an unverified but plausible cross-fit worth checking against exact dimensions before ordering.48

docs.title: MasterKit 77A1188 — front repair kit with grease notes (Aug 2025)
docs.text: MasterKit 77A1188 front caliper repair kit (piston seal, dust boot, and guide-pin seals — "resinки"/rubbers) documented with part numbers found via Ozon marketplace. Caliper guide pins are directional and have specific dimensions that must be verified during rebuild. High-temperature anti-squeal grease and caliper guide-pin grease should both be applied during installation.565758 (See also the Zekkert BR-1325 entry below, which is compared directly against this same 77A1188 kit.)

docs.title: KitParts vs Kitzap — piston sizing reliability
docs.text: For front caliper rebuild kits specifically, Kitzap-sourced kits often have piston diameters that don't fit (too small); KitParts brand is recommended instead, though it may have a longer lead time. Community recommendation: contact community member mastergtr75 for sourcing assistance if stuck.59606162

docs.title: Front caliper piston cross-compat: Nissan Qashqai / Mazda CX-5
docs.text: OEM X80 front caliper pistons can be replaced with parts from Nissan Qashqai J10 or Mazda CX-5 T31, with proper verification of diameter and height. One owner tested Zekkert-brand repair kits from Ozon: one size (labeled for QASHQAI/CX-5) worked with correct dimensions, while another, smaller piston from the same brand line did not fit — measure with calipers before purchase rather than trusting the listing.63646566676869

docs.title: Front seal kits and dust boots — additional cross-references
docs.text:
• Front brake caliper seal kit (seals + piston): part numbers B5CA0339RK or B5CA02646Z (note: B5CA02646Z is the same number documented elsewhere in this card as the standard rear kit — treat with care and verify axle/product category before ordering). Compatible cross-brand alternatives reported available from Gazelle and FAW Besturn B50 models, including rubber seals and piston.70717273747576
  • Brake dust boot (SHRUS-type outer boot): part B5DA122530. Multiple suppliers carry these; a Lanos-sourced dust boot has also been fitted successfully by one owner when the OEM part wasn't in stock locally.73747576

docs.title: Zekkert BR-1325 — front repair kit cross-brand alternative
docs.text: Zekkert BR-1325 caliper rebuild kit (designed for Mazda CX-5, X-Trail T31, Qashqai J10) has been fitted successfully to X80 front calipers by community members; community consensus treats this as a proven compatible alternative. The native part number 77A1188 (Masterkit brand, see above) is also viable at a lower cost (~350 RUB; RU market, March 2026) but is less tested than the Zekkert option.7778798081

docs.title: Caliper repair kit seal failure — real-world consequence
docs.text: Aftermarket brake caliper repair kits (ремкомплект) can have seals that fail under load. One reported case: the piston seized and the brake disc overheated during highway driving, requiring a full caliper replacement (2 discs + 2 calipers) — a costly outcome from a cheap kit. OEM or proven aftermarket parts are recommended over unverified repair kits for this reason.8283

docs.title: Complete front caliper — OEM part number and pricing (Jul 2026)
docs.text:
• Factory FAW front caliper (left/right, суппорт тормозной передний): article B5CA03399ZA. Price: 35,420 RUB (Jul 2026) from Russian parts distributors, with standard 5–7 day delivery to Moscow.84
  • Pricing tiers reported across the community (Jul 2026): OEM (B5CA03399ZA) 35,420 RUB; branded/OEM-adjacent alternatives 12,000–18,000 RUB; historical pricing as low as ~11,000 RUB, with a peak around ~28,000 RUB — significant variance across sources and quality tiers, so shop around rather than assuming one price.858684

docs.title: MASUMA MBC-0008 piston — reconfirmed
docs.text: The MASUMA MBC-0008 piston (already documented above as a compatible front-caliper piston option) is independently reconfirmed by two further community reports as the recommended piston when rebuilding or replacing front brake cylinders.8788

docs.title: Front dust boot — Lancer cross-fit (stretch fit)
docs.text: Separately from the SHRUS-type boot above, the front caliper piston dust boot can also be sourced from Lancer models as a cross-fit; it requires some stretching to fit and the original/stock part is still preferred when available.89

docs.title: Front repair kit — FAW Besturn B50, part FC013501020
docs.text: Front brake caliper repair kit (seals and piston) FAW Besturn B50 part FC013501020 is compatible with the X80 — B50 front-axle brake components are broadly interchangeable with X80 (consistent with the B50 cross-fit notes elsewhere in this card). Sourceable from Chinese parts suppliers such as kitzapchasti.ru.90 The reverse is also reported: when a search returned the B50 kit FC013501020, one member said it does not fit the X80, and the X80 front kit is listed as B5CA0339KIT (rubbers, piston and seals).9192

docs.title: Front piston boot sourcing and early MasterKit 77A1188 reports (Jul–Aug 2024)
docs.text:
OEM front/rear caliper piston boot: part B5CA03326X — one article for both front and rear, reported in stock at the dealer.93 Cross-brand alternative reported to fit better than OEM (the OEM boot runs oversized): MasterKit 77A1188 (for Mazda 6 GH, 2007–2013, 2.0L), available on Ozon.94959697 This is an earlier, independent field confirmation of the same 77A1188 kit documented in more detail elsewhere in this card (see the Aug 2025 grease-notes section and the Zekkert BR-1325 comparison below) — another owner separately confirmed this exact kit "fits perfectly."9899 Mazda 6 GG (2.0L) calipers themselves may also be compatible on some X80 models.94959697

A third report from the same period found Frenkit-brand front caliper repair kits fit well and are readily available; separately, a Mazda GH 2.0L caliper repair kit (ordered from an online catalog) also fits X80 front calipers and reportedly seats tighter/better than the original. Before committing to a full kit, check the caliper cylinder for rust/wear — sometimes only the gaskets need replacing.100101102103 The MasterKit 77A1188 kit (gaskets and seals) is available via Ozon: https://ozon.ru/t/LydBM6D.101

docs.title: Rear caliper piston corrosion repair — sandpaper/grease method
docs.text: A seized rear caliper piston with light surface corrosion can usually be restored rather than replaced: disassemble the caliper, inspect the piston (light surface rust is acceptable), clean it with 0-grit sandpaper, and apply caliper-guide grease under the dust boots. Use a full repair kit with a replacement piston only if the corrosion is severe. Full caliper replacement is unnecessary in most cases — repair kits run roughly 6,000–7,000 RUB (RU market, Sept 2024) at an independent shop vs. 10,000–12,000 RUB at an official dealer (RU market, Sept 2024 pricing, Irkutsk region); availability and pricing for specific caliper models vary by region.104105106

docs.title: Early field reports: screw-in rear piston, rear kit part number, and no-battery release (Mar 2024)
docs.text:
Independent early confirmation of the rear caliper's screw-in piston design (see the dedicated section above): the piston must be rotated in, not pushed — the caliper should be cleaned, guides lubricated, and a possible air lock in the caliper checked if the piston won't budge.107108109 For the motorized (rest/facelift AKPP) parking-brake caliper specifically, one method reported: disconnect the motor's electrical connector and apply battery voltage directly to the two motor contacts to drive the piston in/out — an alternative to the screw-in tool, requiring no special tooling beyond jumper wires.110111 Manual methods (turning the piston by hand or with a generic adapter) are also reported.112 After any of these rear-piston service methods, a brake adaptation procedure is needed before the system is fully functional again.107108109110111112

Separately, an early record of the same B5CA02646Z rear caliper repair kit documented elsewhere in this card: sourced from kitzapchasti.ru.113 A kitparts listing for the X80 rear brake gives B5CA02646Z as the caliper repair kit but titles it as the front caliper kit; the B50 rear caliper kit is FC013502010 / FC013502020 (seals and piston).114115

docs.title: Rear caliper — cylinder is not a separate part (independent corroboration)
docs.text: A separate community group corroborates the rear caliper design already noted above: the rear caliper cylinder (задний суппорт) is not sold as a standalone part — it is integrated with the caliper body and bracket. Only the internal piston and seals can be replaced through disassembly. If the seals leak or the piston is scored, an internal overhaul is attempted first; if damage is severe, the entire caliper assembly must be replaced — there is no way to buy just the cylinder.116117118119120121

docs.title: Uneven rear pad wear — guide-pin/piston-seal diagnosis (independent report)
docs.text: Consistent with the guide-pin/dust-boot diagnosis documented above for disc overheating, a separate report describes one rear pad (e.g. left rear) wearing much faster than its pair: likely causes are a degraded piston seal in the brake cylinder or a worn/corroded caliper guide. Diagnostic steps: check the piston seal condition and guide cleanliness/lubrication before assuming a caliper or suspension fault.122123124

docs.title: MasterKit 77A1188 fitted; guide kit 77A1538 (Aug–Oct 2025)
docs.text: One owner fitted the MasterKit 77A1188 caliper repair kit: all the rubbers fit and the piston is included in the kit; the Ozon listing was posted again in October 2025.125126 For the guide pins, MasterKit 77A1538 (caliper guide kit, Mazda 6 GH) was listed on Ozon in August 2025.127

docs.title: Brake fluid reservoir cap
docs.text:
Tags: #brake-fluid · #part-number

The brake fluid reservoir cap is small and easily lost during service — several owners report losing theirs.1

OEM part number: B5CA04355YA.2

New caps are reported as hard to find in regular retail channels. Owners recommend checking used-parts dealer networks and auto-dismantler ("разборка") sites, or searching specialist FAW parts resellers like kitzap, rather than expecting to find it in a generic parts catalog.32

docs.title: Brake fluid type and flush
docs.text:
Tags: #brake-fluid · #abs

Recommended brake fluid: Rosdot DOT 4 Class 6. A full system flush (changing the fluid at all four corners) takes approximately 910 ml.12

One owner who flushed to this fluid while also replacing the front caliper dust boots reported a ~90% improvement in braking feel versus the factory-fill fluid, tested specifically on mountain-pass driving (Caucasus serpentine roads) with frequent, sustained braking — a scenario that stresses fluid quality (heat, moisture absorption) more than flat city driving.2

docs.title: Bleeding sequence — diagonal Z-pattern (ABS)
docs.text: Because the X80 has a Bosch-type ABS module, the brake bleeding order follows a diagonal ("Z") pattern, not a simple front-to-back or side-to-side sequence: start with the wheel furthest from the master cylinder and work diagonally — right rear → left rear → right front → left front. Nut/bleeder-screw tightening during the job follows the same diagonal logic throughout. The same diagonal principle is also how the ABS system itself is wired/functions, which is why the bleed order matters more on this car than on a simpler non-diagonal system.34567

docs.title: Brake pad noise and quality
docs.text:
Tags: #brake-pad · #noise · #front-axle · #caliper

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Brake pad squeal is a recurring, cross-brand complaint in the community. No single supplier is squeal-free across all reports; the pattern below is useful for setting expectations, not a definitive verdict on any one brand.

docs.title: Mytishchi pads — split experience (April 2024)
docs.text: Community split on Russian-manufactured "Mytishchi" pad quality: some report 1000 km with no issues and a good price; others report squeaking starting around 1000 km, reduced braking effectiveness (especially cold/in traffic), and high-temperature howling. Likely explanation: installation quality or pad-batch softness variation rather than a uniform defect.12345 Conflict: kosta77777 reports a good experience after 1000 km, while Dmitriy (id 451764349) reports severe squeaking and Arapin reports reduced effectiveness; differences may stem from disc condition and driving style.23

docs.title: Chinese-sourced vs Russian-sourced pads
docs.text: Russian-manufactured ("Mytishchi") pads reported to squeal and generate excessive dust. A Chinese-sourced alternative (from mainland China suppliers, ~150–160 CNY (RU market, Oct 2024), obtained as a gift rather than purchased) performed better — less noise, cleaner. Durability not yet confirmed at time of report.678910

docs.title: Aftermarket pads from "kitzap" — persistent squeal
docs.text:
One owner ordered front pads from kitzap (Chinese-sourced supplier); pads began squeaking after one week and continued. Low-cost aftermarket pads often have squeal issues; pads with proper anti-squeal shims (like original FAW parts) are recommended instead.1112

Separately, multiple owners report front pad squeaking from new, sourced from different suppliers (KitZap, Ozon) — one owner tried 3 different sets with continuous squeaking. Root cause unclear: candidates are pad quality, disc surface finish, or installation error. Recommendation: try a different supplier, or have a shop verify installation and disc condition.1314151617

docs.title: KORWIN KWBP0119 — early impressions and break-in
docs.text: Tested 2024-10-10: no squeaking, noise, or dust on day one. A break-in period of ~400 km is needed before final judgment; one report notes squeaking may develop after 1000 km. Pads seated well with no mounting play. By comparison, unspecified China-sourced pads squealed within 10 km and produced significant dust — KORWIN looked superior in early use.1819202122 (See the front-brake-pads card for the KORWIN part number and fitment.)

docs.title: Pad color as a quality signal
docs.text: Black-colored brake pads from budget vendors are reported as poor quality and prone to squeaking; original grey-compound pads are reported superior for both noise and longevity. Several other cards in this section independently recommend light-gray pads over darker compounds for the same reason.23

docs.title: Squeal on new discs+pads — brand undecided (Jul 2025)
docs.text: One owner installed new front discs together with unbranded "kitzap"-sourced pads and got severe squealing immediately — initially suspected the old worn discs were the culprit, but the squeal appeared even with the new discs, pointing at the pads. General mechanism cited: high metallic content in the pad compound squeals more as it heats up. The owner was still deciding between TRIALLI ceramic pads and another mid-price ceramic option at the time of the report — no firm brand verdict, but the takeaway is to prefer ceramic-compound pads at a mid-range price point over unbranded budget pads to avoid this failure mode.2425

docs.title: Deep-dive: Mytishchi squeal troubleshooting and root-cause discussion (Jun 2024)
docs.text: A long community thread revisited the Mytishchi-pad squeal problem (see the split-experience section above) with more diagnostic detail: - One owner went through 4 sets of Mytishchi pads, resurfacing the discs and replacing pads each time, with the squeal returning within a week.26 Rear pads on this car occasionally creak too, especially when reversing — a separate, apparently minor symptom.2728 - Lubrication as a fix: applying MS1600 grease to the caliper/pad contact points and (carefully, sparingly) under the anti-squeal shim can help — but not all Mytishchi pads have an anti-squeal shim/plate to lubricate under in the first place, which limits this fix for some batches.2930313233 - Conflict on OEM pads: one participant states original FAW pads are not a guarantee against squeal either — it has happened even on originals.34 - Overall Mytishchi verdict is mixed, not uniformly bad: they were originally suggested in the group specifically as a low-cost option, no one is forced to buy them; complaints in the chat are a minority of reports (a couple about squeaking, plus some about "wooden"/vague pedal feel under braking); many owners run them without complaint. Result variance is attributed to luck-of-the-batch plus disc condition.35 A contrasting report: discs+pads both sourced from Mytishchi squealed loudly, not immediately but after a few brake applications; switching to a different pad brand resolved it; these Mytishchi pads reportedly ship without anti-squeal shims at all.36 - Extended field report (>3,000 km on Mytishchi pads): squeal occurs specifically when braking gently in traffic/at lights, plus a "wooden" (vague/spongy) brake feel; discs were labeled Japan-made (authenticity unverified) and matched to Mazda GG sizing; for comparison, the originally-fitted B50/Masuma-brand pads had knocked (loose in the ears/retention lugs) and also squealed badly despite biting hard. Net assessment: Mytishchi pads are ~800 RUB (RU market, June 2024) but perform at roughly a ~1,200 RUB quality level, and are reliably in stock — the best available option until something more consistently quiet is found.37 Independently confirmed: Mytishchi pads whistle under braking on another owner's car too.38 - Community suggestion following this: whoever finds a pad that is 100% non-squealing and reasonably priced should post the specific product link, so the group can standardize on a known-good option instead of everyone individually gambling on brands.3940 - Most-cited root causes, from an owner who has diagnosed this repeatedly: (1) the transverse groove in the friction material clogs with debris — a small stone gets lodged and can't escape, causing scraping/squeal (see also the separate stone-in-caliper case below); (2) the pad retention-ear contact plates get gunked up and the pad doesn't retract from the disc by the correct clearance during normal driving — some owners make this worse by over-greasing these plates, since the grease itself then attracts and traps dirt, which can eventually block pad retraction entirely. Suggested fix: disassemble, resurface, and clean thoroughly; if that doesn't hold, spray brake cleaner onto the described contact points with the wheel off and the disc spinning by hand.41 - Ozon listings referenced in this thread: B5CA03328ZA (OEM FAW front pads) at 2,249 RUB, and Mytishchi-brand pads around 800 RUB (RU market, June 2024).42434445

docs.title: Stone/foreign-object lodged in caliper — intermittent noise
docs.text: A small stone or pebble can become trapped inside the brake caliper assembly, causing a squealing or grinding noise that comes and goes with driving conditions (may worsen in turns or under gentle braking). One reported case turned out to be a glass shard rather than a stone. This matches the "clogged transverse groove" mechanism described in the Mytishchi deep-dive above — a second, independently-reported owner suspects they had the same issue previously, based on matching symptoms (noise that later disappeared on its own once the object presumably worked its way out). Diagnosis requires disassembling the brake area to visually inspect and remove the object.4647484950

docs.title: Front whistle from uneven pad wear — check the divider before replacing the caliper
docs.text: Front brake whistle is often traced to uneven pad wear (more wear on one side, typically the left). Before replacing an expensive caliper (суппорт), first check it for a stuck piston or dried-out/seized guide pins — these are cheaper to fix with a repair kit (piston-only or guide-pins-only; see the brake-caliper-repair-kits card) than a full caliper swap. The brake-force divider (тормозной кран/regulator) can also fail and cause uneven pad wear, so it should be checked alongside the caliper rather than assumed to be a caliper-only problem. Replacing individual worn components (guides, piston, seals) separately is cheaper than a full caliper replacement.51525354555657

docs.title: UIDNU YD52002 ceramic pads — whistle returned after initial success (conflict)
docs.text: The front-brake-pads card documents UIDNU YD52002 as resolving earlier whistling complaints on the restyled X80. A later report complicates that: after switching to UIDNU YD52002 — which initially performed well — the whistle reappeared after about 2 days of driving, showing that even a well-regarded ceramic pad can develop noise over time, not only on first install. Community observation from the same thread: whistle risk looks roughly similar across cheap and expensive brands alike (e.g. "Mytishchi" pads at ~700 RUB; RU market, July 2024), and a comparison from a Camry owner needed 4 different pad sets before finding a quiet combination — reinforcing that pad noise is highly batch/installation dependent rather than a reliable brand signal.585960 Conflict: earlier messages in the same community thread (see the front-brake-pads card) praised UIDNU YD52002 as whistle-free; this later report shows the whistle returned after 2 days on at least one car.

docs.title: Budget pad squeaking within 500 km (shop-installed)
docs.text: One owner installed aftermarket budget pads (likely from the Zikert/Zekkert family, sourced from a local shop) that produced severe squeaking within 500 km, described as comparable to a UAZ truck's brakes at traffic lights. Installation was performed by shop mechanics, not the owner — ruling out an obvious DIY installation error as the sole cause.61

docs.title: General squeaking diagnostics checklist
docs.text: Squeaking on budget pads is relatively rare; when it happens, check: (1) the caliper piston stroke for partial binding/sticking, which causes uneven pad wear, disc overheating, and unpredictable braking; (2) caliper guide-pin condition and lubrication (see the guide-pin maintenance section on the brake-caliper-repair-kits card). Genuine OEM pads are available for roughly 10,000 RUB (RU market, March 2024) as a known-quiet fallback if aftermarket squeal persists. Community consensus: squeaking is more often an installation or pad-material issue than a defective part.62636465

docs.title: Rubber-like squeal when braking: silent blocks or grit
docs.text: A rubber-like squeal when braking can come from upper front-arm silent blocks (rubber-metal bushings, сайлентблоки) that are due for replacement, or from grit lodged between a pad and the disc. The grit cause often follows driving through mud or puddles and can also cause vibration. No fix or cost was given.66

docs.title: Brand differences and checking fitment before buying
docs.text:
• A factory video claims that many pad brands are made on one line for different customers and differ mainly in formulation or specification; the factory's robotic line was not shown on camera. A member replies that a shared factory is plausible but the products may still differ by each customer's technical specification, so the claim does not make brands equivalent.6768
  • To find pads that fit the X80, search online parts shops for pads listed "под X80" (for X80), ask the seller to check the stock against a fitment measurement and send a photo of it, and buy only if the measurement matches.69

docs.title: Brake pad wear rate — front vs rear
docs.text:
Tags: #brake-pad · #wear · #front-axle · #rear-axle

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Front brake pads wear roughly 2x faster than rear pads, attributed to weight transfer during braking (front axle carries ~70% of braking load, rear ~30%). Typical owner-reported replacement intervals: front pads ~40,000 km, rear pads ~60,000–80,000 km. Community consensus is that front pads should wear faster under normal braking.1234567

Conflict: a minority of owners report the opposite — rear pads wearing faster — possibly due to wear-indicator quality differences or driving style.1

Separately, in aggressive urban driving several owners quantify this as roughly 2 front pad changes per 1 rear pad change. Rear pads on the X80 have no wear sensor, so rear wear must be checked manually/visually rather than via a dashboard warning. Pad life overall is highly dependent on driving style — aggressive braking accelerates wear on both axles.891011121314

Conflict: one owner in this second discussion also reported the opposite wear pattern (rear wearing faster), again likely explained by individual driving style.8

docs.title: Price vs. lifespan trade-off
docs.text: Following on from the same discussion: premium pads cost roughly 2x the price of budget pads but deliver roughly 2x the lifespan, so the per-kilometer cost is similar — the main practical difference is service frequency, not total spend. Typical full lifespan for quality pads: 100,000–150,000 km before they're worn out. Cheaper pads (around 8,000 RUB in one reported case, RU market, June 2025) tend to fail quickly, while higher-priced quality pads are seen as justified by the extended service interval.15

docs.title: Conflict: OEM pads wearing much faster than the ~40,000 km norm (independent report)
docs.text: A separate community group reports OEM/factory pads are not special and can wear out far faster than the ~40,000 km typical figure documented above: one owner's OEM pads lasted only ~20,000 km, with rapid rotor wear alongside them — roughly half the expected front-pad life. Community advice from this thread leans toward accepting OEM parts and the associated maintenance cost regardless, since aftermarket performance also varies.16171819 Conflict: this ~20,000 km OEM-pad lifespan directly contradicts the ~40,000 km front / 60,000–80,000 km rear figures reported above from the larger discussion — likely explained by the same driving-style variance already noted as a source of disagreement in this card, though it could also reflect a batch-quality or model-year difference in the OEM pads themselves.

docs.title: Caliper guide-pin dust boots
docs.text:
Tags: #caliper · #part-number

Front brake caliper repair kits can include an incompatible dust boot (пыльник) — trial-and-error sourcing needed: one owner (Arсhi 77) replaced the repair kit on his front calipers, but the guide-pin dust boot included in the kit did not fit; he sourced a compatible boot from a different kit instead. He quietly swapped the mismatched boot back into its box and returned it to the marketplace seller rather than raising the mismatch — noting he has never had a return refused, even when returning several mismatched parts (e.g. CV joint parts) from the same order at once, and that dealing with fitment mismatches this way is just part of owning this car 12.

Confirmed compatible source — Zekkert BR-1364 caliper repair kit (also fits Subaru Forester SH): after searching by trial and error, owner KASPER identified a specific working source for the front caliper guide-pin dust boots: the Zekkert BR-1364 brake caliper repair kit. This kit is catalog-listed for Hyundai Santa Fe (2001+), Hyundai Sonata III–IV (1993+), Kia Cerato (2004+), Kia Spectra (2004+), and Mitsubishi L200 III (1996+) — none of which are FAW or Mazda models, illustrating that the correct cross-fit source is not obvious from the catalog application list alone. KASPER additionally confirmed the same guide-pin dust boots are available from a Subaru Forester SH source. Fellow owner Arсhi 77 confirmed the general sourcing lesson: for this part, you simply have to search by trial and error rather than relying on a listed part-number match 3456.

Practical takeaway: don't assume a caliper repair kit's included dust boot will fit the X80 even if the rest of the kit (pistons, seals) works — verify guide-pin boot fitment separately, and expect to try more than one source. The Zekkert BR-1364 kit and Subaru Forester SH parts are the two confirmed working sources reported by the community so far.

docs.title: Drilled and perforated brake discs
docs.text:
Tags: #brake-disc · #part-number · #front-axle · #rear-axle · #mazda-6-compat

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Owners disagree on whether drilled (perforated) discs are worth buying for the X80. For standard discs see front brake discs and rear brake discs.

docs.title: Owner impressions
docs.text:
• One owner bought perforated discs on Ozon and has run them on all four wheels for about a year; he says they look good and do their job.12
  • Another member disagrees: perforation only changes the look and costs extra, because the discs brake the same. Neither side gave a braking measurement.3

docs.title: Painted drilled discs: strip the paint?
docs.text: A buyer of drilled discs for another car asked whether the paint must be removed before fitting, because buyers had reported poor braking until the paint wore off. The reply was not to remove anything, since the paint wears off in use; no measured result was given.45

docs.title: NiBK sets fitted (Oct 2026)
docs.text: One owner listed NiBK parts for the car: front disc set RN1515DSET with pads PN8009, and rear disc set RN1208DSET with pads PN5203. The "DSET" suffix most likely means a disc set; this is inferred, not stated. His photo after fitting (24 October 2026) shows drilled discs painted magenta behind an alloy wheel with 215/60 R17 IKON Tyres winter tyres.67 Mixed reviews of RN1515DSET from earlier threads are in the front brake discs card; a rear Ozon pair listing is in the rear brake discs card.

docs.title: NiBK listings on Ozon
docs.text: Ozon lists NiBK RN1516DSET (front perforated disc for Mazda Atenza / CX-5) and NiBK Performance RN1515DSET (front sport disc for Mazda 6 GH); a member reports poor reviews for the sport disc, and fitment to the X80 is not confirmed. See front brake discs.8910

docs.title: Electronic parking brake
docs.text:
Tags: #parking-brake

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The X80's electronic parking brake (rear-axle) clamps the rear calipers with a motor/servo, not a cable. Before rear pad replacement the system normally needs to be released or put into a "service mode", otherwise the caliper stays clamped and error codes are likely.1 Community members report several different working procedures; these are not necessarily mutually exclusive — reliability varies by trim/generation and by report, so this card documents all of them together with the conflicts between reports.

docs.title: Normal parking use and wear
docs.text:
Standard procedure: keep the transmission in D, apply the foot brake to stop, pull the electronic handbrake switch up to engage it, then release the foot brake and gas pedal.23 The owner's manual describes this exact sequence (including a "dynamic" very-low-speed parking case) and explicitly warns not to drive with the handbrake engaged.2

Holding the car stationary via P (mechanical parking pawl), D + foot brake (all four hydraulic cylinders engaged), or D + electric handbrake (the two rear cylinders engaged) all place broadly similar load on the drivetrain according to the manual — none of the three is inherently damaging when used on level ground.43

However, frequent use of the electric handbrake while merely parked increases wear on the rear brake pads and on the handbrake's motor/servo drive specifically — using P or the foot brake more often is gentler on these parts.56 Never engage the electric handbrake (or the mechanical/hydraulic brakes) while the car is in motion, except in a genuine emergency.7

docs.title: Emergency-stop behavior at speed
docs.text: Per the owner's manual, activating the electronic parking brake while driving at speed (the community discussed the case of ~60 km/h on a highway) triggers the ABS system and causes hard emergency deceleration. The manual documents this as an emergency-only function for when the normal (foot) brakes fail — not something to test casually, since it risks damaging the parking-brake motor/actuator (a costly part) if misused.8910 Normal (non-emergency) parking-brake engagement requires the car to already be stopped or moving at roughly ≤3–3.5 km/h.29 One owner also describes engaging it while rolling: pull the switch up and hold it, it beeps and engages after a long hold, and it releases when the throttle or brake is pressed while the stability system can intervene; he used it for controlled slides in snow. His explanation is loose, so check the exact sequence in the owner's manual.11

docs.title: Reported procedures for releasing the handbrake to replace rear pads
docs.text:
No single procedure is confirmed as universally reliable across trims — different owners report different sequences working for them. Try them in roughly this order of accessibility:

  1. Button-hold + ignition-off sequence (most commonly reported, no tools needed): with the brake pedal pressed, press and hold the electric handbrake button down, then turn the ignition off while still holding the button/pedal — the caliper piston releases enough clamp force to begin the swap.121314 A reported variant: with the engine running and the transmission in N, press and hold the handbrake button for about 5 seconds, then shut off the ignition while still holding the button.15
  2. External 12 V supply directly to the caliper motor: disconnect the electrical connector near the caliper/handbrake actuator and apply a 12 V battery directly to the motor leads to drive it open; a couple of owners describe simple two-wire jumper setups for this, sometimes combined with pulling the handbrake fuse first — described by one owner as "the method for connoisseurs" (unconventional, but reportedly effective as a budget/no-dealer-tool option).16171819
  3. Scan-tool service mode: OBD tools such as Diagzon PRO put the brake system into a dedicated pad-replacement service mode alongside other functions (ABS/ESP diagnostics — one report found a faulty left rear ABS sensor this way — plus TPMS reprogramming); reported as more capable for FAW-specific functions than basic Bluetooth OBDII dongles.2021 Dealer/shop-level scan tools are also used by some services to enter and exit service mode cleanly.2223
  4. Bypass the electronics mechanically: one owner reports simply pulling the handbrake fuse and unplugging the connector, then doing the pad swap by hand without any electronic release step at all — contrasted by others with just entering service mode and replacing normally; both are reported as working, at the cost of extra fiddling for the fuse-pull route.242526

Conflict between reports: which single sequence "just works" is disputed. One owner found that pressing the handbrake button and turning off ignition alone did not fully release their (pre-restyle) caliper and had to add a direct 12 V feed to the motor to finish the job, while others report the button-only sequence working fine on its own — likely a generation/trim difference rather than user error.2728 Two different working procedures end up documented across these threads; if method (1) doesn't fully retract the piston, fall back to (2) or (3) rather than forcing it.29301731

docs.title: Critical warning: never work with the engine running
docs.text: Never remove a rear wheel/caliper to replace pads while the engine is running. The ECU can detect wheel rotation while a wheel is physically off the car and interpret it as the vehicle moving with a brake disassembled — this can lock the handbrake's electronic control module into a fault state (an expensive part to replace), not just throw a clearable error code. Always fully shut the engine down (ignition off) before removing the wheel/caliper.3233 The accepted safe methods are: a proper scan-tool service mode, or the button+ignition sequence above performed with the engine off. Some shops additionally cycle the brake pedal about 5 times after reassembly, before the next ignition-on, on the belief this reduces the chance of the re-clamp timer firing into an error.34

docs.title: Piston retraction and the rear friction-plate debate
docs.text:
Releasing the electronic clamp (via any method above) only removes the resting clamp force — the rear caliper piston is a screw-in design (see the brake-caliper-repair-kits card for full mechanical detail) that must then be manually rotated in with a dedicated tool, not just pushed, to make room for new, thicker pads. A scan tool's "release" step is not a substitute for this manual screw-in step.3536373839

Conflict — installing pads without their anti-squeal friction plates: on one difficult rear-pad job, the friction plates supplied with the new pads would not allow enough clearance for the caliper to seat over them (the bracket has very little slack — roughly one-and-a-half pad-widths of total clearance). That owner installed the pads without the plates after retracting the piston via OBD scan-tool service mode plus manual rotation, and reported good, quiet, effective braking afterward with no issues after testing.4041424344 Another community member pushed back, arguing the plates are functionally necessary for proper braking/noise suppression and that the omission was risky pending more testing/mileage; a third view was that decent-quality pads shouldn't need the plates to avoid squealing regardless of whether they're fitted.454647484950

docs.title: Diagnostics tooling
docs.text: Beyond the pad-replacement service mode itself, scan tools like Diagzon PRO are reported to unlock a broader set of FAW-specific brake-adjacent functions in one package: ABS sensor/module diagnostics, ESP diagnostics, and tire-pressure-sensor reprogramming — worthwhile if buying a tool anyway rather than relying on a generic Bluetooth OBDII dongle.2021

docs.title: Troubleshooting: handbrake button unresponsive after service work
docs.text: If the electric handbrake button stops responding to presses after exiting service mode — and standard recalibration attempts plus disconnecting the 12 V ground both fail to fix it — pulling the 30 A fuse under the hood performs a full system reset. Reinstall the fuse once the handbrake responds normally again; this fixed the issue for one owner after all standard procedures failed.51

docs.title: Frozen/stuck parking brake (winter thaw)
docs.text: During a winter thaw, the electronic parking brake can appear stuck or slow to release because water has frozen between the pad and disc, typically during temperature swings around -5°C to +5°C. Reported fixes: warm the disc with a heat gun (fast and effective), or pour boiling water on the disc to melt the ice — one owner reports success with the latter using water carried in a thermos.5253 Opinions differ on prevention: some suggest pre-emptively drying the brakes in winter to avoid this; others argue the handbrake's servo motor is strong enough to break free of the ice regardless, making preventive drying unnecessary — treat as an unresolved community debate rather than settled advice.54

docs.title: Facelift vs pre-facelift release without the engine running
docs.text: A distinct, simpler release procedure is documented for releasing the EPB without the engine running: on facelift (2019+) models, press and hold the brake pedal, press the parking-brake button, and turn off the ignition while still holding the button. On manual-transmission cars, simply holding the button while shutting the car off is reported to work on its own. Do not release the button until the engine is fully off. The procedure is reported to differ on pre-facelift models, where the brake can be disabled more easily — treat this as a lighter-weight companion to the fuller numbered-procedure list above, for the specific "engine already off" starting condition.55565758 A member of a pre-restyle (дорест) car reports that the shorter variant (press the brake, release the parking brake, hold the brake, switch the engine off) does not work on pre-restyle cars; the owner's 31-second video shows it on a restyled automatic.5960

docs.title: Parking-brake motor is not sold separately (reconfirmed)
docs.text: Reconfirming and consolidating two independent reports: the parking-brake motor (моторчик ручника) cannot be purchased as a standalone part — it is only available as a complete assembly together with the rear caliper itself. If the motor fails, the whole caliper assembly must be replaced.61626364

docs.title: EPB stuck/unresponsive after a battery replacement
docs.text: After replacing the vehicle battery, the EPB can become stuck and fail to release. Reported partial fixes: holding the button longer, or pressing the brake pedal while pressing the EPB button simultaneously — these work for some vehicles but not all; some cars remain unresponsive even after these attempts, indicating a possible need for a dealer diagnostic scan.6566676869 (If the button itself becomes unresponsive after service work rather than after a battery swap, see the fuse-reset fix documented above.)

docs.title: Reference video: rear pad replacement with the electronic handbrake
docs.text: A community-shared YouTube walkthrough demonstrates the rear brake pad replacement procedure on the X80 with the electronic handbrake system, including the piston retraction technique and handling of resulting error codes: https://youtu.be/eM3lffCobnE?si=MKEJD_Griw2Jd7bk70

docs.title: Reset procedure after brake service (if the EPB misbehaves post-service)
docs.text: If the e-brake misbehaves after a rear pad replacement, a full reset procedure is reported: (1) disconnect the battery for 2–3 minutes; (2) reconnect it; (3) turn on the ignition; (4) press the brake pedal and pull the e-brake lever down; (5) hold the lever while turning the ignition off. A dealer performing this recalibration charged ~1,400 RUB (RU market, 2023 pricing). Best practice: disconnect the battery and release the e-brake before starting rear brake work in the first place, to avoid needing this recalibration step at all.7172

docs.title: No-battery-disconnect rear pad replacement — reported working methods (with timing conflict)
docs.text: Beyond the numbered release procedures above, owners report the rear pads can be replaced without disconnecting the battery, via any of several sequences: (1) shift to neutral, engine off, hold the brake, release the handbrake; (2) neutral, engine off, release the handbrake, then proceed; (3) some owners change pads with the engine running (reported as taking about 10 minutes) — this directly conflicts with the critical warning elsewhere in this card against ever working with the engine running, so treat engine-running removal as a risk some owners accept rather than a safe recommendation. Mechanical steps once released: remove the caliper with its bracket, leave the brake disc in place (held by friction only, no bolts needed for this step), screw the piston in, fit the new pads against the disc surface, and reassemble. A service-shop alternative: use a scan tool to electrically open/close the pads in service mode rather than doing it by hand.7374757677787980 Conflict: reported sequences disagree on whether the engine should be on or off, and on when exactly the handbrake should be released relative to the other steps — reliability likely depends on trim/generation as with the other release-procedure conflicts documented above.

docs.title: Дело техники 820005 piston tool and no-motor-removal rear pad procedure (Aug 2024)
docs.text: A specific branded tool for the rear caliper piston screw-in step: Дело техники, model 820005 (available on Ozon: https://ozon.ru/t/lYVkWqd), originally designed for Audi/VW/Skoda platforms but confirmed working on X80 rear calipers. The tool has 2 pins that insert into holes in the piston head, letting you screw the piston back into the cylinder rather than pushing it.818283 Full procedure reported using this tool, without removing any electric motor: (1) open the brake-fluid expansion tank before screwing the piston in (fluid gets pushed back as the piston retracts); (2) insert the tool's 2 pins into the piston head; (3) screw the piston fully into the cylinder; (4) fit the new pads; (5) reassemble. Reported as taking about 10 minutes per side, with no battery disconnection or motor connector work needed — consistent with, and an earlier instance of, the no-battery-disconnect method documented above.84838586

docs.title: Restyled vs pre-restyled service-mode entry — early confirmation and error-code risk
docs.text: An earlier report reinforces the facelift/pre-facelift service-mode distinction documented above: on restyled models, the car can be running in P or N — press and hold the handbrake button down while turning off the ignition with the other hand to release the caliper. On pre-restyled (doresto) models this sequence does not work the same way: as soon as the ignition is turned off, the handbrake automatically re-engages on its own, regardless of the button.8788 If the pads are serviced with the ignition left on at any point during the job (rather than fully off), this can store fault codes that only a dealer can clear via diagnostic software — reinforcing the critical "never work with the engine/ignition on" warning documented above.8990

docs.title: Parking-brake control module (ECU) — part number and availability
docs.text: The electric parking-brake control module itself (separate from the motor/servo already documented above as not sold standalone): part number 5CA044020A, priced around 70,000–75,000 RUB from official FAW dealers (RU market, Sept 2024). This module is extremely hard to find in the aftermarket — scrapyards rarely stock it, making used units nearly impossible to source. Reported common failure mode: in cold weather, the parking brake may fail to auto-release, requiring manual intervention.9192

docs.title: Retracting the rear piston without removing the motor — internal adjustment bolt (Aug 2024)
docs.text: An independent report of the full rear-pad procedure with the electronic handbrake, sourced from an Avito-purchased pad set: (1) engine running, shift to Neutral; (2) press and hold the handbrake button, then turn off the ignition while still holding the button; (3) disconnect the battery terminals; (4) remove the old pads; (5) retract the caliper piston using the caliper's internal adjustment bolt (hex socket) — this achieves the same result as the dedicated screw-in tool above, without removing the motor; alternatively, a strut/clamp can mechanically compress the cylinder, also without motor removal; (6) reinstall the new pads and adjust the caliper; (7) reconnect the battery; (8) turn on the ignition and press the handbrake to trigger auto-adjustment; (9) bleed the brakes before driving. As with the critical warning elsewhere in this card: do not change the ignition state mid-service, or fault codes will be stored that only a dealer can clear via software.939495

docs.title: Dealership misdiagnosis: "clinched" caliper claimed to need replacement
docs.text: A cautionary field report: an owner (Anna) took the car to a Bosch dealership to replace rear pads. The shop claimed the rear caliper on one side was "clinched" (заклинило) and needed a full caliper replacement. However, the car had driven 35 km to the shop without issue, and the brake discs showed only normal wear marks — not the damage pattern expected from a genuinely locked caliper.96979899100 Community consensus was that the dealership either mishandled the EPB service-mode/piston-release procedure (see above) or was upselling unnecessary work — a real caliper seizure severe enough to need replacement should have prevented the car from driving normally beforehand. Recommended response: get a second opinion at a different shop, and make sure any shop follows the proper release/retraction procedure (screw-in, not push; correct service-mode entry) before concluding the caliper itself is faulty.101102103104

docs.title: Uneven parking-brake cable length after rear pad/disc replacement (Aug 2026)
docs.text: One owner replaced rear discs and pads, screwed the caliper pistons back in, and reassembled everything, but found the parking-brake cable had become about 1 cm longer on each side afterward, so the EPB no longer applies in its emergency/mechanical-backup mode even though the caliper lever sits at the correct zero position.105 Community responses: (1) always release the parking brake before lifting the car / removing the wheels — most owners are asked to do this by the shop lift operator as a matter of course, and skipping it is a likely root cause of length drift; several owners who service rear pads regularly report never having to disconnect/pre-release the parking brake at all, suggesting the release step is normally unnecessary if the cable geometry is otherwise undisturbed.106107108109 (2) One owner speculated the issue could stem from leaving the ignition on during the job (the caliper re-clamping mid-service) and asked whether disconnecting the battery terminal is the fix — this remains an open, unresolved question in the thread rather than a confirmed cause.110 Conflict/gap: no owner in this thread confirmed a working fix for the already-lengthened cable; general good practice (per the rest of this card) is to keep the ignition fully off throughout the job and use a proper service-mode/piston-retraction procedure rather than freehand reassembly.105106107108110109

docs.title: More release methods and dealer delay (2025)
docs.text: Besides the button-hold sequence, two further ways are reported for retracting the EPB to change rear pads: release the EPB with the engine running, disconnect the battery negative, then switch off; or have a mechanic connect the EPB motor's two leads to a 12 V source with crocodile clips, reversing the polarity to retract and then re-extend the piston. One owner reports that a dealer's diagnostic procedure took a long time before it worked. The methods differ and none is confirmed as universal; see the numbered list above.11111211315 The service-mode and piston-tool procedures are also covered in rear pad replacement with EPB; wiring, fuses and diagnostic codes are in ABS and EPB: circuits and DTC codes.

docs.title: Front brake discs
docs.text:
Tags: #brake-disc · #front-axle · #mazda-6-compat · #part-number

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

docs.title: OEM part numbers (pre-restyling vs restyle)
docs.text:
X80 front brake discs have two different OEM part numbers depending on generation: - Pre-restyling X80: front disc 5DA033251.12 - Restyle X80 (2018+): front disc 5DA133251.1

Both are 299 mm diameter, but restyle and pre-restyle discs have different internal design/part numbers — they are not interchangeable by number, though some owners report both fitting across generations with correct adapter rings.34 One owner adds more nuance: 5DA033251 is the disc that also fits the Mazda 6 GG, while 5DA133251 is the "native" restyle-only part — in practice several owners consider the two functionally interchangeable despite the different numbers, though this view is not universal (see the cross-compat note above).56

The baseline OEM rear disc number (for reference) is 5DA026251.7

Overall disc spec: 299 mm diameter, 25 mm thickness for the front disc (confirmed independently by two owners).89

docs.title: Mazda cross-compatibility
docs.text: Several owners confirm Mazda 6 discs work as direct alternatives to the FAW front disc: - Mazda 6GG discs reported as fitting front FAW X80 discs directly.10 - Mazda 6 (GH generation, 2002–2007) front discs, 299 mm / 25 mm, cross-ref to part Nisshinbo ND5024K; verified compatible and installed successfully by a community member, cross-checked via the DRIVE2 parts database.111213 - Specific branded options confirmed compatible: Marshall M2000480 (ventilated, sold on Ozon) and Sangsin Brake SD4417 (also sold as Hi-Q SD4417, pricier than the Marshall).9141516 - Other Mazda 6 cross-reference numbers mentioned (fitment not fully confirmed): DF4974S, G33Y3325X, G33Y3325XA.1718

docs.title: Mazda 6 disc + caliper as a combined upgrade (early report, Sept 2024)
docs.text: Independent of the individual Mazda 6 disc cross-references above, an earlier community discussion frames the swap as a combined disc + caliper upgrade: Mazda 6 (especially the GG series and earlier) discs and calipers together are reported as mechanically compatible with the X80, with the Mazda discs slightly larger in diameter. This combined cross-fit is presented as a fix for the known front-pad-rattle design flaw (see the front-brake-pads card's "upper holes need 133.1mm" section) — since swapping in the Mazda caliper alongside its disc avoids the pad-width mismatch entirely, rather than hunting for a correctly-sized 133.1 mm pad. Installation requires fitting the Mazda caliper as well as the disc, not just a disc swap on the stock caliper.19202122

docs.title: Pricing (RU market)
docs.text:
As of 2024-09-13, Irkutsk supplier kitzapchasti.ru: - Front disc 5DA033251 (pre-restyling): 1900 RUB (RU market, Sept 2024). - Front disc 5DA133251 (restyle): 2330 RUB (RU market, Sept 2024).232425

REMSA-brand discs were also mentioned as available from other suppliers around the same time, without a confirmed price.23

SP2449 was separately mentioned by one owner as a recommended alternative disc option, rated as more trustworthy than the "Comi One" brand (incomplete website/support); note this code is also used elsewhere in the community for a Hi-Q brake pad, so treat SP2449 with care and verify the product category before ordering.26

docs.title: Quality warning
docs.text: Zecer-brand front discs are reported as poor quality: one owner had a Zecer disc crack completely after only 10,000–12,000 km, becoming unusable. Community consensus strongly advises against Zecer brake discs.272829

docs.title: Wear limit and disc-retaining screws
docs.text:
• Discs are unsafe once worn below 23 mm thickness — this is the absolute minimum for the X80.30
  • The disc is held to the hub by three small screws torqued to ~15 Nm. These screws only stop the disc falling off during assembly — the actual clamping load comes from the wheel bolts once installed. Over-torquing these screws to 30+ Nm can cause the disc to seize onto the hub. If over-torqued, removal may need an impact driver/wrench, heat, or (as some owners prefer at replacement time) simply drilling the screws out.3132

docs.title: Maintenance notes / troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Noise at 90+ km/h that scales with wheel speed and is independent of braking usually indicates corrosion/scale buildup (окалина) on the disc rim. Fix: remove the wheel, inspect the disc edge for a corrosion ridge, and knock the oxidation off with a hammer. Also check that the anti-squeal backing plate is seated straight — if mounted crooked it can contact the disc during rotation and cause noise too.333435363738
  • Mixed-manufacturer front discs: even with the same part number, discs from different manufacturers can have different friction coefficients — one owner noticed two "identical" discs had different paint in the non-working zone, indicating different makers. In theory this could cause uneven braking; in practice several owners report it works fine (pads "bed in" to each disc), but it should be monitored. Community is split on how much this matters.39404142434445464748
  • If the disc is seized/rust-stuck to the hub, use a proper mechanical brake disc puller tool, not a hammer.4950

docs.title: 2025 part-number and pricing consolidation (BN-1655, Lynx)
docs.text: By mid/late 2025 the community settled on a widely-cited front disc part number and brand: - BN-1655 (front) / BN-1651 (rear) — sold under the Lynx brand; confirmed as a perfect fit replacing both front and rear discs together.5152535455565758596061 - Lynx BN-1655 front disc pricing: 4,257 RUB (Ozon, RU market, Sept 2025); 2,800 RUB (RU market, Sept 2025) on Wildberries via seller "apstore" — one owner got a second car's discs at that lower price on the same day, same seller.62636465666768 - General OEM front/rear disc sourcing note: multiple Chinese-supplier and local-retailer options exist; disc sizing is consistent across model years for a given generation (see the rest/doreset part numbers above).69707172737475

docs.title: Mazda GH cross-fit reconfirmed, restyled fitment, and pricing (Sept 2025)
docs.text:
• Mazda 6 GH front discs fit the restyled X80 directly — one owner states this generation (not GG) is the correct cross-reference for discs.767778
  • LYNXAUTO-brand Mazda 6 GH front discs available on Wildberries/Ozon for ~4,200 RUB (RU market, Sept 2025); the community recommendation is to "buy without hesitation."798081
  • Original (OEM-sourced) disc option via Kitparts: 2,800 RUB (RU market, Sept 2025), but with a ~1-month factory delivery wait; these arrive pre-painted from the factory, a quality detail that's uncommon among aftermarket options.828384

docs.title: Sizing conflict: undersized pads on 300 mm aftermarket discs
docs.text: One owner installed SNLS 300 mm front discs and found the accompanying pads seemed undersized for the disc's pad area, raising the question of whether +5 mm larger pads could be sourced as an upgrade; this remains unverified — it's unclear whether larger pads are a direct bolt-on or would require caliper modification.697085 Conflict/uncertainty: no other owner in this thread confirmed a larger-pad option exists; treat as an open question rather than a recommendation.

docs.title: Front disc diameter emphasized: 299 mm is mandatory
docs.text: Reconfirming the 299 mm spec above: one owner specifically asked about a disc offered at a smaller diameter and was warned it does not fit — FAW X80 front discs must be 299 mm; smaller discs (e.g. 280 mm) cause pad misalignment and uneven pressure distribution. Always double-check diameter, not just part number, before ordering.86878889

docs.title: Front disc longevity report
docs.text: One owner's original front discs lasted to 255,000 km before replacement — a useful upper-bound data point for expected disc life.9091 Separately, another owner reports having to replace front discs at only ~48,000 km, suggesting individual driving style and disc-brand quality can produce a very wide range in practice; monitor disc thickness at regular maintenance rather than assuming either extreme is typical.92

docs.title: Restyled-model hub mismatch — pre-restyle discs don't fit
docs.text: Original brake discs from a pre-restyle model do not attach properly to a restyled (post-restyle) model's hub — the hub mounting interface differs between generations. M8 disc-retaining screws physically fit, but threading/seating on the restyled hub prevents proper seating of a pre-restyle disc. Always match the disc generation to the hub generation, not just the bolt pattern.9394

docs.title: Brand alternatives compiled by one owner (Mazda GH-spec cross-reference)
docs.text: For front discs cross-referenced to Mazda GH spec (part G33Y-33-25XA): SANGSIN SD4417 (Hi-Q), MARSHAL M2000480, PATRON PBD1515, ZEKKERT BS-5162; ATE also mentioned as an option.95

docs.title: Full brake-system upgrade — total cost breakdown
docs.text: A full four-wheel pad+disc upgrade totaled roughly 18,000 RUB (RU market, July 2025) for one owner; another owner who replaced front pads only spent about 9,000 RUB (RU market, July 2025). Parts were sourced across Ozon, Yandex Market, and Wildberries, comparing prices between the three. Marshal-brand discs were a popular choice among community members — one owner paid ~500 RUB more (RU market, July 2025) than the cheapest Marshal listing specifically to get discs that come factory-painted (corrosion protection), and emphasizes selecting by exact disc dimensions rather than by price alone. Pad brand/model choice is described as "personal taste" — the practical approach is reading Ozon, Yandex Market, and Wildberries reviews before buying rather than relying on a single recommended brand.969798

docs.title: Mazda 6 GH front disc brand options — NiBK RN1515DSET and Tayga (Jul 2026)
docs.text: Continuing the Mazda 6 GH cross-reference documented above, community members compiled specific perforated/ceramic disc listings while shopping for a front hub replacement: NiBK Performance RN1515DSET (a sport/perforated disc for Mazda 6 GH, sold on Ozon) received mixed reviews — not universally recommended. Tayga BDF043 perforated discs (299×25 mm, Mazda 6 GH fitment, sold on Avito) received positive feedback, with one owner reporting 30,000+ km with no issues after buying from the same seller. Community advice remains to cross-check against a Mazda-sourced equivalent (e.g. via Emex) and compare part numbers before committing to either option.99100101102103104105106107108

docs.title: Field report: SD4417 + SP2449 combo — 21,000 km including mountain driving
docs.text: One owner reports 21,000 km on the Sangsin Brake SD4417 front disc (see the Mazda cross-compatibility brand list above) paired with Hi-Q SP2449 pads (see the front-brake-pads card for the pad's own fitment/part notes), across two vacations of mountain-pass (serpentine) driving. Result: very satisfied — discs remain flat with no grooves or chips, only a barely audible whistle under heavy heat. Rated as an excellent price/quality combination. By contrast, the same car's original (OEM) discs and pads wore unevenly and needed replacement by 48,000 km.109

docs.title: NiBK RN1515DSET with PN8009 pads fitted (Oct 2026)
docs.text: One owner fitted the NiBK front disc set RN1515DSET with pads PN8009 (the "DSET" suffix most likely means a disc set; inferred, not stated). This adds a positive field fitting to the mixed reviews above; see the drilled and perforated discs card for photos and opinions on perforated discs.110111

docs.title: Catalogue split, fitment reports and judder fix (2024–2025)
docs.text:
• A commenter reads the catalogue as: 5DA133251 is the facelift (рест, "NEW") front disc and 5DA033251 the pre-facelift (дорест) one; he adds that 033 is also listed as a rear disc in some catalogues, possibly a typo.24 Another member calls 5DA033251 the analog of the original 5DA133251, says the disc cross-references between the X80 and the X80 NEW and that it is 299 mm on both; a buyer in the same family received smaller-diameter discs, which the 299 mm member takes to be a wrong item sold.1121133
  • Front discs that began to judder (бьют) when braking from speed: members suggested Marshall front discs for the X80 (Mazda 6 GH), SD4417, with SP2449 pads. The owner who fitted them reports ~21,000 km with no grooves or chips, a near-perfect surface match and only a faint squeal under heavy heat on mountain roads; another member fitted a disc from a different product link and reports ~30,000 km with no problems.114115109
  • Front disc numbers listed for the X80 / Mazda 6 GH: Marshall 5DA026251, G33Y3325X, G33Y3325XA and SD4417, plus TRW DF4974S listed as a Mazda 6 GH disc.114 The Lynx BN-1655 (Mazda 6 GH) carries OEM number G33Y3325X (Ozon listing, October 2025).116
  • NiBK on Ozon: RN1516DSET (front perforated disc for Mazda Atenza / CX-5) and NiBK Performance RN1515DSET (front sport disc for Mazda 6 GH); a member reports poor reviews for the sport disc, and X80 fitment is not confirmed. See also drilled and perforated discs.117118107

docs.title: Prices, brands and life reported in the Sept 2024 thread
docs.text:
• Slotted or vented front discs start at about ~15,000 RUB (RU market, Sept 2024) and a full front brake upgrade (calipers and discs) from about ~180,000 RUB (RU market, Sept 2024); the unit of both figures is inferred from context. The owner thinks slotted or drilled discs make no real difference in normal driving.119
  • The owner says a dealer quoted its own cost for the discs at ~5,000 RUB and sells them at ~7,000–8,000 RUB (RU market, Sept 2024); the dealer promised parts close to original quality, while a commenter says the cheap new discs are a soft alloy that warps after the first puddle and wears fast.120121
  • REMSA discs and pads are reported both ways: one commenter says they wore out quickly and were poor quality; another says they are good, and a third reports a REMSA set past 100,000 km with a small lip that can be sanded off and says 50,000 km or more is safe. The owner notes REMSA is not stocked in Irkutsk or Novosibirsk.122123124
  • At about 237,000 km the owner says his original front pads lasted ~140,000 km and he has since gone through several sets of aftermarket pads (his messages say both a third and a sixth set); the original discs still have ~3 mm of lip, which he does not consider worn out.125126

docs.title: Front brake pads
docs.text:
Tags: #brake-pad · #front-axle · #mazda-6-compat · #part-number

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

docs.title: OEM part numbers and critical dimension
docs.text:
FAW OEM front brake pad part numbers reported: B5CA03328ZAKAT1 and B5CA03328ZA2 (community reports both codes for what appears to be the same/related OEM pad family — treat as OEM front pad regardless of the exact suffix).

Community-verified critical dimension is the upper mounting hole width: - OEM base dimension: 133.1 mm3, also documented at 133.3 mm ± 0.1 mm in a technical comparison of several brands.4 - Official OEM drawing dimensions: 133.4 mm width × 56.6 mm height × 17 mm thickness (×2 shims).2 - Pads shorter than ~133 mm cause detectable play/rattle; do not use pads under this width.3 - Thicker (135 mm) or thinner (132 mm) pads than spec require mechanical forcing to fit and reduce pad lifespan.4

Confirmed OEM-fitment compatibility: Mazda 6 Gen 1 (GG hatchback, GY station wagon, GG sedan) shares the front pad footprint with X80.2

Preference note: several owners say OEM pads give better durability and more consistent quality than aftermarket, resulting in less wear on the discs, though aftermarket alternatives exist and work.2

Noise comparison for OEM vs. aftermarket sourcing channel: OEM pads bought via OZON showed no squeaking after 20,000 km; pads bought from AliExpress squealed initially for the first ~1,000 km, then the noise resolved. Both are reported as functionally adequate for normal driving once past any break-in noise.56

docs.title: Mazda-pad width mismatch — conflicting field reports (conflict)
docs.text:
Multiple owners confirm the critical 133.1 mm upper-mounting-ear width (consistent with the dimension notes above) and warn that Mazda-sourced pads, including Zekkert brand, typically measure 129–130 mm — a ~4 mm shortfall that creates play in the caliper bore, producing a knocking/rattling noise under braking. This is flagged as a safety concern, not just a cosmetic annoyance — the 4 mm gap looks small but is enough to cause detectable play. Mytishchi-brand pads are confirmed to fit at the correct width. Conflict: some owners report Zekkert or other Mazda-sourced pads working fine with no issues, while others measure and report them as 129 mm vs. the needed 133.1 mm, causing caliper play and unsafe knocking. The measurements themselves are not disputed — the disagreement is over whether the resulting play is perceptible/acceptable in practice; owners reporting "no problem" may not have detected the play, or may be accepting the risk unknowingly.789101112131415

Zekkert (Germany-branded) pads specifically measure 129 mm at the bore against the X80's 133.1 mm requirement — a confirmed 4 mm gap causing severe caliper play/clunking; one owner tested a set and removed it immediately. A Yandex Market listing for nominally the same product had the identical undersizing issue. Zekkert is not recommended for the X80 front axle. Conflict: an owner initially reported a Zekkert set from Yandex Market with no squeaks, but later analysis of the same pad line showed it undersized for the X80 — the early positive impression did not catch the dimensional problem.1617

Masuma-brand pads measure 130 mm at the bore, versus the 133.1 mm the X80 needs — dimensions confirmed by the seller directly. One owner drove 25,000–30,000 km on Masuma pads before symptoms appeared: squeaking, chirping, and clunking in the caliper, worsening after a disc cleaning.181920

Budget pads with the correct 133.1 mm bore sizing do exist, around 600 RUB (RU market, March 2024); several owners report using them with no squeaking. The catch is sourcing them: most budget listings (Zekkert, Masuma among them) are actually sized for Mazda (129–130 mm) and mislabeled/sold as "X80-compatible" regardless. Practical workaround: request exact bore measurements from the seller before ordering rather than trusting the listing title.2122
