docs.title: Mazda cross-compatibility (non-OEM sourcing)
docs.text:
• Mazda 6 (GH generation) front pads fit X80 fronts with slight modification — one owner had to shave ~1 mm off the pad to fit. BMTEIL and SLNS brand pads (for the GH fitment) documented as suitable, ~2,000 RUB (RU market, March 2025 price).29303132333435 Separately, another owner using unspecified Mazda 6 (1st-gen) cross-fit front pads reported an imperfect fit with a ~4 mm gap, while the matching rear pads from the same Mazda 6 1st-gen family fit fine — front and rear fitment tolerance is not identical, so check front fitment carefully even when the rear cross-reference is confirmed.363738

Technical dimensions from the listing diagram: 131.3 mm outer width, 118.8 mm inner width, 15.5 mm thickness, 8.4 mm mounting-boss diameter, with upper mounting holes slightly undersized ("hole size 1-2") versus some aftermarket alternatives; lower mounting has solid contact.3940
  • General fitment rule for undersized upper holes: if the caliper bracket shows no lateral play/movement, undersized-hole pads will still fit and function adequately with unaffected friction performance. If there is play/movement in the caliper mounting, choose pads with tighter hole tolerances instead.40

docs.text:

docs.title: Restyle vs pre-restyle
docs.text: Restyle (facelift) front pads are longer than pre-restyle pads. Part numbers differ between the two generations; mounting locations are identical, but pad length differs, so pads must be selected for the correct model year.6263

docs.title: Fitment problems and troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Counterfeit / mis-dimensioned "OEM" pads: pads sold as OEM-spec from online retailers can be counterfeit or wrong-dimension. Clone pads have been found up to 2 mm off the correct 133.3 mm thickness, causing rattling. Accurate 133.3 mm dimension is critical for fitment without modification.646566
  • Caliper grinding/rattling under braking is often caused by undersized pads (reported ~2 mm shorter than the original 133.1 mm spec) — e.g. Mazda B50 pads fit the caliper but are too short. Fixes: (1) verify correct OEM pad dimensions before buying; (2) shim/weld the pad retention ears; (3) add anti-squeal shims (often missing on aftermarket pads); (4) use verified-fit pads such as Hi-Q 131.7 mm or Masuma (Masuma needs shimming). There is some debate over whether guide-pin wear or pad dimension is the primary cause of this noise — likely both contribute.67686970717273
  • Reconfirmed field pattern (Sep 2024): the upper mounting holes specifically require 133.1 mm pads; the remaining mounting points are Mazda-compatible (129–130 mm), which is why partial cross-fit pads rattle only at the top ears. Two fixes reported: (1) source Mazda 6 discs and calipers together as a combined alternative (see the front-brake-discs card); or (2) find correct 133.1 mm pads specifically sized for the upper holes and verify fit at the remaining mounting points before finalizing the swap.74757677

docs.title: Anti-rattle mounting clips
docs.text: Metal spring clips pre-tension the front pads against the caliper to prevent rattling/clanging against the disc over bumps. These clips are often missing from aftermarket pad kits even though they're needed for a proper install; source separately as a "mounting kit for front brake pads" if missing, or salvage from old parts.137138139140

docs.title: Rest vs doreset dimension debate (with disc-corrosion side benefit)
docs.text:
A detailed community thread converged on: doreset (pre-facelift) front pads = 131 mm; rest (facelift) front pads = 133.4 mm, with an acceptable working range of 133.1–133.3 mm. Cross-fitment from Mazda 6 (131 mm, doreset-sized) is possible on a rest car but may require shim adjustment to prevent rattling — one owner warns strongly against this cross-fit ("will rattle"), so treat it as workable-but-risky rather than a clean swap.141142143144145146147148149150151152 Bonus of the 133 mm rest size: no need to scrape rust off the caliper bracket ears to fit, unlike the narrower Mazda-sized pad.149 When installing, preserve the retention "ears/whiskers" on the pad backing — doing so gives a more secure fit even for owners uncertain about exact dimension compatibility.152 Always verify model year (rest/doreset) before purchasing to ensure fitment without modification (consistent with the Restyle vs pre-restyle section above).

Earlier, conflicting mini-thread (Jun 2024): before the detailed 133.4 mm vs 131 mm consolidation above, an earlier exchange reached the opposite initial conclusion — one participant stated front pad size is the same between rest and doreset. That was immediately contradicted by another owner who reported their (rest) front pads are physically bigger than the doreset ones. This earlier thread is superseded in detail by the later 133.4/131 mm consolidation, but is kept here as a record that the same/different-size question was already disputed a year before it was resolved with hard numbers.153154155156

docs.title: Miles ceramic pads — cross-model recommendation (B50/X80)
docs.text: One owner reports standardizing on Miles ceramic-series pads across both the B50 and X80, citing the two models' brake systems as not very different from each other; long service life reported with no problems, drawing on past experience with a burnt/warped rear disc caused by a different pad issue on the B50 (unrelated to Miles specifically). This is a general brand recommendation rather than a confirmed part-number cross-reference — verify fitment/dimensions before ordering, consistent with the 133.1 mm rule documented above.157158

docs.title: UIDNU YD52002 — resolves earlier whistling complaints
docs.text:
UIDNU YD52002 ceramic front pads fit the restyled (post-2019) X80 and are reported to resolve the whistling/squeaking that plagued earlier pad changeouts on this model — sized to the X80 itself, not a Mazda cross-fit. Available on Ozon and other RU retailers; multiple owners confirm good fit and quiet operation.159160161162163164 Separately documented: UIDNU YD52002 is recommended as an OEM-equivalent pad featuring a ceramic friction compound with professional manufacturer branding, available on Ozon.165166167

Update/conflict: a later report (see the brake-pad-noise-quality card for the full account) found the whistle returned after about 2 days on one car after UIDNU YD52002 initially resolved it — even this well-regarded pad is not a guaranteed permanent fix for every car.168169170

docs.title: LED brake-light transmission fault
docs.text:
Tags: #automatic-transmission · #part-number

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Installing an LED bulb in the rear brake-light position (replacing the stock incandescent bulb) can confuse the transmission control unit: the ECU reads the LED's electrical signature differently from an incandescent bulb and can interpret it as the brake being continuously engaged. This causes the automatic transmission (AKPP) to behave erratically and overheat.

This has reportedly led to real financial harm: some services have misdiagnosed the resulting symptoms as transmission failure and charged around 50,000 RUB (RU market, Sept 2025) for an unnecessary overhaul — when the actual fix would have been reverting the bulb. The community speculates some shops may not even genuinely perform the overhaul, quietly swapping back to a normal bulb or a properly-resistored LED instead and still billing for the repair.

Prevention: use original incandescent bulbs in the brake-light position, or if using LEDs, ensure the LED solution includes proper load resistors so its electrical signature matches an incandescent bulb. Not a common failure, but the financial risk if it happens is real and significant.1

docs.title: Confirmed-fit replacement bulb: Blitz BRO173
docs.text: One owner reports the Blitz BRO173 bulb fits and installs successfully in the X80 brake-light position (personally installed and confirmed).2 This is a specific brand/part option for owners looking for a known-fit replacement bulb — verify it matches the incandescent electrical signature described above before using it as a drop-in replacement.

docs.title: Manual parking brake lever stiffness
docs.text:
Tags: #parking-brake · #unresolved

Reported symptom (low confidence, minimal detail, unresolved): the manual parking brake (handbrake) lever becomes increasingly difficult to release from the applied/parking position, described as needing to be "yanked" out of the parking position on and off 1. Community response included a dismissive note referencing negative owner sentiment about this model elsewhere online, but no diagnostic detail was recorded in this thread 2. Root cause not established — possible candidates worth investigating (not yet confirmed for this specific report) include mechanical binding in the lever/ratchet mechanism, cable stiffness/ corrosion, or a hydraulic issue if this trim uses a hybrid mechanism; this entry should be extended once a root cause is confirmed in a future message batch.

docs.title: Rear brake discs — type, thickness, Mazda cross-compat
docs.text:
Tags: #brake-disc · #rear-axle · #mazda-6-compat

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

docs.title: Disc type and thickness vs front
docs.text:
Rear discs on the X80 are solid (not ventilated), and roughly half the thickness of the front discs. Front discs are single solid rotors of uniform thickness. Some aftermarket listing photos make the rear disc look like a two-part/floating construction because of a visible ridge, but it is a single solid disc — the ridge is just a visual artifact, confirmed by comparison photos and the owner's manual thickness diagram.1234

Because the rear disc is thinner and rear pads/discs see roughly half the wear of the front in aggressive urban driving (see the wear-rate card for detail), this is consistent with what owners report for typical service intervals.5

docs.title: Mazda cross-compatibility
docs.text: Rear discs sourced from Mazda 6 (GH generation, 2003–2007) are usable and available for purchase on Ozon. Front discs are reported as noticeably harder to source than rear discs; rear discs are more readily available on the aftermarket. Exact fitment should still be verified against the specific Mazda model year before buying.678910

docs.text: One owner's understanding, confirmed by another member: front discs are cast iron (чугун), while rear discs appear to be steel — described as standard configuration for this vehicle class rather than something unusual.1112

docs.title: Rear brake pad replacement — EPB and piston tool
docs.text:
Tags: #parking-brake · #part-number · #conflict

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Community members disagree on this topic — both positions are reported.

Core mechanical fact — the rear caliper piston is threaded, not push-in. Unlike a typical front caliper, the rear brake piston sits on a worm/threaded shaft ("червячный вал") and cannot be pressed/pushed in like a conventional piston — it must be screwed in (rotated) to retract. Using a standard push-type piston compression tool will not work and risks damaging the piston if forced. This mechanical detail is the reason the whole procedure below differs from a typical front-pad job.12345678

Piston retraction tool. A dedicated tool with a screw-in spindle (not a push-type spreader) is required to rotate the piston fully home. A confirmed working tool is available on OZON, product code 2413649314. Reported improvised alternatives that also work by applying rotational torque: a gas-pipe wrench or an angle-grinder spindle-lock key, applied horizontally to the worm shaft.12345678

Do you actually need a diagnostic scanner to release the parking brake motor? (2026-08 report). Before attempting a DIY rear-pad job, Маksim questioned why he'd been told a diagnostic scanner ("компьютер") is needed to put the electric parking brake into service mode, when a simple button/ignition manipulation could release it without one.910 Игорь Игорев replied with a button-and-ignition sequence: hold the parking-brake release button down, turn off the ignition, remove the key while continuing to hold the button — the car is off and the parking brake stays released.11 Марина described a close variant: hold the brake pedal, press the handbrake button down, and — without releasing either — turn off the car, then proceed to pad service.12 These button/ignition sequences are consistent with the other release procedures already documented above and confirm a diagnostic scanner is not strictly required for this step on many cars.9101112

DIY alternative — powering the caliper's parking-brake motor directly with 12V (2026-08 report). Маksim separately reported finding a different way to release the caliper when the button/scanner methods aren't available or trusted: disconnect the parking-brake motor's terminal at the caliper and apply 12V directly from the car battery — this drives the motor and spreads the pads apart (equivalent to what the scanner's service-mode command or the button sequence achieves electronically). After installing the new pads, reverse the polarity of the 12V feed to run the motor the other way, which draws the pads back together/closes the caliper.1314 Note this addresses only how to move the parking-brake motor/piston mechanism itself — it does not replace the separate threaded-piston retraction step documented above if the piston also needs to be screwed in. Arсhi 77 pushed back that this was overcomplicated — in his view it's genuinely simpler to just release the parking brake with the button/ignition trick and skip messing with the caliper's motor wiring at all.15 Василий Егоров reported doing the whole job with the engine left running, taking about 10 minutes.16 Treat the 12V-direct method as a documented but disputed shortcut — most of the community leans toward the simpler button/ignition release.

Electronic parking brake release procedure — pre-restyle models. To safely release the electric parking brake for pad service: (1) with the ignition ON, shift to N; (2) apply the footbrake; (3) press the parking-brake release button; (4) turn the ignition OFF — the parking brake stays released through this sequence. After replacing the pads, minimize the time before first engine start to avoid triggering BCM adaptation errors.1718192021

Conflict — restyle models use a different sequence. A separate, later-model ("restyle") procedure was reported: shift to P, turn off ignition, hold the footbrake while releasing the parking brake, then release the brake pedal and remove the key. This is a genuinely different sequence (P instead of N, different hold/release order) from the pre-restyle procedure above — confirm which generation your car is before following either one, since using the wrong sequence risks the parking brake re-engaging mid-service or a BCM error.1719

Simplified/alternate restyle-era procedure, second report. A related but slightly different write-up: engage the handbrake button down before shutting off the car; press the brake pedal firmly before opening the caliper; use the screw adjuster (not a piston-push tool, consistent with the threaded-piston note above) to compress the piston; after reassembly, apply the brakes several times before driving to properly seat the new pads; use a scanner to reset the electronic caliper if the car's system requires it.222324

Quick electric-handbrake release (general reference). A simpler community-reported shorthand for releasing the electric handbrake for any wheel/brake service: hold the brake pedal down and press the handbrake button downward.2526

Earliest documented release sequence — a third variant (2024-04 video report, predates both sequences above). An early video walkthrough documents yet another service-mode entry sequence, distinct from both the pre-restyle and restyle procedures above: (1) start the engine with the parking brake applied; (2) press the brake pedal; (3) press and hold a button while continuing to hold the brake pedal; (4) turn the ignition off; (5) remove the key; (6) release the button and the brake pedal. Following this sequence, the parking brake does not re-engage, allowing pad service; the car exits service mode automatically once the brake pad work is complete. Given this predates the other two documented sequences chronologically, treat all three as reflecting either different model years/generations or different valid button-press variants of the same underlying service mode — confirm against your specific car before relying on any single sequence.27

General lubrication procedure, applicable to front or rear pads (2024-06 report). Beyond the rear-specific threaded-piston mechanics above, a proper pad replacement — front or rear — should include: inspecting the caliper cylinder for cleanliness, applying lubricant to the guide pins and under the piston dust cover, and checking pad-to-caliper fit before final installation. Typical job time: 10–15 minutes per side. Community observation: many shops skip the lubrication step, which is cited as a common contributor to future brake squeal/whistle complaints — this is a useful DIY checkpoint even at shops that "just swap pads."28

One owner's rear-end accident caused door and rear-fender damage plus a dent in the spare-tire well. The insurance assessment came in at a modest amount; the owner obtained an independent estimate of roughly 70,000 RUB (Nov 2025, RU market) covering color matching, dent removal, door straightening, and bumper repair 123. General guidance from the thread: using insurance-covered repairs is generally recommended over paying out of pocket, mainly to preserve the vehicle's warranty status 67891011121314.

docs.title: Assembly quality — Kaliningrad vs China sourcing
docs.text:
Tags: #corrosion · #vin

Trunk lid rust (Kaliningrad assembly): Trunk-lid rust is a widespread issue on the X80, especially on white-colored vehicles and cars assembled at the Kaliningrad (Russia) plant 12. Kaliningrad assembly was a "screwdriver" operation — assembling pre-made kits with selective or insufficient zinc treatment 34. Pre-restyled models (pre-2015) are reported as more affected. Warranty replacement is reported slow (7+ months) and dealer repainting is often poor quality; anticorrosion treatment is recommended immediately after purchase 567.

Conflict: brown/dark-colored cars reportedly rust less than white ones; one owner reports no rust issues at 95,000 km on a 5-year-old car that never received anticorrosion treatment 8910. Photo (media 21236) shows a trunk lid after anticorrosion (zinc) repair.

Panel mismatches: FAW vehicles assembled at Autotors (Kaliningrad) can show quality-control issues such as mismatched panels or incorrect components — one reported example is a dashboard panel from the automatic-transmission version (with PRND indicators) installed in a manual-transmission vehicle (which should only show PRN) 1112131415. This suggests the assembly line sometimes uses whatever parts are on hand rather than strictly matching components to the ordered configuration.

Pre-facelift assembly and sourcing: The pre-facelift (pre-restyle) X80 appears to be Chinese-assembled, based on OEM component sourcing patterns, in contrast to the Russian (Kaliningrad) assembly used for later cars 161718. Fog-light control on the Russian-market (domestic) version is more limited than on the Chinese restyle version 1920. Service shops in Russia often avoid working on the X80 due to unfamiliarity with the model and its non-standard component sourcing 21.

Panel misalignment and VIN legibility (another Kaliningrad report): One owner's Kaliningrad-assembled car has misaligned doors and trunk, plus chrome trunk trim that developed rust 22; the same owner notes "our people can mangle any equipment, just let them" — a wry community remark about domestic assembly quality 23. Another Kaliningrad-assembled 2019 car, owned a few months, reports no water-intrusion problems so far 24. Community VIN tip: check the VIN prefix — if it starts with "X" the car is Russian-assembled 25. Some buyers reportedly specifically sought out Chinese-assembled examples over Kaliningrad ones 26. One further owner's car also appears Russian-assembled but has had no issues over its ownership period 27. Kaliningrad-built cars are reported to have very weakly stamped VINs, and if the passenger footwell has had water intrusion, the VIN in that area can become illegible over time (see the dedicated VIN forensic-examination and re-marking card) 28.

Assembly location (community-repeated note): The X80 is assembled in Kaliningrad, at the same plant that previously assembled BMW and Kia vehicles 29. Some owners raise assembly-quality concerns by analogy to Volkswagen Polo sedans built at the Kaluga plant, though community reply notes the Polo sedan/hatch are different cars and most Kaluga-built Polos are in fact well-regarded on the resale market — Kaliningrad assembly is generally perceived as higher quality than Kaluga 3031.

VIN digit pattern as a Kaliningrad-vs-China indicator (August 2026 thread): Community members compared VIN suffix digits while joking about assembly quality (~3,200 Kaliningrad-built units estimated by one member, unverified) 32. One owner's VIN suffix ends in "2306" 33; another reports "2978" with no complaints 34. Discussing the pattern, one member proposed a rule of thumb — a VIN with a run of zeros before the final digits indicates Kaliningrad assembly, while the absence of such zeros indicates Chinese assembly 35. Two other owners then compared full or partial VINs: one gave "3060" as the digits before the final group 36, and another shared the full VIN "306000002978" 37 and a similar one ending "957" 38 — both were judged Kaliningrad-built under the same rule 39. Note: the rule as stated in the thread is a rough, community-derived heuristic (not confirmed against FAW's official VIN/WMI documentation), and the specific examples discussed ("306...") do not contain literal leading zeros — members appear to be using "zeros" loosely to mean a low/padded-looking digit run in the middle of the VIN rather than a precise digit-position rule. Treat as anecdotal until cross-checked against a documented VIN structure.

docs.title: Replacement battery quality and lifespan
docs.text:
Tags: #battery · #buying-guide

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Low-cost generic replacement car batteries fail rapidly — one owner reports a lifespan of only about 6 months before failure (media 18975 shows the failed unit) 1. Investment in a quality brand battery is recommended despite the higher upfront cost.

Battery disconnection/reconnection — what actually resets (February 2026): Removing the battery to recharge it does not cause major electronics problems on the X80. The main side effects reported: the clock/time resets, and the window auto-up (one-touch) function needs to be re-learned/re-programmed 234. Multiple owners confirm they've disconnected the battery repeatedly — including during winter cold-soak voltage drops and during shop repairs — with no lasting issues: one owner had the battery removed "very many times" during a repair with nothing lost 567. One extreme data point: a car sat without its battery installed for about a month with no resulting problems once reconnected 8. Only the clock and radio/EQ settings need re-entry afterward — described by owners as "nothing critical" 96. Caution — this does not generalize to all cars: one owner cites a colleague's BMW X3 as a contrasting case, where disconnecting the battery carries roughly a 50/50 risk of triggering a major electronics fault requiring 50,000+ RUB to fix — underscoring that the X80's tolerance for battery disconnection is a specific, reassuring trait rather than something to assume applies to every vehicle 10.

docs.title: Brake disc/pad wear and sourcing quality
docs.text:
Tags: #wear · #part-number

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Wear reports: Original-equipment brake discs lasted 120,000 km on one vehicle (2017 model, pre-restyle) 1. Another owner replaced discs at 200,000 km 2. A defective disc warped at only 48,000 km, damaging the pads in the process — uneven wear is a commonly reported issue 34. SD4417-branded discs are recommended by the community as a quality upgrade.

Marketplace sourcing challenges: Sellers on online marketplaces (especially Ozon) sometimes misrepresent brake parts — for example, advertising Mazda GG-spec parts but shipping GH-spec parts, or mislabeling the part number on the packaging (media 29584) 56. A common workaround: Hi-Q brand pads have no X80-specific part number listed, but the correct pad dimensions (e.g. 132.4 mm) still fit 7. When ordering through marketplaces, verify exact dimensions on arrival before installing. Local auto-parts shops are more reliable but may have limited stock; pre-ordering from authorized suppliers gives better quality control 89.

Cumulative wear-part spend: One owner reports that his minimal wear-part spending (discs, pads, mounts, including a replaced front-right hub) has reached about 100,000 RUB (Oct 2026, RU market), and he still plans to keep the car for years; he attributes the wear to his driving style and rough-road use 1011.

docs.title: Chinese-brand vehicle quality perceptions
docs.text:
Tags: #reliability · #buying-guide

Community discussion touched on quality issues with Chinese-brand vehicles generally (FAW, Geely, Chery). Examples cited: taxi fleet operators replacing Geely vehicles with used Japanese alternatives after warranty expiration; multiple owners reporting significant repair costs within the first 20,000 km 12. This contrasts with individual users' experience of problem-free operation. Variable quality control in Chinese manufacturing is noted; the community is divided on reliability, with some members recommending used Japanese cars over new Chinese imports at a similar price point 3.

FAW maintenance costs vs. other Chinese brands (June 2024): Community members pushed back against popular-media claims that FAW maintenance is unusually expensive compared to other Chinese brands. One data point offered: five years of maintenance on a Haval F7x (another popular Chinese crossover) can cost as much as a new car, undercutting the narrative that FAW is uniquely costly 45. The general view expressed: online "analysts" and expert-community gurus commenting on Chinese-brand costs often lack real ownership experience, and actual owners using proper parts suppliers and not overpaying for services report reasonable maintenance costs in practice 6.

New-buyer reliability inquiry (November 2025): A prospective buyer considering a 2020 X80 asked the community directly whether the car suffers from production defects and "many shortcomings," comparing concerns to American SUVs 789. Community response: the X80 is a compact crossover comparable in class to the Sportage or Tiguan, front-wheel drive only (no AWD option), with a 2.0L engine suited to typical family use 10. On reliability specifically, one experienced owner's verdict: no major design defects, common issues are minor and predictable — the thermostat is a known early replacement item and should be sourced in good quality from the start, and there's the well-known water-intrusion issue — but nothing rising to the level of a fundamental reliability concern; spare-parts availability is confirmed good 11.

docs.title: Balancing difficulties with generic Chinese-brand tires
docs.text:
Tags: #tires

Generic, low-price Chinese-brand tires are difficult to balance due to soft sidewalls and uneven internal construction — one report describes needing three balancing sessions: the first added 40 grams of weight per wheel, the second session was still problematic, and only the third session produced acceptable results ("a parade of balancing weights" as one member put it) 123. In contrast, branded tires manufactured in Chinese factories for established brands (Hankook, Bridgestone, Viatti) balance normally without issues 45. Recommendation: avoid unbranded low-price Chinese tires; choose branded options from reputable manufacturers even if made in China.

docs.title: Cold-start AKPP behavior at -10°C
docs.text:
Tags: #automatic-transmission · #cold-start · #winter

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

At -10°C ambient temperature, reverse gear engagement is slow/sluggish on the first shift after a cold start, even after roughly one minute of idling; D gear is also slow to engage before the transmission warms up. This is considered normal behavior due to cold AKPP fluid viscosity 1234. To check the fluid level properly on this transmission: open the drain plug and verify that a thin, steady stream flows out — if no flow appears, the level is too low; refill incrementally in 200ml steps, checking after each addition until a proper stream is achieved 5.

docs.title: Used-car comparison — FAW X80 vs Chery Tiggo 5
docs.text:
Tags: #buying-guide · #reliability

For a used-car purchase decision, the community recommends the FAW X80 over the Chery Tiggo 5 for several reasons: (1) simpler electronics and fewer complex systems reduce repair costs 12; (2) the X80 avoids the variator (CVT) transmission problems reported on the Tiggo 5 34; (3) FAW ranks among the Chinese brands with better corrosion resistance according to an independent study cited in the discussion 56; (4) general mechanical robustness and simpler controls are preferred by owners 78. No advantage of the Tiggo 5 is mentioned beyond appearance; its variator transmission is specifically cited as a drawback 910.

General buying guidance from the thread: when choosing between two similarly appealing used vehicles, prioritize technical condition and maintenance history over looks; perform anticorrosion treatment if the previous owner did not; research the specific vehicle's condition rather than relying on brand reputation alone 111213. Owners report 6+ years of ownership without major issues on well-maintained X80 vehicles 141516. Photos (media 19238, 19239) show both models for comparison.

docs.title: FAW X80 vs FAW B50 — reliability and feature comparison
docs.text:
Tags: #reliability · #conflict

Community members disagree on this topic — both positions are reported.

Community members with X80 and/or FAW B50 (sister model) experience compare the two (July 2024).

One owner reports needing to take apart and repair "basically the whole car" within a year of X80 ownership, contrasting it with a previous FAW B50 that never gave him that kind of trouble 1. A more measured counter-view: both the X80 and B50 have relatively few problems overall — the one known B50 issue is a coolant leak nobody has managed to trace the source of, while the X80's only issue in this owner's experience has been water intrusion through the corner trim near the sunroof drain, with nothing else wrong; both models are otherwise satisfying to own 2. A B50 owner with 7 years and 160,000 km on the clock reports no problems beyond replacing two wheel hub bearings 3. Another B50 (automatic) owner, who bought used at 90,000 km and is now at 125,000 km, reports needing only a timing-belt replacement and rear bushings, with the previous owner having done nothing beyond consumables (oil, fluids) 4. That owner names the B50's downsides as: no headlight-level corrector, low ground clearance, and a comparatively weak engine on the highway 5 — and states an overall preference for the B50 over the X80 6. The thread's closing balance: the X80 is "quite good for the money," with a peppier engine and noticeably more interior space than the B50 — if the B50 had the X80's engine, it would be a "race car" 7.

Conflict: opinions genuinely diverge. Two owners (6261, 6270) rate the B50 as more reliable or simply prefer it overall; two others (6257, 6273) prefer the X80 for its performance and interior space. Both camps, notably, describe their respective preferred model as fundamentally sound, with only minor and specific issues rather than systemic problems — the disagreement is about degree and priorities (space/power vs. a slightly cleaner ownership record), not about either model being broadly unreliable.

docs.title: FAW X80 vs FAW B70 comparative driving experience
docs.text: The FAW B70 (sedan) shares an identical transmission and engine platform with the X80. The B70 tested is equipped with a turbo engine (~220+ hp) and provides significantly better acceleration and responsiveness than a stock X80; both were tested on 99-octane fuel. B70 performance is described as "excellent," while the X80's dynamic response is adequate but noticeably less powerful. Both vehicles use the same transmission type, but the B70's turbo setup gives a noticeable advantage in highway passing and acceleration scenarios 1.

docs.title: Long-distance comfort comparison — X80 vs KIA Rio
docs.text:
Tags: #buying-guide

An owner who previously drove a KIA Rio reports the X80 is significantly more comfortable for long-distance highway driving. On monthly 1000 km round trips (500 km each way), the owner rests/relaxes in the X80, whereas driving the Rio left them exhausted 1. Overall, X80 comfort is rated clearly superior for extended-distance travel, despite some other owners' complaints about seat discomfort 2.

Additional long-distance data point (Irkutsk–Novosibirsk, ~2000 km, 19-hour non-stop drive): One owner drove non-stop from Irkutsk to Novosibirsk, about 2,000 km in 19 hours. Their assessment: seating comfort was excellent for the extended drive, with only a minor seat-position adjustment needed partway through; the seat design and ergonomics were described as supportive throughout. This is cited as further evidence the X80 suits long-distance highway use well 34.

docs.title: Used-market price vs Mazda CX-5 and Dongfeng AX7
docs.text:
Tags: #price

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Used-market price comparison (RU, as discussed February 2025): FAW X80 — 1.2–1.6 million RUB (used, 2020+ models) 12. Mazda CX-5 — 2.5 million+ RUB for newer-condition examples, with 10-year-old examples around 2.0 million RUB 34.
