Overall takeaway from the thread: the used-car market has limited modern alternatives in the X80's price range.

docs.title: Interior space comparison — X80 vs Renault Duster
docs.text:
Tags: #buying-guide

The FAW X80 offers noticeably more interior space than the Renault Duster, particularly rear seat room — a wider seating surface and greater door-to-door distance 1. Shift-lever ergonomics are also rated better in the X80: the lever naturally falls to hand on the armrest, versus a harder-to-reach position in the Duster 23. Both vehicles are described as urban crossovers rather than true SUVs 4.

docs.title: Dealer vs independent parts and labor pricing
docs.text:
Tags: #price · #dealer · #part-number · #buying-guide

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Right-side CV joint (in assembly) for the X80: 29,200 RUB, ordered from Kitz Zapchasti in Naberezhnye Chelny with a 10-day delivery window (December 2024 pricing, RU market) 12.

Broader pricing comparison (May 2024, RU market): official FAW dealers charge roughly 2–3x markup on parts versus independent suppliers, with labor rates of 3,000–4,500 RUB/hour. Example (May 2024, RU market) — a thermostat costs 10,000–12,000 RUB with labor at the dealer, versus about 6,900 RUB at an independent shop using the same part sourced from KitZapchasti (≈2,000 RUB part + 4,500 RUB labor). The right outer CV joint (гранат) costs about 13,500 RUB (May 2024, RU market) plus 2,800 RUB labor at the dealer, versus roughly 3,000–4,000 RUB sourced online plus 2,000–3,000 RUB labor at an independent shop 3456.

Factory headlight (tail light, outer right, part number 5CA151150) is available for 9,500 RUB (June 2025, RU market) from official parts vendors; some third-party sellers offer an aftermarket "OOOVE"-branded alternative at 12,500 RUB — buying a counterfeit at a higher price than the genuine part is flagged as a market risk (media 27289) 789.

Independent service-center itemized quote (July–August 2024, Moscow, RU market): A complete suspension and brake job at an independent Moscow service center totaled 54,500 RUB with a VIP membership discount (versus an original estimate of 60,000+ RUB), covering front/rear brake-pad replacement, brake-disc replacement, front suspension arm rods, rear hub-bearing replacement, and wheel alignment 10. Individual line-item labor rates at this center were seen by the community as high (August 2024, RU market): 4,300 RUB for front arm-rod work alone, 4,250 RUB for alignment/toe-in, and 580 RUB just for handbrake cable adjustment — a fee mocked as "the cherry on top" since it covers only tightening/loosening the cable on one side 11. For comparison, another owner reports doing the equivalent front control-arm-bushing replacement work themselves in a garage over the same winter, at presumably far lower cost 12. Many community members questioned whether these individual labor rates were reasonable even accounting for the independent-shop discount.

docs.title: Dealer warranty claims and service trust
docs.text:
Tags: #warranty · #dealer

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Warranty claims process: Warranty coverage varies by component (30,000 km for some parts, 60,000 km for others); the overall warranty period is 5 years 1. To claim warranty: present the vehicle with the defect to an official FAW dealership; the dealer submits the claim to FAW's representative office, which makes the final determination. Remote/photo-based decisions are not possible — an in-person inspection is required. Warranty details are listed in the service booklet, not the owner's manual. Dealers sometimes resist valid warranty claims 2.

Dealer trust issues: Several owners report difficulties with official FAW dealers: service books are sometimes marked "electronic only" with no physical book provided 34; dealers have reported incorrect vehicle status/history to deny service claims 56; diagnostic equipment errors occur (e.g., one dealer's system misreported a wheel-speed sensor reading of 1,480 km/h) 78; general business practices at some dealers are described as untrustworthy 910. Recommendation: verify a dealer's standing on the official FAW website before purchasing or servicing there; independent shops are sometimes reported as more reliable 111213.

Poor dealer workmanship — Samara official dealer (August 2024): A customer reports careless work after a dashboard leak repair at an official FAW dealership in Samara: panels were not properly reassembled/aligned, some parts were not fully reinstalled, and plastic trim may have been damaged in the process 1415. Steering-wheel alignment was also not done correctly, and the factory head unit's Bluetooth stopped working after the visit (suspected wiring disconnection). The customer's blunt characterization of the dealer's technical staff: "криворукие" (ham-fisted/incompetent) 16. Beyond the careless workmanship itself, the customer notes a dismissive attitude toward customers as an additional complaint 17. The dealership manager did apologize and offered to fix the issues on a return visit, and the customer planned to go back the next day to have the problems addressed 18 — illustrating that official-dealer staff unfamiliarity with Chinese-vehicle specifics can extend beyond diagnostics into basic reassembly quality.

Finding a qualified independent electrician (Moscow): One owner asked the community for a recommendation for an auto-electrician in Moscow familiar with the FAW X80's electrical system 1920. Community response: the X80's electrical system is described as "standard, without quirks" — if a general auto-electrician refuses to work on it, that reflects unfamiliarity/reluctance rather than any special technical difficulty with the car itself 21. A separate owner of 4 years notes a general feeling that not every shop will take on their car, reflecting the same service-network hesitancy pattern seen elsewhere in the community 22.

Dealer versus certified independent service station (STO, Taishet): One owner in Taishet services the car at a certified independent STO (service station) that stamps the service book and, he says, keeps the warranty valid; he has not visited a dealer in 60,000 km 23. Another owner prefers dealers, calling independent shops sloppy, and says dealer work costs more but he trusts it 24. The owners therefore disagree on whether a certified independent STO protects the warranty as well as a dealer does 2324.

docs.title: Design heritage — Infiniti platform basis
docs.text: Community speculation (unverified but circulated as a plausible explanation) suggests the X80's chassis design was copied/derived from Infiniti models, specifically drawing on Infiniti's four-wheel-steering rear-suspension architecture 1. Chinese engineers are believed to have replicated the Infiniti rear suspension layout but omitted the functional rear-wheel-steering actuation in the production X80. One community member connects this theory to a concrete observation on the front end: the presence of bearing supports ("опоры с подшипниками") on the front suspension that appear to be legacy design elements inherited from a donor platform that was originally engineered to support steering actuation hardware, rather than being purpose-designed for the X80's actual (non-steering) front suspension 2. Understanding this heritage is offered by the community as a possible explanation for otherwise puzzling hardware choices on the car's suspension.

docs.title: Emergency lockout procedures and prevention
docs.text:
Tags: #alarm

If locked out without a spare key or fob: (1) Check whether the installed StarLine alarm has a GSM module — if so, it may allow remote unlock via the phone app 12. (2) Contact a professional door-opening/locksmith service — this is generally faster than retrieving a spare key from elsewhere 34. (3) Prevention: always carry a spare key, or rely on remote unlock when available. Some owners have been locked out mid-drive after forgetting the key in the ignition 56.

docs.title: Engine durability — Chinese vs Japanese standards
docs.text:
Tags: #mazda-6-compat

The X80 uses Mazda/Ford-derived engine architecture but is built to a lower cost using cheaper metals and materials than the Japanese originals. Japanese OEM engines prioritize durability and longevity with stronger materials, while Chinese production of the same architecture focuses more on cost reduction. Chinese-built vehicles with this engine architecture may last 250,000–300,000 km if well maintained, but Japanese-built counterparts are reported to run significantly longer. One owner from the Russian Far East notes the local market's preference for Japanese imports over Chinese vehicles, despite higher prices, specifically due to perceived reliability differences 1.

Small turbo engines — Haval reports: An owner of a second 1.5-turbo Haval reports no engine problems so far, changing oil at least every 5,000 km and naming the turbo as the weak point 2. A 2016 Haval H6 used as a taxi reached about 320,000 km, with a turbo replacement at about 200,000 km 2. Another member is sceptical of small turbo engines and says Chery owners report electronics, gearbox and suspension problems 3. Low confidence: these are single anecdotes, and the two members disagree on small-turbo reliability 23. See also Chinese-brand vehicle quality perceptions.

docs.title: Engine oil brand experience and change practice
docs.text:
Tags: #engine-oil

No abnormal oil-consumption tendency is reported on well-maintained X80 engines under normal conditions. Oil brands tested by community members: Лукойл (Lukoil) Genesis — no complaints 12; Газпромнефть (Gazpromneft) 5W-40 — poor marks, noted for consumption 3; ZIC 5W-40 — noticeable consumption and engine noise reported 4; Eneos — acceptable 56. Fresh oil can be hard to read on the dipstick; thermal expansion is normal (warm vs. cold readings differ, but not dramatically) 78.

Separately, one owner who has worked with used/imported contract engines (Japanese, German, and UK-sourced, 50,000–160,000 km) observed: Japanese-sourced engines are cleaner internally despite higher mileage; German-sourced engines are dirtier at lower mileage; UK-sourced engines fall in between (media 30712 shows a Japanese ex-Renault contract engine at 157,000 km). European service intervals (20,000–30,000 km) mean less frequent oil-change maintenance there, while Eastern European/Autobahn-heavy usage accumulates mileage comparable to aggressive urban driving. Overall observation: frequent small-volume oil changes (every 5,000 km) with a quality synthetic oil produce visibly cleaner engines than infrequent large-volume changes 91011121314.

docs.title: X80 too small for families — larger SUV/van options
docs.text:
Tags: #buying-guide

Family buyers in the group say the X80 is too small once there is a second child plus luggage, and they consider larger SUVs such as the Skoda Kodiaq, Renault Terrain or Mitsubishi Pajero Sport instead 12. One owner, after a 1,500 km family trip, considers a minivan such as the Toyota Noah or Nissan Serena, though he notes that low ground clearance is a drawback of vans 3. Low confidence: these are a few individual opinions. For interior-space figures see Interior space comparison — X80 vs Renault Duster; for clearance see Off-road capability and ground clearance; for owners who left the X80 for other brands see Owners switching to Jetour/JAECOO after X80.

docs.title: X80 visual impressions vs premium brands
docs.text: Owners describe the FAW X80 as visually appealing, with styling comparable to the Infiniti QX50 and to Mazda models 12. Several owners report being mistaken for driving a premium brand (Infiniti or Mazda) 34. The vehicle is regarded as reliable and comfortable for long-distance travel 56. One owner reports being the only FAW X80 owner in their city in Russia, making an on-highway encounter with another X80 owner (video, media 34690, recorded on the MKAD ring road) a notable event, where the two owners communicated between vehicles 78. Overall design is described as elegant and well suited to highway touring with family comfort 910.

docs.title: Fuel consumption reports by year and conditions
docs.text:
Tags: #fuel-consumption · #buying-guide · #mkpp · #automatic-transmission

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Community-reported fuel consumption varies substantially by model year, transmission type, engine load, and driving style: - 2019 facelift, manual (МКПП): ~10 L/100km city and highway (at 53k km mileage) 12. - 2018, manual: 8.2 L/100km city (at 110k km mileage) 3. - 2018 pre-facelift, manual: 7.1–7.3 L/100km reported in practice 45. - 2017, manual: 7.1–7.3 L/100km (238k km, tank not fully drained during test) 67. - Automatic (АКПП): 7.2–7.4 L/100km on highway with 4 passengers 89. - Highway trips at 90–100 km/h: 6.5–6.7 L/100km reported 1011. - A/C use and higher speeds increase consumption 1213. Some tests found 92-octane fuel gives lower consumption than 95 14. - Tank capacity: 50 liters; full-tank range 610–780 km depending on conditions 1516. Dashboard photo shows 5.6 L/100km at 33,005 km on one vehicle (media 11320).

Later reports (November 2024 – April 2025) add further data points: on one vehicle with a touchscreen "lux" trim, fuel tank capacity is quoted as 58 liters with 11.6–11.8 L/100km typical automatic highway consumption; ECO mode is available but disliked by users ("annoying") 1718. A 2025-04-30 tracked trip of 410 km (70 km highway, rest city/mixed) showed 12.0 L/100km overall (≈12.6 city, ≈9 highway), attributed to aggressive acceleration; manual-transmission drivers report reducing city consumption to 11–11.5 L/100km with gentler driving 1920.

July 2024, highway trip report (2000 km round-trip planning, Domodedovo–Lazarevskoe): For a roughly 3,600 km round-trip drive south, community estimates budgeted 5–6 full tanks of fuel 2122. Discussion emphasized tracking overall consumption per 100 km rather than the instantaneous readout, since the latter is misleading for trip budgeting 23. Regional fuel-quality notes: fill up before crossing into Crimea, since fuel there is reported as lower quality than on the mainland 24; in Krasnodar, the Teboil-branded station (formerly Shell) was rated good, while Rosneft fuel was considered suboptimal by at least one owner 25. A follow-up trip report from late July 2024 to Lazarevskoe, factoring in traffic delays, recorded 8 L/100km on the trip computer while sustaining 110–120 km/h on mountainous, winding roads — a reasonable efficiency result for the 2.0L engine at that pace 26.

January 2026, winter cold-weather report: Driving from Tula in -11°C weather on 92-octane fuel, one owner recorded their lowest-ever fuel consumption reading, attributing it to gentle acceleration; they note they typically avoid exceeding ~140 km/h and that consumption crept up over time as driving habits became less conservative after the initial post-purchase period 27282930.

August 2026, community poll on normal city/highway consumption: Asked what "normal" consumption looks like, owners reported a wide spread: 12.5 L/100km city (transmission not stated, highway not driven) 31; 12 L/100km city in summer, rising to 13 L/100km in winter (transmission not stated) 32; 9.5 L/100km summer city/highway combined 33; automatic transmission (АКПП) 10.5 L/100km city 34; and a highway trip of 8.4 L/100km over 640 km at a reduced ~100 km/h pace (driving without a roof box, amid a regional fuel shortage that slowed traffic generally) 35.

September 2026, manual vs. automatic baseline at high mileage: One owner running a manual-transmission car at 215,000 km mileage reports 8-9 L/100km on the highway and 11-11.5 L/100km in the city, with no significant increase in consumption despite the high mileage 36. A separate owner shared a trip-computer photo (media 1903) captioned "here's my consumption on automatic" 37, illustrating that automatic-transmission cars in the community's reports tend to run somewhat higher than the manual figures above.

docs.title: Fuel octane compatibility — 92 vs 95
docs.text:
Tags: #fuel · #octane

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

The X80 owner's manual specifies a minimum of 92-octane fuel, and owners confirm 92 is the design-intended grade 12. Switching to 95-octane fuel yields no appreciable improvement in power or throttle response on stock engines, increases fuel consumption, and can trigger light detonation (pinging) on some units 34. Community recommendation: use 92-octane for standard operation — it is both correct for the engine and more cost-effective 567.

Fuel quality and the K5 label: One member argued that since autumn 2025 (with an extension to 1 July 2027) some Russian refineries have been allowed, under decree No. 819, to sell Euro-3-spec fuel (sulfur up to 150 mg/kg instead of 10 mg/kg) that is still marked K5, so a K5 label would no longer guarantee Euro-5 fuel 8. This is a claim made in the chat and was not checked against the decree. Two other members countered that their fuel near Moscow was good, with no problems, including from a Tatneft station 910.

docs.title: High-mileage ownership reports (100k–400k+ km)
docs.text:
Tags: #reliability · #buying-guide · #automatic-transmission

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Multiple community members report on the X80's long-term reliability at high mileage:

  • 170k–240k km: Owner purchased at 53k km in 2021, now at 170k km — reports good overall reliability, few factory defects, with most issues traced to STO (service station) improper maintenance rather than the vehicle itself 12. A second owner approaching 240k km had the transmission fluid changed at 200k km and reports smooth running 40k km later 34. A third owner (owner since Jan 2019, at 130k km) did a suspension refresh at 100k km, otherwise normal wear 5. General takeaway: reliability correlates more with owner understanding — gentle driving, preventive care, avoiding unnecessary tinkering — than with raw mileage; high-mileage owners in this thread suffered fewer issues than some 100k-km owners who had shop-induced problems 67.
  • 105k–200k km: Users report 105k km (2020 model) and 147k km (2019 model) with typical wear items — hub bearings, stabilizer links, disc/pad replacement 89. At 200k km with proper maintenance the mechanical drivetrain is reliable; however, robotized CVT transmissions are reported problematic, with failures reported around 100k km. Manual transmissions are reported as more durable 101112.
  • 400k+ km (automatic): One vehicle in service since May 2019 has passed 400,000 km on an automatic transmission with no reported oil-consumption issues. Community sentiment: the car has proven reliable contrary to early skepticism that the motor "wouldn't last 200k km" 131415. Odometer photo confirms 400,089 km (media 19714).
  • 245,000 km (mixed driving): Owner confirms galvanization visible on doors and hood; vehicle driven roughly 50% paved / 50% off-road (gravel, sand, clay, stumps, rough terrain) with no major rust and no oil-consumption issues 161718. Odometer photos confirm 245,782 km (media 19997, 19998).
  • 110,000 km (2.0 AT Max trim, 2021 model): Aggressive highway driving (repeated 180+ km/h cruising, 6000 rpm) plus 80% city aggressive driving (hard braking, rapid acceleration). Zero oil consumption up to 90,000 km; slight consumption began at 110,000 km in hot summer highway conditions (cause unclear — engine wear, poor dealer oil, or counterfeit oil). No misfires, smoke, or check-engine lights; instant cold starts; clean manual-mode shifting. Only oil, filters, brake pads, and discs were replaced over the full 110,000 km — the car "never failed" across Russian regions 1920.
  • 250,000+ km: Another owner accumulated 250,000+ km with only routine maintenance (oil, filters, pads, discs) and no major breakdowns; a separate owner reports the X80 tolerates any fuel quality and oil grade, though higher-quality products improve longevity 21222324.
  • 308,000 km (automatic): After an 11,000 km driving stretch the car consumed 300g of oil; suspension components wear faster on this vehicle due to varied terrain and speed. Reliability rated favorably against major brands; the car operates in temperatures down to -35°C. A partial transmission fluid change was done at 200k km with no issues; no oil leaks despite high mileage. Catalyst replacement (~306k km) and possible air-inlet valve work anticipated 25262728. Odometer photo confirms 308,000 km (media 37567).
  • 50k–163k km (five-owner survey, 2019–2020 models, Jan 2026): A 2020 model at 25,000 km reports excellent acceleration and road handling with only minor electrical glitches (sensor oxidation, intermittent ECU faults) 2930. A 2019 model at 58,000 km reports a comfortable interior suited to a 3-child family, full luxury package, stiffer-than-expected suspension (noted by an owner who switched from a Lada Vesta), and non-functional parktronic/TPMS sensors 313233. A second 2019 model at 82,000 km (purchased for 1.4M RUB, Jan 2026, RU market) reports good comfort and space, minor rust spots, a loud cabin (sound-dampening recommended), and mediocre stock audio 343536. Additional owners in the same thread report generally positive experiences up to 163,000 km, with issues limited to routine wear items 37383940414243444546.
  • 110,000 km (minimal service history): One owner reports 110,000 km with only an EGR valve replacement and no rust, contrasted against another owner at just 65,000 km who already experienced rust and drivability issues — maintenance history and unit-specific condition matter more than raw age or mileage 4748.
  • 320,000 km (owned 5+ years, purchased at 28,000 km): Engine described as robust; transmission has had only one half-drain with no complaints; no water ingress into the cabin; corrosion rare. Oil changed twice yearly (spring and fall). BCM (body control module) connector oxidation occurs regardless of water exposure 4950.
  • 200,000–400,000+ km (engine/transmission durability): Multiple owners report engines and transmissions (both manual and automatic) still functioning without major overhauls at very high mileage — one at 211,000 km (bought at 200,000 km, prior owner since fall 2021), another past 300,000 km. Regular maintenance remains critical, but the drivetrain itself is reported as durable long-term 51525354.
  • 300,000–400,000+ km ("workhorses"): Community reports vehicles in this range still running reliably with regular oil/filter changes and preventive care; post-restyling models are particularly valued in the secondary market despite some known design flaws 5556.
  • 165,000–202,000+ km (multiple owners): One owner at 165,000 km replaced the front hub bearing and an engine mount; another at 100,000 km changed only the front hub bearing; one at 180,000 km changed brake pads, a wheel bearing, and lamps; one reports 202,000+ km in ongoing daily use, calling the car reliable ("hasn't let me down since 2020"), comfortable, with good clearance and decent power. Common complaints across all mileages: interior squeaks/creaks and a transmission jerk on takeoff from rest 57585960616263.
  • 105,000 km / 5.5 years: Only one significant electrical failure over the ownership period — a wiring-harness short circuit under the driver's seat — otherwise the electrical system has been reliable. Owner recommends professional diagnostics over trial-and-error troubleshooting for non-obvious electrical faults 64.
  • 237,000 km (2017 model, purchased new July 2018, as of 2024-09-02): Only the rear hub assembly was replaced; the automatic transmission fluid received a partial change at 200,000 km (oil did not darken, appeared normal); no engine work and no oil consumption on Mobil-brand oil. Suspension components (lower arms, bushings, struts, links) needed refresh at this mileage — described as normal wear for the X80. Overall assessment: reliable, resourceful car that drives well despite its age 656667686970.
  • 177,000–420,000 km (community confirmation): One member reports an X80 with 177,000 km still in operation; others in a related WhatsApp group report vehicles at 350,000–420,000 km, reinforcing the pattern of long-term durability potential 7172.
  • 181,000 km (manual transmission, 6 years): Only the clutch has needed replacement (just starting to feel stiff when shifting); the rest of the drivetrain has been completely reliable despite hard use — 4 accidents, rough off-road driving, and gravel roads. Owner's verdict: "extremely durable vehicle" 7374.
  • 193,000 km (survived 4 collisions): Owner reports the car remains roadworthy and satisfying to drive despite the accident history and high mileage, and explicitly does not plan to sell it — cited as a real-world durability test 75.
  • 2017 model, four years in (Feb 2024): owner reports the car is "all great" entering its fourth year of ownership, with no specific issues volunteered 76.
  • 2020 model, one year of ownership (May 2025): zero problems in the first year; the owner has not personally faced a parts-sourcing issue and cannot speak to that concern from direct experience; highway-stable at 160 km/h and possibly beyond; average fuel consumption 7–8 L/100km on the highway when driven gently; overall comfort assessment is relative to whatever car the buyer is switching from 77.
  • 2019 restyle, 90,000 km, bought roughly two months earlier for 1,150,000 RUB (Dec 2025, RU market): rock-stable at highway speed with plenty of interior space; parts needs so far limited to an upper control arm (sourced via Ozon, Mazda 6-compatible, 2,700 RUB, direct fit) and stabilizer links (also Mazda-sourced, found in stock locally); leather interior in good condition; the car looks new enough that acquaintances are shocked to learn it is a six-year-old Chinese import; fuel consumption 8 L/100km highway in eco mode, 11.5–13 L/100km city depending on driving style 78798081.
  • 2020 model, 41,000 km, two years of ownership (Dec 2025): owner reports being "very satisfied in all respects" — interior, exterior, and technical specifications; has the financial means to buy a new car but cannot bring himself to part with this one, since nothing currently on the market matches its specification for the price; rock-stable at 160 km/h; fuel consumption 8 L/100km highway (calm driving), 10–12 L/100km city; only complaint is a long winter warm-up before the windshield defroster clears frozen glass (unclear whether unique to this unit); the car is rare enough in traffic to draw attention and stand out 82838485.

docs.title: Common ownership issues at specific mileage intervals
docs.text:
Tags: #maintenance-interval · #buying-guide

Community-reported typical maintenance milestones: 1. ~56,000 km: automatic transmission fluid service recommended 1. 2. 75,000–82,000 km: rear suspension springs commonly fail or require replacement, especially on vehicles purchased used 2. 3. 140,000+ km: rear brake pads are typically still original at this mileage; brakes can safely be extended or renewed as needed 2. 4. 2–3 years: battery replacement likely needed 3.

Normal wear-item replacement should follow manufacturer guidance supplemented by this community experience.

docs.title: Manual vs automatic — first-owner transition
docs.text:
Tags: #automatic-transmission · #mkpp · #buying-guide · #conflict

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Community members disagree on this topic — both positions are reported.

Community discussion converges on a few practical points for buyers choosing between manual (МКПП) and automatic (АКПП) X80s, and for owners transitioning from a manual car to their first automatic.

First-time automatic owner, transitioning from a string of manuals (July 2024): A buyer who had previously owned a VW Golf, a Renault Sandero, and a Renault Duster — all manual — bought a 2019 X80 automatic and found the switch intimidating at first, describing her first short drive from the shop to home as "scary." She asked how to disable ECO mode (present as a dedicated button on the Duster but not obviously available on the X80), since the car felt underpowered in that mode, and sought advice on D-mode-in-city/S-mode-on-highway versus the reverse, having read conflicting community opinions 1. She separately asked about non-dealer service options in Moscow, citing official-dealer prices as too high 2. In a fuller account of the purchase, she describes an intensive week-long search across official Moscow dealers (Rolf, Major, Avilon, Avtomir) — even trying and failing to afford a new car — before finding a red 2019 pre-restyle X80 in a dealer lot she hadn't previously heard of, being immediately taken with the top trim and features (coming from a bare-bones 2016 Duster with only air conditioning and an aftermarket Teyes CC3 head unit), then discovering via Avtoteka that it had a prior side-impact accident (A-pillar, side airbags, and seatbelts replaced). Undeterred, she found and bought a black 2019 example from Avilon the very next day, despite having read substantial negative community sentiment about the model beforehand 34. Another member's take on that negativity: FAW draws about as much criticism online as any other brand on average; some parts can be a hassle to source, but that is equally true of other marques on price or availability, and the car is fine if properly operated and maintained 5. The new owner affirms she takes good care of her car 6.

Manual-to-automatic comfort transition (Duster owners): first-time X80 owners coming from a Renault Duster report a significant comfort improvement after moving to automatic: no more clutch operation, electric seat adjustment far more convenient than a manual mechanism, and generally superior seat comfort. Initial anxiety about AKPP complexity and the fear of expensive repairs typically fades after about a week of regular driving, once the comfort benefits become apparent 78. One such owner clarifies that taxi/rideshare driving is not something she'd do regardless of transmission — she simply wanted to drive more for its own sake, and had specifically wanted (and long feared) an automatic because of AKPP-failure worries before finally choosing one 8.

AKPP vs MKPP for commercial (taxi) use — cost debate: one view holds automatic is not suited to taxi work because it adds a cost manual doesn't carry: the recurring AKPP fluid change 9. A counter-view: the only meaningful extra AKPP expense is that fluid change — everything else, roughly 99% of running costs (chassis/wear items), is identical between the two transmissions 10. On interval specifics, one participant states the factory manual gives no explicit AKPP fluid-change interval, but recommends roughly every 30,000 km in practice 1112. The original skeptic elaborates that for taxi driving specifically, every recurring cost compounds fast — fuel, monthly engine-oil changes (at roughly 10,000 km/month of taxi usage), food on the road, and the fleet operator's percentage cut — so adding an AKPP fluid change on top makes manual meaningfully cheaper to run commercially 13. The thread's consensus: MKPP is cheaper to run for taxi use, but AKPP is more comfortable, and a fluid change roughly every six months is judged a reasonable trade for that comfort in non-commercial, personal use 14.

Community reliability consensus — no meaningful difference: across separate discussions, members converge on both МКПП and АКПП being equally reliable long-term, with the choice coming down to personal preference rather than a reliability trade-off 15161718. One member's framing: "get an automatic and enjoy your life" — it will last if cared for 15. A manual-transmission owner disagrees on preference grounds (not reliability): he simply doesn't enjoy automatics and prefers the feel and control of shifting himself, especially wanting to hold 5,000–6,000 rpm through an overtake 19; he separately reports the engine "revs like a dream" and that he regularly drives in both S and M modes 16 — illustrating that manual-vs-automatic preference and shift-mode preference are both about driving feel, not reliability. A manual-transmission owner reports 185,000 km with only a clutch replacement needed to date 20. When asked directly which transmission is more reliable, one member's reply: "both are great" — noting that body style (pre-restyle vs restyle) affects only appearance, gearbox choice is a matter of personal driving preference, and neither transmission type has produced reliability complaints in the community 21172218.

Sport-mode acceleration vs Skoda Rapid: the X80's 2.0L engine on automatic transmission can accelerate competitively in Sport mode against a Skoda Rapid (VW Group compact) 2324. The engine itself is responsive; the limiting factor in normal driving is transmission "hunting" behavior rather than lack of power, and Sport mode reduces that hunting 2526.

docs.title: FAW X80 Mazda 6 platform — parts compatibility
docs.text:
Tags: #mazda-6-compat · #part-number · #buying-guide

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

The FAW X80 shares Mazda 6 platform architecture across several systems — suspension (control arms, bearing hubs), transmission fluids, and steering specifications 1. Mazda part cross-references are increasingly appearing in X80 parts catalogs. Practical implication: sourcing Mazda 6 parts is often more reliable than relying on X80-specific catalogs 2.

X80 models from 2017 onwards generally have excellent parts availability at moderate pricing, and many components cross-compatible with Ford and Mazda vehicles provide practical alternatives to OEM FAW parts — one owner notes that new-car (post-2017) parts are actually more expensive and harder to find than parts for the earlier/pre-facelift model, which has better availability 3456. One long-term owner confirms no problems sourcing Mazda 6 (pre-2006) parts specifically: consumables (filters, brake pads, timing belt) and wear items (bearings, sway-bar bushings, brake discs) were all sourced from non-Chinese Mazda 6 (pre-2006) OEM suppliers with zero compatibility failures — for example, a full bearing/bushing/disc replacement at 105,000 km cost about 60,000 RUB (July 2025, RU market) using this sourcing approach 7.

docs.title: Model-year documentation discrepancy (VIN)
docs.text:
Tags: #vin · #buying-guide

Some X80 vehicles show a document year (ПТС/СТС registration papers) that differs from the year decoded from the VIN — one example: documents show 2018 while VIN decoding shows 2019 12. This is reported as normal for FAW vehicles and does not indicate fraud; it reflects a gap between manufacturing date and registration timing 34. Practical note: when ordering parts online, catalog systems may pull the VIN year (e.g. 2019) as the primary model year even when the documents say 2018 56.

docs.title: Odometer and speedometer accuracy (GPS-verified)
docs.text:
Tags: #speedometer · #diagnostics

A user tested odometer accuracy against a GPS bike tracker over a 13 km city drive: the odometer showed 12.9 km versus 12.9 km on GPS — verified multiple times against kilometer markers on the highway as well 12. Conclusion: odometer readings are accurate enough for fuel-consumption calculations, but the speedometer is unreliable for actual speed estimates on the stock tire size (see the tire-upsizing card for reported speedometer error at other tire sizes) 34.

docs.title: Off-road capability and ground clearance
docs.text:
Tags: #buying-guide

The FAW Besturn X80 is a classification "urban crossover" (паркетник), not a true off-roader 1. It is adequate for paved rough roads, dirt roads, and light rough terrain thanks to relatively high ground clearance and large tires, but it is not suited for genuine off-road conditions — deep mud, deep water crossings, or steep grades 23. Ground clearance is comparable to a Renault Duster 4.

Additional community testing found the X80 can traverse flat fields, dirt roads, and light mud confidently, but its heavy front end and weight distribution limit steep-slope performance 56. On sand hills, the electric handbrake can engage unexpectedly and halt uphill progress 7. The X80 is not 4WD — it is front-wheel-drive (or a compromised all-wheel-drive variant on some trims) 8.

Overall community verdict: the X80 is better for city/highway comfort, while vehicles like the Duster are better suited for serious off-road use. Attempting muddy field driving risks undercarriage damage — wire breakage and component exposure have been reported 23.

docs.title: Owners switching to Jetour/JAECOO after X80
docs.text:
Tags: #buying-guide

One X80 owner sold his car (offering leftover Mazda 6 GG-compatible spare parts — fog-light trim and front-suspension control-arm forks — that no longer applied) and reported buying a new Jetour Dashing: full-time all-wheel drive, classic torque-converter automatic (Aisin-based, not a dual-clutch "robot") 123. Asked whether he had also considered the JAECOO J7, he said he had wanted to but ultimately passed on it: exterior and interior looked good, but the dual-clutch "robot" transmission felt very unresponsive and "dumb" in his test; having previously owned a Volkswagen with a DSG-type robot gearbox, he knew what a well-behaved robot transmission should feel like, and the J7's didn't measure up — it also simply didn't feel right to him 4. Another community member reacted by noting she is likewise wary of robotized/dual-clutch transmissions generally and prefers the time-tested classical torque-converter automatic — she specifically chose a Belgee with an Aisin gearbox (the same transmission family as her FAW) for that reason 5.

This is a single, low-confidence data point rather than a broad trend, but it is a useful cross-shopping reference for X80 owners considering a move to newer Chinese-brand crossovers: dual-clutch "robot" automatics on some competing models (JAECOO J7) draw specific criticism for sluggish, hesitant behavior compared to classic torque-converter automatics like the X80's or the Jetour Dashing's Aisin unit.

docs.title: Paint, coating quality, and rust resistance
docs.text:
Tags: #paint · #corrosion

Coating-layer variation by assembly batch (Kaliningrad, June 2026): One owner reports their car — Kaliningrad-assembled, apparently from an early production batch, 9 years old at time of posting — has a full 4-layer protective system on the sills: zinc, cathodic e-coat (катофорез), primer, and paint, with zero rust anywhere despite the age 1234. Community discussion raised the question of whether this level of coating is universal or batch-dependent; one participant noted their own Kaliningrad-assembled car has a "crooked" (uneven-quality) build but is still holding up ["ничо пойдёт" — "it'll do"] 5. Another participant pushed back on generalizing "Kaliningrad assembly = bad," asking for the specific VIN to confirm assembly location before drawing conclusions, since not everything attributed to Kaliningrad assembly may actually be Kaliningrad-built 67 — illustrating that even within the community, attributing quality problems confidently to a specific plant is contested without VIN verification (see the assembly-quality card for the VIN-prefix check method).

White paint corrosion pattern (2012–2017-era cars, June 2024): Multiple owners report rust/discoloration issues specifically on white-painted cars within 2–3 years, most visibly as a "рыжик" (rust-orange) spot in the lower-left corner of the rear hatch/trunk area — one owner who inspected three white examples at a dealership found the same lower-left rust spot on all three 891011. The pattern is reported as far less common on other colors; some owners half-joke that they wish they'd ordered gold/brown paint instead specifically to avoid this white-paint-linked corrosion issue, and there's community interest in gold-colored examples reportedly becoming available in the Russian market (including Tatarstan) as an alternative 121314.

Long-term galvanization performance (2017 model, 109,000 km, July 2025): One 2017-model owner with 109,000 km reports no corrosion issues at all 15. A second owner states their car is fully galvanized and expects 3–5 more years of trouble-free driving on that basis, despite acknowledging some family skepticism about Chinese-brand durability generally 16.

docs.title: OEM vs aftermarket parts and filter quality
docs.text:
Tags: #part-number · #oem · #aftermarket · #counterfeit · #engine-oil

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

OEM availability and quality: OEM FAW parts are limited and relatively expensive, so many owners resort to aftermarket parts sourced through Kitzap and similar suppliers 12. Community debate: OEM parts are reliable but costly, while Mazda/VW-sourced alternatives often don't fit or work properly despite sharing an engine/transmission origin 34. Cited example: upper control-arm spheres rated for roughly 150,000 km life in OEM form versus about 50,000 km for aftermarket equivalents. Counterfeit parts sold as genuine OEM ("claims genuine, is actually an analog") are also reported on the market.

Unreliable "OEM" parts from Chinese suppliers: one user reports multiple defective FAW-branded parts sourced from Chinese suppliers — a thermostat that tested fine on the bench failed once installed, and filters that failed prematurely. Recommendation: consider Mazda/Ford donor parts from established suppliers as a more reliable alternative to FAW-branded Chinese-sourced parts 56.

Filter and consumables brand quality (extended community discussion, June 2025): ZEKKERT-brand filters are rated low quality by multiple contributors 789. MANN filters often face counterfeiting on the market 1011. LYNX filters are marketed as Japanese but are actually Chinese-origin 1213. BARDAHL synthetic oils are recommended for quality and cold-climate performance 1415. Quality among major suppliers (Stellox, Patron, etc.) varies even within the same brand — for example, a Patron upper engine mount is rated good while the same brand's lower mount is rated poor 161718. Recommendation from the thread: find a trusted local seller with a track record rather than relying on brand names alone; warranty coverage for auto parts is limited in practice 192021. Photos (media 26908, 27008) show example filter products and a brake disc discussed in the thread.

Conflict: extensive debate on brand quality and warranty validity — some members claim major brands hold reputation but lack real substance, others trust branded products specifically to avoid counterfeits; no consensus was reached on a single "best" brand, but all agree quality varies significantly even within the same brand's product line 222324.

Bad-supplier report — KitZapChasti (August 2024): One buyer reports a poor experience ordering from the KitZapChasti supplier: a CV joint (гранта) started clicking/crunching after only 10,000 km, and an upper control-arm ball joint loosened within 6 months. Parts arrived with worn-looking part-number markings, and return shipping is at the buyer's own expense — the buyer recommends caution when sourcing from this vendor 2526.

Discount sourcing tip — Chinese e-commerce sales (June 2026): Chinese e-commerce platforms run periodic "Great China Sale" events with steep discounts; one example cited was a pre-restyle (2013–2016) FAW Besturn X80 front headlight lens cover (12-pin connector type) listed at 4,249 RUB (RU market, posted May 2026) with a 55% discount during the June 2026 sale. Availability of specific pre-restyle parts during these sales is sporadic, so it's worth checking during sale windows specifically 27.

Extended conflict — cheap hub-bearing durability vs. brand/factory differences (July 2026): A community member reported buying a wheel hub bearing on Ozon for around 2,000 RUB (RU market, July 2026) that failed after only about 1,000 km, reigniting the debate on cheap aftermarket parts. Conflict: Василий (a parts seller in the community) argues the real issue is manufacturer/factory identity rather than price alone — the same "product" sold under different price points can come from genuinely different factories or be a different revision/design (he cites an example where two catalog numbers for the same nominal part are actually different hardware revisions, with a newer revision correcting a design flaw), and that group members sourcing parts through him have not reported the same failures as buyers on open marketplaces 2829303132. Arсhi 77 counters that dismissing a part as inherently "4x less durable" than a pricier alternative is not fair without controlled comparison, since price differences can reflect market/inflation factors as much as genuine quality differences 33.

docs.title: Pre-restyle X80 (2017) known issues
docs.text:
Tags: #sunroof · #springs · #head-unit · #parking-brake · #buying-guide

The community has documented a recurring list of issues specific to the pre-restyle X80 (2017 and earlier), most of which were addressed on the restyled (2018+) model:

  1. Sunroof drain-tube corner design defect: the pre-restyle sunroof drain tubes use plastic corner fittings with a flawed design at the drain-tube angle/elbow — it's not that the tube "pops off," but that the corner-fitting geometry itself is wrong, causing water leaks into the cabin over time. The restyled model corrected this specific design flaw 1234. Remedy reported by the community: replace the plastic elbow/hose with a silicone equivalent or apply sealant at the joint.
  2. Front springs settle/sag over time and may eventually break, requiring replacement — see the dedicated suspension-wear card for detailed spring-life data across driving styles 14.
  3. Touchscreen head unit overheating: the pre-restyle touchscreen unit (where fitted) lacks adequate cooling and is prone to overheating and burning out 14.
  4. Parking-brake glitches are commonly reported on pre-restyle cars 14.
  5. Wheel-arch trim strips work loose over time, which can allow water into the interior along the arch line 14.
  6. Engine valves require periodic manual adjustment, since the pre-restyle engine lacks hydraulic valve-lash compensators (hydraulic tappets) — this is routine maintenance rather than a defect, but it's an extra service item pre-restyle owners should budget for that restyle-engine owners generally don't need to worry about 14.

docs.title: Suspension wear — springs, dampers, repairs
docs.text:
Tags: #springs · #wear

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Spring longevity: Original front-spring durability varies widely with driving style — light city driving yielded only about 120,000 km on one 2017 model, while heavy hauling (700 kg every weekend) extended to over 200,000 km on another 2017 model, and one single-spring failure occurred at only 90,000 km — suggesting quality variation or manufacturing defects rather than a consistent wear pattern 123.

Rear damper wear on a road trip: During a 645 km highway leg of a 5,100 km trip (Kislovodsk to Volgograd, including mountain sections), average fuel consumption was 9.7 L/100km with full load and a roof box; actual tank capacity measured about 62L versus the 58L nominal spec. Rear dampers were barely functional at 50,000 km, bottoming out repeatedly on speed bumps; front suspension showed brake noise/creaking throughout the trip, suggesting upcoming maintenance needs. The roof box significantly increased drag. Recommendation from the report: budget for replacement rear dampers within about 1 year of noticing this wear 456789101112.

Two-year ownership, major suspension/axle failure: After 2 years with only minimal maintenance (oil and heater fan replacement), one owner discovered: a drive-axle seal leak, a failed right front strut (fluid had leaked out), a left front spring fractured in two places, and a subsequent drive-axle failure. Repairs performed: drive-axle replacement, suspension repair (strut and spring), and power-steering fluid replacement. Result: suspension functioned properly again, traction improved, and cabin vibration during acceleration was eliminated — all the issues needed to be resolved together to fully fix the suspension and noise 13.

Wheel hub bearing premature failure (pre-facelift, 2023 model, 58,000 km, May 2026): One owner experienced hub-bearing failure at only 58,000 km — unusually early for a modern sealed cartridge bearing, which is normally expected to last 150,000+ km. Symptom was an audible grinding/howling noise from the wheel area; community discussion raised the question of whether the noise was actually the hub bearing or a CV-joint/driveshaft support bearing on the right side instead, since the two can be confused 141516. The owner suspects a manufacturing defect or improper bearing preload during assembly rather than normal wear; OEM bearing-assembly replacement is recommended, though aftermarket alternatives are available.

Suspension upgrade with Mazda GG (Mazda 6) components (June 2026): After a community recommendation, one owner had a shop install Mazda GG-derived front control-arm forks with ball joints and Japanese Kayaba shocks, describing the result as excellent — "like a rocket" — with no cutting or drilling of the original suspension mounting points required. The shop quoted roughly 100,000 RUB for the full job (June 2026, RU market) but the owner ultimately paid about 15,500 RUB for labor (parts cost separate); the car was out of service for about 4 months during the work. The owner's overall verdict: "good machine but has its quirks," and highly recommends the Mazda GG suspension swap 17181920.

Pneumatic rear-spring assist (237,000 km vehicle): Installing a pneumatic air-spring balloon on the rear coil springs improved ride comfort and load handling on a high-mileage (237,000 km) car — it reduced harshness over bumps and supported heavy loads (2–3 passengers) better than springs alone. At roughly 0.9 bar pressure, the ride was described as smooth and pliant, "like a Volga on spring suspension," while the suspension remained responsive to the road surface 212223.

docs.title: Tire load index vs softness — not the same
docs.text:
Tags: #tires

Tire load index (e.g., 94 for city driving, 98–102 for highway/sport use) does not directly correlate with tire softness or hardness. Load index relates to the thickness of the cord/carcass and the tire's rated load capacity, not its compound stiffness 12. Tire noise comes primarily from tread depth and compound characteristics rather than load index; old tires (6+ years) become noisier as the compound degrades — one member described this as an "air micro-pulsing" effect 34. Load-index selection should match the driving pattern (94H-class for city, 98+ for highway), but the actual ride feel depends more on the specific brand and model 56.

Conflict: one member (Валерий) asserted that load index indicates tire softness; others in the thread disputed this. The consensus reached in the discussion is that load index is strictly a capacity rating, while softness is a separate material property set by the manufacturer's compound choice 78.

docs.title: Fitting oversized tires — 225/60R16 and 225/65R17
docs.text:
Tags: #tires · #fitment

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

225/60/16 without offset change: One owner installed 225/60/16 tires without changing the wheel ET offset from the original ET45 spec. Reported handling: normal to good in snow, holding better than the stock 215/60/17 size 123. Some owners report occasional rubbing on the wheel arches during extreme steering angles with this size, especially on restyle-model (2018–2019+) vehicles 45.

Conflict: restyle and pre-facelift models reportedly have different arch geometry/depth, which explains why some owners see no rubbing while others do 678.

225/65R17: A larger-than-stock 225/65R17 size can also be fitted, but requires heating the plastic wheel-well trim with a hot-air gun to press it inward and prevent rubbing (media 35385) 910. After the swap, the speedometer read about 3 km/h faster than actual speed — more accurate than the stock setup's roughly +7 km/h error, because the change in tire circumference shifts the speedometer's calibration offset 111213.

docs.title: Used-market value and resale liquidity
docs.text:
Tags: #price

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

January 2026 (RU market): Community pricing survey found the FAW X80 used market ranging roughly 840,000–1,350,000+ RUB. A pre-facelift 2019 manual "Lux" trim with 106,000 km sold for 840,000 RUB (October 2025 purchase, RU market) 1. A 2020 facelift model with 92,000 km (second owner, max trim, automatic) sold for 1,220,000 RUB (Jan 2026, RU market) 234. A 2020 facelift automatic with 40,000 km (second owner) sold for 1,350,000 RUB (October 2025, RU market) 5. General market consensus: fair baseline price is around 1,000,000 RUB (Jan 2026, RU market) with ±200,000–300,000 RUB variation depending on condition; a review of 49 Avito listings found prices ranging 600,000–1,699,000 RUB, with participants noting even AI pricing tools estimate the model around 1 million RUB; asking prices above ~1.4 million RUB are considered overpriced by the community 6789.

April 2026 (RU market, Moscow): A 2019 model with roughly 99,000 km sold for 1,140,000 RUB. Initial asking price was 1,200,000 RUB (April 2026, RU market) with no buyers; the seller dropped to 1,170,000 RUB, then accepted 1,140,000 RUB after an in-person inspection 1011. Market observation: few X80s are available for sale overall; most listings are pre-facelift cars with 300,000–400,000+ km, while facelift models with lower mileage (~100,000 km) are considered the optimal used-car pick. A separate buyer reported paying 1,150,000 RUB in January 2026 (RU market) for a car with 79,000 km, broadly consistent with this pricing band 121314.

April 2025 (RU market): A 2020 X80 with 40,000 km, in ideal condition with original paint, priced around 1.5 million RUB (automatic transmission) 1516. Prices had declined compared to summer 2023, when comparable units with 20,000–50,000 km sold for 1.55–1.65 million RUB 17.

April 2025 (RU market), liquidity concerns: A 2019 X80 with 46,300 km was valued at 1,266,000 RUB. Market view: the Chinese FAW brand is considered illiquid on the Russian secondary market — asking prices range 1.5–1.7 million RUB, but selling time is unpredictable, and some buyers decline immediately upon learning the brand is FAW (Chinese, rare in Russia). Quick-sale scenarios may net 30–40% below asking price; holding for the right buyer interested in the specific vehicle's condition is recommended over expecting a rapid sale 1819.

December 2025 (RU market): A restyle X80 with 106,000 km actual mileage (55,000 km shown at listing time), top trim, white interior, fitted with an aftermarket phone/remote autostart system, was listed around 350,000 RUB privately; an official dealership offered only 130,000 RUB trade-in value (for resale at 140,000–145,000 RUB). Private-sale estimates for a pristine example in this range: 140,000–150,000 RUB (Dec 2025, RU market) depending on negotiation 202122. For comparison, the FAW T77 (a restyle-era competitor) was noted for a responsive pedal and more interior options, but criticized for its turbo/robotized transmission and weak warranty 2324. Photos and video (media 36181, 36194) show the X80 interior and owner commentary from a T77 comparison test drive.

September 2026 (RU market, Saint Petersburg): A used 2020 automatic X80 with 50,000 km was advertised for sale in Saint Petersburg at 1,400,000 RUB 25.

docs.title: Used X80 (2017-era) — pre-purchase inspection checklist
docs.text:
Tags: #buying-guide · #glass

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Community checklist for buying a used 2017-era X80: 1. Check paint quality carefully, especially the rear door — a common defect area 1. 2. Inspect for water ingress in the cabin: check floor mats, door seals, and sunroof drainage 2. 3. Valve-cover gasket leaks and condensation are common; budget for gasket replacement 3. 4. The stock head unit is problematic — plan on replacing it 4. 5. No factory soundproofing is a common complaint 5. 6. Rear wheel arches use fabric fenders rather than metal, giving inadequate mud protection — check underneath for rust/corrosion 6. 7. Automatic-transmission fuel consumption is typically 11.6–11.8 L/100 km, varying with driving style 4. 8. Always check the VIN before buying. A real case: a car presented for sale had flood damage (water pooled in the front-passenger footwell); the seller claimed it had been fixed, but water intrusion can hide electrical and drivetrain problems that are hard to diagnose later — get a professional inspection before buying, especially in private sales 78. 9. Water and corrosion checks (community-repeated, 2026): Look for water in the front-passenger and driver footwells and under the spare tire in the trunk; test rear parking sensors (parktronic) by engaging reverse — they should either work correctly or beep without fault codes; listen for engine ticking (possible stuck hydraulic tappets); check for corrosion above the rear license plate under the trim visor and along the bottom of doors (especially the 5th/tailgate door) — this rust is reported as nearly universal on older X80s (owners from Moscow and St. Petersburg confirm it) and is treated as cosmetic rather than structural, so a low price can still justify buying 91011121314151617. 10. Tire-pressure sensors (TPMS): if the sensors have not been replaced by the time of sale, assume 99% of them have already failed (they have roughly a 6-year battery life) 18. 11. No reliable way to check accident history at inspection time — buyers note there is no tool to confirm whether a car has been in a collision; some dealerships lend a paint-thickness "tester" (тыкалка) on request to check for bodywork/repaint, and community members recommend asking the dealer to test the car in front of you, or sourcing your own tester from Ozon beforehand 192021. 12. A fogged/condensed window can be present at time of sale from the dealer. One owner purchased an X80 with a fogged/condensed window already present at time of sale (as of 2024-07-22); it has been driven normally for several months since with no functional issues arising from the defect 22. A second owner reports the same experience — a fogged window does not affect vehicle operation 23.

Positive aspects reported: spacious interior, attractive styling, and an overall reliable platform.

docs.title: Unreadable VIN — forensic and re-marking
docs.text:
Tags: #vin · #buying-guide

A used-car buyer whose X80's VIN turned out to be unreadable at registration walked the community through the full bureaucratic process required in Russia to get such a car legally registered.

Process (as experienced, took about 2 months): (1) the car fails the initial registration inspection because the VIN cannot be read 1; (2) the vehicle is referred to a specialist company for a forensic examination (криминалистическая экспертиза) to certify the VIN's original, unaltered status; (3) once cleared, an accredited re-marking (re-stamping) company applies a new VIN marking under the applicable regulation; (4) the owner returns to the traffic-police registration office (РЭП ГАИ) with the new marking certificate, which then issues a referral/instruction for the additional marking step and completes registration 23. The owner's car in this case was a 2017 model, Kaliningrad-assembled 4.

Root cause: this owner's case is attributed to the same weak VIN stamping reported on Kaliningrad-assembled cars (see the assembly-quality card) — the factory-applied VIN can wear away or become illegible over time, especially if the passenger footwell has experienced water intrusion, accelerating corrosion in that area of the body 2.

Related detail — no felt/sound-deadening pad at the VIN location: in the same discussion, another owner notes their car never had a felt/sound-deadening pad at this body location at all, which may be a contributing factor to accelerated wear or corrosion of the stamped VIN on some units 5.

docs.title: Winter tire choice — studless ("lipuchka") experience
docs.text:
Tags: #tires · #buying-guide

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

One owner switched to winter studless tires (Nordman 7 mentioned specifically, the type commonly called "lipuchka"/липучка in Russian) after 5 years of seasonal studded-tire changes 12. Studless tires can be effective in winter depending on driving style and road conditions 34. Community consensus: the studded-vs-studless debate is often unproductive — personal preference, individual driving technique, local road conditions, and the specific tire model matter more than the studded/studless classification itself 56. Some owners report a good experience with studless tires; the safety debate remains ongoing among other members 7. Photos (media 12511, 12512) show the installed winter studless tires' tread pattern and wheel setup.

Manual-transmission-specific winter driving concern: A prospective automatic-to-manual switcher expressed anxiety specifically about winter driving on a manual transmission, noting they know how to handle winter driving on a manual but were uncertain how it compares on an automatic 8. One experienced driver's advice, prioritizing tires over transmission type: studded tires ("шиповка") get the car through winter conditions "like a tank," even though not everyone likes them, because they genuinely help with grip 9. The same driver pushed back on dismissing studded tires as unprofessional or unnecessary, warning that if you ever start to spin out on studless ("lipuchka") tires, you'll remember that studded tires were an option — technique (gentle acceleration, avoiding hard throttle inputs) matters as much as the car itself, but good winter tires provide a real safety margin outside city centers and on rural roads that aren't always well-maintained 10.

Studded tire size question: Asked which size to choose for studded winter tires (225/65 R17 or 215/55 R17), one member recommended "215 65 17" as optimal 11. That size matches neither option offered, so it may be a typo for 215/65 R17 or 215/55 R17; verify it before buying (low confidence) 11.

docs.title: X80 market rarity and smart-key scarcity
docs.text:
Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Market rarity: The FAW X80 is considered rare in the Chinese domestic market; early production runs were limited 12. The FAW Oley, a similar model from the same limited-edition production runs, is extremely difficult to source parts for in China 34. Pre-facelift X80 models feature Chinese-assembly-specific components not found on later versions.

Smart key scarcity: Complete replacement smart keys for the X80 are extremely rare on the market — reportedly only one supplier in Siberia has occasional stock. Replacement physical key blanks and key heads have some parts articles available, but complete assembled keys remain scarce; Chinese suppliers have no such keys in their catalogs at all 56.

Finding rare trim parts at Avito salvage yards: For a small missing trim part, one member suggests asking Avito salvage yards (dismantlers, "razbory" / разборы) that break donor cars: describe what you need and ask the seller whether they have it, even if it is not in the search results. He found a passenger-side dashboard ventilation part this way; knowing the OEM part number makes the search easier 78.
