docs.title: A/C condensate drainage
docs.text:
Tags: #hvac · #water-ingress

Dripping under the car is normal. Water dripping from underneath the vehicle while/after A/C use is expected condensate from the A/C evaporator, not a leak to worry about.12 Whether it drips depends on ambient conditions (humidity/temperature) — it won't drip every time.2

Short drain tube routes condensate onto the steering rack / passenger floor. The A/C condensate drain tube on the engine side is short and can drip water directly onto the steering rack and toward the passenger footwell area, rather than clear of the car. This is a common, independently confirmed issue.345 Fix: extend or reroute the drain tube so condensate is directed clear of the steering components and cabin — a fellow owner noted that dripping is fine as long as it stays outside the cabin, but should not be allowed to migrate to the interior side ("не нутра").5 Note: a separate tube in the same area belongs to the steering-rack circuit, not the A/C drain — don't confuse the two when tracing hoses.6

Water pooling under carpet = blocked drain, not normal operation. When drainage is blocked instead of dripping outward, water pools inside the cabin under the carpet/floor mats. Tell-tale sign: a stale-water smell from the A/C vents even when the A/C has been off/dormant for a while.7 Diagnosis: if the drain tube isn't dripping at all after previously dripping normally, suspect a clog.1 Fix: disconnect the A/C drain hose and clean it with A/C-system foam cleaner (aerosol spray) or compressed air; also clear the condensate collection pan of debris; inspect the full drain-tube routing for kinks or blockages.89 Preventive maintenance: periodic use of A/C foam cleaner to keep the drain path clear.10

Distinguishing from sunroof/cowl drainage. Water intrusion into the cabin is not always the A/C drain — check the sunroof drains (both sides) and the cowl (жабо) drainage holes as separate possible sources before assuming it's the A/C system; these are independent drain paths that can also clog or leak.1112

Sunroof drain leaks — seal lubrication fix. A separate, confirmed sunroof-specific issue: the sunroof starts leaking water as the weather warms up. Fix: lubricate the sunroof seals with silicone grease. Many units begin leaking after their first heavy use, so periodic seal lubrication/maintenance is worthwhile preventive care, not just a one-time fix.1314

Drain-clog diagnosis when condensate floods the passenger footwell. A second, independently reported case of the same blocked-drain pattern described above: when A/C condensate floods under the passenger-side carpet instead of dripping outward, the two leading suspects are (1) a clogged drain tube where it exits toward the engine bay — the most common cause — or (2) a missing or kinked rubber extension hose on the drain outlet (it should have an angled/bent hose fitted). Diagnostic order: check the drain tube in the engine compartment for blockage first; if it's clear, inspect the outlet-hose routing and the seal at the evaporator junction next. In stubborn cases, full disassembly may be needed to trace the exact leak source.151617181920

Corroborating report — short drain hose causes cabin flooding, fix by extending it. A separately reported case (different Telegram group) confirms the short-drain-hose problem documented above: water pooling under the driver/passenger floor mats, especially on the passenger side, traced to a factory A/C drain hose that is too short and drips inside the cabin instead of outside. Fix: extend the black drain hose located at the A/C unit with additional tubing so it reaches clear of the vehicle body — consistent with the reroute/extend fix already documented on this card.212223242526272829303132333435

Corroborating report — sunroof drain as a separate, easily confused water source. A second confirmation of the sunroof-vs-A/C-drain distinction already noted above: water under the floor mats can also originate from the sunroof/moonroof drainage system rather than the A/C. Check the white drain tubes under the front panel where they connect to fittings on the engine shield (visible after removing the lower panel) — these tubes can disconnect or clog independently of the A/C drain; reconnect or clean as needed.21223637

docs.title: Air conditioning — refrigerant system and diagnosis
docs.text:
Tags: #hvac · #bearing · #mazda-6-compat

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Refrigerant capacity. The X80's A/C system holds 500 g of refrigerant (freon).12 The refrigerant type/spec is printed on a nameplate sticker, reportedly on the radiator top or in the owner's manual — check under the hood for the exact marking before a recharge.34 Whether the system is single-circuit or dual-circuit was raised as an open question by one owner and not conclusively answered in this thread.5

Compressor mechanics. The A/C compressor is mechanically driven via belt and pulley (not electrically driven) — it directly loads the engine through the belt, not indirectly via the alternator/generator.67 Internally it uses pistons to pump refrigerant and build pressure.8 Clutch engagement (turning the compressor's drive on/off) is purely electrical; the ECU does not directly control compressor output pressure.7 When the compressor engages, the cooling fan also engages automatically at its first speed.9

Voltage-drop "nudge" sensation — disputed. One owner reports a voltage drop to 7–8V during simultaneous fan+compressor activation, producing a subtle engine "nudge" felt through the car, and attributes any perceived jolt specifically to the A/C clutch disengaging (not the fan).910 Another owner reports never noticing this sensation despite extensive driving with the fan continuously on (e.g. mountain driving), and doubts the effect is generally perceptible.1112 Document as a live disagreement rather than settled fact — the underlying electrical behavior (7–8V dip) is described consistently, but perceptibility in the cabin is disputed.

Fuel consumption from A/C use. Running the A/C increases fuel consumption versus not running it, but by less than driving with the windows open at speed.13 Basic operation: press the A/C button, set an initial cooling temperature (commonly 18°C to start), and select fan speed 3–4; once the cabin cools, raise the set temperature. An Eco mode is confirmed present on pre-facelift/дорест trims; presence on facelift/рест trims (even in Luxury spec) is unconfirmed/unclear in this thread — one owner with a рест Luxury car wasn't sure if theirs had it.141516

A/C not cooling after winter — refrigerant-first diagnosis. A recurring seasonal complaint: A/C blows warm instead of cold after winter dormancy. First check: refrigerant level — the system is described as very sensitive, where even a 30–50 g deficit (well under the 500 g full charge) can cause the system to fail to cool or auto-shut-down as a protection behavior.1718 Check for leaks before simply recharging. One owner also heard an unusual squeaking/hissing sound from the climate-control motor when switching modes, suggesting a possible motor-bearing issue in the climate unit as a secondary/unrelated cause worth ruling out.19 Recharging itself is described as an inexpensive procedure; some minor issues have reportedly self-resolved over time without intervention (unexplained, possibly a self-sealing micro-leak).2021 Official dealerships can charge with the correct refrigerant type; independent shops report they can also do the job if the correct spec is confirmed first (see capacity/spec note above).2223

Freon-leak detection method. To locate a small A/C refrigerant leak, use a dedicated freon "sniffer"/probe (пробник) — a tool that detects freon particles in the air. Place the probe near suspected leak points (e.g. inside air-intake ducting) and watch/listen for its detection signal. This method found an internal leak in at least one case and is reported as more effective than visual inspection alone for small leaks in A/C lines and connections.2425

High-ambient-temperature performance. One owner reports the A/C performs like an aircraft's — very strong — even at 35°C+ ambient temperature, including in mountain passes, suggesting the system has solid cooling-capacity margin under extreme heat.26

Insulating the refrigerant lines improves summer performance. One owner wrapped both the supply and return A/C refrigerant lines with heat-insulating pipe foam plus foil-backed tape. This noticeably improved cooling performance in summer heat and prevented compressor overheat shutdowns.27

Compressor engagement threshold and external-sensor accuracy. The A/C compressor typically engages around -5°C external temperature and not below it.2829 However, the external-temperature sensor feeding the climate display is reported as significantly inaccurate: e.g. reading -1°C when actual temperature was -11°C,30 +3°C after a cold start at -22°C, and as high as +73°C after ~30 minutes of slow driving (20–30 km/h) on a ~31°C day — the sensor reportedly doesn't stabilize until the car reaches speed.3132 Note: the Auto-mode indicator on the climate display shows whenever Auto mode is selected — it does not by itself indicate the compressor is actually engaged; don't confuse the two.30

Compressor grinding noise = bearing wear. A grinding/grating noise from the A/C compressor that increases with RPM, especially after a refrigerant recharge, points to a worn/failing compressor pulley bearing rather than the compressor body itself. Diagnosis: remove the serpentine belt and manually rotate the compressor pulley by hand, checking for radial play — play confirms bearing wear. Community experience: bearing failure is more common than full compressor failure when this noise appears right after a routine recharge.3334353637

Compressor cross-reference parts (2.0L engine). For the FAW Besturn X80/X80F 2.0L engine (2013–2022), aftermarket A/C compressor alternatives are: KCZ2158YU (Krauf brand) and 5DA161450A (KPR brand). These are also reported to fit the Hongqi H5 2.0L (2023+).38

Compressor failure — common cause and repair cost (restyled 2.0L automatic). On the restyled X80 with the 2.0L automatic, A/C compressor failure is often caused by one of the internal gaskets/seals leaking oil, which drops refrigerant pressure and stops the A/C from cooling properly.39 A full replacement compressor (matching the specific part number for a 2019 2.0L automatic) costs from roughly 38,000 RUB (July 2026, RU market) — a price one owner found discouraging enough to ask the community for cheaper sourcing options.4041424344 A cheaper alternative for this specific failure mode is to replace just the leaking gasket/seal instead of the whole compressor, at roughly 25,000 RUB (July 2026, RU market).4546 See the cross-reference part numbers above (KCZ2158YU/Krauf, 5DA161450A/KPR) for full-compressor replacement options.47

ECON vs full A/C mode. The A/C has two operating modes: ECON (Economy) cycles the compressor on/off at roughly a 50% duty cycle, producing slightly more humid cooled air and lower engine load — a reasonable highway-speed comfort compromise. Full mode runs the compressor continuously at full capacity for dry, cold air; at high fan speed this can get cold/dry enough to frost the inside of the windshield.48495051 Live disagreement on why ECON air feels more humid: one owner attributes it purely to on/off compressor cycling; another attributes it instead to a different air-vent/humidity routing in that mode — both explanations are reported without resolution.

Compressor clutch cross-compatibility — Mazda 6 GH. The A/C compressor clutch assembly from a Mazda 6 GH (part CLMZ019, 6PK pulley, 138×134×105×35 mm) fits the FAW Besturn X80 pre-restyle and is cheaper than sourcing the OEM FAW clutch. Confirmed by an experienced mechanic after a successful service installation; labor was about 2 hours plus ~2,500 RUB for a subsequent refrigerant charge (May 2026, RU market).5253545556

Compressor clutch failure — oil starvation from a leaking pulley. A separate, common compressor-clutch failure mode: refrigerant oil leaks out through the pulley seal, starving the internal friction surfaces of lubrication and accelerating bearing wear. Symptoms: abnormal noise during operation, increasing bearing play, and eventual seizure. Preventive check: inspect the pulley periodically for oil weeping and monitor belt condition — distinct from, but related to, the pulley-bearing grinding-noise pattern described above.57

Cold-start compressor rattle — usually benign, watch for it worsening. A rattling/knocking noise from the A/C compressor specifically on cold start, which disappears once the engine warms up, is reported as often normal on older systems — but if the noise becomes excessive or persists after warm-up, treat it as a possible early sign of bearing wear or a refrigerant issue rather than dismissing it outright (low-confidence single report).58

Mazda 6 compressor as a full-unit alternative — fitment disputed. Beyond the clutch-only swap above, a full Mazda 6 A/C compressor (LUZAR LCAC 2550) has also been tried as a cross-platform alternative; visual/photographic comparison suggests it's close, but the same reporting user separately noted it "doesn't quite fit" (не совсем подходит) — document as an open fitment question, not a confirmed swap. Other confirmed compressor cross-references for the 2.0L engine restated here for completeness: OEM 5DA161450A (KPR brand), aftermarket KCZ2158YU (Krauf).535759

AC clutch jamming — continuous-runtime and cold-weather seizure risk. Low refrigerant charge or worn clutch bearings can cause the compressor clutch to stay engaged continuously instead of cycling normally — one driver reported clutch overheating after roughly 14 hours of continuous runtime on a long highway trip (Rostov, overnight). Seasonal risk: if the clutch is engaged and then jams as ambient temperature drops below the ~-5°C compressor cutoff (see the temperature-threshold note above), the owner may not notice anything wrong because A/C use naturally stops for winter — but a clutch jammed engaged through the cold season accumulates wear and can seize. Symptom to watch for: unusual A/C noise, or cooling that persists even with A/C switched off. Fix: check refrigerant charge level and inspect the clutch for proper disengagement before winter. Live disagreement recorded: one owner disputed whether the compressor can genuinely jam mid-season at all, while another specifically flagged the fall-to-winter transition (when A/C use is toggled on/off) as the highest-risk window for an undetected jam.60616263646566

AC compressor pressure-cutoff protection — separate from the temperature-based cabin logic. The A/C compressor has a dedicated pressure-cutoff switch: when refrigerant pressure reaches a critical level (overcharge or a blocked system), the pressure sensor shuts the compressor off to prevent damage (e.g. line/radiator rupture) — a protective mechanism, not a temperature-based one, operating independently from the cabin-temperature sensor that decides whether cooling is currently wanted. Both systems work together in the X80's overall climate-control strategy.676869

Continuous high-speed fan even in AUTO mode — a separate multi-cause fault. Distinct from the mechanical-noise issues above: some owners report the HVAC fan running continuously at high speed even with the climate control set to AUTO, causing noise and over-cooling. Reported root causes span several systems: (1) a failed climate-control pressure sensor, (2) a malfunctioning cabin-temperature sensor, or (3) a compressor-control fault. Because the causes are varied, professional diagnostics with a dealer-level scan tool is recommended rather than guessing at a single sensor to replace; fixes range from sensor replacement to ECU reprogramming depending on findings.70717273

AC not cooling with a working fan — suspect the pressure sensor, not a missing relay. If the A/C fan runs but the compressor never engages, the cause is unlikely to be a missing/blown relay — there is only one general A/C relay in the fuse box, and it either works or the whole system is dead. The more likely suspect is the A/C pressure sensor, located on the refrigerant tube (has its own electrical connector): low refrigerant pressure prevents the compressor from being allowed to engage, as a protection behavior consistent with the pressure-cutoff logic described above.7475767778

AC failure with a bad smell in traffic — refrigerant leak, diagnose at a charging station. A distinct failure pattern: A/C develops a bad smell ("кондей завонял") followed by the system blowing hot air instead of cold, specifically during traffic congestion. This combination points to a refrigerant leak; recommended diagnosis is a proper A/C charging-station check to verify remaining refrigerant quantity and pinpoint the leak location, rather than guessing and simply recharging.7980

AC hose replacement — access point and procedure. To replace an A/C refrigerant hose, the main practical access point is from the passenger side, under the dashboard below the glove box — the hose runs from there to the evaporator unit. Full interior panel removal is not always necessary: reaching in from below or removing just the lower dashboard panel is often enough, though some jobs may still require removing additional trim pieces depending on the exact hose run.81828384

Evaporator refrigerant leak — dye-and-UV diagnosis, and full-replacement cost. A separate refrigerant leak specifically from the evaporator area inside the cabin: possible sources are the thermal expansion valve (TXV), the sealing rings at connection points, or the evaporator core itself. Diagnostic method: add fluorescent dye to the refrigerant charge and inspect with a UV light — this located leak evidence inside the cabin in one confirmed case. Repair scope depends on the exact failure point (TXV seal rings vs. full evaporator), which typically requires evaporator removal to confirm; full evaporator replacement costs approximately 28,000 RUB (RU market, June 2026) because it requires complete dashboard removal — a labor-intensive job.85868788899091929394

Refrigerant type and compressor oil — factory label reference. A factory under-hood label confirms the system uses R134a refrigerant with RAG 100 compressor oil — a definitive spec reference alongside the 500 g capacity figure noted above.959697

docs.title: AKPP — ATF temperature management
docs.text:
Tags: #automatic-transmission · #atf · #cooling · #temperature

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Optimal transmission (ATF) temperature on the X80 is 92–95°C; a 105–110°C threshold is considered critical. The factory heat exchanger for the АКПП is undersized for sustained highway driving in S mode or in hot climates — sustained temperatures over 100°C have been observed in testing. Modern ATF oils can tolerate up to 140°C, but the aluminum АКПП housing itself may fail at lower temperatures, so an additional (auxiliary) ATF cooler/radiator is recommended for longevity, not treated merely as a performance luxury upgrade.1

A real-world field report backs this up with numbers: on a 2024, 7,000 km summer road trip with fresh ATF, transmission temperature never exceeded 102°C, despite 36–39°C ambient heat, intensive highway overtaking in S mode, and Tbilisi/Baku city traffic. Fresh oil and a correct fill level were called out as critical to this result. The same owner's conclusion: an additional radiator is likely unnecessary for moderate drivers who avoid aggressive S-mode use, but is recommended for performance-oriented/harder driving.2

Checking ATF level (no dipstick). The X80's automatic transmission has no visible dipstick. Level is checked via the drain plug: crack open the drain plug and watch the small internal tube — when the level is correct, fluid begins dripping from that tube.3 When changing fluid, drain whatever comes out and refill with the same volume; the transmission reaches the correct level naturally once refilled to match the drained amount.4

Harsh/jerky shifting — diagnosis order. Hard or jerky automatic shifts can have several causes, and owners should check them in this order: (1) dirty or old ATF — check first;5 (2) a clogged filter or fluid that hasn't been changed in a long time — for more precise diagnosis, a service visit is recommended;6 (3) the transmission has no internal serviceable filter, only a strainer/mesh.7 Community characterization: the X80's transmission is "archaic" with no fixed shift schedule — behavior varies almost like it depends on the weather.89 One owner reports that flashing a Euro-2 ECU map resolved harshness for them, implying transmission tuning/mapping can also be a factor — though this requires expert ECU reprogramming and should be a later step after fluid/filter checks.10

AKPP overheating up to 180°C — undersized factory cooler. Some X80 units suffer ATF overheating as high as 180°C due to an undersized transmission cooler from the factory. Symptom pattern: after roughly 30 minutes of aggressive driving, the transmission starts hunting between gears and hesitates on acceleration, then recovers after about 10 minutes of rest. Reported diagnosis: ZF engineers (the transmission's design lineage) confirmed the factory cooling capacity is genuinely inadequate for sustained hard use, consistent with the "additional cooler recommended" guidance above. Fix: install an additional/auxiliary transmission fluid cooler (radiator), and in summer remove the engine under-tray to improve airflow to the transmission area.11121314

Transmission breather (sapun) location. The transmission's breather/vent ("сапун") is mounted near the battery, hanging off a bolt on the battery mounting bracket/stand.151617 Useful to know when ruling out pressure-related causes during cooling/fluid diagnostics.

Protection-mode temperature thresholds — two-stage response. The АКПП's built-in overheating protection operates at two distinct temperature levels: the 1st level, around 127°C, activates a dynamic shift-point adjustment mode (DSP) that shifts into higher RPM ranges to reduce heat generation; the 2nd level, around 150°C, reduces engine torque outright. Without an auxiliary cooler, transmission temperature can reach these thresholds during heavy traffic or repeated hard acceleration, because the OEM cooling capacity is limited — consistent with the broader "undersized factory cooler" pattern already documented on this card.18192021

Auxiliary cooler — Hayden OC-1405 installation, confirmed by two independent reports. Corroborating and adding installation/product detail to the "additional cooler recommended" guidance above: a Hayden OC-1405 auxiliary transmission-fluid cooler (round heat exchanger) has been installed by more than one owner to prevent overheating and K2 friction-pack failure. Installation: remove the stock small rectangular heat exchanger, install an adapter fitting under the tube connections, then plumb in the round Hayden cooler alongside the factory radiator-mounted exchanger. Reported cost: 12,000–15,000 RUB (July 2024, RU market). Recommended timing: install before extended highway driving or frequent towing rather than waiting for symptoms.22232425262719

Partial ATF drain/top-up — remember the gasket, not just the fluid. For a partial automatic-transmission-fluid service (a top-up/partial drain rather than a full fluid change), you need a new gasket/seal in addition to the fresh ATF itself — don't order fluid alone. Confirm the exact gasket requirement with your mechanic before starting, since it's easy to overlook when focused only on the fluid volume.282930

docs.title: HVAC blower motor — failure and repair
docs.text:
Tags: #hvac · #part-number · #mazda-6-compat

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Symptom pattern. The HVAC blower doesn't activate on a cold startup, but may kick in after the engine/cabin warms up, then runs with fluctuating power — pulsing on and off at intervals rather than running steadily.1

Root cause. The X80 blower motor is a brushless type (electronic contacts, not a traditional brush/commutator design). When the contacting surfaces oxidize or start arcing, the motor becomes intermittent: hesitant to start, and pulsing even after warm-up.23 Historically, some service centers have replaced only the brush/contact parts when available, which restores function for a few hundred hours of operation before the issue tends to recur — full motor replacement is recommended for a durable fix rather than repeatedly re-servicing the contacts.3

Access and removal — no glove-box removal required. The motor sits under the dashboard, below the glove box. Reported procedure: (1) glove-box removal is not necessary (it's an optional, easier-access alternative if you prefer to remove it); (2) access from underneath by kneeling in the footwell; (3) unfasten the engine-cover/undertray panel below the glove box; (4) remove 3× 10 mm bolts holding the motor assembly; (5) disconnect the motor's electrical connector.456 Total install/removal time is roughly 30 minutes.7 Caution before buying a replacement: some owners found the motor's contacts still functional after full disassembly and cleaning — suggesting contact oxidation, not a dead motor, may be the actual fault in some cases, worth trying before spending on a new unit.2

Intermittent stop-restart failure — motor inspection. A separate but related failure pattern: the blower stops intermittently and won't restart for extended periods. Likely causes: worn brushes/contacts, water ingress into the motor, or seized bearings — consistent with the brushless-contact root cause above but presenting as a total stall rather than pulsing. Diagnostic order: (1) check the fuse and relay first, (2) if those are fine, disassemble the motor to inspect and clean the brush/contact surfaces. Possible water-ingress source: leakage from the cooling/ventilation system into the blower housing.891011

Blower motor part numbers and cross-compatible alternatives. Original FAW Besturn X80 blower motor part number: GV7D61B10, priced roughly 4,000–8,500 RUB (RU market, December 2025). Dealers quote around 8,500 RUB for the original; supplier "KitZapchasti" reportedly stocks it for 4,000 RUB (RU market, December 2025).1213141516 Mazda 6 GH blower motors are reported as potential alternatives — part numbers RF1853, PFN305, LFH25LF, GS1D61B10 — but the rotor diameter differs: Mazda rotors are narrower than the X80's original, so the Mazda unit generally cannot be dropped in whole; only the motor housing is reported cross-compatible if you reuse the X80's native rotor. Two further alternative part numbers were mentioned with unconfirmed compatibility: HB100K26A and 5GA061B10.171819202122232425

docs.title: Burnt-plastic smell from the heater
docs.text:
Tags: #heater · #catalytic-converter · #egr

Symptom and candidate causes. A burnt-plastic smell while the heater is running, with a seasonal/wet-weather pattern, has been traced to a few different possible origins: (1) heater blower motor overload — check by removing the cabin air filter and inspecting the fan blade for debris or physical resistance/rubbing; (2) the catalytic converter, especially noticeable when driving through standing water; (3) possible EGR (exhaust gas recirculation) contamination. In one confirmed case, an owner found debris physically lodged in the blower intake from underneath the hood — a purely mechanical obstruction rather than an electrical/overheating fault. The wet-weather-specific pattern in several reports suggests moisture or an exhaust-related root cause rather than a constant electrical problem.123456

Catalytic-converter removal case — smell moved but didn't fully disappear. One owner removed the catalytic converter entirely; the burnt smell disappeared from inside the cabin but remained perceptible near the rear of the vehicle — consistent with the exhaust/catalytic-converter theory, since the odor source simply relocated to where the exhaust itself exits rather than being eliminated. This case's smell was also specifically wet-weather-dependent, matching the broader pattern above.7

docs.title: Coolant system — capacity and air-bleeding
docs.text:
Tags: #coolant

Total capacity and drain behavior. FAW X80 coolant system total capacity is 7.5–7.7 liters (owner's manual specifies 7.5 L with G30-91 extended-service coolant, year-round use; a separately confirmed manual page gives 7.6 ± 0.5 L with the same G30-91 spec, applicable to model codes CA6462MTE5AG1 and CA6462ATE5AG1).1234567 Draining through the radiator cap filler opening only removes about 5–6 liters; roughly 1.5–2.5 liters remain trapped in the engine block and lower passages. To drain fully: locate and open the lower block drain plug, or use the lower radiator hose as a bypass drain point — some residual coolant is still difficult to access even then. Tilting/elevating the front end improves drainage completeness. A manual drain requires removing the radiator cap and thorough flushing.12

Normal coolant level. Level should sit at the 50% mark on the expansion tank when the engine is cold; when hot, it rises roughly 1 cm higher — this is normal thermal expansion, not a leak.8

Air-bleeding methods after any coolant work. Two field-tested approaches: (1) Incline method — find roughly a 60° slope, point the front of the car uphill, start the engine and rev to ~3,000 RPM until the cooling fan engages (about 20 minutes), then top up with ~250 ml coolant and drive. (2) Top bleed method — let the engine cool completely, remove the upper hose from the throttle-body/manifold connection (the system's highest point), loosen the radiator cap slightly, pour coolant in slowly until it flows out of the opened hose, then reconnect and seal. Community experience: most air-pocket complaints trace back to a defective radiator cap — in the majority of reported cases, replacing the cap resolved the issue rather than the bleeding procedure itself.9 A simpler variant reported independently: after refilling coolant or replacing the thermostat, simply tilt/raise the front of the car and listen for circulation sounds until air pockets stop escaping — corroborates the incline method above as a routine, low-effort finishing step after any coolant work.101112

Post-thermostat-work checklist if temperature doesn't stabilize. After a thermostat replacement, the system may still hold trapped air. Monitor whether temperature stabilizes normally during a drive. If the gauge fluctuates or never reaches normal operating temperature: (1) check coolant level in the expansion tank, (2) check the radiator cap seal — a cap that isn't fully sealing (non-hermetic) is a common contributor, consistent with the radiator-cap finding above, (3) bleed remaining air by driving until circulation stabilizes. If temperature instead overshoots (runs hotter than normal), suspect the thermostat itself is faulty rather than just an air pocket.131415161718

Loss of circulation after cylinder head work. If coolant circulation is lost or reduced after cylinder head removal/repair, the leading suspects are: (1) a new water pump seal that has failed, (2) blocked passages in the cylinder head from improper reassembly, (3) an incorrect/incompatible head gasket, or (4) debris left in the cooling channels during the job. Targeted diagnosis (pressure test, passage inspection) is needed to pinpoint which of these applies before further work.19

Sudden idle/traffic overheating (120°C spike) — air-pocket-first diagnosis. A separate, detailed field report: engine temperature suddenly spiked to 120°C at idle or in slow traffic after an otherwise normal short drive.20 Priority order of suspects: (1) an air pocket (пробка) in the cooling system — the most common cause, especially after any antifreeze drain/refill; (2) thermostat failure (stuck closed); (3) the cooling fan not engaging properly.2122 Diagnostic routine: monitor fan engagement temperature (should start ~98–99°C, cool the engine to ~92°C, then cycle off), and check whether the lower radiator hose gets hot (confirms the thermostat is opening).23 In this case the owner resolved it by topping off antifreeze (~200 ml) and elevating the front of the car on a ramp while revving, then monitoring fan cycling over an extended highway drive — after which the car ran without recurrence for 40+ minutes of idle without climbing back near 100°C.2425 Preventive takeaway: always check coolant level after any cooling-system work, and monitor over ~500 km after such a fix to confirm the thermostat is behaving normally.26

Overheats while driving with a cold lower hose — air-pocket, not necessarily thermostat. A distinct but related symptom pattern: temperature is normal at idle, then the engine overheats specifically while driving, while the lower radiator hose stays cold despite the thermostat opening and the fan running. Root cause here was an air pocket in the cooling system rather than a failed thermostat. Remedy: bleed the air out following thermostat/coolant work (see air-bleeding methods above); if bleeding alone resolves the overheating, no thermostat replacement is needed — don't jump straight to a parts swap.272829303132

Proper coolant-level checking procedure — radiator first, expansion tank second. On a cold engine: (1) open the radiator cap on the radiator itself — coolant should be visible at the bottom of the filler neck; (2) if no coolant is visible, add until the level appears; (3) only after the radiator itself is confirmed full should you adjust the expansion-tank level to its center mark. Check the radiator level first, not the expansion tank, because the expansion-tank cap can malfunction and give a misleading level reading. If the coolant is old and hasn't been changed recently, drain completely and refill rather than topping off — and remember to bleed air from the system afterward (see the air-bleeding methods above).3334

Air-bleeding confirmation specifically after a thermostat swap. A field-tested confirmation of the air-bleeding methods already documented above, applied specifically after thermostat replacement: bleed air by either (1) starting the engine at high throttle and letting it cycle, or (2) on a lift — raise the front of the vehicle, start the engine, apply throttle, then release. Confirmation the bleed worked: the heater should blow hot air immediately afterward. If it doesn't, air remains trapped in the system — treat lack of heater output as the diagnostic signal that bleeding isn't complete yet, rather than assuming a thermostat or heater-core fault.3536373839

docs.title: Coolant specification — G12/G12+/G13/G30
docs.text:
Tags: #coolant · #part-number

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Baseline spec. The FAW Besturn X80 uses coolant type G12+ or G12++. G13 (a more modern formulation) can also be used as an alternative, but compatibility with whatever coolant is already in the system must be carefully verified before mixing.1 Factory-fill reports vary: most commonly red G12/G12+, though some early cars reportedly shipped with yellow G13 from the factory (source of this unclear/unconfirmed).2

Chemistry and why it matters. G12/G12+ is ethylene-glycol-based, carboxylate-technology, traditional and considered better suited to aluminum/iron/magnesium radiator/engine materials. G13 is propylene-glycol-based — the European eco-spec, less toxic. Separately, G30/G40 (BASF nomenclature) use OAT (organic acid technology) and are considered an evolution of G12, offering improved corrosion protection and longer service life; G12+ and G30 are roughly performance-equivalent. VAG's naming (G11/G12/G12+) and BASF's (G30/G40) describe overlapping technology tiers, not competing products.23

Color is not a reliable indicator of type. Color (red, yellow, green, blue) varies by brand within the same specification — e.g., G12 has been seen in both red and green from different manufacturers, and green G12 should not be confused with the older G11 spec. Always check the specification printed on the bottle/label, never rely on color alone.4

Community debate on mixing G12/G13 — document both positions. Strict-spec followers say G12 and G13 must never be mixed because of their different chemical bases (ethylene vs. propylene glycol). Pragmatists report that in practice, field mixing has caused no visible harm. Recommended conservative approach given this disagreement: when simply topping off, match whatever coolant type is already in the system; when doing a major coolant service (full drain + refill, e.g. during thermostat replacement), flush the system fully and refill with fresh G12/G12+ concentrate diluted 50% with distilled water rather than top up a mixed system.5

Compatibility matrix (G11/G12/G12+/G12++/G13). A shared community diagram ("Правильное смешивание антифризов" — proper antifreeze mixing) lays out concrete mixing rules across five coolant types: G11 cannot be mixed with G12; G12 is compatible with G12+, G12++, and G13; G12+ is compatible with G12++; G13 stands alone (not listed as freely compatible with the others beyond G12). Never mix incompatible types — doing so risks damaging the cooling system. The same source also flags a related caution: never dispose of used engine oil into the coolant.6

Refill procedure and practical spec guidance. For the X80, G12 or G12+ (carboxylate-based, pink/rose-colored) is the recommended coolant; avoid older G30 concentrate without first verifying compatibility, and pink coolant is the community-recommended safe default. When topping off low coolant: (1) never add to a hot engine, (2) add to the radiator itself (not just the expansion tank), roughly 0.5–1.0 L to bring the level between the MIN/MAX marks, (3) keep the expansion tank between MIN and MAX when cold. Low coolant is called out as a cause of both poor heater performance and potential overheating — consistent with the air-pocket/level guidance in the capacity card. If the previous fill type is unknown, G12+ is described as a safe default choice; avoid mixing different coolant colors/types per the compatibility matrix above.789101112131415161718

CARBOX G12+ red antifreeze — confirmed compatible. CARBOX brand red liquid coolant (product Felix 430206032) is confirmed compatible with a 2019 FAW X80 and available for refill. General takeaway restated: any coolant meeting the G12+ specification works for the X80, regardless of specific brand.192021

Corroborating brand recommendation — G12+ red as the common X80 choice. Independent confirmation of the community's default coolant choice already documented above: G12+ antifreeze in red is the common pick for the X80. Reinforcing the mixing warning elsewhere on this card: never mix green and red antifreeze — mixing causes clumping and coolant-system damage. If the existing coolant's type/history is unknown or the system has been neglected, drain and refill completely with fresh fluid rather than topping off an uncertain mix.222324

G13 compatibility, restated with an aluminum-radiator rationale. Confirming and adding chemistry detail to the G13 note already on this card: G13 is safe for 2019+ FAW X80 models with aluminum radiators. G13 is glycerin-based (vs. G12+'s glucose-based chemistry per this report) and is described as more practical, compatible with all the other listed coolant types, and providing longer-term protection for systems with aluminum, magnesium, or copper components.25262728

Service-manual spec G30-91 and VAG/BASF naming. The service manual lists the coolant as G30-91.29 A member explains that G11, G12 and G12+ are VAG classes while G30 and G40 are BASF classes, and that G12+ is roughly equivalent to G30.30 Another member holds that the names are simply different labels for the same standard.31 A Sintec MULTIFREEZE G13 universal antifreeze (1 kg pack) was listed on Ozon (Russian marketplace) in October 2025, but the chat does not confirm that it meets the G30-91 spec.32

docs.title: Cooling fan motor failure and parking sensor glitches
docs.text:
Tags: #cooling-fan · #price

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Root cause — cooling fans and parking sensors share wiring (2026-08 report). One owner brought the car in for a routine service task (blowing dust out of the fuse box) and drove away to find the parking sensors glitching. Diagnosis traced this to the radiator cooling fan motors being electrically connected to the same circuit as the parking sensors — so a fan-motor failure shows up first as parking-sensor malfunctions.1

Consequences of driving with dead cooling fans. The owner unknowingly drove roughly half a year without working radiator cooling fans. No fault ever appeared on the dashboard/instrument cluster for the fan failure itself — the only visible symptom was the parking-sensor glitching.12 Over that period, this led to oil consumption starting to appear, which the owner flags as a knock-on engine-condition concern worth monitoring after this kind of prolonged no-cooling-fan operation.1

Symptom pattern reported. At highway speed, airflow through the radiator was sufficient and temperature stayed normal even with the fans dead; the problem showed up at idle/low speed — e.g., queuing at a gas station with the A/C on, hot air started coming from the A/C vents and coolant temperature climbed.3 On a subsequent ~90 km trip the owner kept a close eye on the temperature gauge and reported it staying normal throughout.45 Another member confirmed the underlying issue was simply that the radiator cooling fan was not running/spinning — noting that a working fan is normally audible.678 One member also suggested computer diagnostics as a general troubleshooting step for this kind of issue,9 and reacted to the full story with a resigned "well..." once the cascade of consequences was laid out.10

Fix and part cross-compatibility. The owner replaced the fan motors with Mazda-sourced motors, described as a direct, one-to-one fit (no modification needed) — after replacement the issue was fully resolved ("now it sings").11 Another member asked which specific Mazda model the motors came from; the owner did not identify the exact model in this thread but offered to check if needed.1213

Price (Russia, 2026-08 report). Cost for 2 replacement motors was about 2,500 RUB total (parts, as reported by the owner — installation/labor cost not separately broken out in this report).13

Community takeaway. The owner explicitly flagged this for future reference: if parking sensors start glitching for no obvious reason, check the radiator cooling fan motors before assuming a parking-sensor-specific fault.14

docs.title: Dashboard panel removal — A/C and heater access
docs.text:
Tags: #dashboard · #hvac · #heater

To reach the evaporator core for A/C repair (leak fix, clog clearing, etc.), the dashboard must be substantially disassembled: (1) remove the hood-release lever by carefully prying it with a flat tool and pulling downward; (2) disconnect the multiple clips and fasteners in the steering column area; (3) remove the main dashboard retaining bolts; (4) remove the iron support tube/brace below the steering column; (5) remove the heater housing, which likely needs to be split open to reach the evaporator itself. This is a moderate-complexity project requiring several hours with breaks — not a quick job. Along the way, note that the comfort module (BSM) is located under the driver's left knee area, useful to know if you're also troubleshooting comfort-module-related electrical issues while the dash is open 123456789101112131415161718.

Multi-day project — reinforcing confirmation: consistent with the "moderate-complexity, several hours" characterization above, a separate report confirms full dashboard removal is a labor-intensive job requiring multiple working sessions — it cannot realistically be completed in one day. Careful documentation of components and fasteners during disassembly is recommended for reassembly, given the number of disassembly steps involved 1920.

docs.title: Fan, A/C and water-pump relays and fuses (EWD)
docs.text:
Tags: #relay · #fuse · #cooling-fan · #wiring-diagram · #water-pump

Source: the factory electrical wiring diagram (EWD) pages shared as PDFs in the group. Values below are as printed on the diagrams; one rating is inconsistent on the page itself (see PWM fan).1

Cooling fans. The R12 Medium Speed Fan Relay switches the Main and Additional Fan Motors through fuse Si9 "Medium Speed Fan" 40A, controlled from ECU (2.0L) pin 50. The R16 High Speed Fan Relay uses Si11 "High Speed Fan" 30A, controlled from ECU (2.0L) pin 68. The R21 PWM Fan Relay (2.0L) is shown with Si11 "PWM Fan" at 50A, which conflicts with the 30A printed on the high-speed fan fuse label; confirm against the PDF before relying on either value.1 For fan-motor failure stories see Cooling fan motor failure and parking sensor glitches.

A/C compressor relay. R1 A/C Compressor Relay uses Si25 "Compressor" 10A to drive the compressor magnetic clutch; its ECU pin is 69 on the 2.0L, 42 on the 1.8T and C_L4 on the 1.8TD.1

Electric water pump relay. R20 Electric Water Pump Relay uses Si21 5A for the electric water pump (1.8T, 1.8TD and 2.0L variants), with ECU pin 39 on the 1.8T and B_N3 on the 1.8TD.1

A/C circuit page. The A/C wiring page shows fuses Si25 "Compressor" 10A, Si5 "Blower" 40A, Si67 "Seat Heater" 5A, Si7 "Defroster" 40A and Si1 "BNT" 40A, with main fuses Si13 125A, Si71 (generator) 175A and Si72 (main) 175A. The compressor magnetic-clutch connector is E12 (2.0L), E11 (1.8T) or E75 (1.8TD); the triple pressure switch is F39. The blower is I18; the page also covers the temperature damper motors (driver-side and front-passenger-side temperature, ventilation, mode, inner/outer circulation), the automatic A/C control unit (ATC) and the rear-window defroster relay.2 See Air conditioning — refrigerant system and diagnosis for the refrigerant side.

docs.title: Engine operating temperature and fan engagement
docs.text:
Tags: #temperature · #cooling-fan · #automatic-transmission · #hvac · #cold-start

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Baseline (no A/C). Normal FAW X80 engine operating temperature is 92–95°C. Auxiliary cooling fans engage at 98–99°C and pull the temperature back down. Under traffic/idle conditions temperature can climb to about 100°C — still within the range considered normal, as fans should cycle automatically to hold thermal balance.1 This is independently corroborated: normal city-driving/idle temperature is commonly reported around 99°C, with fan activation at that same threshold considered typical and normal — the thermostat is functioning properly if temperature stabilizes there and doesn't climb further during traffic or low-speed driving. Investigate further (fan motor, thermostat quality, coolant level) only if temperature consistently exceeds 100°C at idle/traffic.23

Highway gauge reading and dashboard-mark calibration. On the highway, a "4 divisions" gauge reading (roughly the middle of the scale, or slightly above) corresponds to 90–93°C — described as ideal. Rough gauge-mark calibration: 1st mark ≈ 70°C, 2nd mark ≈ 75°C, middle mark ≈ 90°C. Readings above 95–96°C trigger the cooling fan. In winter, even at -10°C to -40°C ambient, the same thermostat/fan behavior applies — don't expect the gauge to read lower purely because the outside air is cold.456789

With A/C engaged. Normal engine temperature stabilizes slightly lower, around 87–90°C, with anything above 90°C potentially triggering the fans. Two cooling fans are expected to run when A/C is on: a primary fan that runs continuously, and a secondary fan that cycles as needed — frequent fan engagement in this state is normal, not a fault sign. If temperatures run high with A/C on, check in order: both fans are actually operating, the radiator is clean/unobstructed, coolant level is adequate, and water pump condition (a weak pump causes temperature instability).10

With АКПП (automatic transmission) load. On automatic-transmission X80s, temperatures commonly reach 98–100°C in traffic specifically because of hydrodynamic transmission heat generation feeding into the shared cooling system. On the highway at steady throttle, temperature typically drops back to 90–92°C. A reading of 99–102°C sustained on the highway (not just in traffic) is not normal — it points to a thermostat or other cooling-system problem rather than ordinary АКПП heat load.11

Cold-start warm-up timing (winter). A owner logged a cold start at 9°C ambient: the engine reached 60°C in roughly 11 minutes at idle, with transmission (ATF) fluid warming about 4°C slower than the engine. On the analog/graduated dash gauge, each mark represents roughly 10°C.121314 Recommended winter procedure (-5 to -20°C): idle the engine until coolant reaches 60–80°C, then drive gently at 1,300–3,000 RPM for about 5 minutes before normal use; modern Euro-5-class vehicles are said to tolerate moving off after just 5–10 minutes for emissions-standard reasons, but the transmission and engine oil should still reach working temperature before aggressive driving.1516 One community member pushed back that this "gentle idle first" approach is unnecessary and that any oil just needs to reach working temperature by driving, not idling — presented as a live disagreement rather than settled practice.17

Slow cabin-heater warm-up on a cold start — normal, not a fault. New-car owners commonly report the cabin heater staying cold during the initial warm-up (15–20 minutes at around -5°C) even after the engine itself reaches temperature. This is expected behavior, not a defect: the small coolant circuit (before the thermostat opens the large/radiator loop) has to warm first, and once the thermostat opens to the large circuit, distributing that warmth to the cabin heater core takes additional time. This is not a fault as long as: (1) the engine does reach normal operating temperature, and (2) the heater does eventually warm up while driving. Patience is the fix — engine oil tends to warm faster than coolant, so allow another 5–10 minutes. Only suspect a real problem (stuck thermostat, low coolant, or an air pocket) if the heater still hasn't warmed after 30+ minutes or a stretch of moderate-speed driving.1819202122232425

Hot-climate traffic case study (Krasnodar) — before/after a thermostat-and-hose fix. A field report from a hot-climate region (Krasnodar, June data) illustrates the traffic/A/C temperature pattern already documented above with concrete before/after numbers: before fixes, temperature in heavy traffic with A/C on reached 106–108°C; after replacing the thermostat and repairing a cracked hose, temperature stabilized around 99°C in the same conditions (minimum ~89°C when the fans activate, rarely exceeding 99°C). This corroborates the fan-activation-around-89°C baseline noted above and shows that a properly functioning thermostat/hose set keeps traffic-heat temperatures near that ceiling even in hot regional climates.262728

docs.title: LPG/GBO installation — cooling-system effects
docs.text:
Tags: #overheating · #thermostat · #water-pump

Multiple owners who installed an LPG/GBO gas-conversion system reported cooling-related overheating symptoms afterward. Two independent case threads are combined here because they converge on the same diagnostic logic.

Case 1 — 115,000 km, 2017 X80, post-GBO overheating. After installing LPG on a 2017 car with 115k km, the owner saw a check-engine light and coolant temperature of 99–102°C both at highway speed and idle — abnormal for those conditions.12 An initial antifreeze top-up (coolant had been low, topped to max) did not resolve it.3 Diagnosis narrowed to a combination of: (1) an air pocket introduced in the cooling system during GBO installation and component relocation (the GBO reducer is commonly mounted above the original coolant hose routing, which the installer's own forums flag as an air-trap risk);4 (2) possible thermostat malfunction — a cold lower hose indicates the large cooling circuit isn't opening;56 or (3) radiator blockage/cleanliness. The gas installer in this case struggled at length to get the thermostat to circulate both loops properly.7 Community consensus in this thread: thermostat failure and air pockets are the primary suspects — GBO itself does not directly cause overheating by design, but poorly installed or poorly maintained GBO plumbing can.8

Case 2 — general post-LPO overheating pattern. A second, broader thread on post-LPG-installation overheating narrowed the cause list to: (1) air pockets in the heater-radiator circuit from incorrect hose routing during install; (2) incorrectly positioned LPO hoses; (3) a defective thermostat; or (4) a failing water pump.9 Diagnostic test: rev the engine on gas and check whether the lower radiator hose heats up — if cold/barely warm, the thermostat is likely at fault; if it heats normally, the water pump is functioning.1011 Also check the radiator cap — a cap that doesn't hold pressure was flagged as a contributing factor in at least one case, and cap replacement was recommended alongside the other checks.12 Multiple owners in this thread reported the same symptom pattern resolved specifically by thermostat replacement.13 There was live debate on which component to test first (pump vs. thermostat); the resolution reached was that a cold/barely-warm lower hose while revving on gas points to thermostat first, since a failing pump would still let some warmth through via circulation, whereas a stuck-closed thermostat blocks the large loop outright.14

Air-pocket formation after component relocation. When a GBO reducer or other add-on component is mounted above the original coolant hose routing (a common LPG-install pattern), air pockets can form in the system and prevent proper flow through the large cooling circuit. Purge methods reported: gentle acceleration with the front of the car raised, or repeating several heat cycles (drive/cool/drive) to work the air out gradually.415

Thermostat/fan behavior runs 4–5°C higher on gas than on petrol. A separate report describes the baseline thermostat operating pattern by fuel type: on petrol, the thermostat opens at 99°C, initially dips to 93°C, then stabilizes around 84°C in normal operation. On gas (LPG), the same pattern repeats but shifted 4–5°C higher throughout, with the cooling fan typically engaging at 99°C and disengaging at 95°C — attributed to gas burning at a higher combustion temperature than petrol. Separately noted as a contributing design factor: the X80's thermostat sits in an unusual location (not at the end of the cylinder block, where temperature is normally highest), which is described as a general contributor to the model's cooling challenges regardless of fuel type.161718

docs.title: Heater blower motor fan — no separate part
docs.text:
Tags: #heater · #hvac · #part-number · #price

If the heater blower motor's fan blade ("крыльчатка мотора печки") cracks or breaks, it cannot be purchased separately — only the complete motor assembly is available as a replacement part. Buying the full assembly just to replace a broken blade is not economical compared to a full new heater-unit-level part. Some owners have looked into sourcing a compatible fan/motor from other vehicle platforms as a cheaper workaround, but fitment compatibility is uncertain and unconfirmed — no specific cross-compatible part number has been established by the community 1234567.

Blower motor uses a graphite bushing, not a ball bearing — cold-weather whistle fix: the X80 heater blower motor uses a metal-graphite sleeve bushing, not a ball bearing. A whistling noise in cold weather can come from either the bushing or debris/leaves caught in the impeller. First attempt: spray aerosol penetrating lubricant (WD-40) into the unit without disassembly. If that fails: remove the motor (held by 3 self-tapping screws under the glove box), clean out any debris, and re-grease the bushing. Full motor replacement is available if the bushing is too worn. Check for debris before assuming a bushing replacement is needed 891011121314151617.

Heater motor for restyle model — visual reference (low confidence): a visual reference photo of a replacement heater blower motor (вентилятор печки) for the FAW X80 restyle model was shared in the group, documenting the part's location and appearance — useful as a visual identification aid alongside the sourcing notes above 18.

docs.title: Heater-core coolant leak into the cabin
docs.text:
Tags: #hvac

Symptoms. A dripping sound from the passenger side, moisture found under the driver-side floor mat, and the heater ceasing to produce heat — together these point to coolant leaking from the heater core or its associated hose circuit directly into the cabin, rather than a rainwater/sunroof/condensate source.12 Context in this case: the car had a prior air-lock (air pocket) in the heating system, after which coolant had been refilled — a possible link between that earlier service and the later leak was suspected but not confirmed.3

Locating the source. Note which footwell is wet: dampness centered on the driver's side rather than the passenger's side points toward the heater hoses/core routing on that side rather than a more general source.4 Diagnostic steps: check the antifreeze/coolant level under the hood first (a drop supports an internal leak rather than condensation);3 then inspect the heater hoses and the heater-core connection points for wetness or corrosion.5

Fix. Replace the heater core, or repair/replace the specific cracked/degraded tube(s) feeding it, once the exact leak point is confirmed — most reports in this thread pointed to the hoses themselves rather than the core body.54

docs.title: Heater fan motor failure — diagnosis and repair
docs.text:
Tags: #heater · #hvac · #part-number

Symptom: heater fan motor stopped working in cold weather.1

Diagnostic step. A direct electrical bypass test — powering the fan motor via the cigarette lighter circuit — temporarily restored function. This indicates the motor itself is likely still functional; the fault is in the control circuit feeding it, not the motor.123

Likely cause: the heater regulator/resistor (rheostat) has burned out or failed — this component controls fan speed and sits between the switch and the motor. Part: "реостат отопителя резистор" GV7D61B15.45

Fix: replace the heater resistor/regulator module — not the fan motor itself, since the motor tested functional via the bypass.45

docs.title: Heater hose and coolant-tube sourcing
docs.text:
Tags: #part-number · #sourcing
