Ozon NFC sensors reportedly did not work at all (a different protocol from the standard cloneable type), so check the protocol before relying on the Diagzone/Autel cloning route 31. One owner instead bought universal German-made sensors with a wheel purchase from Rimzone; the car was already in the dealer's database, they programmed without fuss and were judged more reliable than the Chinese ones 32.
  • Valve only. The TPMS valve without the sensor is hard to find separately: kitzapchasti.ru lists it for 2,350 RUB (RU market, October 2025), but most suppliers sell only the complete valve+sensor assembly, about 2,300 RUB locally. Given the high cost of online delivery, check local availability first 33343536373839404142.

docs.title: TPMS sensor programming, cloning and tools
docs.text:
Tags: #tpms

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Detail card of the overview TPMS tire pressure sensors. Related: TPMS sensor cloning when installing aftermarket wheels · TPMS sensors — 5GA/5BA reports, programming, IDs.

  • Programming is mandatory. New or replacement sensors must be programmed/registered before they work 123. Reports on how much is needed differ by generation: pre-restyle cars are said to auto-adapt to new sensors, while restyle cars need ECU reprogramming by a dealer or specialist, so verify the model year before buying 45. Self-programming was reported not possible, so there are two routes: transfer the original sensors from the old wheels to the new ones (preferred, no reprogramming) 67, or have a FAW dealer program new ones with its diagnostic equipment 8.
  • Broken sensor during tire work. Extract the code from the old (dead but still readable) sensor and program it into the new one before installing it; keep the old sensor if it still reads at all 91011.
  • Cloning vs. a new UUID. Either clone the original sensor's UUID/ID into the new sensor so the ECU keeps recognising the old identity, or program a fresh UUID and make the ECU learn it. OEM FAW sensors cannot be cloned; they must be programmed as new, by extracting the UUID from ECU memory and writing it to the new sensor with a tool such as an Autel 1213141516.
  • One original sensor needed for auto-programming. New sensors cannot auto-pair unless at least one original sensor stays on the car as a reference; otherwise a technician must program them one by one 1718.
  • Per-wheel programming, then sleep. After replacement each sensor is programmed individually per wheel location (Autel confirmed to work) 192021. Sensors then sleep after roughly 4 hours of inactivity and do not report until the car has been driven 1.5-2 km 22232425192021.
  • Second (seasonal) wheel set. FS43X0L5 sensors can be programmed into the BCM with an Autel T508 in minutes, but a sensor ID cannot be duplicated onto a second wheel set: each ID is locked to one position, so seasonal swaps need either reprogramming at each changeover or a fully separate sensor set 26272829.
  • Autel walkthrough (June 2026). Use an Autel scanner with the FAW/Bestune library: searching "FAW" returns nothing, so open the "BESTUN" brand menu and expand to "X80" and the sensors then pair 3031323334353637383940414243444546474849505152. After fitting, a sensor can be woken by driving with the tire inflated (pressure alone activates it) or by holding a powerful coil magnet against its body, which switches on the transmitter 5245. Genuine FAW sensors are proprietary and need special reprogramming matched to their battery model 3031.
  • Scanners. Plain OBD readers cannot bind or read TPMS 53. Recommended: Autel TS508 Wi-Fi with MaxiTPMS (sold on Ozon), or a Mucar BT200 on the DiagZone PRO platform with its TPMS service function 54555657. The Autel TS508 was confirmed by an experienced member to support the X80; borrowing a tire shop's unit is a good alternative to buying one, and Autel sensors suit the car too 5859. An Autel MX-Sensor 433/315 MHz programmer was 7,579 RUB at a 58% discount on AliExpress (April 2025) 60; a Launch-type programmer costs about 7,800 RUB (RU market, October 2026), so most owners pay a shop instead 61.
  • Remote/outsourced programming. A community member offered paid programming or ID cloning with a proprietary programmer for 7,500 RUB (RU market, May 2026); remote handling works if the customer supplies the sensor IDs, read off the sensor or via Launch/Diagzone Pro diagnostics from the ECU 62636465. An Avito specialist might program four sensors for about 1,000 RUB (RU market, October 2026), though this is hearsay 66.
  • Conflict on older sensors. Some technicians report success reprogramming sensors made before about 2016 with aftermarket scanners, others cannot bind any replacement sensor at all because of equipment limits (unresolved) 676869707172.

docs.title: TPMS sensors — 5GA/5BA reports, programming, IDs
docs.text:
Tags: #tpms · #sensor · #part-number · #tire-pressure

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Supplement to TPMS tire pressure sensors: part-number reports, programming pitfalls and ID-reading limits from the 2025 threads. Related cards: TPMS sensors — part number and pricing, TPMS sensor cloning when installing aftermarket wheels, TPMS sensor battery type and design; the sensor's controller wiring is in Wiring diagram (EWD) circuits and connectors.

Part numbers: 5GA037973 vs 5BA037973. The X80FC2 parts catalog lists the TPMS sensor as part code 5GA037973 in the wheel-and-tyre group 3700A01X80F; the same group lists tyres 215/60R17 96V (Hankook, FQ9062016717) and 185/70R17 (Wanli, FQ9062017687). The catalog gives no frequency, battery or price 1. One member fitted 5BA037973 bought on Ozon and reports it working through a winter, about a year on. A member says 5BA037973 is for the pre-restyle X80 and the X40 and that the X80 sensor starts with 5GA, whereas one supplier told another owner that 5BA037973 is the restyle number; the two statements conflict. A set of 4 sensors listed on AliExpress as 5GA037973C for FAW Bestune 2018-2024 (T77) was priced ~7,459 RUB (RU market, Nov 2025) 23456.

A new sensor must be programmed. A replacement 5GA037973 has to be programmed after fitting: either the old sensor's ID is read and cloned into the new one, or the ID is read from the car over OBD and written into the sensor 78. A Launch TPMS LTR-03 tool (433 + 315 MHz) was listed for this in Nov 2025 9.

New sensor not accepted / dead after a battery swap. One owner's new 5GA037973 was not accepted by the car and the supplier said it belongs to a different system; the workaround described is to leave the old battery in place with its tabs cut and fit a new cell outside 1011. In another case a sensor did not work after a battery swap; the replies blamed wrong polarity or failing to disconnect the old cell, and the sensor eventually proved dead 1213.

Reading and cloning IDs. One owner pulled the sensor IDs from the ECU via OBD-II with an Autel scanner; another says Diagzone Pro reads the IDs virtually from the ECU. A member states a sensor ID cannot be cloned onto a second wheel set because the sensors are not programmable 141516.

Aftermarket FS43X0L5 and the OEM label. Aftermarket sensors for the X80 are sold as FS43X0L5; one owner bought an Autel-branded 4-pack, other options mentioned are a metal-bodied 4-pack and an NFC-type set. The OEM sensor label reads FS43X0L5-181218-050549BD with a DataMatrix code 17181920.

docs.title: TPMS tire pressure sensors
docs.text: Tags: #tpms · #tire-pressure

docs.title: How the system works
docs.text:
Each wheel carries its own TPMS sensor with a sealed, non-replaceable battery and a unique ID that must be programmed into the vehicle computer; sensors cannot be paired as a group, each is registered individually 1234. Owners describe the X80 system as a Japanese-origin design: unlike Hyundai or Geely models, which reportedly auto-detect new sensors, the FAW system needs a diagnostic tool for every new or replacement sensor, and a professional Autel programmer can handle several sensors in one session 567. Later part-number reports, programming pitfalls and ID-reading limits are in TPMS sensors — 5GA/5BA reports, programming, IDs.

  • Wheel-position binding. Sensors are bound to a wheel position and cannot be freely moved on rotation; rebinding is required whenever they are rotated 89. The car keeps reporting a moved sensor's data under its original position until re-paired, and after rotation readings may show on the wrong position until the computer updates; the receiver can pick a sensor up from about 10 m away 10.
  • Frequency. The system runs at 434 MHz or 433 MHz depending on vehicle/market and the frequencies cannot be mixed 1112; X80 sensors are described as 433 MHz (the Europe standard; US is 315 MHz, Japan 434 MHz) 1314151617181920. The parts catalog and owner's manual, however, point to 315 MHz for the OEM sensor 212223, yet several owners measured or ordered "433 MHz" sensors that worked when matched to the correct part number, so treat the part number as authoritative over the marketed frequency and check both 24252627. Sensors made before about 2016 are reported at 315, 433 or 434 MHz depending on the manufacturing batch 282930313233. Universal sensors for Asian/Korean vehicles exist in the correct FAW frequency 343536. The FAW carrier frequency encoding is reportedly several MHz off generic aftermarket sensors, apparently by design to push owners to dealer programming 3738.
  • Reading the sensor ID. The ID is printed on the sensor body (the last 8 digits of the identification number, near the torque/thread area) 3940; it can be read by eye once the tire is dismounted, or through a compatible scanner/OBD-II interface 1314151617181920. It is how you match a physical sensor to its registered ID when troubleshooting or ordering a replacement 3940.
  • Checking sensor function on the dashboard. Turn the key to ON, wait 2 minutes, then open the reading with the steering-wheel info button: down, OK, OK 4142. Signal registration can take 2-3 minutes after startup 434445.

docs.title: TPMS warnings and fault finding
docs.text:
Tags: #tpms · #tire-pressure

Detail card of the overview TPMS tire pressure sensors.

  • Low-pressure warning. Pressing OK on the steering wheel only acknowledges it for now; if it returns after the next ignition cycle, pressure really is below spec, so check and inflate 12.
  • "Check TPMS system" (проверяйте систему TPMS). Usually means the batteries in the wheel sensors are exhausted (Victor, October 2026); the dashboard photo at 42,657 km shows the yellow warning with a tyre icon and a "stop reminder" prompt 3. The sensors are potted and cannot be opened, so owners replace them and clone the IDs 45. Dead sensors cannot broadcast their IDs, so reviving them is pointless: read the ID printed on each sensor, or with an OBD2 scanner, and have a tyre shop program the new sensors with those IDs when the wheels are mounted 67.
  • Dead-sensor warning (2026). The warning appears when a wheel sensor stops reporting and the dashboard shows which wheel has no reading. One owner said only replacing the sensors clears it 8; another said the only way to remove it is to make the sensors work 9; a third pointed to the cabin fuses without explaining how, which is unclear 10.
  • After a car wash. Try resetting through the dashboard menu, then disconnect and reconnect the battery terminal; if it persists suspect a dead sensor battery or failed sensor. One thread names a CR2032-type cell, others CR2450/BR2450 (see TPMS sensor battery life and replacement); because opening a sensor takes knife-and-soldering-iron skill, the practical fix is usually replacing all four together for consistent recalibration 1112131415161718.
  • All dashes/blank on the trip computer with the light on. Check in order: sensors physically present on all four wheels; sensor battery status (most common failure near the ~5-year mark); physical sensor damage. None can be confirmed without removing the wheels, as there is no non-invasive diagnostic for individual sensors 192021222324252627.
  • Intermittent signal loss can come from a weak end-of-life battery (~6 years), poor contact at the receiver module, or the normal registration delay 282930. Cold can cause temporary failures that recover after about 10 km of driving 3132333435.
  • "Info" button unresponsive / no data. A new owner of a manual-transmission restyle X80 found neither parking nor tire-pressure sensors working, and the "i" button, which should open the tire-pressure menu, did nothing 3637. Others see the menu open but show no readings, so there are two failure modes: the menu does not open, or it opens empty 3839. Community advice: first decide whether the button itself is faulty, since a working button with blank data points to dead sensors/batteries; complete failure needs a scanner 404142. One owner ordered new sensor batteries to troubleshoot before a full swap 4344.
  • Battery-only service. A lower-confidence report says some sensors can be serviced by changing the internal battery, and some owners simply ignore the light as a non-critical convenience; either way re-registration needs technician-grade equipment 454647484950.

docs.title: Trailer wiring adapter fuse damage
docs.text:
Tags: #fuse

Connecting a trailer wiring adapter with an incorrect pinout can short circuits and blow vehicle fuses, particularly the rear-light fuses. Symptom: rear brake lights stop working right after a trailer hookup 12. Solution: identify the blown fuse and replace it. To prevent recurrence, use a properly matched adapter/harness or add relay isolation between the trailer circuit and the vehicle's own lighting circuit rather than a direct tap 3.

docs.title: Transmission warning light and adaptation reset
docs.text:
Tags: #automatic-transmission · #warning-light

Yellow gear-icon warning light — what it means and first checks. A yellow gear icon with an exclamation mark in the instrument cluster indicates a transmission fault. Possible causes: low transmission fluid level, overheating (with risk to the K2 clutch pack), internal clutch pack issues, solenoid failure, or the transmission having entered limp mode. Always check the transmission fluid level first, since it's the simplest and most common cause. If the light persists after confirming fluid level is correct, a diagnostic scan is needed to read the specific fault code and narrow down the cause further 123 4.

Adaptation-reset procedure for acceleration hesitation. A separate, practical procedure some owners use when the automatic transmission hesitates during acceleration (without necessarily throwing the warning light above): (1) turn the ignition key 2-3 times without actually starting the engine; (2) press the gas pedal hard; (3) turn off the ignition and wait 3 minutes; (4) turn the key to the same accessory/on position again and remove it; (5) press the gas pedal hard again; (6) release the pedal and start the engine normally. This sequence is reported to reset the transmission's adaptation values. Noted caveat: this procedure was confirmed to work with a traditional metal key ignition (AKPP); it's unclear whether/how it translates to push-button start systems, which may need a different sequence — treat this as unconfirmed for push-button-start cars 5678 9.

docs.title: Trunk lock water ingress and repair
docs.text:
Tags: #trunk · #water-ingress · #connector

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Two related failure patterns are reported for the trunk/boot lock, both traced to the same underlying cause (water ingress into the lock solenoid/connectors).

Case 1: lock stopped opening manually, remote still works. Symptom: the trunk clicks open when triggered manually from inside the car but won't actuate from the outside handle/latch at all — only the remote keyfob opens it 1. Diagnosis: check whether the latch lever ("лепесток") itself moves freely — it can get stuck/bind mechanically — and separately check whether the electrical contacts it's supposed to close are actually making contact, since a free-moving lever can still fail to close a fouled contact 23. Root cause confirmed by the owner: water — noticeable because water visibly pours out when opening the trunk right after a car wash, and winter cold makes the problem worse 45. Temporary workaround: manually push the latch lever into the locked position, then use the physical key to open it from outside 1. Fix: remove the trunk trim panel, clean all electrical terminals/connector pins ("клеммы и фишки"), and dry them 6. One owner's drying+silicone-grease treatment stopped a related symptom (a clicking sound) entirely 7. Preventive measure: apply butyl sealing tape around the trunk seal/lock area to keep water out during future car washes.

Case 2: trunk button doesn't work, remote does. Symptom: the trunk opens fine via the remote keyfob, but the physical trunk-release button does nothing 8. Because the remote-triggered release works, the lock mechanism itself is confirmed functional — the fault is isolated to the button/its switch contact, not the lock 910. Fix: same approach as case 1 — remove the rear/trunk trim, inspect and clean all electrical terminals and the button's contacts, spray the lock mechanism with a light lubricant (WD-40 or equivalent) 11. This class of fix (cleaning contacts) resolves roughly 90% of these complaints according to community experience; check the emergency mechanical trunk release first if the trunk needs to be opened urgently while diagnosing.

docs.title: Trunk power outlet availability
docs.text:
Tags: #trunk · #fuse

Availability by model year/generation: on the pre-facelift X80 (2015–2018), a trunk power outlet is factory-installed on some trims, protected by a dedicated 15A fuse in the cabin/dash fuse panel. On the facelift (2018+), there is no factory trunk outlet, but a placeholder hole exists for DIY installation. Power for this outlet comes from the interior (cabin) wiring — it is not separately fused from the trunk area 123456789101112131415. ⚠️ Conflict: some facelift owners report a factory outlet is present; it's unclear whether this is present on all trims or only higher-spec models. Pre-facelift models definitively have it.

Fuse rating and location: the trunk/cargo power outlet is protected by a dedicated 15A fuse, located in the salon/cabin fuse panel, separate from the salon power-outlet fuses. It is rated for 15A continuous — suitable for small chargers, small air compressors (~3W rated), and tools under 100W. Higher-power devices will blow the 15A fuse 101116171819202122.

Wiring troubleshooting: if the trunk power outlet has no power: (1) check the 15A fuse in the cabin panel (top/middle area of the dash); (2) if the fuse is blown, replace it with a 15A fuse and retest; (3) if there is still no power after fuse replacement, check for loose connectors in the wiring harness running to the outlet; (4) verify the outlet itself is not disconnected. A high-power surge (e.g. a short in a trailer plug) is the most common cause of fuse failure 23242526271728292030.

docs.title: Cabin water ingress and electrical faults
docs.text:
Tags: #water-ingress · #engine-bay

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Overnight battery drain from comfort-block/immobilizer moisture shorts. A distinct symptom pattern: complete battery discharge overnight after a normal shutdown, with all lights/switches checked and ruled out. Root cause: water intrusion into the comfort-block connector or the immobilizer module causes a short. Diagnosis: check for water in the driver's/passenger's footwell carpet by touch, and examine the comfort block and immobilizer connectors for corrosion from rainwater ingress — a short in these block connectors, caused by water breaching the weather seals, is what produces the parasitic drain 12.

Engine-bay water pooling near the BCM. Water can also accumulate in the engine bay during rain, especially around the BCM (Battery/Body Control Module) area — after storms, standing water has been observed in certain recesses there. Diagnosis: remove the BCM cover and visually inspect contacts for oxidation (green coloring); clean any oxidized contacts with cotton swabs and isopropyl alcohol. In one inspected case, water had been sealed around the connections with sealant (герметик) previously, and the BCM contacts were found clean and functional — i.e. a prior sealant repair can hold up, so check whether one was already done before assuming fresh damage 345.

A known issue on the X80: water can leak into the passenger compartment, leaving wet carpets and standing water in the cabin. This water intrusion causes intermittent electrical faults and system malfunctions 6. Practical takeaway for diagnosing seemingly-unrelated electrical gremlins: rule out water damage as the root cause before chasing individual component failures. The leak issue reportedly persists even after "recent fixes," and is treated by the community as an underlying design/manufacturing weak point rather than a one-off 6.

Specific case: VSM (body/vehicle control module) moisture causing gauge and light malfunctions. Symptom: lights and gauges malfunction — e.g. the dashboard indicator shows the rear lights should be on, but they don't actually light up 7. Likely cause: moisture infiltration into the VSM connector 8. The affected connector is located in the fuse block area 910. Diagnosis/fix: (1) locate the VSM connector; (2) clean it with contact cleaner or isopropyl alcohol; (3) prevent recurrence by packing a silicone-based grease (not aerosol spray) around the connector — SILICOT universal silicone grease with fluoroplast (ВМПАВТО brand, ~30g tube) was the specific product recommended 111213.

Alternative/parallel cause: blown parking-light fuse and bumper wire chafing. A similar-looking symptom (gauge/light electrical glitches) can instead trace to a blown fuse for the габариты (parking-light) circuit, or to wiring damage/chafing near the front bumper (corrosion or insulation breakdown at that point is a recurring failure spot on this car) 1415.

Specific case: comfort-module and immobilizer-block flooding (push-button/keyless-start cars). On cars with push-button start, a flickering "key/lock" icon on the dash means the immobilizer can't read the key — a possible sign of the same underlying moisture problem 16 1718. Water can reach the comfort control module (блок комфорта) and the immobilizer block through two distinct paths: (1) a poor seal around the right fender below the windshield; (2) a loose hood-release cable grommet (прокладка тросика открытия капота). One owner found the comfort-block flooded — it sits by the driver's left foot, just behind the cabin filter 19. Diagnosis: check for water under the driver's left foot area or under the passenger-side carpet 2021. Repair that resolved the issue: dry the affected blocks thoroughly, then coat exposed circuit-board areas/contacts with epoxy resin to seal them, and pack silicone grease into all connector pins to prevent recurrence 2212232413. As a preventive check, disassembling the plastic trim by the driver's left foot and inspecting/ reseating connectors there is also suggested 25. Multiple owners report this class of fault causes seemingly random electrical gremlins that are otherwise hard to diagnose 202627.

BCM water damage causing multi-symptom failures — reprogram when replacing. The Body Control Module (BCM) itself can fail from water intrusion, producing a cluster of seemingly unrelated electrical symptoms at once: the parking brake won't release, lights won't activate, and the instrument panel flickers or dies 2829. Critical when replacing the BCM: parameters must be cloned from the old module to the new one, or the vehicle won't function correctly — a straight swap without cloning leaves the car broken 3031. Official dealers often decline this reprogramming work; independent specialists in the Moscow region (e.g. Odintsovo) have been reported to do it 3233.

Car won't start, all dashboard lights flashing — BSM/GLONASS water ingress. Symptom: the car won't start, all dashboard lights flash continuously, and the key gets no response. Cause: water ingress to electrical modules. Check, in order: (1) the BSM (body control module), located under the left A-pillar/left footwell area; (2) the GLONASS module under the driver's seat — its connector can end up fully submerged. Fix: remove the affected module, dry it thoroughly, clean the connections with isopropyl alcohol, and check for corrosion/oxidation. Also inspect the roof drain tube (under the dash panel) for a disconnect or blockage that lets water pool, and dry any wet carpet areas. One owner resolved the fault simply by disconnecting the GLONASS connector 343536373839 404142434445.

Radio/climate control unit failure traced to water under the carpets. If the integrated radio/climate-control dashboard unit stops working, first check for water under the carpets, especially in the driver/passenger footwell, and inspect the connectors under the seats and the BSM (comfort block) at the lower-left pillar for oxidation/corrosion — water reaching the unit causes connector oxidation. A repair shop can open and inspect the unit's internals; if it's beyond repair, an aftermarket Tesla-style touchscreen unit (no physical buttons) is a reported replacement option — see the head-unit card for more on that swap 46474849.

A minimal, generic confirmation of the pattern. One brief, low-detail report reinforces the general "oxidized contacts → intermittent electrical malfunction" pattern documented throughout this card: an unspecified intermittent electrical issue turned out, on inspection, to be caused by oxidized contacts somewhere in the system; cleaning them resolved it and the system returned to normal 50. No specific location or symptom was given in this report, so treat it as corroborating evidence for the broader pattern rather than a new diagnostic lead — when troubleshooting an otherwise-unexplained intermittent fault on this car, contact oxidation (see the specific locations documented elsewhere in this card and the BSM/BCM card) is worth checking early.

Complete dashboard illumination with no start, traced to a corroded connector block under the driver seat. One owner's case: all dashboard lights illuminate as soon as the battery is connected, regardless of key position, but the engine will not start. Root cause, found only after two weeks of undiagnosed trouble and a professional electrical inspection: wires inside the connector block under the driver seat had corroded, causing a short circuit. During the repair, two additional high-risk corrosion points were discovered in the same harness — reinforcing that this connector block is a recurring weak point worth inspecting proactively, not just after a fault appears 5152.

Severe intermittent power loss traced to water in the electrical distribution box plus a defective throttle body. A related but more severe case: intermittent, severe power loss (check-engine light plus the car becoming unresponsive unless shut off and left for ~10 minutes). Diagnosis found water inside the electrical distribution box causing contact oxidation, compounded by a separately defective throttle body (дроссель). Repair: clean the oxidized contacts and replace the throttle body. The fix held for 4+ years afterward with no recurrence; the repair was initially covered under dealer warranty 535455 5657.

Tail lights staying on after shutdown — comfort-block water damage, same fix pattern as elsewhere in this card. Symptom: rear lights stay on when the car is parked and alarmed. Cause: water damage in the comfort block's connectors, located to the left of the driver's footwell inside the trim. Fix, following the same pattern documented throughout this card: (1) disconnect the battery for 30+ minutes to force an ECU reset; (2) inspect the connector under the driver seat for water/corrosion; (3) if wet, dry the components and apply a thin solder coating to the contact pins for protection; (4) for a permanent fix, find and seal the actual water-entry point — common culprits are the windshield seal, hood seal, sunroof drain, or heater core. The underlying circuit issue can present as either a short or something immobilizer-related, but if the car still starts normally, a connector fault (rather than a deeper electrical failure) is the more likely explanation 585960616263646566 676869707172.

Dashboard cutting out mid-drive plus automatic-transmission lock — same comfort-block (BSM/VSM) water-damage root cause. A more severe variant, same underlying module: the dashboard (gauges and climate) cuts out completely while driving — the radio keeps working — the automatic transmission locks up when stopped, and the fault sometimes clears itself after about a minute. Cause: water intrusion into the comfort block (BSM/VSM module, to the left of the driver's footwell), corroding the connector pins. Fix: (1) disconnect the battery for 10 minutes to reset; (2) remove and inspect the comfort-block connector for corrosion/water; (3) lubricate all pins, optionally with a thin solder coating; (4) locate and seal the actual leak source. If the fault persists after connector service, a factory diagnostic tool is needed to clear the stored fault codes 727374757677.

Intermittent (not total) starting/power problems from the same GLONASS/BSM water path — plus an alternative diagnosis. A milder, intermittent variant of the BSM/GLONASS water-ingress pattern documented above: instead of a total no-start, the symptoms are intermittent starting/power problems and odd dashboard behavior, again pointing to water accumulation under the driver's seat affecting the GLONASS module and the body control module (BSM) connections there 7879. Drying the connections out and removing modules that aren't strictly needed was suggested as a way to resolve it 80. No standing water was found in this particular case, but the area under the seat remained suspect 81. Alternative diagnosis, same symptom picture: a failing ignition-switch contact group can produce very similar intermittent starting/power symptoms without any water involved, so if drying/cleaning the seat-area connectors doesn't fix it, check the ignition switch's contact group next rather than assuming water is always the cause 8283.

docs.title: Power-window auto-mode reset procedure
docs.text:
Tags: #window · #battery

Symptom: after disconnecting the battery terminal, the power windows' one-touch auto up/down mode stops working — windows only move while the button is held, with no single-press full travel.

Reset procedure (standard on most car platforms, applies to the X80): (1) fully open the window; (2) press and hold the window switch — listen/ feel for a characteristic click, which indicates the relearn has registered; (3) repeat for each window individually, and also for the sunroof; (4) do this with the ignition/key in the on position. Some owners report needing several attempts, or trying slightly different button-press patterns (quick double-press, then hold to the end position) before the relearn takes — one owner found success by relearning the rear windows before the front ones, using two quick taps down followed by holding the button through full travel; another simply pressed every button repeatedly until it worked; a third noted the sunroof and all window switches need the same "hold until you feel/hear the click" treatment 12345678910.

Video tutorial for the relearn procedure: a Rutube video walkthrough of the same auto-mode relearn procedure (needed after any battery disconnect or electrical service) is available and shows the process step-by-step for restoring one-touch window operation 111213.

Additional independent video reference: another walkthrough of the same reset/relearn procedure was separately shared on Rutube: https://rutube.ru/video/336d8fb9d761fbfee33324a736a1a654/ 14.

Confirming report — also triggered by alarm/StarLine installation: a separate report confirms the same symptom and fix after a StarLine alarm installation (not just a bare battery disconnect): close the car door, press and hold the window-up button on the key fob until the window closes, then immediately press it again to reprogram; repeat for other functions. This also restores the automatic window-drop behavior on alarm closure 151617.

Simplified timing — hold 5 seconds at each end of travel: a separate report confirms the relearn works with simple fixed timing: for each window individually, raise it fully and hold the switch for 5 seconds, then lower it fully and hold for 5 seconds. Repeat the up/down sequence a second time if the first attempt doesn't take. If the problem persists after two attempts, check the window fuse 1819202122.

docs.text:
Tags: #aliexpress

Replacement window control modules are available on AliExpress as aftermarket parts, but quality is inconsistent 1. One owner's purchased module only operated the left-front window and mirrors after installation (i.e. it was defective) 2. The fault could be in the electrical connector rather than the module itself, so proper diagnosis (checking the connector first) is recommended before assuming the replacement part is bad 3.

docs.title: Window lock buttons — low-speed malfunction
docs.text:
Tags: #door · #window

The door/window lock buttons auto-activate at low driving speeds as a factory safety feature. If the buttons stick or fail to respond correctly: (1) disconnect the battery and let the system reinitialize — some cases self-recover with this simple reset; (2) check the door connectors for water infiltration or corrosion, since moisture ingress is a known issue on this platform; (3) inspect the contact surfaces inside the button assembly itself for wear/corrosion; (4) if the above doesn't resolve it, disassembly is needed for detailed diagnosis — this may require replacing the internal contacts or cleaning oxidized surfaces 12345.

docs.title: Windshield washer motor replacement
docs.text:
Tags: #part-number · #pre-facelift · #restyle

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

The OEM windshield washer motor is a known failure point on the X80. Replacement options differ by generation:

  • Post-facelift: a Nissan/Infiniti dual-outlet washer motor (Ozon listing 2090641451) has been confirmed to install as a direct replacement and work correctly.
  • Pre-facelift: a FAW X80 Startvolt-brand motor, part 5ca067482sv (Ozon listing 2303811007), fits pre-facelift models.

Confirm your generation before ordering — the two motors are not interchangeable across the facelift split 123 45.

Non-responsive motor despite being mechanically sound — fuse and contact-oxidation checklist. If the washer motor itself is confirmed mechanically fine (spins freely, not seized) but doesn't respond to the washer switch — i.e. no power reaching it (+) — check in this order: (1) the relevant fuse first; (2) if the fuse is good, contact oxidation in the wiring/connector near the steering-wheel area is the next suspect 678.

Weak or no spray despite a full reservoir — frost, orientation, and blockage. A separate failure mode: the reservoir is full but spray is weak or absent. Three causes to check, roughly in order of likelihood in cold weather: (1) frozen/frosted nozzle tips — most common in winter, carefully clear with a needle, avoiding excessive force that could damage the nozzle 91011; (2) incorrect nozzle orientation — nozzles should point upward; (3) debris blocking the nozzle orifices. Additional winter-specific remedies: use washer fluid rated with antifreeze rather than plain water/weak mix, run maximum defrost/windshield heat to help warm the nozzles from residual heat, and if the system is fully frozen, park in a warm location (e.g. a shopping mall garage) to thaw it out before attempting to clear nozzles by force 12131114.

Pump not spraying at all — check the fuse and relay before assuming motor failure. Before concluding the motor itself has failed (as documented above), rule out the simpler electrical cause: if the washer pump doesn't run at all, check (1) the fuse in the cabin fuse block, located below the driver's left knee, and (2) the relay next to it in the same block — both need to be checked, since either one failing alone produces the identical no-spray symptom 15161718 1920212223.

docs.title: Windshield wiper auto/rain-sensing mode not functioning
docs.text:
Tags: #wiper · #rain-sensor

Symptom. On some X80 units, the automatic/rain-sensing windshield-wiper mode doesn't work correctly: manual wiper mode works fine, but the auto/rain-sense mode fails to trigger the wipers appropriately.12

Possible causes and diagnostic approach. Three candidate causes were raised: (1) a relay failure — though relays are considered unlikely to be the direct cause given the system architecture; (2) a BCM (Body Control Module) malfunction — the BCM controls all wiper modes centrally, not via a dedicated per-mode relay, so a BCM fault can plausibly take out just the auto mode while leaving manual mode intact; (3) a wiper stalk/column switch failure. Recommended diagnostic approach: visually inspect the BCM connectors for moisture/water damage first (a known failure vector for other BCM-controlled features on this car), then check voltage/signal at the BCM's inputs and outputs to the wiper motor to isolate whether the fault is upstream (BCM/wiring) or downstream (motor/stalk).12

docs.title: Wiper relay spontaneous activation
docs.text:
Tags: #wiper · #relay · #corrosion · #water-ingress · #bsm

Symptom: the wipers activate on their own even when the control stalk is in the OFF position, and the relay(s) stay engaged after the stalk is turned off 12. A temporary fix some owners use: physically strike the fuse block with a hand — this can jolt the stuck relay(s) back to a normal (open) state 34.

Root causes, most to least likely. (1) Water intrusion into the cabin fuse block, leaving visible green/blue oxidation on the contacts — check by pulling the connector blocks off and inspecting for green residue 567. (2) A short circuit elsewhere in the vehicle's electrical circuits — one owner found relays clicking even after removing the relay, suggesting current bypassing the relay entirely through a short 891011. (3) General relay/connector contamination unrelated to a leak.

Fuse/relay locations (pre-facelift/"doreste"). In the cabin, on the left side: the wiper relays and fuses are among the lower fuses/relays in that block, with front/rear wiper relays specifically noted as the two lower ones 12131415. Fuse rating: 5 or 10A, located under the steering wheel 1213.

BSM as a secondary suspect. Even once the fuse block is identified as the primary problem area, the BSM (body control module) block is also worth opening and inspecting, since it shares exposure to the same moisture ingress pathway 1617.

Permanent fix. Open the fuse block(s), inspect for green/blue corrosion on the contacts, clean them with electronic contact cleaner, and replace any relay whose contacts are too corroded to clean. The diagnosis worsens the longer the water sits — earlier intervention gives a better chance of a successful repair rather than needing a full block replacement 1817. One owner reported checking under the carpet regularly for water intrusion (from the driver's footwell area) as a possible entry point to also address, since he suspected water tracking in from there even without visible carpet wetness at the time of inspection 1920.

docs.title: AKPP filter and pan gasket — listings, prices
docs.text:
Tags: #automatic-transmission · #part-number · #price · #conflict

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Community members disagree on this topic — both positions are reported.

Part numbers and prices for the automatic transmission (AKPP) pan gasket and filter, as listed in the group. For the verified-fit discussion see AKPP seal and pan-gasket leaks; for the service itself see AKPP fluid change.

Pan gasket 35168-TFA050. A kitparts.ru listing offers the AKPP oil pan gasket 35168-TFA050 for the X80 from ~6,066 RUB (RU market, October 2024). A member who had bought from the same shop says their parts were fine, unlike marketplace purchases12.

Filter MAHLE/KNECHT HX169KIT. Given as the AKPP filter element; the gasket number was asked about but not stated. Listed on Wildberries in October 2025 without a vehicle note, and Emex sold it wholesale from ~4,251 RUB (RU market, February 2026). Conflicting description: one member says the filter is a metal mesh that can be washed and refitted, which contradicts the idea of a replaceable element34567.

docs.title: AKPP fluid change — drain plug and filter
docs.text:
Tags: #automatic-transmission · #engine-oil · #drain-plug

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Drain plug location. The AKPP (automatic transmission) has a dedicated drain plug on the sump/pan, accessible from underneath with a hex socket — a full fluid change does not strictly require removing the whole pan just to drain the fluid, though the filter (a coarse steel mesh, not a paper cartridge) does live inside the pan123.

Partial-drain interval and volumes. Standard community practice is a partial drain ("полупролив") roughly every 30,000 km, with the first one done as soon as possible after buying a used car. One owner drained/refilled 4L at 80,000 km (fluid, gasket, and filter all found in good condition at that service) and planned the next partial drain at 30-40k km later45. Community consensus in this thread settled around 3.7-3.8L as the amount that "sticks" (settles as consistent) for a partial drain without pan removal67.

Filter is a reusable steel mesh, not a cartridge. The AKPP oil filter is a coarse steel mesh strainer, not a disposable paper element. Recommended service: remove it, blow it out with compressed air, and clean with kerosene/gasoline solvent, then reinstall — no need to replace it outright, and shops that charge extra for "complex filter service" are pushing an unnecessary markup89. Filter part number and full ordering link: 35330-TFA060 (kitzapchasti.ru); draining is not fussy about catching old fluid separately — a partial drain settles at almost exactly 4L, and if the pan is also dropped, add roughly +1L (total ~5L)1011. When removing the pan filter/cover, also clean and wipe the pan cover and check the drain magnets for metal shavings — on a well-maintained AKPP the pan cover should come out clean, without sludge buildup12.

Bleeding air after a fill. After pumping fluid in, work the gear selector through the positions (this is how trapped air is bled from the system) — a competent mechanic should already know to do this1314. Air/pressure venting itself happens through the AKPP breather ("сапун"), which clips onto the battery bracket151617.

Level-check procedure and temperature requirement. To set/verify the level on a partial drain (no pan removal): warm the transmission to 35-47°C (ideally the higher end, ~47°C) before the fluid has fully expanded, then — with the engine running — cycle the selector through D (3 sec), R (3 sec), N (3 sec) a few times, then open the drain and wait until the stream slows to a trickle before closing it. Without pan removal, this yields about 3-3.2L718.

Fill-point location. Multiple owners struggled to find the correct fluid fill access point on this transmission (one reported spending ~20 minutes searching); a reference video/article for the "AKPP X80 part 2" procedure (2L, 2017 model) circulated in the group to help locate it, alongside photos pointing to the exact fill opening192021.

Later interval reports — 40,000-45,000 km, and a "no factory interval, just checks" claim. Later, separate threads add conflicting interval information on top of the ~30,000 km partial-drain practice already documented on this card: one report gives 40,000-45,000 km as the partial-change interval, explicitly stating a full fluid change is not recommended (no benefit, and risk of transmission damage from an improper full-flush procedure) — the reusable steel-mesh filter should simply be cleaned, dried, and reinstalled rather than replaced, consistent with the filter-service guidance already on this card2223. A separate later report frames it differently: the factory maintenance schedule does not include an AKPP oil-change interval at all, only a fluid level check every 30,000 km — but for used cars, especially at 80,000 km+, a full fluid change with filter service is strongly recommended regardless. Service-center cost for this full change (including pan-gasket replacement): 5,000-6,000 RUB (RU market, July 2024). Fluid capacity is roughly 4+ liters; a partial fill without dropping the pan will not achieve a complete change242526272829. Conflict: interval guidance ranges from ~30,000 km (community practice already on this card) to 40,000-45,000 km (later report) to "no factory interval, just periodic checks" (another later report) — not resolved within this data batch, and may reflect the factory-vs-community-practice distinction the "no interval" report explicitly raises.

Factory vs. realistic interval, and expected transmission lifespan. A further, separate report gives yet another framing: the factory (Aisin) recommendation is a fluid change every 20,000 km, while community specialists consider 30,000 km more realistic in practice. Expected AKPP resource life before a major repair is cited as 130,000-190,000 km; delaying fluid changes and skipping an auxiliary cooler (see the AKPP-longevity card) are said to compound and significantly shorten this lifespan, while early cooler installation can extend it30.

AKPP pan gasket — part number, from the second Telegram group. A separate community (FAW BESTURN X80 group) gives the AKPP pan-gasket part number: 100 139 0002. The same message reconfirms the filter-cleaning practice already documented on this card: during a fluid change, the old filter is not replaced — it's washed/cleaned and reinstalled31.

AKPP oil filter pricing spread — scam warning, from the second Telegram group. A separate report from the second group: an owner (non-facelift, 2017, ~93,000 km) shopping for the AKPP oil filter (part 35330-TFA060, already documented on this card) found prices ranging from ~2,000 RUB to ~8,000 RUB for apparently the same item (comparing kitzap.ru against a Wildberries listing). Community reply reinforces the guidance already on this card: the filter is metal and can simply be cleaned/rinsed well rather than replaced — some sellers are marking up an otherwise identical product, so cross-check sites before paying the higher price32333435.

Filter replacement at high mileage — restated as a full-assembly swap. A separate report describes the filter as a mesh screen rather than a cartridge element, and frames the job as an outright replacement (mesh screen plus gasket seal) rather than clean-and-reinstall: at the 190,000 km service interval, this replacement can be done at the same time as an oil change, and the filter element comes out completely as a single removable assembly, with no complex disassembly required — consistent with the ease-of-access already noted on this card, though this source treats replacement (not cleaning) as the default approach363738.

Where the community disagrees

  • AKPP fluid-change interval guidance conflicts across threads: ~30,000 km partial drain (earlier community practice), 40,000-45,000 km partial-change interval with full change discouraged (later report), factory Aisin recommendation of 20,000 km vs. community-realistic 30,000 km (another report), and "no factory interval at all, only 30,000 km level checks, but full change recommended for used cars at 80,000 km+" (yet another report). Not resolved within this data batch.

docs.title: AKPP fluid specification — conflicting claims
docs.text:
Tags: #automatic-transmission · #atf · #conflict

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Community members disagree on this topic — both positions are reported.

This card collects several different, sometimes conflicting claims about the correct ATF spec for the X80's automatic transmission, reported by different owners at different times. Treat this as raw community data rather than a single confirmed answer — cross-check against the manual/dealer before committing to a fluid.

"ATF 3309/DAM 3309" claim. One owner reports having changed the AT fluid and used Reinwell ATF 3309/LT, having been advised against Mobil-branded ATF because its price doesn't justify the amount of counterfeiting in that segment; filled to about 8L total including the auxiliary cooler circuit1. This exchange included photo evidence of the Reinwell bottle/packaging, with other members asking "where exactly [does it go]?" and "like this?" while sharing photos back and forth confirming the product23456789. An unrelated side-question in the same thread — about sourcing a rear wheel-bearing part — was answered with part number FC012615X, available from WB, Avito, Ozon and similar marketplaces, noted as mostly no-name equivalents of similar quality regardless of listed price101112. When directly asked "what oil and how many liters," another owner in the same thread answered "ATF 3309 [sic — written "3308" in the reply text], 8L for a full change, ~4L for a partial change"1314.

"JWS, approval/допуск 3309" claim (Aisin G09). A separate owner states the transmission (Aisin G09) spec is: type JWS (synthetic), with approval/допуск 3309 — meaning any synthetic ATF fluid carrying the 3309 approval code should qualify, not a specific brand1516.

"JWS-3309, Aisin 09G/09K/09M" claim with capacity figures. Elsewhere in the group, the automatic transmission (Aisin 09G) is described as requiring ATF meeting the JWS-3309 specification, with capacity 6.4L for a complete fill, approximately 8L for a full replacement, and 4L for a partial replacement — sourced from a manual excerpt/photo17. A separate reply agrees "if it's the AT, yes, with допуск 3309" and adds that Idemitsu is fine for both the AT and the engine1819.

"TF60/61SN, lifetime fluid per manual — but owners dispute this" claim. Another thread identifies the transmission model as 09G/09K/09M, spec TF60/61SN, and notes the official FAW manual states the fluid is filled for the vehicle's service life and only the level should be checked — but the owner community instead cites Volkswagen-group service documentation recommending periodic changes around 60,000-80,000 km, with kakoemaslo.ru cited as a reference for looking up the ATF spec2021. This claim was directly disputed by another long-time member, who argues such third-party "regulations" articles are unsubstantiated ("I could write dozens of these myself"), that official dealers under warranty follow only the manufacturer's stated schedule, and that trusting random published schedules over the manual is not something they're willing to do22. The original poster maintains their position is based on personal experience plus specialist advice they trust specifically for Aisin transmissions, and points back to VAG-manual screenshots with change-interval tables2324.

"75/90, допуск GL5" claim (context: differential/axle use, labeled by the source as AKPP-related). One thread states "75/90 допуск GL5. Допускается работа в мостах" — i.e. a 75W-90 gear oil meeting GL5 is acceptable, explicitly noting it's also approved for use in the axles/differentials, which suggests this reply may be answering a differential-oil question rather than (or in addition to) the torque-converter ATF question; the same owner filled this oil about 8,000 km prior with no issues, noting GL5 has higher requirements than GL4, suited to hypoid gears2526. This claim should not be read as contradicting the ATF specs above without more context — it may describe a different fluid circuit (differential/axle) rather than the torque-converter fluid. Separately, the AT pan gasket part number is 35168-TFA050, around 6,066 RUB (RU market, Oct 2024) from a supplier called Kitparts27.

"3309 or Toyota Type IV" claim. A separate, later report simplifies the requirement to: the AKPP requires either 3309 or Toyota Type IV transmission fluid28.

Official approvals document — full cross-brand list. A photographed official specifications page states the transmission is a 4-speed automatic with JWS 3309/3314 approval per official spec, and lists a broad set of cross-manufacturer equivalences shown on the same page: MAN 339 Type V1/Z11/Z2, MB-Freigabe 236.9, Voith 55.6335, ZF TE-ML 04D/14B/20B/25B, plus recommended-equivalent approvals including Aisin Warner JWS 3309/3314, Allison TES 295/389, BMW LA-2634, Chrysler ATF+3/+4, Ford M2C195-A/922-A1, GM 9986195, Honda Z1, Hyundai/Kia/Mitsubishi SP-II/III, MB 235.71/236.8/236.10/236.11/236.91, Nissan Matic-D/J/K, Toyota T-IV/JWS 3309, Voith H55.6336, Volvo 97341/5-Speed, VW 50 160/TL 52 162/G 052 990/G 055 025, and ZF TE-ML 02F/11B/14C. Note this document describes the fluid as a 4-speed-class approval, which sits alongside the "6-speed" transmission descriptions used elsewhere for the X80 — treat the transmission speed-count as unresolved across this card and the transmission-identity notes in the engine-identity card29.

Universal vs. mono-spec ATF — a conflict, and a fix for post-change problems. When transmission issues appeared immediately after a fluid change, one specialist's advice was to move away from universal (multi-spec) ATF and toward a single-type ("mono") fluid, spec 4 or 3309, then perform two fluid changes about 1,000 km apart to fully purge the old fluid and confirm compatibility. The reasoning given: universal oils satisfy multiple approval labels at once but may not be genuinely ideal for any one of them, unlike a dedicated single-spec fluid30313233. Conflict: this directly disagrees with the "universal fluid is fine, any 3309-approved ATF qualifies" framing used elsewhere in this card — presented here as a distinct, dissenting recommendation, not a resolved consensus.

Dextron III — accepted per factory spec, with caveats. In a separate power-steering-fluid discussion, one owner explicitly chose the safer, familiar Dextron III over an unfamiliar alternative for their power-steering system. For the transmission itself, Dextron III is described as acceptable per factory spec, though a specialist recommended instead ordering fluid meeting spec 3309 specifically. The owner went ahead and performed a full transmission fluid replacement using Dextron III. Toyota Type IV was mentioned as another possible alternative but was not recommended without further confirmation34353637.

Manual's fluid-change interval claim disputed. One owner posted that a diagnostic error appeared for the transmission (alongside ESP/ABS errors) and asserted the AT fluid should be changed every 60,000-70,000 km. Another member immediately challenged this, asking directly where that figure is documented; the original poster admitted they thought they'd read it in the manual, but the challenger states flatly that no such 60-70K interval appears in the manual — the only related text is that the fluid level should be checked every 30,000 km, with no separate change interval specified at all38394041. This is a distinct, procedural claim from the fluid-type conflicts collected above, but touches the same "what does the manual actually say about maintaining this fluid" question.

Partial-drain service practice — real-world interval and fluid used. One owner shares a practical maintenance pattern: the AT can be serviced in stages via partial drains (no pan removal), each draining roughly 2.1-2.2 liters. In this owner's own practice, partial drains were done at 80,000 km and 110,000 km on the odometer — i.e. about 30,000 km apart — with a full pan-removal/filter-clean service planned for the 3rd service interval. The fluid used was Totachi ATF (Multi-Vehicle, fully synthetic), added via syringe through the fill access point (photographed). A noticeable improvement in transmission responsiveness was reported after the partial change — a second owner in the same thread reports the same subjective effect ("felt the car got peppier") after their own partial drain4243444546.

Level-check procedure — no dipstick on the X80F. The Besturn X80F automatic-transmission variant has no transmission fluid dipstick. To check the level: open the drain plug/bolt at the bottom of the transmission pan. If fluid trickles out, the level is correct. If nothing comes out, add fluid via syringe until it just starts to seep from the opening — the transmission pan should be kept full to that point4748.

Power loss reported after a partial fluid/filter change. One owner performed a partial AT fluid-and-filter change and afterward experienced loss of power and sluggish acceleration. The fluid used was Rowe 9000 multi-spec ATF, which may not meet all of the FAW AKPP's requirements — consistent with the universal-vs-mono-spec concern raised above. Suggested troubleshooting: verify fluid level, check the fuel-system filter for blockages, and reconsider fluid-type compatibility with the transmission (identified elsewhere in this KB as TF-70SC)49505152535455565758.

AKPP oil change with Mannol (early report, low detail). One owner performed an AKPP transmission fluid change using Mannol-brand ATF; a change interval was recommended by the owner despite the factory manual omitting a fixed schedule — no specific frequency was settled on in this exchange5960.

ATF 3309 restated as non-negotiable — universal ATF explicitly rejected. A separate, later exchange restates the requirement in the strongest terms yet: the AKPP requires ATF 3309 specifically; so-called "universal" ATF oils that claim broad compatibility are not suitable for this gearbox due to differing viscosity profiles. The fluid is described as mineral-based with synthetic additives, not fully synthetic61626364656667. Conflict: some owners in this same exchange experimented with other fluids (Titan 4400, ZIC, Dextron) with mixed results; the community consensus nonetheless leans toward strict adherence to 3309.

Jerky/harsh shifts after a partial fluid exchange — traced to wrong spec or adaptation lag. After a partial AT fluid exchange, some owners reported jerky/harsh shifts and reduced acceleration. Root cause identified in this thread: using a universal ATF instead of the exact ATF 3309 spec, or simply an insufficient adaptation period after the fluid swap. Fix: switch to the exact ATF 3309 spec and allow the transmission to relearn its shift patterns through normal driving — different fluid viscosity is said to disrupt the calibrated shift timing686963707172. Conflict: one owner resolved the issue by switching to ATF 3309, while another noted the restyled (2019+) gearbox differs internally from the older version, which may affect how it responds to fluid changes.

AKPP fill capacity and methods — restated with method-specific figures. Factory-stated capacity is 6 liters. In practice the figure depends on method: a partial drain without pan removal removes/replaces roughly 3 liters out, 3 liters in; a full drain and refill takes 8-12 liters total; after any fill, expect roughly 1 liter to subsequently drain out of the lines during operation. Verify the final level with the dipstick after driving73747576.

AT filter part number (2017 model) and simplified fluid spec. For the 2017-model automatic transmission, the filter part number is 35330-TFA060. Recommended fluid: JWS 3309 or Toyota Type IV — consistent with the "3309 or Toyota Type IV" claim already on this card7778798081.

Fluid change volume — 6L over 2 cycles, restated. A separate report states the standard AT fluid change is 6 liters total across 2 cycles. Without pan removal, a partial drain yields 2.5-3 L; with pan and filter removal, 3-3.5 L. Practical consensus in this exchange: 4 liters is a safe working amount, with more cycles possible if desired — broadly consistent with the partial/full-drain figures already on this card828384.

Manual "lifetime fluid" claim vs. preventive-maintenance camp — restated with concrete intervals. Factory documentation again states the fluid is rated for the vehicle's full service life, and official dealers typically skip an AT fluid change during standard maintenance. Practical owner experience clusters into two camps: (1) change at 40,000-60,000 km first, then every 60,000-70,000 km as preventive maintenance; (2) one owner with 220,000 km has never changed the fluid, with no issues reported. Some owners use a "recycled oil" method — siphoning old fluid through a filter and returning it — to cut cost while still refreshing the fluid periodically85868788899091929394959697. Conflict: this restates and reinforces the existing lifetime-vs-periodic disagreement already documented on this card (, ).

Polymerium ATF — retracted after poor oil-analysis results. Polymerium transmission oil, previously recommended elsewhere in the community, is now flagged as a fluid to avoid: independent used-oil analysis on the Oilclub forum found elevated wear metals and a short effective service life. Recommended alternatives with better track records: BARDAHL (verified by owner experience) and NGN. General guidance: prioritize verified oil-analysis results over brand reputation or price. TOTACHI ATF Multi-Vehicle (synthetic) and TOTACHI ATF Type T-IV are cited as acceptable, reasonably priced alternatives9899100101102103104.

TOTACHI ATF — restated with packaging detail. Both TOTACHI ATF Multi-Vehicle (synthetic) and TOTACHI ATF Type T-IV are again confirmed as suitable, sold in 4 L containers; multiple owners recommend buying via Wildberries105106107.

AT filter kit and gasket-quality note (MAHLE HX169KIT). The automatic transmission uses the MAHLE HX169KIT filter kit, which includes the pan gasket. Some owners report needing a custom/aftermarket gasket because OEM gasket quality has reportedly declined in recent production years. Separately, the manual transmission has no breather (сапун) in the factory design108109110111.

Partial vs. full-change volume — restated, with a disputed 8L outlier. Total AT capacity is again cited as approximately 6 liters. Partial change without pan drop: 2.2-2.5 L. Full change with pan drop and filter change: typically 3-3.5 L, though one owner reported 8 L going in after a pan drop — treated as an outlier/disputed figure rather than representative. Most owners favor 3-4 L for a proper partial change with pan removal, or 2-2.5 L without. As of October 2025 (RU market), one owner paid 1,800 RUB per 4 L of ATF112113114115116117118119120121122.

Pan filter with gasket — MAHLE HX169KIT. Automatic-transmission pan filter with gasket: MAHLE/KNECHT HX169KIT, which also fits as a MINI Cooper equivalent. Available on autorus.ru and Wildberries. Reported price ~2,000+ RUB (RU market, Oct 2025), with a note that the same part was purchased a month earlier for 2,500 RUB — treat pricing as volatile123124125126127128.

Pan gasket installation without sealant, on repeat services. For AKPP pan gasket replacement, sealant is not required on the second and subsequent times the pan is serviced — reuse the original metal spacer bushings from the previous gasket, or transfer new 0.2mm spacers from the old gasket to the new one. This method prevents leaks without additional sealant129.

AT fluid type and change interval — restated. Automatic transmission fluid type 3309 is used in the FAW X80. At 93,000 km on a 2020 model, a partial drain plus filter cleaning was recommended; at 200,000 km, one owner performed a partial drain and cleaning without major issues. Original factory fluid can last through high mileage if the transmission is otherwise performing well; check manufacturer specs for full change-interval details130131132133134135.

Specific retail product — CHEMPIOIL Multi ATF JWS 3309. A specific branded product matching the JWS 3309 spec: CHEMPIOIL Multi ATF JWS 3309, sourced from Wildberries and other retailers. For checking fluid color/condition when cap access is limited, a 5 ml medical syringe works to draw a small sample136137138139140.

"KIXX DXIII carries our JWS-3309 approval" — restated, with a "Multi ≠ universal" caution. An owner confirms KIXX DXIII shows the JWS-3309 approval on the bottle and was told by a shop this fits the 4-speed AT. Community reply: nominally, any fluid showing the JWS 3309 approval is suitable — multiple shops and the manual itself reportedly cite only "3309" with no brand restriction, and Mannol Multi ATF is the most commonly-used fluid among owners in this group. A caution is raised, though: "Multi" fluids are sometimes described online as intended for 6-8 speed gearboxes rather than being universal, and it isn't clear whether "Multi" labeling is itself sufficient proof of 3309 suitability, prompting one owner's cynical "paper accepts anything" remark. One long-time contributor's personal view: he only trusts Mobil for a strict 3309 match (an older-generation approval; the newer standard being Type IV), comparing "universal Multi ATF" fluids to all-season tires or a do-it-all kitchen appliance — i.e. broadly capable but not necessarily ideal141142143144145146147148149.

Mobil 3309 pricing and counterfeit risk — restated with an early, lower price point. Mobil 3309 (1L) listed on Ozon at around 1,000+ RUB, described by one owner as "a lottery" given inconsistent seller quality. Pushback from another member: Mobil has the highest counterfeit rate of any 3309-approved brand on the market, so there is little reason to insist on it specifically — many other oils carry the same 3309 approval, and more frequent changes matter more than brand loyalty150151.

Transmission filter cross-fit — Mini Cooper part, Sumomoto vs. Zekkert. The AKPP filter cross-fits with a Mini Cooper transmission filter, listed as Sumomoto SM-24347566358 (OEM equivalent 24347566358), sold on Ozon and confirmed compatible with the X80/X80F. Reported prices (RU market, Apr 2026) ranged from ~900 RUB (Sumomoto, single) up to 2,400-2,500 RUB for other listings, with one owner having paid as much as 3,500 RUB when the exchange rate was less favorable; a 4-piece kit was quoted at 2,500 RUB. Zekkert-brand filters were explicitly rejected by one buyer as poor quality; Sumomoto was the preferred brand in this exchange. The filter is also available via AliExpress152153154155156157158159160161162163164.

"Mobil ATF 3309, no dipstick, partial drain at 60,000 km" — from the second Telegram group. A separate community (FAW BESTURN X80 group) gives another data point consistent with several claims already on this card: the AKPP has no dipstick for checking fluid level (an electronic level-sensing system instead — consistent with the "no dipstick on the X80F" claim already documented above), the fluid used is Mobil ATF 3309 synthetic per the vehicle's paperwork ("по паспорту"), and a partial drain ("полупролив") is performed at 60,000 km165.

AKPP capacity — 8 liters, Mobil 3309 synthetic, 60,000 km change interval — from the second Telegram group. A separate, related report from the same second group states the AKPP holds 8 liters total, using Mobil 3309 synthetic fluid, with a full-change interval of 60,000 km — broadly consistent with the "8-12 liters total for a full drain/refill" and "3309" claims already documented on this card, though this report frames 8L as the total capacity rather than a full-change volume specifically166.

Where the community disagrees

  • The claim that AT fluid should be changed every 60,000-70,000 km per the manual was directly disputed by another member, who states the manual only specifies a 30,000 km level-check interval with no separate change interval given. Not resolved — the original poster did not produce a manual citation to support the 60-70K figure.
  • This recommendation (switch from universal/multi-spec ATF to a dedicated mono-spec fluid such as 3309, with a double change to purge old fluid) directly conflicts with the "any 3309-approved universal ATF should qualify" framing used elsewhere in this card. Not resolved within this data batch — may depend on specific transmission wear state or specialist preference.
  • This batch of Telegram messages contains at least four distinct spec labels for the same X80 automatic transmission across different points in time: "ATF 3309/3308", "JWS допуск 3309", "JWS-3309" (with Aisin 09G/09K/09M), and "TF60/61SN". These may partly be different ways of naming the same underlying Aisin approval, or may reflect genuine confusion/drift in the community — not resolved within this data batch. Cross-check against an authoritative Aisin/FAW parts catalog before purchasing fluid.
  • Direct community disagreement: one side argues (citing VAG/Volkswagen-group documentation) that the "lifetime fluid, check level only" claim in the FAW manual is wrong and periodic ATF changes (~60,000-80,000 km) are warranted; the other side argues third-party "regulation" articles are unsubstantiated and the manufacturer's own manual/warranty schedule should be trusted instead. Not resolved within this data batch.
  • The "75/90, допуск GL5" reply explicitly mentions axle/differential use, which may mean it answers a different (differential) fluid question rather than describing the torque-converter ATF — flagged here rather than merged as a contradiction.
  • Despite a strong restatement that ATF 3309 is required and "universal" ATF is unsuitable, some owners in the same exchange report experimenting with other fluids (Titan 4400, ZIC, Dextron) with mixed results — not fully resolved within this data batch.
  • One owner resolved post-partial-change jerky shifting by switching to ATF 3309; another separately noted the restyled (2019+) gearbox differs internally from the older version, which may affect its sensitivity to fluid type/change method — whether this fully explains the jerky-shift cases is unresolved.

docs.title: AKPP longevity — philosophy and auxiliary cooler
docs.text:
Tags: #automatic-transmission · #overheating

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

"If it's not broken, don't fix it" philosophy. One experienced owner's overall take: the AKPP is robust but temperamental, and if it's running without problems, it's best left alone rather than subjected to unnecessary deep maintenance. At around 240,000 km, this owner was specifically advised by experienced mechanics not to touch the transmission despite it being past typical service intervals123. Normal wear-and-tear seal leakage of roughly 50-100g/year is considered acceptable, addressed with partial fluid top-ups as needed rather than a full service45. A full disassembly/rebuild (~200,000 RUB, RU market, Oct 2024) is recommended only if the transmission slips badly or won't shift properly — otherwise, leave a running transmission alone6.

Overheating failure case. One owner experienced repeated overheating episodes over the course of a year (coolant/fluid temperature 102-108°C), and multiple different service stations were unable to accurately, correctly, or promptly diagnose the cause. This eventually led to the transmission failing outright at 164,000 km, requiring a full AKPP replacement7. The overheating symptom pattern: after sitting in traffic or sustained high-load driving, the transmission would show power loss and a whining/roaring noise until temperature normalized8. Regular overheating at these temperatures is understood to accelerate ATF degradation and friction-pack wear, contributing to the eventual failure78.

Auxiliary cooler installation (prevention). To prevent a repeat of the overheating problem, an auxiliary ATF cooler radiator was installed. It sits without requiring front bumper removal9. One owner following the thread asked how to change AKPP fluid given the cooler sits well above the transmission's own level, and whether the plumbing bypasses, parallels, or series-connects with the main radiator's circuit10 — the installer's answer is captured below. Key installation notes from the thread: the OEM heat exchanger (which normally routes ATF heat into the main engine coolant loop) is disconnected/bypassed since it's no longer needed, with an adapter fitting connecting the transmission lines to the new auxiliary radiator instead — the main radiator continues to handle only engine coolant separately, while the auxiliary radiator circulates ATF1112. Adding the auxiliary cooler increases total system fluid capacity by roughly 1.5 liters; a full fluid fill after installation came to about 8L total13. Oil drains separately from both the transmission itself and from the new cooler13. The change procedure otherwise stays the same as before the cooler was added13.

Community-wide durability concern — restated. Multiple owners more broadly report worn transmissions, reinforcing a community-level view that the factory cooling (heat exchanger) is insufficient for the Aisin AKPP under real-world use. The preventive recommendation matches the case above: install an auxiliary AKPP radiator to reduce thermal stress and extend transmission life. Without a cooling upgrade, the perceived risk of premature solenoid/transmission failure is said to increase with vehicle age1415.

Aisin 09G thermal stress — VW cross-reference and cooler recommendation. The X80 uses the Aisin 09G automatic transmission, the same unit used in the VW Golf/Jetta, where it reportedly lasts 200,000-230,000 km without a supplemental cooler, and 300,000-500,000 km with one. On the X80, this is the smallest, most thermally stressed configuration of that transmission, paired with a minimal stock cooler; fluid temperature can reach 180°C in traffic, producing weak shift feel and eventual failure. A supplemental transmission cooler is strongly recommended for hot climates or heavy traffic driving; without one, typical lifespan is estimated at roughly 150,000-200,000 km161718.

Normal fluid-temperature range — restated with real numbers. AKPP fluid temperature runs roughly 80-90°C in spring conditions (around +10°C ambient) and similarly in other mild weather, per scan-tool readings; no significant overheating was observed192021.

Gentler throttle input reduces heat buildup. Avoiding aggressive throttle input reduces transmission heat generation, extending transmission life and helping prevent overheating — particularly relevant for high-daily-mileage city driving (e.g. Moscow-style commuting, 50-250 km/day), where wear is better tracked in motor-hours than distance22.

Shifts better cold, worse hot — possible pressure/tuning issue. The AT is reported to shift better when cold and worse once at operating temperature, suggesting an oil-viscosity or hydraulic-pressure drop-off with heat. It may hold load through 4th gear when cold but struggle to maintain load when warm — pointing to oil type/pressure or transmission-side ECU tuning. Note: the engine ECU is a Bosch unit, but the transmission may run its own, harder-to-read/reprogram ECU232425262728.

AISIN 09G lightest variant — no dedicated radiator, adaptation sensitivity, and reset workaround. Restating and adding detail to the Aisin 09G thermal-stress picture already on this card: the X80's AISIN 09G is the lightest variant of that transmission family and is prone to overheating, consistent with the "smallest, most thermally stressed configuration" already noted. It has no dedicated transmission radiator, only a small heat exchanger (consistent with the "minimal stock cooler" already documented). Typical lifespan 200,000-300,000 km, based on older Volkswagen applications (2006-2012) that also lacked extra cooling — from 2012+, VW-platform applications gained additional radiators. Known issue: transmission adaptation is sensitive to driving style; resetting the adaptation (via key-cycle manipulation or a battery/module reset) can temporarily improve shift feel. Overall verdict: comfortable for careful drivers, problematic under aggressive driving2930313233343536.

Earlier, independent operating-temperature measurement — 85-97°C under normal driving. An earlier, independent report gives concrete scan-tool-verified AKPP temperatures: 85-97°C under normal mixed-mode driving (37°C ambient, 5-hour test), measured with an OBD diagnostic device (a Mucar BT200 running Diagzone software) capable of reading real-time AKPP temperature — the standard dashboard only shows engine coolant temperature, not gearbox temperature, which the owner notes makes assessing the need for an auxiliary cooler difficult without such a tool. The manufacturer's critical threshold is cited as 127°C3738394041424344.

Earlier, independent statement of the Aisin 09G cooling gap. Consistent with, and predating, the Aisin 09G thermal-stress case already documented on this card: an earlier thread states plainly that the Aisin 09G in the X80 has an inadequate factory heat exchanger — many other manufacturers add a supplemental radiator to this transmission from the factory, but FAW omitted it as a cost-cutting measure. Community specialists recommend installing an auxiliary AKPP cooler for reliability and longevity, particularly given that (as also noted above) transmission temperature isn't visible on the stock dashboard383945.

docs.title: Automatic transmission (AKPP) parking procedure
docs.text:
Tags: #automatic-transmission

Correct AKPP parking procedure reported by owners: (1) drive to the parking spot and apply the foot brake; (2) shift to Park (some sources say shift to Neutral first, then Park); (3) apply the electronic parking brake; (4) release the foot brake; (5) the engine shuts down automatically and the parking brake engages automatically. Important: keep your foot on the brake until the parking brake is fully engaged, to prevent the vehicle from rolling/lurching and to avoid load on the transmission's parking pawl 12345678.

Conflict: some owners recommend shifting Neutral → Park during parking to reduce transmission load; others argue this is unnecessary and potentially harmful to the transmission. The majority use the standard Drive → Park sequence per the owner's manual 910.

docs.title: AKPP selector stuck locked — end-stop spring-clip fix
docs.text:
Tags: #automatic-transmission

The AKPP (automatic transmission) gear selector can become mechanically locked even when the brake pedal is pressed/released correctly — a different failure mode from the electronic P081929 shift-correction issue documented elsewhere in this section. Cause: the spring clips inside the selector's end-stop mechanism (концевик — the shift-lock solenoid/switch assembly) bend out of shape over time, preventing the lock from releasing properly.
