Fix: remove the AKPP shifter frame/surround trim, reach in by hand to the left side of the selector, unclip the end-stop mechanism, and manually re-bend the spring clips back into their correct shape. This solution — found on Mazda forums, given the X80's Mazda-derived drivetrain lineage — permanently resolves the selector-lock issue without needing a service-center visit 1 2345.

Shifter does not leave P on the first press of the brake pedal (Oct 2026). On an automatic (АКПП) the selector did not release from park on the first brake press; it began the day after the right rear bulb was replaced, and the car works normally again now 678. Victor 🇷🇺 suspects the transmission reads either the brake-pedal switch or the circuit of the centre (third) stop light, and recommends checking them; homemade LED stop-light bulbs often cause trouble where the car had incandescent bulbs 9.

docs.title: Generator (alternator) belt removal procedure
docs.text:
Tags: #alternator · #price · #part-number · #conflict

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Community members disagree on this topic — both positions are reported.

To access and adjust the generator (alternator) belt tensioner and remove the belt, the front wheel and wheel-arch liner/fender guard must be removed — belt removal cannot be accomplished without this access. Multiple community members confirm this is the standard procedure for the X80.12

Replacement interval — inspect, don't just calendar-replace. Recommendations vary: some sources online suggest replacing at 70,000+ km per manufacturer interval to preserve warranty, while experienced owners recommend inspecting the belt for visible wear/cracking instead of blind calendar replacement. One owner at 100,000 km had the belt inspected by a mechanic and it was confirmed to still be in good condition, with the mechanic recommending against replacement. Visual inspection is considered more reliable than mileage alone.34567

Belt and roller part numbers. Serpentine (drive) belt part number: 5DA015909. Tensioner pulley (натяжитель/натяжной ролик): 5CA015980. The idler/bypass pulley (обводной ролик) is also sold separately. Recommendation: replace the belt and both pulleys together as a set. Prices vary significantly between retailers — some bundle at a higher cost, while individual parts can be found cheaper on other platforms.8910111213

Belt length — manual spec vs. practical experience (2025-10 reports). The manual specifies a 6PK2260 belt, but owners report this exact length is very difficult to install. Multiple lengths were tested by the community: 2260 (per manual, very difficult), 2263 (extremely difficult — installation may require crankshaft rotation or special techniques, or cutting the old belt off), 2275 (fits with some difficulty but works reliably — reported as +2–3 mm longer than 2260), plus less-common reports of 2277, 2271, and 2270. Net community conclusion: despite the manual calling for 2260, 2275 is the length that works better in practice.14151617181920212223

Installation procedure and challenges (2025-10 reports). Without a service pit, tension the roller by placing a wrench on the roller bolt and pulling it toward the rear of the vehicle, then fit the belt. A common trick for stubborn fits: press the belt against the crankshaft pulley and rotate the engine by hand using a socket wrench on the crankshaft bolt. Access is easier with the right front wheel removed and the plastic wheel-arch liner taken off. Warning: a belt that sits skewed on the pulleys (not properly centered) will cut/shear over time — verify correct tracking before finishing the job. Removing a stuck belt sometimes requires cutting it or using special tools.24252627282930313233343536373839404142434445

Real-world install at 120,000 km. One owner (Vova) replaced the serpentine belt at 120,000 km: the manual-spec 2260 would not fit, so he used 2275 instead. After 10,000 km on the 2275 belt, it was working properly with no issues.464748495051525354

Belt brand/pricing data points (2025-10). Dongil 6PK2263: ~850 RUB (RU market, Oct 2025), but installation difficulty is extreme (per the length notes above); also seen at 1,160 RUB at Auto-Doc, and 1,400 RUB for the Daico brand. Dongil 6PK2275 is separately recommended after several successful installs, available on Ozon.555657212223 Quality caution: one owner reported durability concerns with a JD-brand 6PK2275 belt purchase — in the same period, that owner's lower front control-arm (left) bushings and ball joint failed at only 30,000 km, and stabilizer-bar links failed at 15,000 km, describing overall poor durability from that supplier batch.56

Mileage-based belt/pulley inspection (2025-10/11 reports). At around 300,000 km, one owner's serpentine belt was still holding up and only the tensioner/idler pulley (~36,000 RUB, RU market, Oct 2025) and the alternator needed replacement (cost not specified, October 2025). Belt tension should visually sit centered on the tensioner's reference marks — check all rollers and tension settings whenever replacing the belt. A separate owner replaced the belt at ~280,000 km due to noise; the replacement belt was of a different type/construction than the original, possibly reflecting a local sourcing/quality issue rather than a design problem.585960

docs.title: Audi 09G and DQ200 gearbox reference notes
docs.text:
Tags: #reference · #automatic-transmission

Reference material shared in the group about two other-brand automatic gearboxes: the Audi 09G (a 6-speed made by AISIN AW) and the VW-group DQ200 dual-clutch box. It is background for comparing with the X80's own automatic (see AKPP longevity); none of it is X80-specific.

09G technical data. Audi code AQ250-6F (AISIN AW TF-60SN), service code 09G, used on the Audi A3 (model year 2004) and TT. Planetary gearset in Lepelletier layout; torque up to 300 Nm depending on version; weight about 82.5 kg (the previous 09A: 102 kg); length about 350 mm. Gear ratios: 1st 4.148, 2nd 2.370, 3rd 1.556, 4th 1.155, 5th 0.859, 6th 0.686, reverse 3.394. Intermediate drive 52/49 = 1.061. Final drive 61/15 = 4.067 (engine code GSY, 1.6 L) or 58/15 = 3.867 (GJZ, 2.0 L FSI); overall ratio 4.316 (GSY) or 4.102 (GJZ); total spread 6.051.

09G selector shift-lock. The selector is held in P by a latch driven by solenoid N110, controlled by the gearbox control unit J217. With the ignition on and the selector in N for more than 2 seconds, N110 is energised and locks the selector in N; this lock stops working above about 5 km/h and is released by pressing the brake pedal or switching the ignition off. If power fails, the selector stays locked in P; the emergency release is done after removing the centre-console trim (per the owner's manual) by pushing the N110 latch out of the P slot. The key-removal lock is solenoid N376 (steering-column control unit J527), which stops the key turning to the removal position while the selector is outside P; switch F319 (normally closed) signals P. Parking for a long time with the selector outside P discharges the battery. On the Audi TT both locks are mechanical cables1.

09G tiptronic steering-wheel shifting. With the selector in D or S, pressing one of the two steering-wheel buttons enters tiptronic mode, which stays active for about 8 seconds after the last shift and then returns to automatic. Several presses can skip gears (for example 6th straight to 3rd). The 8-second countdown is extended while cornering or on engine overrun, and the maximum time from manual back to automatic is 40 seconds. On the A3 the button signal travels over the LIN bus to the steering-column control unit J527; US-export Audi TT have no steering-wheel shifting in D or S1.

DQ200 hydraulic accumulator warning. In a video an owner warns that the DQ200 gearbox hydraulic accumulator is charged with gas to about 60 bar and must not be taken apart without releasing the pressure, because the seal or the gas can blow out. The transcript is fragmentary, so the exact procedure is unclear2.

docs.title: AKPP drive modes and shifting behavior
docs.text:
Tags: #automatic-transmission

Transmission type. The X80 automatic transmission is a traditional hydraulic automatic with a torque converter — not a CVT and not a dual-clutch robotized gearbox. This matters because the hydro-transformer (torque converter) continues to generate heat while the car is stationary in gear, which is relevant to the N-vs-D-in-traffic debate below123.

Available modes. The X80 AT offers D (Drive), S (Sport), R (Reverse), P (Park), N (Neutral), and M (Manual) modes. D automatically shifts across 6 gears during normal driving. S keeps the transmission in lower gears with higher RPM for a more responsive/sporty feel, at the cost of higher fuel consumption. M mode allows manual gear selection via a +/- lever, with the selected gear (1-6) shown on the dashboard45678910.

Mode-switching rules. Switching from P to R/D/N/S, or between R/D/S, requires the vehicle to be at a full stop with the brake pedal pressed1112. Once the car is moving, shifting between the other modes (e.g. D↔S) is possible, but care should be taken to avoid a jarring transmission shock when switching at speed13. Manual up/down shifts are possible while driving; the transmission will automatically downshift on its own if engine speed gets too high, overriding the manual selection for safety13.

D vs. S characteristics. D mode: shorter/lower gearing progression, softer acceleration, quieter cabin, lower RPM in city driving (about 1200-1500 RPM in 2nd gear)141516. S mode: longer gearing, requires higher RPM to hold speed (about 2700-3000 RPM in traffic), noisier and more vibration, but gives better highway performance and more predictable cruise-control behavior; also produces higher fuel consumption from prolonged low-gear operation17181920. D mode is gentler on the suspension and produces less tire noise on smooth roads21222324.

Cruise control interaction with mode. Cruise control can temporarily allow speed to drift ±15-20 km/h from the set point (e.g. to get around an obstruction); if speed drops below the set point (e.g. after braking), pressing the + button resumes the previously set speed2526. In S mode, cruise control responds more predictably/better than in D mode, where it can trigger abrupt downshifts on hills, producing unwanted jerking27. If actual speed exceeds the cruise setting, cruise deactivates automatically27.

ECO-mode downshift logic. The AKPP uses the MAP sensor (manifold absolute pressure) plus throttle pedal position to judge engine load. A sharp/firm increase in throttle triggers an immediate downshift; a gradual increase in throttle keeps the current gear for economy. To force a downshift while in ECO behavior, a brief sharp throttle "stab" works282930. On uphill grades with gentle acceleration, the AKPP can hold a high gear (e.g. 3rd) at low RPM as normal ECO-mode behavior for fuel economy, downshifting automatically once more throttle is applied or load crosses a threshold — this has been observed specifically in mountain driving3132.

6th-gear low-speed noise quirk. At 40-50 km/h in 6th gear at ~1500 RPM, applying throttle can produce a grinding/knocking noise from the transmission. Manually selecting 5th gear (raising RPM to ~2000) eliminates the noise completely. The likely cause is the transmission attempting to sustain a very low RPM in a high gear. One owner reports this symptom persisting after 6 years of city driving333435363738394041.

N (neutral) vs. holding D in traffic — community debate. There is no consensus on whether to shift to N + handbrake or simply hold D + foot brake/handbrake while stationary in traffic. Advocates for N+handbrake argue it reduces heat buildup in the transmission fluid, since the torque converter continues generating heat while idling in D42434445. The counter-argument is that frequent D→N→D mode switching adds unnecessary wear and is not needed with a modern AKPP design46474849. No definitive data was presented by either side12.

Handbrake behavior in D or N (not P). The manual handbrake can hold the car on an incline without shifting to P. However, standard procedure is to keep the car in P when stopped, using the handbrake only as a secondary hold505152. If the handbrake is used on a slope while in D or N instead of P, testing by owners shows the car can be held, but this is not recommended standard practice — some reports suggest ECU/transmission behavior in this state may be inconsistent if the brake pedal isn't also applied5354555657.

Park lock vs. handbrake holding power (separate testing). Direct testing showed that the transmission's Park (P) lock alone does not reliably hold the vehicle on an incline — the car's weight on a slope is primarily held by the electronic/mechanical handbrake, not by the transmission's park pawl5859. The manual's proper parking sequence is: (1) apply the brake pedal, (2) shift to R (Reverse) [not P] — note: this reflects the manual's stated sequence as reported by the source, distinct from ordinary P-based parking described above, (3) engage the electronic handbrake, (4) release the brake pedal6061. On level ground, Park mode provides a secondary safety margin, but on any incline the vehicle can roll if the handbrake isn't engaged; the park lock can slip on grades without simultaneous handbrake engagement62.

Shift jerking — 2017 pre-facelift reports (conflict). Some owners report noticeable jerking during automatic-transmission shifts, particularly on 2017 pre-facelift models. One owner describes a noticeable but slight jerk during shifts; another reports smooth operation on straight roads but a strong "kick" from the transmission after sharp turns at 20-30 km/h. Community response is mixed: several suggest this may be a matter of subjective perception rather than a defect, and the Aisin automatic is generally well-regarded for reliability, with one source citing hundreds of positive reviews. A manual-transmission version remains available as an alternative for owners who want to avoid the AT entirely6364656667686970. Conflict: whether this jerking is a normal characteristic or a real defect is unresolved — some owners accept it, others find it problematic.

D-mode aggressive downshifting and gear-hunting (Aisin-based AT). The Aisin-based automatic exhibits overly aggressive downshifting and what owners describe as incorrect shift logic specifically in D (Drive) mode: the transmission engages 6th gear at as low as 60 km/h — too low a speed for such a high gear — and shifts unnecessarily aggressively during acceleration, causing engine rev-bounce and inefficient power delivery. Some owners believe the firmware calibration may be underdeveloped for this application. Workaround: switch to S (Sport) mode or manual shift mode for better throttle response and more consistent engine revs; S mode maintains higher RPM for optimal traction on grades and prevents gear-hunting. Some owners report that a firmware update improved the behavior7172737475767778798081828384858687.

Howling/grinding noise at low speed under load (conflict). A separate anomaly: when the automatic transmission holds a low gear (e.g. 5th) at low speed (~30 km/h) and the driver applies throttle to accelerate, the transmission produces a distinctive howling or grinding sound (гул). Owners consider this abnormal and suggest two possible causes: (1) transmission fluid degradation or an incorrect fluid level, or (2) internal wear of gear-engagement teeth or bearing wear (шестеренки). Changing the transmission fluid temporarily suppresses the symptom but does not cure it if internal wear is the actual cause. In manual-shift mode (lever moved to the manual gate), gear selection reportedly operates smoothly without the noise, which points toward the automatic shift logic itself as a contributing factor rather than the gearset alone888990919293949596979899. Conflict: members disagree on the underlying cause — some attribute the sound to worn bearings, others to gear-tooth wear; the prognosis (normal resonance vs. sign of wear) is unresolved.

D vs. S — fuel consumption angle. Restating the D/S characteristics above from a fuel-economy angle: D-mode ("economy") shifts into longer/higher gears with shorter shift intervals and nominally lower RPM. S-mode holds lower/shorter gears with less frequent shifting and higher RPM — yet community testing shows S-mode sometimes delivers equal or even lower fuel consumption than D, because fewer total shifts can offset the higher-RPM operation. The net effect varies by individual driving pattern100.

Gearing, RPM at speed, and adaptive shift learning (additional reports). 2nd gear reaches roughly 80 km/h at 5,500 RPM; 4th gear tops out around only 40 km/h before the transmission struggles — gearing is long throughout, and 6th gear is barely used even at highway speeds because of poor synchronization/utilization101102103. The AKPP's adaptive-learning tuning changes shift behavior based on driving style, which can make it feel inconsistent — sometimes smooth and gentle, other times harsh/aggressive with chattering from low gears; this is by design rather than a fault, but can feel unpredictable104105106. In S mode specifically, shifting can be harsh with high engine noise, traced to a short 3rd-gear ratio (4th gear tops at ~40 km/h) and poor gear synchronization; transmission oil burning was also reported in this context. Manual (M) mode is recommended for highway driving to avoid this strain107101108.

Overall gear character and optimal RPM band. Despite feeling responsive off the line, the 6-speed automatic has relatively long overall gearing and is well suited to highway cruising with reasonable economy; shift patterns continue to adapt to driving style and traffic109110111112. Reported optimal engine operation is in the 3500-4000 RPM band for the best dynamic response — running below 3500 RPM in D feels sluggish, while using Tiptronic/manual-shift or S mode at 4000+ RPM gives noticeably better acceleration with similar fuel consumption to conservative D-mode driving; Euro 5 emissions tuning is cited as intentionally limiting low-RPM performance113111. Separately, the AKPP can safely sustain 5.5k RPM under sustained hard acceleration (e.g. an uphill overtake) without the ECU cutting throttle, provided the driver holds a steady pedal through the maneuver114.

Poor highway throttle response — possible causes (AKPP, unresolved). Some AKPP-equipped cars show sluggish highway response: the gas pedal feels ineffective until pressed hard, and releasing the pedal produces no power response even though the engine revs — the transmission doesn't seem to engage smoothly. Community theories (unresolved): mis-tuned air/fuel mixture (excess air causing hesitation), throttle pedal not properly synchronized with the ECU, or suboptimal firmware calibration. The manual-transmission (MКПП) version is reported to have markedly better throttle response by comparison. One owner who had the ECU reflashed with full standard tuning (no deletions) confirmed the car worked correctly afterward115116117118119120121122123124.

Sport vs. Drive — restated with a city/highway recommendation. Restating and reinforcing the D/S guidance already on this card: for city driving, Sport mode is recommended to reduce gear-hunting at intermediate speeds and feel more responsive. On the highway, Drive is adequate; using Sport on the highway makes the transmission hold gears longer, resist shifting into 6th, and keep the engine at higher (noisier) RPM. Manual mode remains available to override automatic shifting on the highway if desired. Performance note: given the engine's modest power, reaching 197-215 km/h takes significant time and fuel. Fuel consumption is reported as comparable between Drive and Sport at highway speeds125126127128129130.

Harsh 4th-6th downshift shudder under hard acceleration. A separate AT complaint: the transmission shudders harshly when downshifting from 4th toward 6th during aggressive (full-throttle) acceleration; smooth acceleration transitions cleanly. Under cruise control on an uphill grade (125 km/h), the transmission downshifts to 4th and holds ~3,100 RPM for about 10 seconds, then delivers a hard jerk on the upshift to 5th. A transmission-fluid change at 68,000 km showed minor metal particles on the sump magnet, described by a mechanic as normal wear. One concern raised: a possible ruptured hydro-accumulator in the gearbox — countered by the observation that a ruptured accumulator would typically put the transmission into limp mode rather than cause this kind of shudder131132133134.

Downshifting on inclines — normal, and a spark-plug-related jerk to distinguish from it. Automatic-transmission downshifts from 6th to 4th gear on inclines are normal AKPP behavior, not a transmission fault. However, a separate symptom — jerking/hesitation specifically while holding 4th gear under load — is often caused by worn spark plugs, not by the transmission itself. Spark plugs have roughly a 70,000 km service interval; inspection is recommended starting around 112,000+ km on used vehicles, especially if this jerk is present135136137138139140.

AKPP low-RPM creep and hum — restated as a general characteristic. Automatic-transmission X80s commonly exhibit low-RPM creep/jerking when accelerating from a stop or rolling start, plus an audible hum/grinding noise in the 1000-2000 RPM range that disappears once the gearbox shifts past 2000 RPM. This is reported as characteristic AKPP behavior rather than a fault in most cases, though severe grinding could indicate worn friction packs. Recommendation: avoid heavy loading/towing until the transmission has been inspected at higher mileage141142143144145146147.

Sport mode — full-throttle standstill launch RPM. Restating and quantifying the Sport-mode behavior already on this card: at full throttle from a standstill in Sport mode, the automatic transmission can hold 1st gear to roughly 6,300 RPM before shifting — noticeably higher and more aggressive than Comfort/Drive mode. Manual transmission cars have no Sport mode equivalent148149150.

Pre-facelift AKPP — two different model identifiers, unresolved. The pre-facelift X80's automatic transmission is identified in the group by two different labels: part number 5CA003000, and separately the designation TF-61SN. Conflict: it's unclear from this data batch whether these refer to the same transmission under different naming conventions (part number vs. transmission-family designation) or are genuinely conflicting sources — cross-check against an authoritative Aisin/FAW catalog before relying on either label alone151152.

Gear selector stuck/locked after extended non-use — mechanical override procedure. After roughly 1+ week of the vehicle sitting unused, the automatic transmission's gear selector can become stuck/locked, unable to switch positions. Diagnostic steps before assuming a fault: (1) confirm the brake lights illuminate when the brake pedal is pressed; (2) listen for a solenoid click near the selector when attempting to shift; (3) turn the ignition on and check selector response. If genuinely locked: there is a mechanical override button under a small plastic cap/cover on the right side of the selector — pressing it should produce a click and unlock the selector mechanically. After unlocking, turn the ignition off and wait 15-45 minutes for the vehicle's electronic systems to fully power down/sleep before trying again; the selector should then work normally. The suspected cause is a transmission solenoid lock or an electronic glitch triggered by the extended idle period, not a hardware failure153154155156157158159160161162163164165166167168169170171172173174175176177.

Delayed downshift on hills — manual-mode workaround, possible thermal factor. A separate, earlier report on hill behavior: in D mode, the AKPP can be reluctant to downshift automatically on steep grades even at full throttle. Workaround: switch to manual mode (S or the +/- gate) for consistent engine braking and power delivery on hills. In D mode, releasing the pedal first tends to trigger the downshift. Specialists in the thread describe this reluctance as normal transmission behavior rather than a fault, though possible thermal factors (transmission temperature) were raised as a contributing variable178179180181.

D-mode vs. S-mode selection guidance for manual-to-automatic converts. Separate, earlier guidance on the D/S mode choice already touched on elsewhere on this card: D (economy) mode suits city driving, auto-shifting to higher gears to reduce consumption; S (sport) mode holds lower gears for better acceleration response. Recommendation specifically for owners transitioning from a manual-transmission car: use S mode for better throttle control and engine-sound feedback, and prefer S mode on the highway with A/C running. If present, Eco mode is described as simply D mode with more aggressive auto-upshifting, and cannot be disabled independently182.

Transmission shift-point tuning via ECU/firmware — unverified claim. A separate, lower-confidence report claims AKPP shift points and shift-quality behavior can be modified via ECU firmware tuning without hardware changes — tuners adjusting DSP (dynamic shift programming) parameters to extend the shifting RPM range or soften shifts. Some tuners reportedly claim they can reprogram the transmission control strategy without vendor documentation, though results are said to vary and this claim is not independently verified within this data batch183184.

Selector requires Park to start; Neutral alone won't start the engine. A separate, more basic behavioral fact: the AKPP requires the gear selector to be in Park (P) to start the engine — Neutral (N) alone does not allow starting, since N is intended only for service use (e.g. allowing the wheels to roll, such as during a tow or a wash). Handbrake position does not affect the ability to start if the selector isn't in P. If the vehicle won't start in N but starts fine in P, the selector is functioning correctly and this is not a fault185186187.

Where the community disagrees

  • Whether AT shift jerking on some (particularly 2017 pre-facelift) X80s is a normal characteristic or an early sign of a problem is unresolved: some owners dismiss it as subjective/normal, others report it as a real annoyance.
  • Members disagree on the cause of the low-speed howling/grinding noise: some attribute it to bearing wear, others to gear-tooth wear; whether it's benign resonance or a sign of developing internal damage is not settled in this data batch.
  • Community split: N+handbrake advocates argue it reduces transmission-fluid heat buildup in traffic; D-hold advocates argue frequent D↔N switching causes more wear and is unnecessary. No definitive data presented by either side.
  • The pre-facelift X80's automatic transmission is identified by two different labels in this data batch — part number 5CA003000 and designation TF-61SN — without clarity on whether these are compatible naming conventions for the same unit or conflicting sources.

docs.title: AKPP jerking — spark plug and fluid fix
docs.text:
Tags: #automatic-transmission · #jerking · #spark-plugs · #conflict

Community members disagree on this topic — both positions are reported.

Symptom — jerky 3→4 shift on pre-facelift AT cars at high mileage. Pre-facelift automatic-transmission X80s can develop a jerky/shuddering shift specifically between 3rd and 4th gear (described as feeling like a KAMAZ truck pushing the car) at high mileage (210,000+ km). A partial (half-drain) fluid change alone did not resolve this in the reported case. Possible causes raised: spark plug condition, or internal transmission wear12. Conflict: root cause varies by report — in some cases changing spark plugs resolved the symptom, in others transmission wear is suspected instead; no single confirmed cause.

Fix — fluid half-drain + filter + spark plug change resolves jerking felt at 60-80 km/h. Separately, jerking sensations during gear shifts, felt specifically during acceleration between 60-80 km/h, were resolved by performing an AKPP fluid half-drain with filter replacement, combined with a spark plug change. Multiple owners in the same thread confirmed the jerks/"рывки" went away after these two maintenance steps together; the working theory is that fresher transmission fluid plus correct spark timing (from fresh plugs) combine to fix the symptom, rather than either step alone345678910. Conflict: one owner (44707) described the shift jerk as something felt/heard during the shift itself rather than specifically induced by acceleration; after a spark-plug change it subsided for them too (44758) — consistent with the same fix working across slightly different symptom descriptions.

Fix — restated: fluid + filter change alone resolved jerking/bucking, with visible wear evidence. In a separate case, changing the AKPP fluid and filter alone (without a documented spark-plug change in this thread) resolved jerking and bucking in the automatic transmission. The drained oil was medium-dirty (not heavily fouled, but not clean either), and metallic particles were visible on the drain-pan magnets — consistent with normal wear debris rather than a sign of impending failure1112131415.

Takeaway. Across these reports, an AKPP fluid half-drain + filter service, together with a spark plug change, is the most consistently reported fix for shift-related jerking/shuddering — see the dedicated AKPP fluid-change-procedure card for the mechanics of the drain/filter service, and the spark-plugs card for plug options1311.

Baseline — small jerks (пинки) on downshift/throttle-release are a normal AKPP characteristic, not a defect. An earlier, independent report establishes a baseline distinct from the fixable-jerking cases above: the AKPP produces small jerking sensations ("пинки") during downshifts and when releasing the throttle — this is described as a normal transmission characteristic, not a defect, occurring especially in stop-and-go traffic. Users report this is inherent to the transmission design, involving engine braking transmitted through the gearbox. This baseline is useful context before assuming any jerk requires the fluid/filter/spark-plug fix documented above — some jerking is expected and not a fault to chase1617181920.

Excessive jerking from low fluid level — check/top-up before assuming a deeper fault. A separate, earlier fix distinct from the half-drain procedures above: excessive AKPP jerking can result simply from insufficient fluid level. Remedy: check and top up the transmission fluid as needed. After any transmission work or oil change, drive approximately 1,000 km and re-check the level, topping up again if necessary — fluid level can settle/drop after a service and a second check catches this2122.

Cold-start shift hesitation — thin/cold fluid, distinct from the jerking cases above. A related but distinct symptom from the shift-jerking cases documented above: cold or thin transmission fluid can cause a noticeable shift lag at low speeds when accelerating from a standstill, feeling like a manual transmission with delayed clutch engagement — normal once at higher speed or once the engine is warm. Consistent with the fluid-quality theme running through this card, a transmission fluid change at 40,000-50,000 km is reported to substantially improve this response. One owner also raised a possible link to a prior transmission reprogramming at lower mileage correlating with increased sensitivity. Conflict: root cause is disputed — one user (Aleksandr) attributes the hesitation to engine ECU cleaning rather than the transmission itself; the discussion was inconclusive on whether fluid viscosity, transmission-map reprogramming, or ECU logic is the true cause23242526272829303132333435363738.

Where the community disagrees

  • Cold-start shift hesitation root cause is disputed: one user attributes it to engine ECU cleaning rather than the transmission; the broader discussion did not conclusively determine whether fluid viscosity, transmission-map reprogramming, or ECU logic is responsible. Not resolved within this data batch.

docs.title: Camshaft position sensor — P0340 and oil seal
docs.text:
Tags: #part-number · #oil-leak

Error code and effect. Error code P3046 / P0340 indicates camshaft position sensor failure. This disables variable valve timing (VVT) and causes a noticeable loss of power1.

Diagnosis. Check the sensor's wiring and connector for damage first — this is reported as the most common failure mode12. The camshaft position sensor is mounted on the cylinder head cover (valve cover)34; a Ford Mondeo 4 2.3L is cited as using a similar sensor placement for reference5.

Part number and replacement. Sensor part number 3602055-37K (FAW Besturn X80). It is described as inexpensive and a roughly 10-minute replacement67. If replacing the sensor doesn't resolve the issue, check the VVT solenoid for clogging or inspect for a stretched timing chain as the next steps8.

Oil seepage from the sensor seal. When the camshaft position sensor weeps oil from its seal, the seal itself can be replaced separately from the sensor; doing so may require removing the valve cover3910. One owner reports the seepage can remain a minor weep — not requiring urgent repair — for up to 2 years111213141516.

docs.title: Catalytic converter removal and P0420
docs.text:
Tags: #catalytic-converter · #ecu-tuning · #emissions · #rattle

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Why owners remove it, and at what mileage. Many X80 owners remove the catalytic converters (there are two catalysts per car) once the check-engine light illuminates with a catalyst-related error code. Reported removal mileages in this batch: 70,000 km, 85,000 km, and 170,000 km. After removal, ECU reprogramming to the Euro-2 emission standard is generally required; some owners report the throttle response feels different (delayed) immediately after the remap. There is concern about catalyst fragments causing cylinder scoring if pieces break loose internally — this is debated within the community: some argue the risk is lower on the X80 than on some Korean-brand vehicles because of where the catalysts sit in the exhaust (one catalyst close to the manifold); KASPER specifically notes the catalyst closest to the manifold is the one whose debris could plausibly reach a cylinder. As an alternative to removal, replacing both catalysts costs 130,000+ RUB for parts, plus labor12345678910. Conflict: Олег Белоусов argues catalyst fragments can cause cylinder scoring; Игорь Игорев argues the risk is minimal on non-Korean vehicles since debris exits via the exhaust; KASPER's middle position is that the catalyst nearest the manifold specifically could shed debris toward a cylinder.

ECU/lambda-sensor side of removal. Removing the catalyst requires one of two ECU-side approaches: (1) disable the lambda/oxygen sensor reading (the car runs Euro-2 logic on this platform), or (2) install an oxygen-sensor simulator ("обманка"). Using a simulator alone, without disabling the sensor logic, may not reliably prevent the check-engine light, depending on the simulator's calibration quality — most aftermarket simulators are reported unreliable, working initially but triggering the check-engine light again later. A professional ECU reflash is recommended for stable operation without a check-engine light1112131415.

Removal without any ECU tuning at all — sometimes viable. The catalyst can be removed without any ECU reprogramming if the vehicle has no pre-existing error codes at the time of removal (confirmed by a diagnostic scan beforehand) — in that specific case, tuning is reported as unnecessary. However, even with a clean pre-removal scan, a check-engine light may still appear after 50,000+ km of subsequent driving. The engine will not stop running if the light activates, but the light stays on the dashboard. One owner reported driving 60,000+ km post-removal with no issues at all1617.

Deletion procedure and flame-arrestor replacement, at higher mileage. Catalytic converters are also removed around 112,000-120,000 km in some cases, with the converter physically replaced by a flame arrestor (пламягаситель) — shops performing this deletion keep the flame-arrestor part in stock. As above, tuning isn't always required immediately if the check-engine light doesn't illuminate right away, but ECU tuning (7,000-10,000 RUB, RU market, Feb 2025) is available to optimize engine behavior after deletion181920.

Non-destructive inspection method (avoids guessing whether removal is even needed). Catalytic-converter interior condition can be checked without removing the part, using an endoscope inserted through the oxygen-sensor ports (located before and after the catalyst). This lets an owner assess internal deterioration or damage before deciding whether to remove or replace. A properly functioning catalyst can reportedly remain in service 200,000+ km without visible degradation when combustion stays clean212223.

P0420 code specifically. The P0420 code ("Catalyst System Efficiency Below Threshold, Bank 1") indicates either catalyst failure or a malfunctioning second (downstream) lambda sensor. Two solution paths: (1) check/replace the second lambda sensor and its wiring, or (2) delete the catalyst with an ECU remap and install a flame guard — one reported price point was 5,000 RUB in Samara, as of April 2024 (RU market). Owners report improved power/performance after catalyst deletion for this code; the vehicle remains drivable with the check-engine light on2425262728.

Exhaust-system fastener corrosion (separate, related maintenance note). Around 250,000 km, the bolts and spring fasteners holding the exhaust system together typically corrode and can shear/lose their heads during removal attempts; using an impact wrench (ударный гайковёрт) is reported to solve the extraction problem — without one, bolt heads often just break off29.

Euro 5 firmware perceived as restrictive — Euro 2 downgrade for performance. Community perception is that the X80's Euro 5 firmware calibration is restrictive and limits engine performance for emissions compliance. Some owners downgrade to Euro 2 firmware for better throttle response and power delivery, trading emissions control for performance3031.

Stage 1 tuning without catalyst deletion — price point. Stage 1 ECU tuning that does not remove/delete the catalytic converter was available in Nizhny Novgorod for 12,000 RUB as of June 2025 (RU market)32.

Catalyst error diagnosis at low mileage. At 57,000 km, outright catalytic converter failure is considered rare on a stock vehicle. If a P0420-type cat-related code appears, check the oxygen (lambda) sensor first with a diagnostic scanner/multimeter before assuming the catalyst itself has failed — specifically the second, post-catalyst sensor. Chinese-vehicle catalytic converters are reported to have a more limited lifespan compared to other manufacturers33343536373839.

Custom ECU remap — O2-sensor disable plus power tuning, a tuner's perspective. A tuner reports the standard remap program disables oxygen-sensor monitoring (supporting catalyst delete/bypass, consistent with the lambda-defeat approaches already documented on this card) and can additionally adjust engine power characteristics on request. A common customer request is more power in the low/mid RPM range; one tuner mentioned adding power there specifically because the car is mostly driven by their spouse40.

Secondary (post-lambda) catalyst removal — disputed practice, restated with more detail. The secondary catalytic converter (positioned after the second lambda sensor) can be removed and replaced with a welded-in flame suppressor, typically paired with an ECU reprogram to clear the resulting error codes — consistent with the general catalyst-deletion procedure already documented on this card. Removal before 100,000 km is recommended to limit catalyst breakdown and the resulting risk of metal debris scoring the engine. Dispute: some owners advocate removal for performance/engine-longevity reasons, while others — specifically Chinese-market tuners — advise against removal on Chinese-built engines, citing lower durability margins than the donor Mazda/Ford design. An alternative to full removal: install a repair/restoration catalytic converter without any ECU reprogram414243444546474849505152535455565758. Conflict: one owner removed the secondary catalyst at 80,000 km after an error code and reported improved performance; another reports catalyst clogging/failure starting at 58,000 km, resolved via removal plus reprogram; the community's rough consensus is to remove only if an error code actually appears, ideally before 100,000 km.

Claimed factory power output — 164 hp design vs. 142 hp as delivered. Per Chinese-tuner sources, the X80's engine (Mazda/Ford-derived) is rated 164 hp in its parent design but intentionally throttled to 142 hp from the factory. An ECU reprogram is claimed to recover roughly 12-15 hp (~10%). Conflict: some tuners (Chinese chip-tune shops) say the factory ECU is already at its practical maximum and advise against remapping; others report a remap mainly improves throttle response and lets the driver customize pedal sensitivity without exceeding safe engine limits — one owner reports 4 years of remap use with no issues, and another states the remap doesn't touch core fuel/timing maps, only removes factory throttle limiters. A related, unresolved debate concerns motor longevity: Mazda/Ford-original engines are assumed good for 1M+ km, while the Chinese-built copies are assumed by some to top out around 300,000-400,000 km555960616263646566.

Chip-tuned AT behavior — even a mild 95-octane remap affects shifting. Even a slight chip tune (a remap for 95-octane fuel mapping) is reported to change automatic-transmission behavior: the transmission can start hunting between gears and become overly sensitive to throttle input — hyper-responsive at intermediate throttle, sluggish under higher load. The reporting owner does not recommend a 95-octane remap given concerns about both engine and transmission resource/durability67686970717273.

ECU block/firmware variation across production batches. X80 ECU hardware blocks are inconsistent across production batches — different blocks need different firmware and tuning approaches, and standard Mazda/Ford tuning software does not reliably support every X80 block because of this variation. The ECU can be read and reprogrammed, but matching firmware is hard to find in public databases; tuners sometimes resort to loading Mazda or Ford firmware as a workaround, with inconsistent results. This block-to-block inconsistency is described as unusual and specific to FAW's production process74757677.

Removal + flame-arrestor retrofit — cost breakdown restated with sourcing options. When a clogged catalyst needs removal: replacement-unit options include a new unit (~35,000-40,000 RUB used, RU market, Oct 2025), a 16,500 RUB alternative (Nissan Qashqai Euro 5 catalyst via Avito), or a universal 63.5mm unit from AliExpress (~1,676 UAH). Alternatively, remove the catalyst and install a flame arrestor (пламегаситель) plus reflash the ECU: reported costs (RU market, Oct 2025) were 5,000-12,000 RUB for tuning, 2,000-5,000 RUB for flame-arrestor welding, and one report of 5,000 RUB total in Samara two years prior. After removal with a correct reflash, expect at most a minor oil smell at startup; without reflashing, the engine over-consumes oil. A chemical catalyst-cleaner fuel additive exists but has limited effectiveness787980818283848586878889. Conflict: side-effect reports disagree — some owners see no oil consumption after removal+reflash, others report a slight oil odor or minimal consumption.

Removal procedure detail — manifold gasket risk, honeycomb inspection, and a repair-converter price point. Removing the catalyst requires removing the exhaust-manifold gasket, which can break during extraction. Before removal, inspect the ceramic honeycomb inside (white ceramic with light passing through = partial blockage but usable; dark/broken sections = failure) to judge whether removal is even necessary. After removal, install a flame arrestor to maintain exhaust safety. A Euro-5 repair converter was available for roughly 8,800 RUB (RU market, Nov 2025, Yandex Market) as a lower-cost alternative to a full new unit — one reported case of proactive removal without any prior failure symptoms90919293949596979899100101102103104105106107108109110111112113114115.

Two-catalyst layout confirmed again. Restating the two-catalyst layout already documented on this card: the X80 has two catalytic converters in the exhaust system, and each can trigger its own independent error code116.

Internal substrate degradation at 121,000 km — no external symptoms. At 121,000 km, internal degradation of the catalyst substrate can begin — the ceramic honeycomb material starts to crumble/flake internally, which may trigger intermittent fault codes. Critically, external inspection alone can show no visible damage or clogging; the deterioration is purely internal and would only be caught by the endoscope method or a substrate check already documented on this card117118119120.

ECU remap + cat removal — 2026 price point and driver feedback. A combined catalyst-removal-plus-remap service (to the Euro-2 map, consistent with the general approach already documented on this card) was quoted at roughly 8,000 RUB (RU market, Mar 2026) for automatic-transmission cars. Owners report the car feels noticeably more responsive ("резвее, шустрее") after the combo, with a slight morning exhaust smell that dissipates and disappears — a flame suppressor is recommended to manage this. Concerns raised: increased engine load, the automatic transmission may shift harshly at first as it adapts, and an oil change is recommended right after remapping. Longevity reports: one owner has run 120,000-190,000 km since removal with no engine issues; another reports satisfactory performance overall. Conflict (consistent with the tuner dispute already documented on this card): tuners warn that adding power stresses the automatic transmission and requires careful adaptation, while some owners report no issues at all121122123124125126127128129130131132133134135136137.

P0420 at ~140,000 km — diagnosis path and a caution against catalyst specialists. After a check-engine light and P0420 diagnosis at ~140,000 km, recommended diagnosis (before assuming the catalyst is dead): use an endoscope to physically inspect the catalyst substrate for soot buildup, melting, or physical breakup; pull and inspect the oxygen sensors, which can simply be clogged; and try sustained highway driving at higher RPM ("give it some gas") to burn off accumulated soot, since low-speed/short-trip driving is what lets soot build up in the first place — mileage alone is not the determining factor, driving style is. Only if the endoscope shows the substrate melted or physically disintegrated should removal be considered. One owner in this thread had recently installed a methane (CNG) conversion, adding a possible contributing variable. Repair-shop skepticism: "catalyst specialists" are said to have a financial incentive to recommend deletion regardless of actual condition, so their diagnosis should not be taken at face value. Self-diagnosis tooling recommended: an ELM327 v1.5 Bluetooth scanner with the dual-board PIC18F25K80 chipset, ~800 RUB (RU market, Apr 2026) on Ozon, to let owners read/monitor codes themselves rather than relying solely on a shop138139140141142143144145.

P0420 traced to poor-quality fuel — Gazprom vs. Rosneft, repeatable. A separate P0420 case: the check-engine light and P0420 code appeared, was cleared, and then reappeared while running out a tank of Gazprom 95-octane fuel purchased in late April 2026. After switching to Rosneft 95-octane, the code cleared and did not return after roughly 45-60 km of driving — confirmed as resolved by a follow-up scan showing no codes. A similar case from a Chery-brand owner reportedly showed an "insufficient octane rating" message on the same Gazprom fuel. Community consensus in this thread: Gazprom-brand fuel quality is a recurring complaint (some say Gazprom stations prioritize their gas/LPG business over petrol quality), and Rosneft, Gazpromneft (a distinct company from Gazprom despite the similar name), or Tatneft are recommended as more reliable fuel sources — one long-time member reports exclusively using Teboil or Rosneft146147148149150151152153.

Rattle from corroded mounting bolts — causes and repair options. A separate rattle symptom, distinct from the codes/removal cases above: the lower catalytic converter can rattle due to corroded mounting bolts. Recommended solution path: (1) check the screen/mesh on the second catalyst (afterburner); (2) remove the corroded mounting bolts — reported repair cost around 1,000 RUB (RU market, Aug 2026); (3) optionally install a flame arrestor after removal, consistent with the flame-arrestor practice already documented on this card; (4) install an ECU "cheat"/simulator module or get a full reprogram. Reported reprogramming price spread by region (RU market, Aug 2026): Tula region 8,000 RUB, Orel 15,000 RUB, Moscow 20,000 RUB — a notably wide regional spread compared to the other remap prices already on this card. The ECU on these cars is a Bosch 7.8.8 unit, which is described as having limited reprogramming options available compared to other ECU families154155156157158159160161.

Front catalytic converter cut out — owner report from Perm (Oct 2026). Konstantin Руммель cut out the front catalytic converter (катализатор) at "40k" (unit not stated, presumably km) and says the car feels great 162163. He left the rear converter in place so the cabin does not smell of exhaust 164. A question whether removing the rear one would matter, and one about chip tuning (чип-тюнинг), received no answer in the batch.

Where the community disagrees

  • Community disagreement on catalyst-fragment risk: Олег Белоусов claims fragments can cause cylinder scoring; Игорь Игорев argues risk is minimal on non-Korean vehicles since debris exits via the exhaust; KASPER notes the catalyst closest to the manifold specifically could plausibly send debris toward a cylinder. Not resolved within this data batch.
  • Community disagreement over secondary-catalyst removal: some advocate removal before 100,000 km for performance and to avoid catalyst breakdown; Chinese-market tuners specifically advise against removal on Chinese-built engines citing lower durability margins than the Mazda/Ford donor platform. Not resolved within this data batch.
  • Tuners disagree on whether X80 ECU remapping for power is safe/beneficial: Chinese chip-tune shops caution against it, citing the factory ECU as already near its practical maximum, while other owners report years of trouble-free remap use with only throttle-limiter removal and improved pedal response, not core fuel/timing changes. Not resolved within this data batch.
  • Reports on oil-consumption/smell side-effects after catalyst removal + ECU reflash disagree: some owners report no oil consumption, others report a slight oil odor or minimal consumption. Not resolved within this data batch.

docs.title: Catalytic converter removal — ECU reflash
docs.text:
Tags: #catalytic-converter · #ecu · #price · #emissions

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

The FAW X80 has two catalytic converters.12

Removal costs (Moscow, RU market, Dec 2024 report): - Service labor for removal: ~4,000 RUB.13 - Flame arrestor (пламегаситель) installation: ~2,500 RUB.1 - ECU reflash to Euro-2: 7,000–10,000 RUB, or ~5,000 RUB if bundled with the removal ("with connections").134 - Basic ECU adjustment down to Euro-2 emission mapping is free if included as part of the removal package; full stage tuning (performance remap) is a separate, additional paid option.4

Catalyst scrap value. Removed catalysts can be either (a) trade-credited toward the service cost, or (b) sold separately — but current market conditions (as of Oct–Dec 2024) mean scrap value is minimal: theoretically valued around 5,000 RUB (RU market, Oct-Dec 2024), but in practice many shops refuse to buy them or credit only a nominal/near-free amount due to low precious-metal content and demand.5678910

Mileage recommendation. Removal is typically recommended around 120,000–200,000 km, once the catalysts are naturally degrading anyway (community members note this is somewhat subjective, but real examples exist: one owner found a second catalyst already partially melted/damaged ("подплавлен") at 80,000 km).2111012

Verification. Shops verify the catalysts are actually removed (not just bypassed cosmetically) using a spectrometer to check for precious-metal content, relevant when trading in the old units.9

Fuel octane after removing the catalytic converter. After removal one owner runs 92 petrol and says it gives the best consumption and pull. Another found 95 and 95+ used more fuel with no real gain, while a third says 95 pulled better before the converter was removed131415.

docs.title: Clutch kit — Mazda 6 GG fitment and parts
docs.text:
Tags: #clutch · #manual-transmission · #mazda-6-compat · #price

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Clutch is shared with the first-generation Mazda 6 (GG). Тимур says the FAW X80 clutch is unified with the first-generation Mazda 6 (GG platform), with a 225 mm disc, so only an original is not required: Trialli, LUK or Sachs aftermarket parts, or Mazda 6 kits, are suggested, after checking the number of splines (шлицы) against the VIN (vehicle identification number) or the removed part. Original FAW numbers to check against: 5CA016460 (disc) and 5CA016410 (pressure plate / basket, корзина) 1. Photos posted by Никита show a disc marked "К МАХОВИКУ" (flywheel side) and a pressure plate whose stamp appears to read 5CA0-16410; the other number was not visible 23.

Triali FR 2750 kit and the OEM brand (Sep 2026). Victor 🇷🇺 notes that Triali FR 2750 is sold as a clutch kit for the X80 (basket, driven disc and release bearing). Its listed diameter is 225 mm although stock is 230 mm (a discrepancy with the 225 mm figure above), and the OEM clutch is made by Exedy, which the parts catalogue naturally does not list. He says the Triali driven disc looks like the Krauf TCZ1128AS, a mediocre make 4.

Price check (Sep 2026). Victor 🇷🇺 plans to replace only the driven disc and release bearing. A Valeo basket costs about 14,000 RUB (RU market, Sep 2026) and an OEM basket was quoted at about 7,500 RUB (RU market, Sep 2026); units are not written in the message and are assumed to be roubles, and he does not believe a genuine OEM basket comes for 7,500, expecting cheap poor-quality Chinese 5.

Replacement measurements: new basket and disc stack (Sep-Oct 2026). While replacing the clutch Victor 🇷🇺 found nothing damaged on the old parts but measured differences: the new pressure plate sits 0.5 mm further from the flywheel and his new driven disc is 1.1 mm thicker, so the compressed stack is about 1.6 mm against a pressure-plate stroke of 1.5-3 mm that the Alisa voice assistant gave him, so every millimetre matters. He considered shims under the cover or another kit, and was unsure whether the pedal also needs adjusting afterwards. Do not overtighten the cover bolts: the anti-rotation bolts are practically impossible to unscrew later 6. The four photos he posted show clutch cover and flywheel assemblies but do not clearly show the worn-versus-new comparison 7. For the pedal itself see the card on clutch pedal adjustment.

Disc thickness: worn vs new. Никита compared photos of his old, worn disc with a new one: in the first photo the new disc is on top, in the second on the right, and he says his worn disc is the same thickness as the new one; no measurements were given 89.

Release bearing grease: plastic vs metal (Oct 2026). Victor 🇷🇺 fitted a metal Valeo release bearing (выжимной подшипник; the factory one has a plastic inner part, which he says should not be greased) and greased it with thick special lithium grease, together with the lever tips, the ball the lever rests on and the splines of the input shaft 10. Disagreement: Victor 🇷🇺 says manufacturers forbid greasing, in their instructions, because dust sticks and the plastic jams 1112; Serega asks why the same dust-abrasion problem would not apply to a metal bearing, since dust packing into grease would act as an abrasive and wear it quickly 13.

docs.title: Manual clutch lifespan and driving style
docs.text:
Tags: #clutch · #manual-transmission

Lifespan is driving-style dependent, not a fixed interval. Community consensus: manual-transmission clutch ("сцепление") lifespan depends heavily on driving style rather than raw mileage. With smooth, unhurried operation, a clutch can typically be expected to last the entire life of the engine/vehicle without needing replacement.123

Aggressive driving can destroy a clutch very quickly. In contrast to the above, aggressive driving or repeated clutch-slipping can wear out a clutch in as little as 2–3 short drives — an extreme case illustrating just how much technique matters versus distance covered.123

Long-term evidence. One owner reports 150,000+ km without any clutch issues across multiple Chinese-brand vehicles, attributing this to consistently smooth driving technique.23

New clutch install cost, real-world data point. One owner asked about replacement cost specifically for a manual (restyled) X80; a separate owner reported installing a brand-new clutch and having it fail/underperform almost immediately, suspecting a defective part rather than a technique issue — a reminder that even a fresh clutch can be a bad unit out of the box, so if a new clutch feels wrong right away, suspect the part before blaming driving habits.14

docs.title: Clutch pedal adjustment (manual transmission)
docs.text:
Tags: #clutch · #manual-transmission

On the X80's manual transmission, the clutch pedal position and bite point are adjustable. The adjustment mechanism is located under the clutch pedal, at the point where the pedal assembly is mounted, and is accessible from inside the cabin 1. The procedure is similar to a Honda Civic 4D — the catch/engagement point is regulated by adjusting a mechanical stop with accessible adjustment bolts — and does not require major disassembly 2. Community members have lowered the pedal position to improve driving comfort and to make sure the clutch-position sensor engages properly. A video walkthrough of the procedure was shared in the group: https://youtu.be/XShCbog_Eak?si=kKvef1R9KhmU6f9z 345678

Clutch pedal squeak — diagnosis: first, localize the noise — squeaking felt/heard in the cabin when pressing the pedal vs. noise from under the hood point to different causes. Cabin-side squeak: check and lubricate the spring and pivot/hinge mechanism at the pedal (use proper grease, not silicone grease, which several owners noted as ineffective here) — worn spring or hinge mechanism may need replacement if lubrication doesn't resolve it. Under-hood-side noise: check the clutch fork and the slave cylinder connection point where the pushrod contacts the fork 910111213. A general troubleshooting checklist shared in the group covers the common causes in order: (1) worn clutch release/throwout bearing (most common cause of a squeak on pedal press); (2) insufficient lubrication of the pedal mechanism; (3) worn/ stretched clutch cable; (4) worn or weakened return spring; (5) improperly adjusted pedal. Recommended checks: inspect/top up lubrication in the pedal mechanism, inspect the clutch cable for wear/damage, check the return spring's condition, and adjust the pedal per the automaker's specification if needed 14.

Related but distinct issue — hard shifting into 1st/2nd gear in extreme heat, traced to clutch hydraulic fluid (2024-07 report). This is a separate clutch-system problem from the pedal-position adjustment above: in extreme heat (above 35°C), some manual-transmission owners experience poor engagement of 1st and 2nd gears — the transmission becomes difficult to shift — while performance is normal at cooler temperatures. Root cause identified by the community: the clutch hydraulic (slave/master cylinder) brake fluid degrades or partially boils at high temperature, reducing hydraulic pressure needed for clean disengagement. Fix: replace the clutch hydraulic fluid with a fresh, appropriate low-viscosity-spec fluid. One reporting owner found their fluid had turned black and was leaking; after replacement with fresh fluid, the heat-related shifting problem was resolved.15161718

docs.title: Manual clutch wear and cylinder issues
docs.text:
Tags: #clutch · #manual-transmission

Clutch wear detected at 90,000 km. One owner detected a clutch smell and noticed the pedal engagement point sitting low at 90,000 km mileage — early signs of clutch wear on the manual-transmission X80. For comparison, another owner noted their previous vehicle, a Geely Emgrand X70, lasted 300,000 km without a clutch replacement, suggesting clutch durability varies significantly by driving conditions/style rather than being a fixed X80-specific number1.

Clutch pedal travel loss with a suspected master-cylinder fluid leak. In a separate case, after a brake-pad replacement, an owner experienced a complete loss of clutch pedal travel combined with a suspected fluid leak in the clutch master cylinder. The timing right after brake work raises the possibility the two jobs are connected (e.g. disturbed fluid lines or reservoir during brake service), though this wasn't confirmed. The owner's plan was to replace the slave cylinder next2.

Clutch replacement need depends heavily on driving style — some replace at 40k km, others go much further. Consistent with the driving-condition variability already noted on this card, clutch wear/replacement need varies widely: some owners report needing a clutch replacement around 40,000 km, while others last much longer. A separate, related symptom — hard/stiff gear shifting after long drives — may indicate a worn clutch or simply insufficient hydraulic pressure rather than a transmission fault; bleeding/checking the clutch hydraulics is recommended as a cheaper first step before assuming clutch replacement is needed34567.

Hard shifting specifically when the engine is hot — clutch-wear diagnosis and a confirmed fix. A separate case with a more specific symptom pattern: the manual transmission shifts stiff/hard when the engine is warm, but smoothly when cold. Community-identified likely causes, roughly in order of what to check first: (1) low manual-transmission oil, (2) brake-fluid problems, (3) a worn clutch disc/synchros, especially with degraded spring retention. One owner confirmed that replacing the clutch fully resolved the issue, after checking (and ruling out) the cheaper transmission-oil and brake-fluid causes first891011121314.

docs.title: Cold start and fuel pressure troubleshooting
docs.text:
Tags: #cold-start · #misfire · #fuel-filter · #diagnostics

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Misfire on cold start, resolves after warmup. Engine misfires that occur on cold start but disappear after the engine warms up are likely caused by incorrect valve clearances; inspect valve clearances if the problem persists12. The symptom pattern is: rough running/misfire in the first few minutes after start, resolving as the engine heats up3.

Poor cold start after a fuel pump replacement — pressure diagnosis. After a fuel pump replacement, if the engine becomes hard to start (especially cold), possible causes include: (1) a replacement pump with the wrong pressure rating for the X80 — different pumps have different pressure specs; (2) the reverse/check valve stuck or installed in the wrong orientation; (3) kinked or restricted fuel lines; (4) fuel system pressure too low or unstable4. Recommended diagnostic: connect a fuel pressure manometer to check system pressure and its stability; inspect all fuel line connections and check-valve orientation, and verify the pump's pressure rating matches OEM spec. If a wrong-spec pump was installed, replacement with the correct part may be required5.

Poor cold start after fuel pump replacement — fuel filter cause. In a separate case, erratic cold starting persisting after fuel pump service was traced to a clogged/sludge-laden fuel filter, not the pump itself; cleaning or replacing the fuel filter normalized starting678. Owner notes this is a separate failure mode from the pump and the two should be checked independently910.

General cold-start diagnostic checklist. When cold-weather starting is poor, possible causes span: a weak battery, failing spark plugs, bad ignition coils, a failing fuel pump, a stuck check valve, a dirty fuel filter, an overly rich mixture from sensor/ECU issues, or valve clearance problems. Best practice: connect a diagnostic scanner at a professional shop to read fault codes rather than assuming a single cause1112131415.

Hard/no start after long idle — fuel system not holding pressure. Symptom: the engine cranks but won't start after sitting for a long time (12+ hours), or starts with difficulty after being parked 1-2 days; once running, it starts normally the rest of the day. Root cause: the fuel system fails to hold pressure — fuel leaks back through the return line or filter connection after shutdown. Diagnostic procedure: (1) turn on the ignition without pressing the brake, to prime the pump and build pressure; (2) turn off; (3) wait 5 seconds; (4) press the brake and turn on ignition again — if the car now starts easily, the fuel system isn't holding pressure. Fix: inspect the fuel filter connection and the rubber seal/O-ring where the return line connects — this is a known weak point on Mazda L-series-derived engines (the X80's engine family); filter replacement or seal re-seating may be needed1617181920.

Hard starting — injector flooding or throttle-body coking as alternate causes. If the engine struggles to start, especially in the first few seconds after a cold soak, also check: (1) the fuel injectors for flooding/excessive fuel delivery, verifiable with a fuel-rail pressure test; (2) the throttle body for carbon buildup/coking, which restricts airflow and causes cold-start stumbles — cleaning the throttle body helps. One owner resolved recurring hard-start issues this way, describing the engine as having "hesitated and choked" on startup until the throttle was cleaned1821.

No-start after 2+ months of storage with a dead battery — flooding diagnosis and clearing procedure. A separate case, specifically after extended storage: (1) check the spark plugs — if wet, the engine is flooded with excess fuel; if dry, fuel isn't reaching the cylinders; (2) listen for the fuel pump activating (a brief click/whirr) when the ignition is turned on; (3) check that the fuel filter isn't clogged; (4) if flooded, remove the spark plugs and crank the engine several times with the pedal to the floor to clear the excess fuel, then reinstall the plugs and attempt a restart. In this case, repeated cranking cleared the flood condition and the engine started normally afterward222324252627.

docs.title: Coolant temperature sensor location
docs.text:
Tags: #coolant · #sensor · #pre-facelift

Pre-facelift (2018, "дорест") location. On pre-facelift X80 engines, the coolant temperature sensor (ДТОЖ) is located at the rear of the engine, near the 4th cylinder, accessible from the engine side. Removal requires a 19mm socket123.

Post-facelift (restyled) location. On post-facelift ("рестайлинг") models, the sensor may instead be integrated into a triple-connector assembly (тройник) rather than standing alone in the same rear-of-engine spot — owners should search the group history for "thermostat/sensor assembly replacement" threads for exact location details specific to their model year, since the sensor's mounting point differs from the pre-facelift layout4.

docs.title: Coolant overheating — a long diagnostic case
docs.text:
Tags: #overheating · #coolant · #thermostat · #water-pump · #diagnostics · #cooling-fan

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

One owner describes struggling with a coolant-overheating problem for an entire year. Over that time they replaced, in sequence: 3 thermostats, 2 water pumps, the cooling fan assembly, and the coolant temperature sensor, plus had the radiator cleaned1. The problem was ultimately resolved only on the next (i.e. yet another/latest) thermostat replacement1. The owner's own summary: "who would have known," underscoring that the same symptom (high coolant temperature) can have multiple plausible hardware causes, and that root-causing it may require working through several components rather than assuming any single part is the culprit1.

Cooling fan activation temperature and algorithm. The main cooling fan activates at approximately 98-99°C engine temperature. A second fan activates separately for air-conditioning operation, using a different control algorithm. Frequent/unexpected fan activation is cited as a sign to investigate the thermostat, water pump, or a clogged radiator — consistent with the diagnostic case above2345.

Metal-stamping quality question (low-confidence, unresolved). In a related coolant-system exchange (same conversation discussing a possible head-gasket leak and air ingress into the cooling circuit), one owner posted a close-up photo of a stamped metal part and asked whether the visible marks were normal stamping technique or a sign of poor metal quality. No answer or resolution was captured in this data batch — flagged here as a low-confidence, open observation rather than a confirmed defect6.

Major engine/cooling rebuild — component list and radiator-swap attempt. A separate, larger repair job on a high-mileage X80 involved replacing, as part of one combined job: the engine panel, radiator, radiator cooling fan, radiator protection/shroud, black bumper cover, ventilation fans, silver trim around the radiator, narrow radiator grille, and the antifreeze/coolant itself. The owner attempted to fit a Mazda radiator (motivated by the overheating issues already documented on this card) but found the original mounting points did not match, so the original-spec radiator was retained instead. All replacement parts used were OEM. Estimated timeline for the whole job: about 1 week of actual work, extended by a 1-week holiday delay7891011121314.

docs.title: Crankcase ventilation hose and rough idle
docs.text:
Tags: #problem

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Location and common failure modes. The crankcase ventilation hose is located between the intake manifold and the engine block. Common issues: the hose isn't reinstalled correctly after service, or it cracks over time. Problems it causes: whistling sounds, breather-system malfunction, and — as the case below illustrates — rough idle and drivability symptoms serious enough to be mistaken for several other faults12345678.

Real-world case — misdiagnosed for weeks after a thermostat/intake-gasket job. After a thermostat and intake-manifold-gasket replacement, one owner (Ксения) experienced: rough idle (RPM staying elevated), jerking on acceleration, a stiff brake pedal, and a non-functional handbrake in Park. A long diagnostic thread considered — and ruled out — throttle-sensor adjustment, the idle air control sensor, spark plugs not fully seated, missing electrical/ground connections, intake-manifold gasket misalignment, and a broken gasket seal leaking coolant into electrical circuits, before the crankcase ventilation hose was found disconnected — the actual root cause. Reconnecting it resolved every symptom9101112131415161718192021222324252627282930313233343536373839404142434445464748495051525354555615758592360616263. Conflict/lesson: multiple plausible diagnoses were proposed and pursued (idle sensor, spark plugs, electrical connections, gasket seal leak) before the crankcase ventilation hose was identified as the actual cause — after any service that disturbs the intake manifold area, checking this hose first can save significant diagnostic time.

Throttle response failure — traced to vacuum-system leak, not just crankcase hose. A separate but related symptom: the gas pedal becomes unresponsive on all pedals (throttle and brake) simultaneously, causing fuel-injection control issues. Likely causes: vacuum-booster failure or a ruptured crankcase-ventilation hose (consistent with the hose failures already documented on this card). Solution: inspect all vacuum hoses on the intake tract for splits or damage, especially the crankcase-ventilation hose; this may require removing the intake manifold for a proper inspection. A FAW service visit is recommended for diagnosis if the issue isn't found by visual inspection646566.

Hissing noise only when hot — loose crankcase-ventilation tube. A separate report: a hissing/whistling sound near the throttle-body area appears only once the engine is warmed up. Cause: the crankcase-ventilation tube (routing blow-by gases) under the intake manifold works loose or partially detaches; it may also cause a slight RPM fluctuation. No dashboard error is logged. A full fix requires intake-manifold removal (labor-intensive — see the dedicated intake-manifold-removal card), but re-tightening the connection from underneath may be enough676869707172.

Jerking at low throttle traced to a cracked coolant/intake tube near the thermostat. In a separate case, jerking in traffic when lightly touching the pedals was traced — during an unrelated thermostat replacement — to a cracked tube running from the thermostat to the intake manifold. Replacing the cracked tube resolved the jerking. Tip noted in the same thread: when refilling coolant, raise the hood and pour slowly to avoid trapping air pockets737475.

No PCV valve at all — the X80 ships with a dummy plug where a Ford Mondeo has a real valve. A detailed diagnostic thread establishes that the X80 has no functioning crankcase-ventilation (PCV) valve — the valve cover has only an empty housing with a dummy tube plugged in where the equivalent Ford Mondeo PCV valve would sit. This is identified as a likely contributor to rough idle/jerking around 1200-1500 RPM, compounded by the X80's electronic throttle pedal: ECU-to-throttle signal transmission has a perceptible delay (one owner reports that on light pedal input the throttle sometimes doesn't seem to open at all — driving with a very light foot can paradoxically feel smoother, "but it shouldn't have to work that way"), and under this theory the fuel/air mixture correction lags the crankcase-pressure swings enough to produce a jerk. Temporary workaround: partially constrict (pinch) the ventilation hose with a small clip, reducing flow by roughly 50% — one owner (Фаб) reported this measurably reduced bogging/hesitation on throttle tip-in and gearshifts, though some light throttle-off twitching remained; this is a single anecdotal report, not a confirmed fix. Permanent fix: source and install a genuine Ford Mondeo PCV valve (~1,000 RUB, RU market, June 2026, via Chinese marketplaces reachable over VPN; not listed on Ozon). Owners who installed the Mondeo valve and also cleaned the MAP sensor (see the MAP-sensor card) report reduced jerking and smoother AT shifting. A related design flaw noted in the same thread: the intake manifold sits low on this engine and accumulates sludge over time, and by ~140,000 km the EGR valve is typically fouled with oil sludge as a result (see the EGR card)7677787980818283848586878889909192. Conflict: one member questioned whether the missing-PCV-valve theory actually holds and whether a muffler/exhaust modification might be the real fix instead — not resolved in this batch.

Rough running and elevated fuel consumption in hot weather — same root-cause cluster. Multiple owners separately report the engine running roughly ("like a diesel"), with increased fuel consumption and rough/jerky idle around 1200-1300 RPM, specifically when ambient temperature rises in summer — despite no stored error codes and normal-testing sensors. This is attributed to the same crankcase-ventilation design flaw, intake-manifold sludge buildup, and a MAP/MAF sensor needing cleaning, all already documented on this card9394958788969798.

Intake-manifold air leak — smoke-test diagnosis. A separate but related case: no error codes were present, but an air leak was traced to the intake-manifold gaskets using a smoke generator (дымогенератор) — smoke visibly escaped around the manifold, confirming the leak point. A replacement silicone gasket kit (5 gaskets, for Mazda/Ford-compatible intake manifolds) costs roughly 500-1,000 RUB (RU market, June 2026) on Ozon; full disassembly of the intake manifold is required (see also the engine-gasket cross-compatibility card)969799100.

Ford donor part number for the crankcase ventilation tube. Consistent with the "no real PCV valve" finding already on this card, one owner (Сергей Елисеев) gives a concrete Ford cross-reference part number for the crankcase-ventilation tube itself (патрубок картерных газов): 1440473 (also listed as FMVQ PTP024589). Symptom pattern matches the rest of this card: a hissing/whistling noise from the engine bay plus fluctuating idle speed points to this tube being clogged or cracked101.

Cold-start roaring/rocking noise — cracked intake bypass tube, inherited from Ford Focus 2 — from the second Telegram group. A separate community (FAW BESTURN X80 group) reports a distinct but related symptom: a loud roaring/rocking sound on cold start or rapid acceleration. The likely cause given: a cracked intake-manifold bypass tube or hose — described as a documented issue inherited from the Ford Focus 2 platform (the same lineage discussed elsewhere on this card for crankcase-ventilation/intake components). The tube/hose part itself is inexpensive, but replacement is reported as difficult, requiring removal of significant surrounding components. An alternative diagnosis offered in the same thread: the noise could instead originate from the timing chain/tensioner area at the front of the engine, more likely at higher mileage, rather than the intake tube — the two causes were not definitively distinguished in this exchange102103104105106.

Where the community disagrees

  • A long diagnostic thread pursued multiple plausible causes (idle air control sensor, spark plugs, electrical/ground connections, gasket seal coolant leak) for rough idle and jerking after a thermostat/intake-gasket service, before the actual root cause — a disconnected crankcase ventilation hose between the intake manifold and block — was identified. Documented here as a diagnostic lesson, not an unresolved factual conflict.
