docs.title: Engine identity — Duratec HE lineage
docs.text:
Tags: #mazda-6-compat

The FAW Besturn X80's engine is identified in the group as a Duratec HE design, of Ford/Mazda origin — parts cross-compatible with Ford and Mazda models are generally expected to fit given this shared lineage1.

"2.3 / 3.0" confusion, clarified. A side discussion arose over whether a 2.3L or 3.0L variant exists for the X80. One member initially suggested a part "might be from the 2.3 engine, or diesel, or maybe 3.0 — needs comparing"2. Another member pushed back sharply, stating there is no such thing as a 2.3 or 3.0 X80 and that this confusion comes from conflating Mazda's engine lineup (which does include 2.3L variants) with the X80 itself3. The original commenter then clarified they meant that Mazda models carry a 2.3, while the X80 has its own single engine configuration4. Net takeaway: displacement variants like 2.3/3.0 belong to the Mazda side of the shared engine family, not to the X80 itself, which has one primary engine configuration1234.

Cross-manufacturer parts sourcing, restated. The X80 uses the Ford Duratec HE 2.0L engine, paired with an AISIN 09G automatic transmission — the same transmission family used in Volkswagen and Mazda vehicles. Parts availability from Ford and Mazda specialists is generally good; some suspension and engine service specs can also be found by consulting Ford/Mazda manuals5678.

Reliability track record. The Duratec HE engine (also installed in various Ford, Mazda, and Volvo models) has a proven reliability record within the community, with some example units reportedly exceeding 500,000 km. Minor oil consumption is possible on some units but is not considered characteristic of the design. Overall durability is described as good, despite some early market skepticism when the X80 was newer91011.

Transmission model identity — conflicting names across sources. Several distinct model/family names have been used in the group for the X80's automatic transmission at different times, and they do not agree with each other: - Aisin 09G — described as the same family used in Volkswagen vehicles12. - Aisin Seiki F21 (2nd generation), alongside a 6-speed manual (МКПП Standard) as the other drivetrain option; manufacturer-claimed fuel consumption of 8.2 L/100km, against a real-world average closer to 9.5 L/100km13. - TF-70SC — shown in a photographed table comparing FAW/Besturn model-lineup engines, drivetrains, and transmission codes, with the X80 (2014+, 1.8L engine row) listed against TF-70SC14.

Conflict — transmission model name unresolved. These three labels (Aisin 09G, Aisin Seiki F21, TF-70SC) may refer to the same physical unit under different naming conventions (e.g. an internal Aisin code vs. a marketing/comparison-table code), or may reflect genuine confusion/drift in what different sources call the transmission — not resolved within this KB. The AKPP fluid-specification card separately notes a "4-speed" designation on an official approvals document, adding a fourth data point that doesn't cleanly match a "6-speed" description used elsewhere. Cross-check against an authoritative Aisin/FAW parts catalog before relying on any single name.

Power/torque specs by variant — CA4GD1 (naturally aspirated) and CA4GC18T (turbo). Per an official specifications table: the naturally-aspirated gasoline engine CA4GD1 EFI produces max power 104 kW @ 6500 rpm (nominal 108 kW @ 6500 rpm) and torque 184 N·m @ 4000 rpm, capable of climbing grades over 30%; manual-transmission top speed 185 km/h, automatic 180 km/h. The turbocharged variant CA4GC18T EFI produces max power 132 kW @ 5500-6000 rpm (nominal 137 kW @ 5500-6000 rpm) and torque 235 N·m @ 2000-4500 rpm, also capable of climbing grades over 30%, with a top speed of 198 km/h15.

Naturally-aspirated engine — inherent low-RPM torque limitation. The 2.0L naturally-aspirated CA4GD1 produces adequate torque only above roughly 3000 RPM — full dynamic performance requires revving the engine, and lazy low-RPM driving feels slow. This is described as inherent to atmospheric (non-turbo) engines generally, not a fault. Turbocharged 1.5T-2.0T variants are cited as the manufacturer's answer for better low-end torque and responsiveness across a wider RPM range; the naturally-aspirated X80 is characterized as tuned for comfort/practicality rather than spirited driving1617.

Same engine across MT and AT variants — mount and parts implications. FAW X80 automatic-transmission (AT) and manual-transmission (MT) models share the same engine (2.0L, 142 hp). As a result, engine mounts are identical between MT and AT variants, and parts sourced by transmission-type designation should be compatible as long as the same engine is used1819202122232425. Conflict: one user reported 147 hp specifically for the automatic variant, but others in the same thread confirmed all X80 models are rated 142 hp; the discrepancy is unresolved.

Community summary — Aisin 6-speed AT, Mazda 6 GH engine lineage, and a body-corrosion note. A concise community summary restates and adds to the identity picture on this card: the automatic transmission is described as an Aisin 6-speed unit, considered reliable — a data point relevant to (but not fully resolving) the transmission-naming conflict already documented above. The engine is described simply as Mazda 6 GH 2.0L, consistent with the Duratec HE/Mazda lineage already established on this card. Separately (outside this card's engine/transmission scope but noted for context): suspension components are described as partially sourced from Mazda 6 GG and GH models, and while the body is factory-galvanized, additional anticorrosion treatment is recommended for the underbody, doors, hood, trunk, wheel arches, and door sills2627.

Platform lineage restated — historical Mazda origin, cross-compat implications. Restating and reinforcing the Ford/Mazda lineage already established on this card: the X80's motor is historically derived from Mazda, and the X80 shares its platform base with the FAW B50. This shared origin is why parts/oils formulated for Mazda's GG-generation models (CX-5, Mazda 6 GG) may fit or apply to some X80 components — platform-sharing is the key mechanism to keep in mind when evaluating any claimed cross-compatibility2829.

Aisin automatic transmission and Mazda 6 engine — independent confirmations from the second Telegram group. A separate community (FAW BESTURN X80 group) independently reconfirms two identity facts already established on this card: the automatic transmission is a Japanese-made Aisin unit, described by one owner as "reliable, nothing more so" ("Надёжнее некуда")3031; and the engine is described simply as "like the one in a Mazda 6" ("Двигатель как на Мазда 6 стоит"), consistent with the Duratec HE/Mazda-6 lineage already documented on this card32.

Mazda 6 (pre-2006) platform and parts compatibility, plus a differing view on parts availability — from the second Telegram group. Further independent confirmation from the second group: the X80 platform is described as based on the Mazda 6 (pre-2006 generation), with many suspension, drivetrain, and engine consumables/parts from that Mazda 6 era reported as compatible or direct replacements — owners report using Mazda 6 parts with no issues, consistent with the Mazda-6-GG-generation cross-compatibility already documented on this card3334. Conflict — parts availability perception. This confirmation of good cross-compatibility contrasts with a separate, more skeptical inquiry in the same thread from a prospective buyer who was hesitant about the X80 specifically because parts availability seemed "scarce" ("по наличию запчастей как-то скудно"), especially body panels — suggesting owner experience on parts availability may vary by part category (consumables/drivetrain vs. body panels) rather than being uniformly good or bad35.

Where the community disagrees

  • This KB records at least four different transmission-model labels for the X80's automatic transmission at different points: "Aisin 09G", "Aisin Seiki F21 (2nd gen)", "TF-70SC", and a "4-speed" JWS 3309/3314 approval document (see the AKPP fluid-specification card). These may be different names for the same unit or may reflect real confusion in the community. Not resolved within this KB — verify against an authoritative Aisin/FAW parts catalog before relying on any single label.
  • One user reported 147 hp for the automatic-transmission variant specifically, but multiple other owners in the same thread confirmed all X80 models (MT and AT) are rated 142 hp. Not resolved within this data batch.
  • One thread reports good Mazda-6 cross-compatibility for suspension/drivetrain/engine consumables, while a separate, unrelated inquiry in the same batch reflects a prospective buyer's concern that parts (especially body panels) seemed scarce. Not a direct factual contradiction — likely reflects a difference between consumable/mechanical parts (good availability via Mazda cross-fit) and body/cosmetic parts (perceived as scarcer) — not resolved within this data batch.

docs.title: Engine and gearbox wiring diagram component codes
docs.text:
Tags: #reference · #wiring-diagram

Electrical wiring diagram (EWD) pages shared in the group name the engine-control and gearbox-control components of the three engine variants. Component codes (E9, F6, ...) are the diagram's own labels. The text extracted from the PDFs is layout-scrambled, so pin-level wiring is not captured; open the PDF for pin numbers.

2.0 L engine (EWD page 1101, file Z001 ECM 2.0.pdf). Intake air pressure/temperature sensor E9, electronic throttle valve body EN5, camshaft position sensor EN6, engine water (coolant) temperature sensor W1, speed sensor E13, accelerator pedal sensor R22, knock sensor E16, EGR valve F10, front and rear oxygen sensors F6 and F7, canister solenoid valve F29, intake manifold long/short solenoid valve F5, intake tumble control solenoid valve F9, OCV (oil control valve) solenoid valve E3, fuel injectors EN1-EN4 ("Nozzle 1-4") and ignition coils F1-F4. The ECU is labelled ECU11.

1.8T engine (page 1102, Z002.pdf). Electric throttle valve body E28, accelerator pedal sensor R22, camshaft position sensor E25, knock sensor E32, speed sensor E33, air mass flow meter E27, boost pressure sensor F48, brake vacuum sensor F47, ambient pressure sensor E35, A/C pressure sensor F41, canister E36, electronic vacuum pump, electric water pump, front and rear oxygen sensors F44 and F43, injectors E17, E19, E21, E23 and ignition coils E18, E20, E22, E24. Some labels are marked "(!2.0L)", possibly meaning parts not used on the 2.0 L2.

1.8TD engine (page 1103, Z003.pdf). Injectors ENT1-ENT4, ignition coils E48, E50, E57, E58, knock sensor E73, front oxygen sensor E60, rear oxygen sensor F37, crankshaft and camshaft sensors, rail pressure sensor ENT5, speed sensor E53, electric throttle valve body E69, intake air pressure/temperature sensors E61 and E62 (before and after the throttle), coolant temperature sensor, intake OCV, canister, supercharger and accelerator pedal sensor R22. Some labels are ambiguous3.

Actuators per variant (page 1115, Z015.pdf). 2.0 L: injectors 1-4, ignition coils 1-4, EGR solenoid valve, intake manifold long/short switch, intake tumble control solenoid valve, OCV valve, canister solenoid valve. 1.8T: injectors 1-4, ignition coils 1-4, exhaust gas control valve, air mass flow meter, variable camshaft timing, canister solenoid valve. 1.8TD: ignition coils 1-4, supercharger control solenoid valve, intake bypass valve, exhaust OCV valve, intake OCV valve, canister solenoid valve. The page also lists the front and rear oxygen sensor heaters of each variant; the ECU pin mapping is not recoverable from the text4.

Oil pressure switch connectors (page 1120, Z020 IC.pdf). E15 on the 2.0 L, E8 on the 1.8T and E71 on the 1.8TD; brake fluid level sensor connector F8 sits on the brake fluid reservoir. The same page lists the gateway control units (131 and 132), the anti-theft controller (161), the generator (118, see page 1112), the PKE (keyless entry) controller (162) and the spiral cable (97 and 99)5.

2nd-generation automatic transmission (page 1104, Z004 TCM.pdf). TCU-controlled parts: pressure control solenoid valves for Clutch 1, Clutch 2 and Brake 1, the main oil line pressure control solenoid valve, a lock control solenoid valve, shift solenoid valves 1 and 2, an oil temperature sensor, input and output torque sensors, a gear position switch, shift switch R33, multi-function switch F25 and the oil temperature and speed sensor F26. The TCU connector is labelled AT and the page cross-references ECU (1.8T) and ECU (2.0L). Ignition switch positions OFF, ACC, IG1, IG2, ST and SL are shown6.

3rd-generation automatic transmission, 1.8TD (page 1105, Z005 TCM.pdf). Pressure control solenoid valves for Clutch 1, 2 and 3 and Brake 1, main oil line pressure solenoid, lock control solenoid, shift solenoid valves 1 and 2, oil temperature sensor, input and output torque sensors, select position switch F23 (positions P, R, N, D, S), multi-function switch F28, oil temperature and speed sensor F34, shift switch R33, battery sensor F54, DC/DC converter F50 and the back-up (reverse) light relay7.

See also engine variants and engine identity.

docs.title: Exhaust flex tube (gofra) replacement
docs.text:
Tags: #exhaust · #price · #part-number · #conflict

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Community members disagree on this topic — both positions are reported.

Correct size — resolved conflict. The correct exhaust flex tube ("gofra") size is 55×120mm, NOT 50×100mm, despite some online sources and kitparts.ru listing the smaller size. Some sources (an older chat discussion, a Drive2 post) had claimed 55×120mm; kitparts.ru listed 50×100mm. Community measurement and consensus: 55×120mm is correct, and 50×100mm may be undersized for this application. When ordering, explicitly specify 55×120. Verify fitment with calipers — the original muffler connection point measures approximately 54mm diameter.12345678910111213141516171819202122232425

Replacement trigger. If the gofra shows visible damage (starting to burn through), replacement is needed. Installation requires welding.12345678910111213141516171819202122232425

Cost. Podolsk region (Moscow suburbs): 1,200 RUB for the gofra part + 1,500 RUB labor (~15 minutes of work) (RU market, June 2025). Moscow city cost was reported higher, at 7,500 RUB total (RU market, June 2025) for the same job — significant regional price variance.12345678910111213141516171819202122232425

Product example. TRIALLI FT 0018 is a 55×120mm stainless-steel vibration compensator/flex tube with wire-mesh reinforcement (Hydra brand line), available on Ozon.ru. Owners inquiring about this part have compared metal-braided gofra options against other construction types.2425

Second product example — reinforced interlock hose (2025-11 report). A separate reinforced/interlocking exhaust gofra, brand EuroEX, part 55x120il, matching the community-confirmed 55×120mm size above, is available on Ozon.26

docs.title: Exhaust heat shield repair options
docs.text:
Tags: #exhaust · #heat-shield

The undercarriage heat shield (thermal screen) protects the cabin from exhaust heat. Options: (1) replace it with a compatible shield sourced from any compatible donor vehicle body; (2) DIY-repair the existing shield with a high-temperature silicone sealant, specifically T-7000 PRO, if it's cracked/degraded rather than missing. Either approach prevents heat transfer into the interior. Source consulted: Yury T, a local expert based in Tolyatti 12345.

docs.title: Floating idle RPM — throttle position sensor
docs.text:
Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Symptoms: idle RPM fluctuates between roughly 1600–4000, and the engine revs up uncontrollably even with the brake pedal held down 1 23. This happened on a pre-facelift automatic-transmission car right after starting it 1.

Potential causes raised by the community: a throttle position sensor (TPS) signal loss or grounding issue — specifically, poor contact to ground at the TPS can cause this, based on a similar case on a different vehicle 456; a MAF (mass airflow) sensor fault; a coolant/ДТОЖ temperature sensor feeding false readings to the ECU, causing a false "cold start" enrichment; or a blocked/dirty crankcase-ventilation hose 74. A computer diagnostic scan can show the throttle position and other live values to narrow this down 89. Suggested remedies, in rough order of being tried: a full diagnostic scan first; throttle-body cleaning (a dealer throttle-wash appointment was booked in this case); DTOZH/MAF sensor replacement if the scan points there 101112. Note: in this specific case the temperature gauge itself displayed normally throughout, which the owner treated as evidence against (but not proof against) a coolant-sensor cause 13.

Conflict: multiple plausible causes were debated without an on-record confirmed fix in this thread — throttle sensor, DTOZH, MAF, and crankcase ventilation were all raised, and a diagnostic scan was recommended to narrow it down rather than guessing 11168.

Baseline healthy idle parameters, for comparison. As a reference point for what a normal, non-floating idle looks like: on a healthy 2019 model-year (post-facelift) engine, cold idle sits around ~930 RPM with 21.3% engine load as read on an OBD2 scanner, with the lambda-sensor reading near stoichiometric. Owners troubleshooting floating/surging idle can use these figures as a rough sanity check against their own OBD2 readings 1415.

Revs rise by themselves when the clutch is pressed. An owner describes a video in which the engine revs on its own when the clutch is pressed, with no throttle input. Advice: switch off, remove the intake hose at the throttle body and check the throttle flap position, since debris under the flap can hold it open1617.

docs.title: Fuel consumption factors and dashboard display
docs.text:
Tags: #fuel-consumption · #dashboard · #automatic-transmission

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Typical consumption and influencing factors. Reported typical fuel consumption: about 7 L/100km on the highway, up to 12 L/100km in city driving1. One owner cautions that self-reported consumption figures circulating in the group aren't always reliable (someone claimed as low as 5 L/100km)1. Factors cited as affecting consumption: fuel quality/brand (95 octane isn't always genuinely better — sometimes it's "just additives")12, driving style, wind direction/strength, tire pressure, wheel diameter and weight, engine cleanliness, and the vehicle's Euro emissions standard (the X80 is Euro 5)1. One owner reported roughly 11.9 L/100km as their approximate figure and considers 95 octane normal for their driving23.

High-mileage oil consumption vs. EGR. At around 170,000 km, one owner observed increased oil consumption (burning through about 5,000 km of fill) and wondered whether this might indicate worn piston rings rather than an EGR-related issue; another owner replied it's hard to say — at 170K km "it could be anything"45.

Hydrogen engine cleaning. One owner performed a hydrogen-based engine/intake cleaning service and reported a noticeable improvement: idle RPM became livelier, revs climbed more readily on throttle (closer to manual-transmission responsiveness), versus sluggish 3-3.5 RPM movement on brief throttle blips beforehand. The service also cleans the throttle body and intake system. Cost: about 3,000 RUB (RU market, September 2024), ~1 hour; recommended every 15,000 km, especially after 100,000 km mileage6.

Fuel-warning-light reserve range. When the low-fuel warning light comes on, the car can typically continue for about 60-70 km under normal driving, with 70 km cited as the average/consensus figure by two respondents; actual range varies with speed, load, and terrain789. The exact trigger threshold for the warning light is configurable in the dashboard menu — one owner set theirs to trigger at 120 km of estimated remaining range instead of the default, noting "however you set it, that's how far you'll go" (i.e. the range shown is itself an estimate, not a fixed guarantee)1011.

Dashboard consumption display modes. The dashboard offers two separate, independently resettable trip-consumption trackers, L1 and L2 — their only purpose is to allow separate trip periods to be tracked/reset independently; if neither is reset, both display identical consumption figures121314. Separately, there are two different consumption readouts: an instantaneous/momentary consumption meter (reflecting consumption at that exact moment — e.g. showing ~20 L/100km during hard acceleration is normal and not a fault) and an average consumption figure over the trip/distance15. The remaining-range display ("Остаток пробега" / estimated distance on remaining fuel) is separate from the L1/L2 trip-consumption trackers10.

Manufacturer claim vs. real-world average. The manufacturer's claimed average fuel consumption is 8.2 L/100km, but the real-world community average is closer to 9.5 L/100km16.

Real-world data by fuel type and driving condition (gasoline, automatic). City driving: 11.6-12.1 L/100km (varies by driving style), with one report of 14.3 L/100km in heavy stop-and-go city traffic — that figure already includes a 7% correction for the speedometer's known over-reading. Highway driving: roughly 9 L/100km. On LPG/propane with a properly installed system: 10-11.5 L/100km in the city; a poorly installed system can push consumption as high as 16 L/100km. Consumption is heavily influenced by driving style, engine calibration/tuning, and vehicle load. Note: the speedometer reads roughly 7% high, which affects any consumption figures derived from odometer/speed readings unless corrected171819202122.

LPG cost-efficiency despite higher volumetric consumption. Propane (LPG/LPO) consumes 1-2 liters more per 100 km than gasoline, but its significantly lower per-liter cost makes overall running cost lower. Community consensus: despite the higher volume consumed, LPG remains economically advantageous for high-mileage owners212324.

Additional consumption data points and cluster-accuracy note (batch restated). Further owner reports gathered separately: city driving on AT ranges 12-14 L/100km, highway/mixed 9-12 L/100km depending on style; the instrument cluster's fuel-economy gauge is reported to understate actual consumption by roughly 1 L/100km — actual consumption should be computed fill-to-fill (fuel volume ÷ odometer distance) for accuracy, since the speedometer itself also reads high (see the speedometer/top-speed card)252627282930313233343536373839404142. One AKPP owner at ~58,500 km reports a consistent 14 L/100km in mixed city/highway driving — well above the manufacturer's claimed ~10 L/100km max — despite testing 95-octane fuel and varying driving style; manual-transmission owners in the same batch report 7.2-8.2 L/100km highway and 9-12 L/100km city434445.

Consumption by driving mode and condition (restated). Consumption depends heavily on driving style, load, tire pressure, road type, and oil quality. Careful highway driving on AKPP achieves 7-8 L/100km; winter consumption rises to 13 L/100km; city driving ranges 8-12 L/100km depending on traffic. Turbocharged 1.5T-2.0T variants were reported to be in development by the manufacturer for better low-end torque46474849.

Fuel consumption data from individual fill-to-fill logs. Highway driving at a constant 110 km/h (manual transmission), on a full tank: roughly 30L per 500km (≈16.7 L/100km). In summer, a full tank on the highway without refilling can reach roughly 700km without hitting the reserve. City driving (commute/errands): roughly 60L for 470km (≈12.8 L/100km). Actual economy varies significantly by driving style and conditions5051525354.

95 vs. 92 octane consumption, with a roof box. With a roof rack box installed and highway cruising at 108 km/h, one owner measured approximately 9.2 L/100km on 95-octane fuel versus 9.8 L/100km on 92-octane — a gap reportedly narrowing on longer trips past 200,000 km on the odometer. The owner planned to standardize on 95-octane going forward55.

Octane rating — no benefit above 95. The Duratec HE engine runs fine on both 92 and 95 octane. Testing with 100-octane fuel showed no improvement in dynamics or fuel consumption versus 95; some owners blend 95+100 in roughly a 70/30 ratio for high-speed driving, but running pure 100 continuously was reported to increase consumption with no offsetting performance gain5657585960616263646566676869707172.

Speed-dependent highway consumption table (2.0L AT, 142hp). Real-world consumption on the automatic 2.0L atmospheric (142hp) engine at steady highway speeds: 100 km/h = 8.6 L/100km; 110 km/h = 9.4 L/100km; 120 km/h = 10.1 L/100km; 130 km/h = 9.2 L/100km; 140 km/h = 8.7 L/100km (with cruise control engaged in D mode — the non-monotonic pattern above 120 km/h is as reported). Other owners cite 9-10 L/100km as typical mixed-driving consumption. Fuel used: 92 octane (AI-92)7374757677.

Consumption by transmission type, restated with concrete figures. Manual-transmission 2019 model: 12.5-12.7 L/100km in active city driving on 95 RON fuel. Automatic 2020 model: highway consumption ranges 7.8-22 L/100km depending heavily on speed (higher speed = disproportionately higher consumption); city driving with frequent stops runs 12.5-14 L/100km, also on 95 RON787980.

High-speed consumption and top-speed behavior. At a sustained ~200 km/h, the instantaneous consumption display shows 29 L/100km, with calculated consumption closer to ~17 L/100km (subjectively it feels even higher). The factory speed limiter is 180 km/h (reported reflashable to roughly 200 km/h). One report of a maximum speed of 221 km/h reached downhill, with 175-180 km/h confirmed achievable on level ground. Steering precision is reported to degrade above 200 km/h818283848586.

Typical consumption range and variables, restated with a computer-vs-actual gap. City driving: 12-12.7 L/100km (the trip computer shows a lower figure than actual; the ~12.7 L/100km actual figure was verified via fuel-pump/fill checks). Summer highway: 7.8-8 L/100km. Summer city/mixed: 10.5-11 L/100km. Variables affecting the figures: driving style, road condition, tire pressure, fuel quality, trip length, and number of cold starts per day. A 2019 mechanical (manual) X80 reported 12.7 L/100km city, 8 L/100km highway. Overall, the dashboard fuel computer under-reports; real consumption typically sums to 12-13.5 L/100km in mixed use87888990919293949596979899100101.

Manual-transmission consumption — restated with a wider range including a very low outlier. Additional manual-transmission data points, consistent with the manual-vs-automatic split already on this card: 13-14 L/100km in city driving with A/C running, 9-9.5 L/100km on highway driving (not exceeding 110 km/h). Consumption varies with trip pattern — short ~8km trips consume more per 100km than longer highway runs — and with fuel quality. One owner with mixed Moscow-region driving reported a notably lower 8-9 L/100km, on the low end of what's typically reported for this transmission type102103104105106.

Automatic-transmission city consumption — restated. A separate automatic-transmission data point, consistent with figures already on this card: approximately 10.5 L/100km in city driving, again varying with driving behavior and fuel quality107108.

2.0L naturally-aspirated engine — city figures, verified-at-pump vs. dashboard gap, tire-size effect. For the 2.0L naturally aspirated engine specifically: typical city consumption 7-10 L/100km, up from a previously reported 5-6 L/100km in an earlier year — consumption varies by driving conditions and traffic. One owner's actual verified consumption (calculated from fuel volume added at the pump, not the onboard trip computer, which under-reads by roughly 4-5%) was 8-10 L/100km in city driving — consistent with the computer-vs-actual gap already documented on this card. Larger tire size is noted as reducing fuel economy. For comparison, a Mazda CX-5 2.0L with AWD reportedly shows a similar 10+ L/100km in city driving109110111112113114.

Fuel-grade choice and octane recommendation — restated with a community split figure. Factory recommendation is 92 RON (АИ-92); chipped/tuned engines require 95+ to avoid knocking. On non-chipped engines, 92 is sufficient — no measurable power difference, and 95 costs more for negligible benefit. Fuel quality/brand is reported to matter more than octane rating alone; consumption is relatively stable across grades. Community split: roughly 80% use 92 RON. Switching between 92/95 is acceptable, but mixing grades within one tank is not considered ideal. Common brands cited: Rosneft, Gazprom, Tatneft, Lukoil, Shell. Conflict: some owners report better highway performance on 95, others see no difference; some chipped cars need 95+ specifically to prevent knocking — consistent with the octane debate already implicit elsewhere on this card115116117118119120121122123124125126127128129130131132133134135136137138139140141142143144145146147148149150151.

Transmission-type consumption correlation, S-mode vs. D-mode. An earlier data point on the AKPP-vs-manual split already documented on this card: AKPP typically 10.3-12.5 L/100km city, 7.5-9 L/100km highway; manual 9.6-10.3 L/100km city, 7.2-7.9 L/100km highway. Cruise control in S mode may show better consumption than D mode despite similar gear selection. Individual factors — driving style, A/C use, oil viscosity, spark plug condition, fuel quality/brand — all significantly affect the numbers152139140141142143148.

City vs. highway spread — an earlier, independent figure. A separate, earlier report: highway 7-8.5 L/100km (smooth cruising), city 10.5-12.5 L/100km (stop-start traffic). AKPP models show similar or slightly higher consumption than manual in this comparison. Fuel grade (92 vs. 95) affects economy less than driving mode does153154155.

Highway speed and economy — 130-140 km/h beats a steady 120 km/h. One comparison found highway driving at 130-140 km/h gives better fuel economy (8.5-9 L/100km) than a steady 120 km/h (9.5-10 L/100km) — suggesting the engine sits in a more efficient operating range at the slightly higher speed, likely due to lower throttle position and more favorable injection mapping at that RPM/load combination156157.

Fuel consumption estimate — restated (2.0L). A later, independent estimate: highway at 120 km/h roughly 10-11 L/100km; city 11-13 L/100km. Premium 95-octane fuel may provide slightly better economy than 92, potentially saving on the order of 50 RUB per tank (RU market, August 2024) — a marginal effect consistent with the octane debate documented above on this card158.

Consumption change after intake/exhaust service — within normal variation, not a mechanical regression. One owner replaced a cracked crankcase-ventilation tube (6-7cm crack), cleaned the intake manifold and throttle body, and changed spark plugs (gap 1.3→1.1mm), then reported a +0.5 L/100km consumption increase over 1,000 km. Conflict: the owner was concerned this indicated a problem from the service work, but community consensus in the thread holds this is within normal measurement variation (city 10.5-12.5 L/100km, highway 7.1-9.0 L/100km spread already seen elsewhere on this card) and likely reflects subjective perception rather than an actual mechanical regression159160161162163164.

Automatic-transmission consumption breakdown, including winter penalty — from the second Telegram group. A separate community (FAW BESTURN X80 group) reports, for 2.0L automatic: highway (≈70% of driving) 9-10 L/100km; city/mixed 10-13 L/100km; winter with pre-heating cycles 15-16 L/100km — a substantial cold-weather penalty of +3-5 L/100km versus warm-engine operation. The dashboard fuel gauge is again reported to under-read actual consumption, by roughly 0.5-1.5 L/100km165166167168169170171172.

Manual-transmission consumption — from the second Telegram group. From the same separate community: 2.0L manual — highway 7.5-9 L/100km; city summer 8.8-9.2 L/100km; city with A/C ~10 L/100km. Manual transmission is again reported roughly 2-3 L/100km better than automatic in comparable conditions, consistent with the transmission-type split already documented on this card171173174175.

City consumption at 30,000 km, automatic transmission — same second Telegram group. The same second community (FAW BESTURN X80 group) reports 11.7 L/100km in city driving at 30,000 km mileage on an automatic-transmission car, consistent with the AKPP city-consumption range already documented on this card. Community reply: this figure is normal for the model and reflects early break-in — smoother driving can improve it somewhat, but a genuinely lower consumption (e.g. matching a Kia Rio 1.4-1.6) isn't realistic for this car176177.

Engine noticeably quieter on Euro 5 (higher-sulfur) fuel — single, low-confidence report. One owner observed the engine running significantly quieter after refueling with Euro 5 grade petrol (described as containing "7.7 sulfur content," likely a shorthand for a specific sulfur spec rather than a standard Euro-5 figure — treat as reported, not verified). The owner noted the change was immediate, on a fill of 40+ liters, while driving the M2 highway near Moscow (2026-09-05). This is a single anecdotal report with no fuel-brand or consumption-figure comparison given — confidence: low178.

Where the community disagrees

  • Fuel-grade debate: factory recommends 92 RON, ~80% of the community uses 92; some owners report better highway performance on 95, others see no difference, and chipped/tuned cars specifically need 95+ to prevent knocking. Not resolved within this data batch.
  • One owner was concerned a +0.5 L/100km consumption increase after intake/exhaust service (crankcase tube replacement, intake/throttle cleaning, spark plug gap change) indicated a problem; community consensus in the thread holds this is within normal measurement variation rather than a mechanical regression. Not a fully resolved factual conflict, documented as a diagnostic-interpretation disagreement.

docs.title: Fuel injectors — cleaning and reliability
docs.text:
Tags: #cleaning · #maintenance-interval · #conflict

Community members disagree on this topic — both positions are reported.

Proactive cleaning recommendation. One guide recommends cleaning fuel injectors every 15,000 km to prevent carburetion issues; by 60,000 km, injectors may start malfunctioning (spraying a stream instead of atomizing a fine mist), which can cause rough idle, misfires, and performance loss. Professional cleaning on a test bench is recommended over a fuel additive12.

Proper methodology — diagnose before cleaning. A separate, more methodical view: don't clean blindly — first test the spray pattern and flow rate to establish whether cleaning is actually needed. Effective methods include professional bench testing with specialized equipment, ultrasonic-bath cleaning with chemical agents, or fuel-system pressure testing. Direct in-field cleaning with additive chemicals is considered less effective and not recommended without first diagnosing an actual injector problem34.

Counter-experience — injectors rarely fail, fuel quality does more of the work. A separate, more optimistic report states X80 fuel injectors are typically in good condition and rarely fail — with high-quality fuel acting as a natural cleaning agent over time. More common fuel-system problems, per this view, are fuel filter degradation and fuel pump failure, rather than injector clogging56. Conflict: this directly contrasts with the 15,000 km proactive-cleaning recommendation above; treat the interval as one community data point rather than a settled schedule, and prefer diagnosing actual symptoms (rough idle, misfire) before committing to a cleaning service.

Where the community disagrees

  • One source recommends proactive injector cleaning every 15,000 km, citing malfunction by 60,000 km; another reports injectors rarely fail on the X80 given good fuel quality, with fuel filter/pump problems being more common than injector clogging. Not resolved within this data batch — prefer symptom-based diagnosis over a fixed interval.

docs.title: Fuel pump vs. ignition diagnosis (quick-start)
docs.text:
Tags: #fuel-pump · #diagnostics

Quick diagnostic method. To determine whether a no-start/hard-start condition is caused by fuel pump failure or an ignition problem: spray quick-start aerosol ("быстрый старт") into the intake manifold while cranking the engine.

  • If the engine starts, the issue is on the fuel supply side (likely pump failure) — the aerosol is providing a combustible charge that the failed pump isn't.
  • If the engine does not start, the problem is more likely ignition (spark/electrodes) rather than fuel delivery.

This rapid test avoids unnecessary part replacement by narrowing down which system to investigate first.1

docs.title: Fuel pump — intermittent pressure drop
docs.text:
Tags: #fuel-pump · #problem · #diagnostics

Symptom. Some X80 owners report fuel pump failures characterized by random, intermittent pressure drops that are difficult to catch with a standard pressure gauge because the pump operates normally most of the time. The pump can suddenly drop to what's described as a low-voltage operating state (roughly equivalent to going from 14V to 10V), causing engine vibration and stalling1.

Diagnostic approach. Because the fault is intermittent, diagnosis reportedly requires listening to the pump directly — with the driver's seat removed for access — to catch a hesitation sound in the pump's operation, rather than relying solely on a pressure-gauge snapshot1.

Circuit protection — dedicated fuses and fuel-rail pressure relief. The fuel pump has its own dedicated fuse under the hood, separate from a distinct fuel-injector fuse. The fuel rail includes a pressure-relief valve that holds the specified system pressure, and a relay also controls fuel-pump circuit operation23.

Service life — worn/metallic by 300,000 km. One pump reached 300,000 km with visible internal wear and metallic debris (described as "в мясо" — worn down to the metal); at that mileage it was failing and needed replacement. By comparison, owners typically don't replace fuel pumps on other vehicles until well past 120,000 km — the X80 pump is reported to hold up reasonably well before showing wear around 300k km. One replacement pump came packaged with its own fuse included45.

Bench-test-OK-but-fails-installed — diagnostic approach. A fuel pump that works fine on a bench test (connected directly to the battery) but fails once installed in the tank typically points to one of three causes: (1) the pump struggles under real load — check the filter/valve; (2) a tank-assembly issue requiring full replacement; (3) a wiring/grounding issue. Recommendation: ensure clean, corrosion-free clamps/connections first, and consider a full tank-assembly replacement if the problem persists after that678910.

Pump silent on ignition-on, only activates on crank — an electrical-circuit fault, not pump failure. A distinct failure mode from the intermittent-pressure-drop case above: the fuel pump stays completely silent when the ignition is turned on, and only activates once the engine is actually cranked. Root cause: an electrical circuit issue, not the fuel pump itself failing — the car can still start because the pump receives its activation signal on crank rather than on ignition-on. Diagnostic steps: (1) check the fuel-pump relay under the rear seat, which can stick; (2) inspect electrical connections under the rear seat for corrosion or loose wires; (3) manually verify the pump itself is functional by removing the fuel line and confirming spray/flow with ignition-only (no cranking) — if it sprays, the pump is fine and the fault is upstream in the wiring/relay. Fix: repair the wiring, or replace the relay if it's found stuck1112131415161718.

docs.title: Fuel pump replacement — VAZ/Lada compatibility
docs.text:
Tags: #fuel-pump · #cross-compatibility

One owner reported successfully replacing the OEM fuel pump with a VAZ (Lada) fuel pump as a cross-compatible alternative.1

Behavior noted: the VAZ pump operates normally, but produces an audible humming noise when the ignition is on and the engine is at full idle/cold-start — this appears to be normal behavior for VAZ-sourced units, not a defect.12

Conflict/caveat: the OEM pump reportedly runs quieter. The community recommendation is to verify this noise level is acceptable to you before committing to the swap — feedback on this specific compatibility is limited to owners who have actually installed a VAZ pump; general community caution suggests treating this as anecdotal rather than a fully validated cross-reference.12

docs.title: Fuel pump seal — behavior and cross-fit
docs.text:
Tags: #fuel-pump · #bosch · #fuel-filter

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Seal ring is critical for pressure delivery. A missing or improperly installed O-ring seal on the fuel pump module (located on the pump housing threads) prevents the fuel system from building pressure — the pump itself runs and pumps fine, but no fuel reaches the injectors and the spark plugs stay dry1. Diagnosing this specific case took some searching before the owner realized they'd forgotten to install the seal ring; once installed, the car started immediately234. Lesson: be careful when disassembling the pump module, and check reference photos/diagrams before reassembly5.

Activation timing — momentary vs. continuous. The X80's fuel pump activates only momentarily during an engine-start attempt, rather than running continuously whenever the key is on (as it does in some other vehicles)16. This is reported to match the behavior of Toyota Corolla, Mazda, and other Japanese-market vehicles using Bosch pumps, several of which use this same start-only activation pattern; the original X80 pump is a Bosch design dating to ~2014178910. The reporting owner notes this is also documented elsewhere online for Japanese vehicles, and states two other members separately confirmed the same behavior on their own cars11. In short: at the moment of start, the pump builds pressure and injectors begin working6. Note: per the candidate analysis of this thread, this "start-only" behavior was itself debated — one view holds the pump runs only on engine start (as described above, matching Japanese-market cars), while another view in the community holds the pump should run on ignition-on for pressure buildup, matching the behavior of typical fuel-injected vehicles generally. The reporting owner's own experience, corroborated by two other members, matched the start-only pattern.

Cross-brand fuel pump compatibility. - A VAZ 2108 fuel pump was asked about as a possible substitute; one reply confirms it matches by geometry, though performance/output specifics weren't confirmed in this thread121314. - Separately, after the factory (Russian-market) fuel pump failed after about 2 years in service, one owner replaced it with a BOSCH pump originally purchased for a Kia Ceed back in 2020 — reported as a working cross-fit, though long-term durability wasn't yet established at time of posting15.

Part numbers and a VAZ 2110 cross-fit confirmation. The FAW X80's fuel pump assembly part number is FA031335XAP1; the individual pump-only part number is FA031335XP1. As an alternative, the VAZ 2110 fuel pump (roughly 800 RUB, RU market, Jan 2025) is reported to fit 1:1 and function equivalently. The associated fuel filter part number is FC0160950 (roughly 340 RUB, RU market, Jan 2025). Some owners prefer the Bosch motor found inside the OEM module over aftermarket replacement modules; a Mapco pump with an integral fine filter was also suggested as an option16171819202122.

Mapco 22760 — a specific fuel pump listing, from the second Telegram group. A separate community (FAW BESTURN X80 group) points to a specific fuel pump product: Mapco 22760, available from the EMEX e-commerce retailer — consistent with the Mapco-brand fuel pump already mentioned as an option on this card, giving it a concrete part number23.

Fuel filter and pump listings, seals (Sep-Oct 2026). A Kittank fuel filter FC0160950 is labelled on the box for the B50 and X80 (photo, Sep 2026) 24. When refitting the fuel pump or filter fitting, fit new rubber seals and make sure they are fuel-resistant (бензостойкие) before assembling the pump 25; Serega's kit also contained a thick seal in addition to the thin one (photo: a small dark rubber O-ring) 26. Arсhi 77 gives the pump article FA031335XAP1 labelled "for B50" and sees it at already "20" at Kitzap (unit not stated, presumably thousand RUB, Oct 2026) 27. Руслан Кот saw this pump at 3,000-5,000 RUB on Yandex (RU market, Oct 2026) and Arсhi 77 says Ozon is about the same (RU market, Oct 2026), noting that all sellers use one article number; fitment on the X80 was not confirmed 2829.

Where the community disagrees

  • Community disagreement on fuel pump activation: one view holds the pump operates only briefly on engine-start attempt (matching Japanese-market cars like Corolla/Mazda); another view holds it should run on ignition-on for pressure buildup, matching typical fuel-injected vehicles. The reporting owner's own car, and two others who confirmed, matched the start-only pattern — not a fully resolved community consensus.

docs.title: Fuel pump: gasket orientation affects fuel pressure
docs.text:
Tags: #fuel-pump · #gasket

When a failed fuel pump is replaced, the small round rubber gasket/seal at the pump-to-tank interface must be seated in the correct orientation — installing it the wrong way changes fuel pressure enough to prevent the engine from starting at all.

One owner's fuel pump died and was replaced, but the car still would not start. The cause turned out to be simple: the round rubber gasket had been fitted in the wrong position during assembly, which altered fuel pressure. After re-seating the gasket correctly, the pump pressurized normally, the car started, and reportedly ran even better than with the original pump.1

Takeaway: if a car won't start after a fuel pump swap, don't assume the new pump is defective — check that the round gasket/seal is oriented and seated correctly before troubleshooting further.1

docs.title: Fuel tank capacity and octane spec
docs.text:
Tags: #fuel · #octane

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Tank capacity and official spec. The FAW Besturn X80 fuel tank capacity is 58 liters per the official owner's manual12. After the pump clicks off on first fill, roughly 5-7 more liters can still be added, giving ~63-65L total usable capacity including reserve1. The manual's fuel specification references standard number "17930" (i.e. GB 17930), unleaded petrol12. Operating temperature range shown on the manual chart: -15°C to +45°C3. One owner pushed back on a rumored 71L figure circulating elsewhere, noting that per the manual it's 58L and 71L "definitely won't fit"4; a third-party spec listing (drom.ru) was also cited in support of the tank-capacity figure5.

Octane requirement. The manual states a minimum octane rating of 92 (unleaded, per GB 17930)26. Some owners run 92 successfully; 95 is more common in the Russian market6. The spec is also printed on the inside of the fuel-filler flap, per one owner's reminder to another7.

Community octane debate. Owners report mixed experience across octane grades: - 92 octane: the traditional baseline — most economical, matches manual minimum89. - 95 octane: preferred by some owners for smoother running1011. - 98 octane: considered unnecessary on a stock engine; several owners report the engine "тупит" (bogs down/pings) on 98, i.e. detonation-adjacent symptoms rather than a benefit1213. - Fuel brand/quality (e.g. Pulsar, Jeddrive were named as acceptable brands) appears to influence smoothness and performance at least as much as octane rating alone1415. - Vehicles that have had the catalytic converter removed/deleted ("евро2" ECU modification) show increased detonation risk on 92 octane and are reported to need a minimum of 95 octane; symptom without enough octane is described as "клапана звенят" (valve/knock rattle)161718.

Additional individual reports. One owner tried "good" 95+ and 98 and found the car ran objectively worse/duller than on 92, describing it as the engine having "heartburn" from the extra additives19. Another switched from habitual 95 down to 92 and noticed no real difference, remarking their wallet was happier for it20. On the catalyst-delete/detonation question, one owner argued the "клапана звенят" rattle may actually be carbon buildup/compression-related rather than purely catalyst-related, comparing it to VAZ ("Tazy") engines that rattle after a head skim + metal gasket but don't last long that way21. A different owner with a catalyst-delete car described concretely: on a half-tank of 92 after the delete the car would barely run; topping up with 98 helped, and a full tank of 95 ran fine, but going back to 92 afterward the car "won't take it" anymore2223. One owner with high fuel consumption (11.6 L/100km, self-described as driving mostly in the city) said she wanted to try 92 to see if it would lower consumption, to which another owner replied some in the group claimed as low as ~7 L/100km2425. A remap/ECU flash done without triggering fault codes was noted as unusual/impressive by another member of the discussion26.

Consumption test comparing 92 vs 95. Suggested test procedure from the community: reset the trip odometer, fill 30-40L of the fuel to be tested, drive exclusively in D mode, and record the resulting consumption27. Results reported: the difference between 92 and 95 octane ranged from no measurable difference up to about 1 L/100km worse on 92, depending on driving style and conditions — the engine is designed to run on either grade2728.

Fuel gauge calibration quirks — additional reports (drop lag, and consumption-based estimate not level-based). Separately, owners report the factory fuel gauge can show 'full' when the tank still has 20L+ capacity remaining (attributed to Chinese gauge-calibration design); after driving begins, the gauge display drops 1.3-1.5x slower than actual fuel consumption. The low-fuel warning light triggers at roughly 10-15L remaining, varying with driving mode/consumption rate29303132. A related, more detailed report states the gauge doesn't purely reflect tank level — it calculates remaining fuel based on consumption rate, which produces a common symptom: the gauge reads 'half' or 'low' yet only ~35L actually fits at fill-up, despite the 58L rated capacity. Workaround: reset the trip meter at every full fill-up and cross-check actual fuel added every ~500km. In one case, the low-fuel warning appeared at 470km into a tank but only 35L went in at the pump. Loose fuel-sender contacts are suspected in some cases, causing gauge errors that persist even after a battery disconnect3334353637383940.

Octane and driving-feel — additional individual reports. One owner reported 92 octane gave poor acceleration and a rough feel, and switching to 95 noticeably improved engine response. A separate owner who tested extensively — 7+ grade/brand combinations daily over roughly two years — found 92 octane optimal for both consumption and efficiency in their own use. Results are reported to vary by individual perception and by fuel quality/brand rather than octane number alone41424344.

92 vs. 95 octane — no strong performance difference, quality matters more. No significant performance difference is felt between 92 and 95 octane fuel on the X80. Reports: 92 octane works reliably even past 102,000 km; 95 octane is preferred by some for more dynamic driving; a few owners updated firmware and then switched to 95. Community view: fuel quality matters more than octane rating (avoid unreliable/sketchy gas stations); the price difference between grades is marginal. General recommendation: 92 for economical driving, 95 for spirited driving45464748495051. Conflict: one user reports no difference between 92/95, another prefers 95 specifically after a firmware update — the variation likely reflects driving style and fuel-quality variability rather than a fixed rule.

Octane recommendation restated concisely. Minimum: 92 octane regular fuel. Recommended: 95 octane for enhanced performance — a brief restatement consistent with the manual-minimum-vs-community-preference split already detailed on this card52.

Fuel pump prices in Russia, late April 2026. 95-octane gasoline ranged 64-71 RUB/liter: Gazpromnieft (a Gazprom subsidiary, separate company from the Gazprom-branded pumps) at 64.80 RUB/liter, Rosneft at roughly 70.50 RUB/liter. Regional variation noted, with the Moscow area running ~69-71 RUB/liter (RU market, April 2026) and other regions somewhat lower5354555657.

Fuel tank filler neck — anti-siphon screen. The fuel tank includes a fine mesh screen in the filler neck (горловина) that prevents siphoning fuel out via a hose — attempts to siphon yield no fuel flow, and the hose stays dry even when fully inserted to the fuel level. This anti-theft design cannot be bypassed without removing the fuel pump assembly5859606162.

Filler-cap marking — "not below 92," and a report that higher octane runs worse. The X80's fuel filler cap itself is marked "не ниже 92" ("not lower than 92") — a physical, on-car restatement of the 92-octane minimum already documented on this card. One report goes further than the "no strong difference" consensus above: use of 95+ octane is specifically not recommended, with owners reporting the engine runs better on 92 — more consistent performance and better fuel economy than on higher grades. Conflict: this stands in tension with the earlier reports on this card of owners preferring 95 for "more dynamic driving" — not resolved within this data batch, and may depend on individual engine condition, ECU calibration, or simply differing subjective impressions6364.

Octane preference on a catalytic-converter-deleted engine — 92 preferred, 95 causes detonation. On one X80 with the catalytic converter removed (deleted at 190,000 km — see the cat-delete card), 92 octane is preferred; 95 octane causes detonation, with audible pinging under throttle. This is a distinct, engine-modification-specific data point rather than a general contradiction of the 92-vs-95 discussion elsewhere on this card. The same owner reports Lukoil fuel specifically reduces consumption by 0.2-0.7 L/100km versus other stations, and that fuel quality varies noticeably by brand/region: Gazprom is described as consistently good, while BR, Rosneft, and regional brands vary. Reported city economy: 8.2-8.3 L/100km on standard fuel, dropping to 7.5 L/100km on Lukoil premium (as of a September 2024 report)6566676869.

During fuel-supply shortages, 100-octane shows better economy and response than 92 or 95. The X80 can run on 92, 95, or 100 octane fuel. During a period of fuel-supply shortages, owners reported that 100 octane gave better fuel economy (lower consumption across multiple reported ratios) and slightly better engine response compared to 92 or 95. No performance degradation was noted on 92 octane in normal, non-shortage driving. The practical takeaway from this report: choice among the three grades depends mainly on local availability and regional pricing rather than any strict engine requirement above the 92-octane minimum already documented on this card — confidence: medium7071727374.

Where the community disagrees

  • Community disagreement: traditionalists favor 92 octane for economy; some owners claim 95/98 is beneficial; owners with catalyst-delete ECU remaps report 92 causes problems and require 95 minimum. Fuel brand/quality appears to matter as much as octane rating itself.
  • Octane preference reports conflict: one owner sees no difference between 92 and 95, another specifically prefers 95 after a firmware update. Not resolved within this data batch — likely depends on driving style and fuel-quality variability.
  • A further conflict layer on octane choice: the filler-cap marking and one report insist 92 is correct and 95 runs worse, while other reports on this card (including [^conflict1], involving catalyst-delete cars) claim the opposite — that catalyst-delete/remapped cars specifically need 95 minimum, and that 95 causes detonation on at least one other catalyst-delete car documented on this card. These reports are mutually inconsistent even accounting for the ECU-remap variable, and are not resolved within this data batch — engine-specific tuning, catalyst-delete status, and individual ECU calibration likely all play a role and should be verified per-vehicle rather than assumed from community consensus alone.

docs.title: Fuel tank drain procedure (siphon method)
docs.text:
Method. There's no dedicated drain valve/plug documented for the X80 fuel tank — the community's approach is the same as on any car: siphon through the filler-neck valve. Use a thin hose that fits freely into the fuel-cap valve opening; the hose must be thin enough to pass through without forcing it.12

Starting the siphon. Getting flow started requires a strong, deliberate inhalation/suction on the hose to pull fuel up and over — one owner joked it takes a breath strong enough "to fill both lungs" before the siphon catches, and another confirmed the hose method alone (without a strong draw) didn't work for them.34

Caution. This is a manual-suction siphon method (not a pump), so there's a real risk of drawing fuel into your mouth — not recommended for casual/inexperienced use. Work with fuel doors closed/contained to avoid spills.1234

docs.title: Fuel tank sender wire contact failure
docs.text:
Tags: #fuel-pump

Known issue. The wire harness connecting to the fuel level sender, located under the driver's seat, is reported as a recurring point of failure — the connector at this location often develops a loose or intermittent contact over time. This is referenced as a recurring complaint on Drive2 (the Russian automotive forum), not just an isolated X80 group report, suggesting it's a broader known weak point rather than a one-off defect.

Diagnostic implication. If experiencing fuel gauge inaccuracy or intermittent fuel pump-related symptoms, checking and reseating this connector is recommended as a first troubleshooting step before assuming a failed sender unit or fuel pump — a bad connection can mimic sensor or pump failure symptoms without requiring part replacement to fix.12

docs.title: Alternator failure — diagnosis and sourcing
docs.text:
Tags: #alternator · #mazda-6-compat

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Failure symptom and initial diagnosis. One owner's battery was boiling/overcharging at 57,000 km, which points to a generator voltage-regulator (реле регулятора) failure; the diode bridge inside the generator may also need replacing at the same time12.

Sourcing components — Mazda 6 GG catalog cross-reference. Generator regulator and diode-bridge components can be sourced by cross-referencing the Mazda 6 GG (2.0L) generator through parts catalogs — the Exist catalog specifically was recommended as a good match-up tool. The generator itself ("гена") from the Mazda 6 GG is expected to fit as a complete unit, though sourcing individual internal components (rather than the whole assembly) may require disassembling and visually matching parts against photos, since exact spec parts aren't always separately listed23. One owner reports their dealership fitted a generator sourced through Ford, with some additional work done on the mounting/bracket side to make it fit4. Separately, complete FAW-branded generators ("гены") are reported available in Moscow5.

Ford generator as an alternative — noted with a mounting caveat. A Ford-sourced generator has been used successfully as a cross-fit, but required custom mounting-bracket modifications to install4.

Replacement cost. Complete replacement generators range from roughly 8,000 to 17,000 RUB (RU market, January 2025) depending on source/condition6. A later restated range narrows this to 8,000-15,000 RUB (RU market, January 2025) for new units, with used units from disassembled cars ("разборки") priced similarly but without a warranty guarantee67.

Replace-whole-unit vs. repair individual parts — cost comparison. Spare parts alone (diode bridge, voltage regulator) cost roughly half the price of a full replacement generator, but there's a real risk/hassle tradeoff: the diode bridge specifically is described as a real hassle to source/replace correctly ("тот ещё геморрой"), and one owner directly asks whether the diode-bridge diagnosis was confirmed, or whether just replacing the voltage regulator (RR) might be sufficient instead — suggesting the diode-bridge diagnosis isn't always clear-cut and is worth double-checking before committing to the more expensive repair path. For reference, the drive belt itself is noted as good for 100,000+ km, i.e. unrelated to this failure78. The owner ultimately decided replacement parts (roughly half the cost of a full generator) weren't worth the trouble relative to buying a complete replacement unit, given the price gap wasn't large enough to offset the extra hassle and uncertainty of a parts-level repair9.

Where the community disagrees

  • The Ford-sourced generator cross-fit required custom bracket/mounting work rather than being a true drop-in; treated here as a caveat, not a confirmed clean cross-fit, distinct from the Mazda 6 GG complete-unit fit reported as more straightforward.

docs.title: Idle RPM spec — cold vs. warm engine
docs.text:
Tags: #cold-start

Cold-start idle and warm-up curve (one report). One community discussion gives FAW X80 normal cold-start idle as 1000-1100 RPM, dropping to 700-800 RPM once the engine is fully warmed. A variation of ±100 RPM around these figures is considered normal. The stated mechanism: cold air has higher oxygen content, so the engine runs a richer mixture and a higher idle speed at start; RPM gradually decreases as coolant temperature climbs toward 90°C123456.

Warm idle and "weak idle" threshold (separate, later report). A separate, later discussion gives somewhat lower figures: normal cold idle around 800 RPM, with warm idle 700-750 RPM considered acceptable, and a broader normal band of 600-1000 RPM depending on how warmed-up the engine is. Idle below 600 RPM is flagged as weak/abnormal. This source also notes the dashboard tachometer display is less precise than the actual RPM, and that slight idle fluctuation is normal78910. Conflict: the two reports disagree on the cold-idle figure (1000-1100 RPM vs. ~800 RPM) — this may reflect different ambient temperatures, engine variants, or simply different owners' dashboards/tachometers; both agree the idle drops as the engine warms and that some fluctuation is normal.

Where the community disagrees

  • Two independent reports give different cold-idle figures: 1000-1100 RPM (dropping to 700-800 RPM warm) in one thread, vs. ~800 RPM cold / 700-750 RPM warm in another, with a broader 600-1000 RPM normal band and a "below 600 RPM is weak" threshold. Not resolved within this data batch — may reflect ambient temperature, engine/ECU variant, or dashboard-precision differences between owners.

docs.title: Idle stalling/shaking at stops — likely air-intake leak
docs.text:
Tags: #problem

Symptom. The vehicle shakes or stalls at stops, sometimes specifically at red lights. When the brake is released after stopping, the engine can momentarily stumble12.

Likely cause. Most likely cause: an air-intake leak causing rough idle12. Confidence: medium — reported by two owners without a confirmed fix documented in this batch; cross-check against the crankcase-ventilation-hose card, since a disconnected hose is a related and confirmed cause of similar symptoms elsewhere in this KB.

Throttle/idle runaway — inspection procedure. Symptom: engine accelerates to 4000 RPM on its own, doesn't respond to the throttle pedal, with a clicking sound from the engine compartment. Diagnostic steps: (1) remove the air-intake hose from the throttle body; (2) visually inspect the throttle-butterfly position — it should move freely; (3) check whether the butterfly is stuck closed (IAC/idle-control issue) or stuck open (mechanical jam); (4) look for carbon buildup or debris under the butterfly; (5) disconnect the battery terminals for 5 minutes to reset the ECU; (6) check whether the rubber fuel line inside the engine bay is cracked, causing a vacuum leak. If the issue persists after this inspection, a service visit for ECU diagnosis and possible throttle-body cleaning is recommended345678910111213.

Diagnostic method — fuel-trim monitoring plus a quick spray test. Air leaks can be located using a diagnostic scanner by watching fuel-trim correction (долговременная коррекция топлива): if the ECU is actively compensating fuel delivery, that indicates an air leak. A faster field test: spray carburetor cleaner or WD-40 around suspected leak points on a running engine — RPM will rise noticeably if a leak is present at that spot, pinpointing the source14151617.

Air-intake leak as the cause of hesitation at 1300-1400 RPM with AT engagement hiccups. A separate case: RPM drop and AISIN-transmission engagement hiccups specifically around 1300-1400 RPM during acceleration, root-caused to an air leak in the intake manifold gasket area — consistent with the general air-leak diagnosis already on this card. Diagnosis used a smoke generator to visually locate the leak point. Fix: replace the intake manifold gaskets and clean the throttle body. Problem confirmed resolved after the repair (Feb 2026)181920.

Hose on the DPF (сажевый фильтр) side of the intake manifold: are clamps needed? (Sep 2026). Vasily Egorov, fighting floating idle revs (плавающие обороты) for two days, was replacing the thin hose that runs from the DPF-side connection under the intake manifold and asked for photos of its routing 21. Romanych says this hose has no stock clamps because they cannot be reached to tighten 22. Vasily fitted washing-machine-type spring clamps as a precaution 23; Сергей Елисеев says the new hose went on very tightly and clamps would have been superfluous 24.

Long-term fuel trim and MAP at idle. After a rough idle and higher fuel use, an owner replaced the thermostat and cleaned the throttle body; the long-term fuel trim at idle fell from about 1.6 to 0.8-0.9. Another member says a vacuum leak shows up as a high long-term trim and suggests a carb-cleaner spray test; the MAP reading at warm idle should be 28-35 kPa, with 35 kPa the upper limit25142627.

docs.title: Intake manifold hose (gofra) replacement
docs.text:
Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Procedure. The intake manifold hose assembly ("gofra") requires careful removal and measurement before ordering a replacement. Measured diameter is approximately 55mm (verified with calipers). Replacement parts are available on Ozon.12345

Difficulty. The job is described as moderately complex but achievable with basic tools; part of the complexity involves working around suspension mounting components near the hose.12345

Separate hose — crankcase ventilation hose rupture causing an air leak (2024-07 report). A different hose from the gofra above: a strong air leak was detected with WD-40 spray around the lower area of the intake manifold, near cylinder 4 — engine RPM audibly reacted when the leak point was sprayed. Likely cause: rupture of the crankcase ventilation hose, sourced under article/part 21317 (available on Ozon). Repair requires removing the intake manifold — one mounting bolt is accessible only from underneath, so a lift or service pit is needed. Estimated repair time: 1–1.5 hours. Fix: replace the ruptured cooling/ventilation hose.6789101112

docs.title: Intake manifold removal difficulty
docs.text:
Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Difficulty. Removing the intake manifold on the X80 is reported as notoriously difficult, caused by 2-3 bolts that are extremely tight and sit in hard-to-reach positions. The community jokingly describes the effort required as needing "Sanskrit incantations" — i.e. special patience/prayers rather than a clean mechanical trick12.

No established procedure. No documented step-by-step procedure for easing this removal was shared in this exchange; the community's practical guidance amounts to persistence, and possibly the use of impact tools on the stuck bolts, rather than any confirmed shortcut12.
