docs.title: AKPP partial ATF change — drain plug, pan, mesh
docs.text:
Tags: #automatic-transmission · #atf · #drain-plug

The routine partial fluid change: draining through the bottom plug, optionally dropping the pan to clean the mesh, and refilling.

Procedure — bottom drain / partial change (the routine method). Warm the transmission to 40–50°C, then unscrew the lower drain plug — a thin, steady stream indicates correct level; if insufficient, add fluid via the drain hole using a technical syringe. Do not check at high temperature (~80°C) — flow is excessive and the reading is inaccurate (though checking near idle temperature ~90°C is also accepted practice by some in the community on service visits — this is a documented disagreement).123456789101112 A partial change at 60,000 km typically drains ~4.5 L, replaces the filter, and refills; a full/complete drain-refill was historically done at 120,000 km. Some owners do partial changes earlier, at 50,000 km, for extended oil life. Draining through the dipstick tube with a hand pump is convenient when no service pit is available. Warning, strongly emphasized by the community: never completely drain the AKPP multiple times in a row — this destroys internal transmission components; partial changes can safely be repeated at 20,000–40,000 km intervals.131415161718192021

Simple pan-plug-only method, no filter access (2025-02 report). For a straightforward partial change without dropping the pan: drain fluid from the bottom drain plug (easy to identify); measure the drained amount using a tube positioned below the drain hole to track level; refill through the side fill bolt near the front of the transmission using a syringe. Multiple owners confirmed this method works well for routine partial fluid changes.2223242526

Partial exchange procedure — mesh filter cleaning and refill methods (2025-06 report, expands on the routine method above). Recommended over a full drain-and-fill: (1) Drain through the bottom pan plug — without removing the pan, roughly 2.5 L drains; with the pan removed, roughly 4 L drains. (2) While the pan is off, check the coarse metal mesh filter inside it and wash it with gasoline, kerosene, or carburetor cleaner. (3) Replace the pan gasket — old gaskets dry out and start leaking. (4) Refill either via the top filler near the heat exchanger, or via the drain hole using a syringe or gravity-fed container (never attempt gravity feed without a supporting container — it takes far too long otherwise). (5) Repeat the partial-exchange cycle 2–3 times total for the best overall fluid turnover. Total system capacity with the cooler is approximately 7.4 L; the base transmission alone holds approximately 6 L.272829303132333435363738394041424344454647

Fluid check and partial replacement without a dipstick (community procedure). The X80 has no transmission dipstick — fluid level is checked by removing the drain plug at the bottom of the pan: fluid flowing out steadily indicates a correct level. A partial replacement uses about 4 liters of fluid; replace the pan gasket during the service. While the pan is off, remove and inspect/clean the transmission filter element (steel mesh) and the interior of the pan for metal debris and magnetic contamination. Don't replace the drain-plug bolts if they haven't seized — reuse them with light lubrication. One reported case: an automatic-transmission car at 91,000 km with a history of jerking on 1-2-3 shifts — the recommended approach is to check the fluid level first, then proceed to a full fluid change if it's found low or dirty.4849505152535455565758

50,000+ km used-car service procedure, restated (2024-08 report). For a used X80 at 50,000+ km: perform a partial (semi-flush) change first as a baseline. On the first pan-removal service (recommended for higher-mileage cars), clean the strainer thoroughly, install a new pan gasket (35168-TFA050), and refill with 4L (no pan removal) or 4–4.2L (with pan removal). ATF must carry the 3309 spec or Toyota TYPE IV equivalent — do not mix green and red fluids. Check used-car service history skeptically, since records may be incomplete.596061

See also: Automatic transmission (AKPP) — ATF fluid & intervals; AKPP pan gasket, filter and part numbers; AKPP fluid level check — plug, tube, temperature.

docs.title: ATF partial vs full exchange and volumes
docs.text:
Tags: #automatic-transmission · #atf

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

How much fluid a partial or full change moves, and what owners report about machine (hydraulic) flushes versus repeated partial changes.

Fill quantity confusion, resolved. Owners have reported conflicting numbers — some say 3 L is a full fill, others say 4–5 L. The dealer's own procedure clarifies the variance: drain fluid (~2.7–3 L emerges on a partial drain), add ~3 L back, then check/top up per the owner's manual procedure in 200 ml increments until correct (professional dealer tooling uses VAS 5051 / VAS 6262 / VAS 6262/2 adapters for precise top-fill). Total system capacity when genuinely full is ~4–5 L. After filling, run through all gears several times before final level check.123456789101112131415161718

Safety warning — external flush machines. Do not use an external "аппарат" flushing device for an AKPP oil change once the transmission has 100,000+ km — it stirs up accumulated internal debris and risks damage. Manual half-drain of ~4 L at 30,000–40,000 km intervals is the safer approach. One owner reported oil condition was still excellent (raspberry-colored) at 80,000 km on this regime. Separately, one owner destroyed a Mazda transmission by overfilling during a half-drain procedure — a caution about being careful with quantities, not just method. Consensus: only intervene on a transmission with actual shift problems beyond the routine 30–40k interval; otherwise leave it alone.192021222324252627282930

3 partial flushes vs. 1 full aerated flush. At 70,000 km, one owner chose 3 sequential partial fluid changes instead of a full aerated flush (the service shop offered both options). Result: noticeably improved shifting behavior, smoother downshifts, better acceleration — the factory fill was suspected to be poor-quality/degraded oil from assembly. Cost was also lower: 3 partial changes ≈ 18,000 RUB (RU market, November 2024) vs. a full aerated flush at 23,000–29,000 RUB (Moscow-area, RU market, November 2024), for comparable perceived improvement. One other community member disputed that 3 partials would typically be cheaper than one full flush, but the reporting owner's actual received quotes showed the gap.3132333435

60,000 km first-change procedure and restyled-model top access (2024-06 report). Recommended first AKPP fluid change at 60,000 km, with two documented options: (1) full hardware/aerated flush — drain, refill with 12–14 L through the top, requires proper equipment and careful pressure management to avoid solenoid damage; (2) semi-drain (preferred under 60k km) — remove the pan, change filter and gasket, drain and refill with the same amount plus 50–70 g increments across multiple cycles, checking fluid level at a 35°C target temperature.36 Unlike pre-facelift cars, the restyled X80 has a top fill access port for transmission fluid — fill from above, drain from below — making the hardware-flush method impractical without proper ports, so the semi-pan-change method remains the practical option even for restyled owners.3738394041

Fluid capacity — exact measured drain (2026-05 report). One partial-drain service measured exactly 4 liters drained from the automatic transmission, corroborating the ~4L figure used in the partial-change procedure card (actual amount can vary by procedure/temperature).4243

Confusion over drained-vs-total volume, restated (2026-06 report, low confidence — single source). A viewer questioned a video's fluid-change procedure: draining via the drain plug removes only 1–1.2 liters, and the refill procedure calls for waiting for a 1-drop-per-second flow before closing the plug. This restates the fill-quantity confusion already documented above — actual total capacity requires calibration against a reference gauge, not just "replace what drained." Do not overfill; excess pressure damages seals. Some commenters suggested checking the service manual for exact specs rather than relying on informal videos.44

See also: Automatic transmission (AKPP) — ATF fluid & intervals; AKPP partial ATF change — drain plug, pan, mesh; AKPP ATF service prices and shops; ATF change interval — AISIN guidance, owner debate.

docs.title: AKPP top-fill access, ports and breather
docs.text:
Tags: #automatic-transmission · #atf

Filling the transmission from above: where the filler ports are, how the method works, and where the breather (sapun) is routed.

Procedure — top-fill method (Aisin G09 factory access point, undocumented in owner's manual). The Aisin G09 has a factory top-fill plug that allows a faster partial change from above instead of only draining from the bottom. One user confirmed with a dealership that this method exists and is faster/easier than the bottom-only approach. Access is difficult on the X80 but noticeably easier on the FAW B50, which uses the same Aisin 0.9G transmission with a more front-facing, accessible filler bolt.123456789 There is community debate about why the manufacturer doesn't document this method — the working theory is that it's to push owners toward full dealer service replacements.

There are two fill holes on top of the transmission: one has a tortuous internal path (slow to refill through), the other accepts oil more easily. Use a syringe to fill from the top. The engine must be running and the oil warm (~38°C). After refilling, cycle the selector through all gears with a 2–3 second pause per gear before rechecking the level via the lower drain plug (thin steady stream = correct level). Top-fill changes typically move 3–4 liters (not 2.2 L) — this is a partial, not full, change.10111213141516171819202122 Note: to shift the selector out of Park with the battery disconnected, lift the plastic trim to find the white release lever — no need to remove the entire console cover.1011121314

Breather/vent (sapun) location (2025-06 report). The AKPP breather tube ("сапун") routes upward from the transmission via plastic tubing and terminates with a cap up near the roofline, to prevent water ingress while relieving pressure/vacuum. Some owners report theirs is missing — check that the tube and cap are present and intact near the transmission.23242526

Fill access, drain-plug thread, and breather location — early Q&A thread (2026-01/02 report, conflicts with breather location above). The AKPP drain plug thread is M14 × 1.5. For a partial fluid change, one owner directed a fellow member to the "technological fill hole" near where the dipstick sits; another owner reported being unable to locate this fitting at all. A separate exchange noted a bolt at the rear of the transmission ("in the back") that can technically be unscrewed to fill from there, but called this "not realistic" in practice — filling through the drain hole is the practical alternative. On the breather: one owner asked whether a breather (сапун) exists to avoid needing an external flush "apparatus"; the reply confirmed a breather is present but is very thin, visible beside the battery (specifically, to the left of the battery when facing the front of the car, at the point where the battery mount attaches) — with a mention that some owners have filled transmission oil via the oil pressure sensor access point instead. This beside-the-battery breather description has not been reconciled with the separate 2025-06 report elsewhere on this card describing the breather terminating near the roofline — treat as an unresolved discrepancy, possibly reflecting different breather routing across model years. A drive2.ru guide ("АКПП X80 замена ATF, часть 3") was shared as a supplementary reference for the fluid-change procedure.272829303132333435363738394041

See also: Automatic transmission (AKPP) — ATF fluid & intervals; AKPP partial ATF change — drain plug, pan, mesh; AKPP fluid level check — plug, tube, temperature.

docs.title: AKPP wear signs, shift symptoms and outcomes
docs.text:
Tags: #automatic-transmission · #atf · #wear

What the drained fluid and pan revealed, shift symptoms that call for a fluid change, and what owners saw afterwards.

Wear evidence at 100,000 km (never previously changed). One owner's first transmission fluid inspection at 100k km (fluid never changed) found numerous small brass/bronze shavings (bearing wear particles), magnetic deposits of ferrous particles on the pan magnets, and a clogged filter screen. Per Aisin's own guidance, fluid should be changed every 20,000–60,000 km depending on driving conditions (more frequent for stop-and-go urban driving). After a full drain (~2.5–3 L extracted) and sump cleaning, subsequent maintenance can be done by partial drain-and-refill through the bottom sump plug; full sump removal is recommended only at that first deep service after 100k km (or longer), not routinely.1234567

Diagnosing shift-to-neutral jerking, and pan-gasket brand caution (2026-02 report). For a car exhibiting AKPP pitching/jerking into neutral unexpectedly, an OBD2 scanner (ELM327-type) is unlikely to show a fault code — check and change the fluid first, not the electronics. Full procedure reported to fix this symptom: unbolt the drain plug and dipstick tube, remove the pan, drop the filter (mesh can be rinsed and reused), install a BRAVE BREK124 pan gasket — buyers were warned not to source the gasket from Kitszap, since a cheap Kitszap gasket reportedly blew out within 2 days of installation — and reuse the OEM distance spacers/washers (they sit slightly shorter than some aftermarket copies). Repeat the partial fluid change 2–3 times at 500–1,000 km intervals for a thorough flush. If the fluid itself looks fine, check for debris in the pan and a clogged heat exchanger (теплообменник) — in summer/heavy city driving this may call for adding an auxiliary transmission cooler.891011121314151617181920212223

Partial-change interval — "still like new" at 80,000 km (2024-07 report). One owner bought the car at 60,000 km and did a partial (semi-proliv) change at 80,000 km; fluid condition was reported as "like new" at that point, corroborating the 30,000–40,000 km partial-interval consensus documented in the overview card.2425

docs.title: Automatic transmission (AKPP) — ATF fluid & intervals
docs.text:
Tags: #automatic-transmission · #atf · #aisin · #transmission-fluid · #engine-oil

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Overview. The Aisin G09 / 09G (TF60/TF80) automatic transmission (AKPP) of the X80 takes ATF to the JWS-3309 spec. The factory manual calls the fill lifetime, but owners overwhelmingly change it: usually a partial change (about 3–4 L drained) every 30,000–40,000 km, with a deeper pan-and-mesh service at the first major service. This card keeps the change-interval discussion and the corroborating reports; each other topic has its own card:

  • ATF fluid spec JWS-3309, brands and counterfeits — fluid spec, brands, counterfeits
  • AKPP partial ATF change — drain plug, pan, mesh — drain plug, pan and mesh procedure
  • AKPP pan gasket, filter and part numbers — pan gasket, filter, part numbers
  • AKPP top-fill access, ports and breather — top-fill ports and breather
  • AKPP fluid level check — plug, tube, temperature — level check, overflow tube, temperature
  • ATF partial vs full exchange and volumes — partial vs full exchange, volumes, machine flush
  • AKPP ATF service prices and shops — service prices and shops
  • AKPP wear signs, shift symptoms and outcomes — wear signs, symptoms, owner outcomes

Related existing cards: ATF change interval — AISIN guidance, owner debate; ATF and power-steering fluid — Dexron III vs JWS3309; Transmission fluid change intervals and costs; AKPP transmission filter — part number and cost.

Factory position vs. community practice. The factory manual states the transmission is "sealed for life" with no scheduled oil change. Community consensus strongly disagrees: because the Aisin transmission has an inherent overheating tendency and is sensitive to oil quality, dirty oil clogs the hydraulic block and its fine channels/solenoid pistons, reducing pressure on the friction-pack clutch cylinders and accelerating clutch degradation.12345

Change interval — disagreement documented. There is real disagreement in the community between owners who prioritize the manufacturer's spec (60,000 km or "lifetime") and owners with empirical evidence favoring more frequent partial changes: - Олег Белоусов maintains the manufacturer specs (60k/lifetime) are the engineering baseline and should be trusted. - KASPER and others counter with real-world examples of extended transmission life (700,000+ km reported) achieved with frequent partial fluid changes every 20,000–40,000 km.6789101112131415161718192021222324252627 - The practical middle-ground that most experienced owners converge on: partial fluid change every 30,000–40,000 km, full/deeper service (sump removal, cleaning) only at first major service after 80,000–100,000 km or when shift quality degrades.1234528 - Other reported interval data points from individual owners: 70,000 km (city driving) is enough to notice improved shift smoothness after a change;29 ~80,000–82,000 km cited as a typical interval by some, though temperature and usage patterns affect frequency;30313233 one owner recommends a minimum of 30,000 km, others prefer 20,000–25,000 km.12345

Repeated corroborating reports (Jan–May 2026) — same guidance, no new facts. Several later threads reconfirm points already established in the topic cards, with no substantive new information beyond what's documented in the topic cards: partial change every ~20,000 km starting around 100,000 km total mileage using MANNOL MULTIVEHICLE JWS 3309 (~3.5 L per change, no drain plug — pan removal required, sourced via Ozon/Yandex Market with filter);3435363738 the mandatory half-drain-only rule (never a full drain) restated in a March 2026 discussion, alongside a reminder to buy a new pan gasket;3940414243444546474849505152 the three documented AKPP service tiers (pan-plug-only partial, partial-with-pan-removal-and-filter, and full-equipment change) restated as a menu of options in April 2026;53545556 the half-drain step-by-step procedure (drain plug → dipstick tube → pan → filter → refill ~4 L → new ~800 RUB gasket, RU market) restated again in April 2026;57585960616263646566676869 the JWS-3309 spec with Idemitsu as an owner-confirmed acceptable brand, restated in an April 2026 thread;7071727374 and Dexron III (3309) named again as the AKPP fluid spec in a May 2026 exchange.7576

Maintenance interval, another data point (2026-05 report). A separate service recommendation set the AKPP fluid change interval at every ~50,000 km, consistent with the 30,000–50,000 km range already documented above.77

Auxiliary transmission cooler as a preventive measure around 80k km (2024-08 report). Owners who fit an auxiliary AKPP cooling radiator preventively (motivated by a reported overheating failure at 165,000 km) discussed it alongside this partial-vs-full fluid-change debate; the reasoning and the cost breakdown are in the auxiliary cooling radiator card.787980818283848586

Change interval and spec — further corroborating reports (2026-01/02). Additional community data points reinforce the guidance already documented in the topic cards: one owner recommends changing every 60,000 km as a safe baseline "you won't go wrong with";87 another argues the change should really happen at 40,000–45,000 km, reporting they changed at 50,000 km and found the difference in transmission behavior before/after clearly noticeable;88 and a third owner, at 45,000 km, had not yet done their first AKPP fluid change, considering it "a bit early" still — consistent with the 40,000–50,000 km first-change window documented in the topic cards.89 On fluid spec, further owners confirm JWS 3309 (and any JWS-3309-approved analog/equivalent) as the correct spec when asked whether a specific canned fluid was suitable for the X80 automatic.909192

docs.title: Brake pad and disc wear intervals
docs.text:
Tags: #wear

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Front pads/discs (city driving, general estimate). Based on owner experience, brake pads typically wear out at 30,000–40,000 km in city driving; brake discs last approximately 70,000 km. Actual wear rate depends heavily on driving style and road conditions (frequent urban braking vs. highway cruising).12

Rear pads/discs — measured data point (2025-05 report). At 48,000 km, one owner measured rear disc thickness at 9.3mm and pad thickness at 6mm, with an estimated safe service life to roughly 100,000 km at that wear rate. Community comparison points: one owner changed rear discs at 170,000 km (all around); another at 125,000 km had already changed rear pads multiple times (5+ replacements) — again showing that wear rate depends heavily on individual driving style and load.3456

Interval consensus and caliper-piston maintenance (2026-05 report). Broader community consensus on front pads: 30,000–40,000 km for normal (non-aggressive-braking) driving. Rear pads often last much longer — one owner reported 90,000 km on the rear — though some owners see shorter 60,000–70,000 km intervals with lighter use patterns; individual results vary. Brake caliper pistons are prone to rust and seizure if pads aren't changed on a regular schedule — regular service prevents piston stiction, and a seized/tight caliper shortens pad life further (a stuck caliper was cited as a contributing factor to a 30,000 km replacement interval). Higher-quality pads tend to wear faster than budget pads but give better performance and heat management.7891011121314

Brake disc surface rust from inactivity is normal, not a defect (2024-07 report). Brake discs rust quickly on the exposed rotor surface when the car sits idle — winter storage or even a single month of parking without driving can produce visible surface rust. Multiple owners corroborate this is normal and not indicative of an underlying problem; the rust is typically superficial and wears off within the first few braking cycles once driving resumes. One owner separately noted that light surface rust traces naturally reappear on the metal disc surface even shortly after an anti-corrosion (anticoat) treatment at a service center — this is expected and not a sign the anticoat service failed.15161718

DIY feasibility (2026-04 report). Brake pad replacement is considered an accessible DIY job — a basic jack and socket set is enough. Procedure: lift the vehicle, remove the wheel, access the caliper, replace the pads. The community view is that no special training is required to do this at a beginner level.19

docs.title: Cabin air filter — debris/water and carbon vs. regular
docs.text:
Tags: #cabin-filter · #air-filter

Debris and water ingestion is a known design characteristic. Cabin air filters on the X80 accumulate leaves, other solid debris, and water — the air-intake system draws in both solid matter and moisture from wherever the intake sits, including water splashed up from puddles. Owner photos document heavy leaf/debris contamination after extended use without a filter change. The recommendation is to simply replace the filter periodically rather than try to clean it.123

Removing the factory "zhaba" intake plug — an immediate, no-cost water fix (2024-06 report). A separate, simpler mitigation than the netting/duct modifications below: removing (or partially covering) the factory air-intake plug, colloquially called the "zhaba" cap, prevents water from accumulating in the air-intake chamber in the first place. The plug is located below the windshield/hood junction area. One owner reports this was an immediate fix installed right after taking delivery of the vehicle, and it eliminated recurring water-saturated cabin filter problems for them — worth trying before investing in the netting or custom-duct approaches documented below, since it requires no purchase or fabrication.4

Reducing intake contamination. Two mitigation approaches discussed: (1) fit mosquito netting over the air-intake windows located under the hood/bonnet, below the windshield, to block leaves and water before they reach the intake; (2) briefly reverse the heater blower motor's polarity to blow accumulated debris back out of the intake duct. The community has also discussed custom 3D-printed or fiberglass air-intake ducts with additional filtration, aimed at stopping water vapor/spray from puddle crossings from reaching the cabin via the intake.567

Regular filters outperform activated-carbon filters for this car. Community consensus is that plain/regular cabin filters are superior to activated-carbon (charcoal) filters on the X80: carbon filters clog much faster and don't provide a meaningful odor-reduction benefit over a regular filter once saturated. A regular filter lasts a full service interval; a carbon filter would need monthly replacement due to rapid saturation, which isn't practical. The most effective way to control cabin odors is reported to be forcing outside/fresh air intake rather than relying on filter media type.8910

docs.title: Cabin air filter — replacement procedure and interval
docs.text:
Tags: #cabin-filter

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

The cabin air filter is located behind the glove compartment. Procedure: (1) open the glove box; (2) disengage the two spring clips/hinges at the top corners of the glove-box opening; (3) remove the spring clip that retains the glove-box door (on the right side); (4) carefully pull the glove box down and remove it; (5) locate the filter housing behind the heater unit — the housing has directional arrows; (6) remove the old filter and install the new one following the arrow direction; (7) close the housing, reinstall the glove box, and re-engage all clips. The green spring clips are strong and require careful handling 12.

Replacement interval: every 10,000 km as preventive maintenance; some owners change the filter at every oil-service interval to fold it into regular maintenance 34.

Alternate quick glove-box removal: a simpler documented method for accessing the cabin filter: (1) press the arrow/button marked "1" at the upper right of the glove box; (2) use both hands to pull the release clips marked "2" outward toward yourself; (3) the glove box detaches completely. No disassembly or force required — a pure clip-release mechanism 5.

Caution — glove-box closer/damper can dislodge: when replacing the filter, avoid forcing the glove box open too far — this can pop the closer/damper (micro-lift) off its hinge/pivot. Symptom afterward: the glove box closes crookedly or won't latch on one side. This isn't a broken glove box, just a dislodged damper — it commonly happens and even dealer service techs simply pop it back in without treating it as a real repair. Fix: remove the trim panel underneath the glove box (unscrew it), then reseat the closer/damper and reinstall the glove box correctly; work gently rather than forcing it wide open 67891011.

Confirming simplified procedure: a separate report confirms the filter location above the glove box is straightforward to reach: (1) open the glove box; (2) disconnect the right-side micro-lift linkage (тяга микролифта) that holds the box open; (3) lower the glove box fully; (4) access and pull out the filter from above — it comes out easily once the box is lowered. Reinstalling the glove box afterward can require some dexterity to realign the lower pivot points correctly 1213141516.

Original vs. aftermarket filter comparison: the original FAW cabin filter has a distinct wave/corrugation pattern. Aftermarket analogs (e.g. Mazda-branded) are about 0.5 cm narrower than the original; Mazda-type filters are confirmed to fit and work. The Marshall MC8665K carbon/ activated-charcoal filter (available on Ozon, link: https://ozon.ru/t/39YlO9P) "fits as if it were original" — good packaging and quality reported. Modern aftermarket filters often have fewer side reinforcements (rigid only front/back) than the original, which can require a slight adjustment of the corrugated (гофра) spring to seat correctly 17181920212223242526272829.

Filter location, driver's-right area — video inspection: the cabin air filter is located behind the right side of the steering wheel from the driver's perspective (i.e. the glove-box area described above). A video walkthrough of removal and inspection showed rust/oxidation build-up on the old filter frame and an attempt to clean the accumulated debris — consistent with the filter needing regular replacement rather than cleaning/reuse 30.

Recommended replacement filter — Ozon sourcing, orientation, and odor removal: a specific scented cabin filter for "FAW Bestune X80 1.8T / B50 / B70 / B90 / Mazda 6 I/II" is sold on Ozon. One owner orders 3 units at a time (about 2-week delivery) since it fits precisely and performs its function well; installing it eliminates cabin odors completely (e.g. exhaust smell from following other vehicles). Installation orientation: blue side up. A supplier-provided installation video is also available 31323334.

docs.title: Common wear items — replacement mileage overview
docs.text:
Community-compiled overview of typical wear-item replacement points on the X80 (varies by driving conditions):

  1. Front wheel hub bearing — approximately 80,000–126,000 km.
  2. Upper suspension arms/rods — approximately 80,000–126,000 km, varies significantly by driving conditions.
  3. Sway bar end links/bushings — interval varies.
  4. Front brake pads — varies by driving style.
  5. Engine oil/filter and transmission oil/filter — per regular manufacturer-recommended intervals.123

docs.title: Counterfeit oil and fluid — sourcing checks
docs.text:
Tags: #counterfeit · #engine-oil

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Counterfeit engine oil: a 2025 raid. A 2025 DRIVE2 post (shared in the group) reports that police in Vladimir region found an illegal full-cycle motor-oil plant in the village of Ileykino (Kirzhach district), operating since March 2023, with 25 pallets of finished oil, two truckloads of goods and over 2 million RUB seized. The counterfeiters filled canisters of known global brands, including Shell, and barrels for service stations and transport companies, and also used tin canisters. The author's point is that marketplace oil cannot be verified by packaging alone: buy from official sellers and keep receipts. Commenters recommend Lukoil and Sintec, noting the official Lukoil store on Ozon and that Sintec is sold at Rosneft stations; no price or lab data is given, so treat this as a caution, not a verified oil list.1

Marketplace oil: two owner positions. One member would not buy engine oil from Wildberries-type marketplaces after a video test showed transformer-type fluid instead of motor oil; another buys only from a seller that provides certificates, in sealed iron cans with several seals, and says his car runs like clockwork.23 The same advice (metal canisters, verified suppliers) appears on the engine oil selection card and for filters on the filter part numbers card.

Counterfeit gearbox oil. The owner (Oleg Belousov) says counterfeit Lukoil-branded gearbox oil was bottled in Moscow for about five years and sold across Russia, but adds that the genuine-looking Lukoil oil he used was fine. Another commenter says to check the supplier's certificates and whether the fluid comes from Turkey, and that a Krasnoyarsk service tested its supply for about three months before using it, so the fluid is not to be trusted without supplier paperwork.45 For gearbox fluid specifications see the ATF and power-steering fluid card.

docs.title: Cruise control activation via ECU reprogramming
docs.text:
Tags: #cruise-control · #ecu

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Cruise control hardware/logic is pre-installed in the engine control unit (ECU) but disabled by configuration on many X80s. It can be activated via ECU reprogramming, a process reported to take about 10 minutes, using service software available either through dealers or purchased informally (e.g., on Avito). One physical prerequisite: the steering wheel multi-function buttons must actually be present on the car — if missing, they can be sourced separately and fitted before activation.123456789

docs.title: Scheduled maintenance pricing — dealer vs. chain
docs.text:
Tags: #price · #dealer

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Autopilot service chain (Moscow/Moscow region), 2024-10-16 report: - Full oil change: free. - Air + cabin filter replacement: minimum 1,200 RUB (RU market, October 2024).12 - One owner's total for a complete service (all filters + oil) at a different, unnamed shop: 9,600–10,000 RUB (RU market, October 2024).3 - Another owner's total at yet another shop ("filter service"): ~6,200 RUB (RU market, October 2024).45

Regional/shop variation is significant; Autopilot's advertised free oil change plus low-cost filters made it cheaper than some competitors for that specific owner, but total costs across the community range widely depending on shop and oil brand used.123456

Official FAW dealer ТО-2 (2nd scheduled maintenance), Nikolaev, Ukraine, invoice dated 2024-10-31: - Total: ~8,000 UAH (Ukrainian dealer, October 2024; approximately 20,000 RUB equivalent at the time, RU market conversion).789 - Includes: engine oil change, filter change, belt inspection, and miscellaneous adjustments.8 - Owner's own estimate for doing the same work themselves (DIY labor + parts): 1,500–2,000 UAH (≈3,500–5,000 RUB, RU market conversion, October 2024) — i.e., roughly a quarter of the dealer price. The owner noted this was likely their last dealer-serviced visit, opting to do it themselves after the warranty period ends.1011

Authorized dealer booking, AutoGermes (Nizhny Novgorod), Dec 2024 report. Authorized FAW dealer offers X80 service and parts sales. Initial diagnostic fee: 4,500 RUB (RU market, December 2024). Expect appointment delays during peak season. Dealer performs standard maintenance including oil changes and a technical wash.121314

Dealer service quality issues — inadequate oil changes (Apr 2025 report). Community members report recurring quality problems at authorized dealer service: over-tightening drain plugs and filter housings, failing to remove undercar protection panels for proper servicing (later requiring welding/cutting when the owner attempts repairs), not actually changing the oil filter despite documented service claims, and questionable spark-plug replacement work. Doing an oil change through the dipstick access alone (without removing the drain plug/filter) is considered inadequate. Practical tip: photograph the filter/parts before and after a dealer visit as a check.15161718

Official FAW dealer package, Sormovskaya location, Russia (2025-08-29). A single quoted service package — engine oil change, oil filter, air filter, and cabin air filter replacement — came to 20,000+ RUB.1920

Typical non-premium shop pricing, Krasnodar region (2025-10). | Service | Cost | Notes | |---|---|---| | Oil change, no shield removal | 600–700 RUB | — | | Oil change, with shield removal | 800 RUB | Shop tried to upsell an unnecessary air filter replacement.21 | | Spark plug replacement | ~1,000 RUB | Per service appointment; separately, higher-end aftermarket plugs bought at ~1,000 RUB each were reported to fail within a year.222324 | | Antifreeze replacement | ~1,500 RUB | — | 2122

60,000 km major service cost comparison (2026-04 report). At the dealership, a full 60,000 km service (oil, filter, antifreeze, spark plugs, air filter) runs about 27,000 RUB (RU market, April 2026); the same scope at a certified multi-brand (non-dealer) service center costs around 17,000 RUB (RU market, April 2026). Note: the dealer's oil-change labor alone is billed separately and was reported as approximately 2,700 RUB (RU market, April 2026) (a figure the owner initially mis-typed as "27 RUB"). Bringing your own oil and an original filter to the dealer can cut roughly 10,000 RUB (RU market, April 2026) off the dealer total.25262728

Suspension-related repair labor costs, Saint Petersburg (2026-04 report). A Saint Petersburg service center quoted 83,040 RUB (RU market, April 2026) for a drive-shaft-related repair job, itemized as: 4× drive-shaft ("привод") repairs at 1,600 RUB each, plus 2× front control-arm bushing/cradle blocks (part MZAB-016) at 1,900 RUB each, with total materials around 43,000 RUB and the balance being labor/markup. For comparison, separately-reported rates in the same city for related jobs: rear hub removal/installation 7,920 RUB (RU market, April 2026) (vs. a typical local market rate closer to ~1,500 RUB (RU market, April 2026), described as a ~20-minute job); control-arm bushing press-out/press-in (перепрессовка сайлентблока) priced similarly high. Community consensus: these dealer/shop prices run roughly 30–40% inflated versus private mechanics — searching Avito for a well-reviewed garage-based mechanic was the suggested alternative for routine work. Note: warranty on shop-performed work only covers defective labor if the customer did not supply their own parts.2930313233343536

docs.title: Emergency tool kit storage in the spare wheel well
docs.text:
Tags: #tools

Practical tip. Keep tools and spare parts in a bag/container stored inside the spare wheel well instead of loose in the trunk. This space-efficient approach allows carrying a full tool set, an air compressor, jump-start cables, a metal sheet (for jack stability on soft ground), rope, a folding shovel, and spare fluids — all without taking up regular cargo space.123456

docs.title: Engine bay cleaning with a pressure washer
docs.text:
Tags: #engine-bay · #cleaning · #conflict

Community members disagree on this topic — both positions are reported.

Recommended safe procedure (2024-06 report). Community-consolidated method for cleaning the engine bay with a Karcher-type pressure washer: (1) remove the engine cover plastic shroud; (2) disconnect the battery to prevent electrical damage; (3) apply a foam cleaner (roughly 1000-concentration dilution), let it dwell for ~10 minutes; (4) rinse gently at low pressure, deliberately avoiding a direct high-pressure spray on electrical connectors, the alternator, or near the ECU; (5) follow up with an air compressor blow-dry to prevent moisture-driven corrosion in connectors and crevices.

Conflict — electrical damage risk (documented disagreement). Some owners express real concern about electrical damage from washing the engine bay at all, citing the X80's known sensitivity around electrical connectors. Others — including several who wash regularly — report no problems whatsoever doing this periodically, provided the low-pressure/battery-disconnect precautions above are followed. Consensus position: the risk is real if done carelessly (high pressure directly on connectors, no battery disconnect, no drying step), but manageable and low-risk if the full safe procedure is followed; several owners with a track record of regular washes report zero issues.123456789101112

docs.title: Engine diagnostics cost (misfire/knock)
docs.text:
