Front suspension height imbalance after Sufix spring install (March 2026): installing new Sufix-brand front springs (confirmed OEM-spec replacement) caused the front of the vehicle to sit ~2cm higher than the rear, an unbalanced stance resembling a "lifted" vehicle. Root cause: the new front spring's stiffness combined with the (separately) worn/ sagged rear springs, not a defect in the front spring itself. Fix: install 20–30mm rubber spacer shims under the rear springs to re-level the stance — Clearance-Plus-brand 30mm spacers made for the Mazda 6 GH were confirmed compatible. No negative handling effects were reported at highway speeds of 140+ km/h after the correction 12345678. Cross-reference: see the rear springs card for the matching rear-spacer fix in detail.

Suspension tuning — how wire thickness, spring rate, and shock condition interact (April 2026): spring stiffness is set primarily by the wire (rod) thickness — many buyers select springs only by physical dimensions (width/length/height/diameter) without considering stiffness, and get caught out. A worn/soft shock absorber can mask a spring stiffness problem: if the shock no longer damps properly, the front end can visibly sag/dip even with correctly-rated springs, which owners sometimes misdiagnose as a spring issue. Victor clarifies: the shock absorber itself does not affect ride height (it only damps motion) — height is set by spring rate, which usually correlates with wire thickness. A thicker-wire (stiffer) spring compresses less under the car's weight and therefore results in a higher final ride height than a thinner-wire spring by roughly 5–15mm; overall front-left/front-right height should still come out even once matched correctly 910.

Cutting a coil to lower the front makes bumps harsher — fix is a full Mazda 6 GG fork + KYB swap: cutting one coil off the front springs lowers the car (leveling out a nose-high stance) but makes the suspension noticeably harsher over bumps — at 30–40 km/h over a speed bump, the impact becomes a jarring hit instead of the shocks absorbing it smoothly. Fix recommended by shops: replace the front struts entirely with longer-stroke Mazda 6 GG forks (not GH — see the shock absorbers card for the GG-vs-GH stroke-length distinction) paired with KYB shocks. This requires a complete fork replacement, not just a shock swap — guides are available on Drive2.ru (https://www.drive2.ru/l/588344000172297904/ and https://www.drive2.ru/l/588012772294411407/). Reported to noticeably improve suspension geometry/compliance after the lowering mod 11121314151617.

SUFIX SZ-1303 — 2020+ models, ~3cm lift, some settling in the first weeks: further corroborating reports on SUFIX SZ-1303 (already documented above): confirmed specifically for 2020-and-later X80 model years, giving roughly +3cm at the front. Some owners observed slight settling/subsidence within the first 1–2 weeks after installation. Owners measured resulting ride height with different reference points (wheel-center-to-arch vs. rocker-panel/порог) — readings are not directly comparable across methods, so pick one measurement method and stick with it before/after. Confirmed stiffer than stock 1819.

LYNXauto SC-1590 — long-term settling, ~1cm over 6+ months: additional owners confirm LYNXauto SC-1590 springs fit the factory struts without modification, but several separately report the same settling characteristic: roughly 1cm of sag after 6+ months of use. Spring diameter matches factory spec; aftermarket coil-material quality is reported to vary between batches 2021222324.

Ride height, boots and settling (Sep 2026 thread). Victor: the stock X80 front spring is about 380 mm free height, not 400 25; the Suffix SZ1303 is also 380 mm, and the one-piece (not two-part) GG-type dust boots (пыльники) add 10-15 mm 26. He says the stock front shock resembles the Mazda GH strut with a GG-style hose lug welded on, so the matching spring has GH parameters, but is the stiffest one 27. Olga fitted yellow reinforced Suffix SZ1303 springs and the front rose a lot — 470 mm — to the point that the car felt as if it would take off 2829; Che Guevara noted the group had blamed the double dust boot from Mazda 30. Settling claims disagree: Victor relays that the Suffix version with a 13 mm rod sags within one to two months according to Mazda owners 31, while Olga reported no sag after two months 32, and Arсhi 77 argued that mileage, not calendar time, decides whether springs settle 33. Victor measured her wire at 13.5 mm rather than 13 mm 34, supported by a caliper photo 35; his own 14 mm-rod Suffix ("too stiff") measured 460 mm right after fitting and 450 mm after settling 36. When reporting height, measure from the wheel centre to the arch, not from the floor, because owners run different tyre sizes 37.

Related cards: Front springs overview; Coil springs — aftermarket numbers and sag (all springs)

docs.title: Front strut dust boots — sourcing
docs.text:
Tags: #part-number · #mazda-6-compat · #sourcing

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Wrong dust boots installed by service shops cause visible ride-height differences: some service centers install an incorrect dust boot (пыльник) type on the suspension struts — sometimes even after being warned, on the grounds that "the listing says it fits." This produces a visible change in ride height compared to a correctly-fitted boot. In one comparison, Turkish/Sufix-brand suspension springs (14mm total thickness) matched OEM new-spring height correctly when the correct boot was used. Separately, pitted/damaged springs have caused their matching dust boots to break as well. Recommendation: avoid cheap marketplace dust boots of unclear origin; buy from reputable suppliers and verify against a known-good reference before installing. Conflict: one buyer purchased Sufix springs (an alternative brand made for the Chinese market) whose original seller claimed a direct fit but which actually needed a coil cut for modification — OEM springs were eventually preferred over the Sufix ones in that case 12345678.

Front strut dust boot (piston rod seal) — FAW part 5CA034015, slow EMEX dealer sourcing: the FAW part number for the front strut dust boot/piston rod seal is 5CA034015. Sourcing through FAW dealers (EMEX) has been slow — one owner's order sat stuck on "assembly" status for weeks with no movement. Possible alternative: a Mazda cross-fit part, but this requires verifying the thread pitch on the strut rod before assuming it fits. After the extended EMEX wait, the recommendation is to check local suspension repair shops for a faster-turnaround option or a confirmed Mazda equivalent rather than relying solely on the official channel 91011121314.

Front dust boots not directly Mazda-cross-fit — X80's extra bearing needs a thicker boot; confirmed alternatives: despite the shared platform lineage, front strut dust boots are not directly interchangeable between the X80 and Mazda 6 (GG) — the X80 has a bearing built into the upper strut support that the GG design lacks, so the X80 needs a dual-part dust boot roughly 10mm thicker than the GG version; fitting a plain GG boot causes improper clearance. Confirmed correct alternatives: SAT STGJ6E34012 or Katsuro KAT19706MAZ (rubber support) combined with a Masuma MAB1062 dust boot, or the complete kit Febest MZSH-BGYFKIT (includes 2 dust boots + 2 bump stops). PR7029 was also mentioned as a potential match, unconfirmed. Sourcing difficulty: many of these parts show as out of stock or with 8–12 day delivery windows — plan ahead rather than ordering when a boot has already failed 15161718192021222324252627.

Kits and strut-top parts. A kit of 2 dust boots and 2 bump stops is listed as KYB 910107 or Monroe PK157. Spring-seat spacers are Katsuro KAT19706MAZ or SAT STGJ6E34012, but their codes carry Mazda markers, so fitment must be checked. A member suggested PR7029 for the boot, while another owner said the boot in the shared photo is the wrong one.282920 The Kitparts listing for the front strut support bearing 5CA03438YA starts at 5,174 RUB (RU market, October 2025).30 A Masuma SAM-4101 front strut mount (опора амортизатора) for the Mazda 6 2002-07 is listed on Ozon; the post does not state fitment to the X80.31

docs.title: Front suspension lift spacers (30mm kit)
docs.text:
Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

30mm front strut spacer kit — Ozon, restyle-fit, requires drilling (Oct 2025): a 30mm front suspension spacer kit (polyurethane, specifically listed for the FAW Besturn X80 restyle/facelift 2018-2022, sold to increase ground clearance) is available on Ozon 12. Important caveat: the spacer's mounting bolts are a larger diameter than the factory bolts, so installation requires drilling out the bolt holes in both the strut top mount and the spring/suspension cup to fit the larger bolts — it is not a bolt-in swap with factory hardware 23.

Drilling procedure for the 30mm spacer: (1) drill out the mounting holes in the strut top mount (tower); (2) drill out the mounting holes in the suspension cup/turret; (3) install the larger-diameter bolts supplied with the spacer kit. This lets the spacer install without forcing an undersized factory bolt into an oversized spacer hole. Installation difficulty is moderate — tool access or a professional shop is recommended rather than attempting it with only basic hand tools 34.

Bump-stop-to-lower-arm clearance after a 2–3cm lift — no alignment impact: after installing 2–3cm front suspension spacers to raise ride height, the gap between the rubber bump stop and the lower control arm should measure about 2–3cm — this gap is what allows normal suspension travel without bottoming out after the lift. Separately, adding spacers of this size is reported to not affect wheel alignment (camber/toe) on its own 56. Some owners additionally use spacers together with stiffer ("tупые"/firm) shocks specifically to prevent bottoming out; a further owner mentions running a full pneumatic (air-spring) setup instead, without giving installation detail; another owner used a slightly larger 3cm spring spacer rather than the more common 2cm size 789.

Height imbalance after new front springs — front sits ~2cm higher than rear: installing new OEM-spec front springs (Suffix brand) can leave the front end sitting roughly 2cm higher than the rear, creating an unbalanced, "lifted-look" stance (as if the whole car were lift-kitted), because the new front springs are stiffer than the worn rear springs still on the car. Fix used successfully: install 20–30mm rubber spacer shims under the rear springs to level the stance — "Clearance Plus" brand 30mm spacers listed for Mazda 6 GH (2007-2013) were confirmed compatible; see also rear suspension spacer shims for the rear-specific spacer details. No negative handling effects were reported at highway speeds up to 140+ km/h with this combination 1011121314151617.

Mazda 6 GG dustboots as an unintended lift — front rises 1–1.5cm: fitting front strut dust-boots (пыльники) from a Mazda 6 GG onto the X80 raises the front end by about 1–1.5cm — an unintended side effect of the parts swap rather than a designed modification, but it does add ground clearance. The reason: X80's front strut has an extra cup/bearing arrangement not present on the older GG strut design (a rotating bearing that barely moves), so the factory dust-boot on the X80 has a thinner base than the GG boot to compensate — swapping in the thicker GG boot effectively acts as a lift spacer. As an alternative to sourcing GG boots specifically, ordinary height spacers achieve the same 1–1.5cm gain 18192021.

Owner-reported height/spacer configuration — front spring thickness vs. rear spacer reality: one configuration reported for reference: front — 455mm total ride height, with 14mm-thick OEM-spec springs on the factory struts; rear — factory soft springs plus spacer plates advertised as +20mm, but the actual measured lift was only +10mm relative to stock (consistent with the spacer over-advertising pattern documented on the rear springs card). Open question in the thread: whether the rear springs had also been swapped, and how a real +40mm spacer stack would perform, was not resolved. Both spring thickness and spacer stack height affect the final ride height and comfort, and there are many aftermarket configurations in use across the community 222324.

Official manual reference height — 435mm, and three measurement methods that don't agree: per the official manual, stock ride height is 435mm measured from wheel center to the top of the wheel arch. In practice, owners measuring the same car with different methods (from above at the fender lip, from below at the rocker/threshold, or by eye at fender height) got noticeably different numbers on the same vehicle in one example (465mm / 445mm / 455mm) — always state which method was used, and don't compare lift results across threads using different methods without normalizing first 2526272829303132.

Rear spacers from Mazda 6 GG (+2cm) — may need trimming, works well as a matched B50 front+rear set: Mazda 6 GG-sourced rear spacers (Ozon: https://ozon.ru/t/HDgTSeb) give roughly +2cm of rear lift, but may need grinding/cutting to fit the X80 properly due to manufacturing differences from the Mazda application. One owner running the same spacer set as a matched front+rear pair on a FAW B50 (the X80's platform mate) reports it worked well as a complete kit 3334353637.

40mm polyurethane spacers, front+rear — 50,000 km update, no increased wear: a fuller account of the 40mm-polyurethane-spacer lift already referenced elsewhere on this card: installing 40mm spacers on both front strut tops and rear springs improves off-road clearance, reduces vibration transmission, and improves ride comfort. Installation notes: loosen all suspension mounting bolts before fitting the spacers, then re-torque everything with the car resting on its wheels (loaded); re-check/re-torque the suspension bushings again shortly after to prevent premature wear. After 50,000 km on this setup: ride is stiffer than stock but with no increased component wear reported, and off-road capability is described as excellent 3839404142434445.

40mm spacer product links (Ozon): the specific 40mm polyurethane spacer kits referenced above — front strut-top spacers: https://ozon.ru/t/QolXB0w; rear spring spacers (2-piece set, AutoDVC brand): https://ozon.ru/t/GKJk4JV. Using the same 40mm size front and rear is recommended to keep the lift proportional 4344.

Front spring + spacer combo — Japanese donor springs (JD Co, 930-0835) with +20mm spacers: one owner sourced non-OEM Japanese front springs — manufacturer JD Co., LTD, model 930-0835, from Kamifugo 1-8-43, Toyama City, Japan — and combined them with a +20mm spacer setup. He reports this combination avoids the sagging seen with unmodified new (non-donor) springs. At the time of the report he was searching for a matching used spring from the same manufacturer to replace the other side symmetrically, implying the donor springs were sourced/replaced one side at a time rather than as a matched pair 46.

Front height with Suffix front springs — 47cm, vs. a rear-only aftermarket-spring settling curve (Aug 2026): with Suffix-brand front springs installed on the factory dampers, one owner measured front ride height at 47cm. Discussing the resulting front/rear imbalance, another owner reported his own (non-stock/aftermarket) rear springs measured 47cm right after installation, but settled to 43cm once loaded — noting that with the factory rear setup the car would instead bottom straight onto the bump stop under the same load. A follow-up measurement after 3,800km of driving with a full load and full fuel tank found the rear had settled further, from the as-installed 47cm down to 44cm. Separately in the same discussion, dust-boot type was raised as a contributing variable: a one-piece (non-factory, GG-style) damper dust boot can add about +1cm versus the stock two-piece boot, and a fresh spacer/spring install is expected to settle further over the first 2-3 weeks — see the rear springs card for the rear-specific spring and spacer options behind these height figures 4748495051.

docs.title: Front suspension overhaul with Mazda 6 parts
docs.text:
Tags: #mazda-6-compat · #part-number · #conflict

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Community members disagree on this topic — both positions are reported.

Overview. The FAW X80 front suspension shares enough design lineage with the Mazda 6 GG/GH generation that owners have successfully upgraded/repaired using Mazda parts: struts/shocks (Kayaba brand recommended), springs, and control arms (Mazda forks/wishbones). Several community members reported successful swaps.123456789101112131415161718192021222324252627282930313233343536373839404142434445

Springs. Mazda OEM springs are softer than stock FAW springs. As a same-vehicle OEM alternative, LYNXauto SC-1590 replacement springs cost approximately 3,000 RUB (RU market, April 2025) and fit the original (FAW) struts. Mazda 6gg springs themselves are narrower than the FAW spring seats but can be made to work with spacers/shims. Several users reported spring breakage over time — the community attributes this to normal material fatigue rather than the springs being undersized/wrong-thickness.123–45

Control arms / forks. Mazda forks (control arms/wishbones) have a larger strut bore diameter than the FAW originals, which means the shock absorber selection must match the Mazda fork geometry, not the FAW spec — mixing FAW struts with Mazda forks (or vice versa) without checking bore compatibility can cause a fitment mismatch.1–45

Disagreement — brake component compatibility (unresolved). One owner asked whether swapping to Mazda front suspension components also requires changing brake components (calipers, rotors). The community did not reach consensus: one position holds that just swapping the forks/control arms is sufficient without touching brakes; another position raised the concern that the larger Mazda fork strut-bore diameter could imply a fitment difference that affects brake caliper mounting. No owner in the thread reported a definitive tested answer either way — treat this as an open question requiring case-by-case verification before assuming brake parts don't need to change.123456789101112131415161718192021222324252627282930313233343536373839404142434445

Related DIY reference. A detailed Drive2 guide covering front suspension replacement (links, joints, bearings) was shared in the group: https://www.drive2.ru/l/701822396251791372/?m=702930703972579894&page=0 — useful supplementary reading for this job, though not X80-specific.46

Consumables sourcing and full replacement cost (2025-07/26 report). One owner (automatic transmission car, 105,000 km) corroborates the Mazda-parts sourcing strategy above at a broader level: "I buy consumables from Mazda 6 up to 2006, never had a miss — and obviously not Chinese ones." At 105,000 km this owner did a complete suspension overhaul — all bushings and bearings plus brake disc replacement — for a combined cost of approximately 60,000 RUB (RU market, July 2025) (2025-07-26). Before that point, only oil filters, brake pads, and the alternator belt had needed replacing. Also reconfirms the AKPP fluid-change interval elsewhere on this KB: "no automatic transmission problems if you change the oil about once every 50,000 km."47

docs.title: Front wheel hub — ABS sensor ring identification
docs.text:
Tags: #wheel-hub · #abs · #sensor · #part-number

Why it matters: front wheel hubs should include an ABS sensor ring — a magnetic ring mounted on the bearing — which is essential for wheel-speed sensing (ABS function). A hub without this ring will not support ABS.

Visual identification: (1) a dark/brown ring indicates the hub has ABS capability; (2) a shiny/bright ring indicates the hub is without ABS. This color difference is the quickest way to tell hubs apart by eye before installing.

Recommendation: always verify with the supplier before ordering, since visual identification from photos/listings can be ambiguous and mixing up the two hub types means losing ABS function 12345.

ABS wheel-speed sensor transfer when upgrading wheels: separate from the hub's built-in ABS ring above, the ABS wheel-speed sensor itself (mounted at the hub, reading the ring) can be unscrewed from the factory wheel/hub assembly and remounted on a new/aftermarket rim in the same position — no new sensor purchase is needed when switching to a same-diameter (e.g. 17-inch to 17-inch) wheel. Restyle vs. pre-restyle sensors differ in wiring-harness thickness, but both variants are removable/transferable 67.

docs.title: Front wheel hub bearing
docs.text:
Tags: #mazda-6-compat · #part-number · #front-axle · #caliper · #tpms · #wheel-hub · #bearing · #price

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

The X80 front wheel bearing is not a separate part: the bearing is pressed into the hub, and the hub is sold and replaced as one bolt-on hub assembly (ступица в сборе). This card covers the front axle and the facts common to both axles (bearing brands, price spread). The rear hub is a different design and has its own rear wheel hub bearing card.

docs.title: Design and serviceability
docs.text:
Hub bearings on the X80 are non-serviceable, sealed integrated units — not individually greasable or adjustable. The hub uses a solid/cast bearing design (литой подшипник); its lubricant depletes over time with no way to top it up.123456789101112131415 Because the front bearing is pressed into the hub, the entire hub assembly is replaced as one unit when the bearing wears out.16 The assembly is bolt-on: a 28-spline shaft and 4 bolts to the steering knuckle, with hub and bearing sold together — unlike the Mazda 6 GG/GH, where the bearing is pressed into the knuckle.171819

No separate bearing is supplied. Andrey Simonov confirmed via the FAW Excelant dealer that only the complete sealed assembly exists, from 6,000 RUB (RU market, May 2025). Professional press-fit replacement of a bare bearing needs an arc-welding torch, nitrogen gas and lathe work, so DIY bearing swapping is not considered practical for X80 owners.20 An earlier (2024) report reached the same conclusion for hub 5CA033047B and described the job as difficult and multi-hour, requiring removal of the lower control arms, ball joints and brake hardware, with little room around the hub without proper equipment. The one reported shortcut — pressing the old bearing out of its housing and pressing in a generic bearing instead of buying the OEM assembly — failed within 1,000 km.21222324

Left and right are identical. The assembly is symmetric (двусторонняя деталь, not a left- or right-specific part), so one part number covers both sides and a single spare can serve either side — handy when carrying a spare on a long trip.2526272829303132 The trailing letter of the part number varies by supplier batch and does not affect fitment (see below).

Replace both sides together. Bearings are a common wear item on this car. Community recommendation: when one side needs replacing, do both at the same time even if only one is noisy, to avoid a ride/noise imbalance between the sides.33

Greasing a new unit. The assembly is often shipped dry and must be greased before installation: put the bearing on plastic film, apply grease generously and work it in by hand with a rotating/massaging motion until excess grease exits the opposite side. The unit is universal and fits either side.34

Conflict — is it serviceable? One report says the front hub bearing may make noise after extended use, that some owners have successfully replaced a failed bearing with a Mazda-equivalent part, and that the bearing is "serviceable and re-greasable on some vehicles". This conflicts with everything above, which consistently describes the X80 front hub as a sealed assembly (5CA033047B) that cannot be re-greased or have its bearing swapped separately and needs arc-welding/lathe work to press-fit. No resolution was found in the source thread; the "serviceable" claim is recorded as unverified against the more detailed sealed-assembly reports.

docs.title: Part numbers and fitment
docs.text:
OEM part: 5CA033047B, X80-specific.3536 ZZAP.ru (an aggregator with several sellers per part number, e.g. "ApalAvto"), KitZap, KitParts and Ozon all listed 5CA033047A/5CA033047B as the same hub; the letter suffix varies by supplier.37383940414243444546474849 The restyled hub is 5CA033047B with 28 internal splines on the outer CV joint (ШРУС); a 5CA033047A variant also exists. Verify the spline count before ordering — variants with 26 splines will not fit. Factory-equivalent parts are available from several sources, including the KitZap catalog.5051525354555657123456789101112131415 The complete pre-assembled hub with bearing 5CA033047B is confirmed to fit the restyled X80 (Feb 2026); before buying, check that the ABS sensor tab/bracket is present on the bearing housing, since some listed variants omit it.585960 Fitment was also confirmed on a 2019 model, and one owner bought 5CA033047B on Ozon and replaced the front-right hub with "everything fit".61626364

Genuine-pattern part numbers typically end in 3304x. An owner-photographed reference part is 5GAO-3304X NTP: 28 splines, 4-bolt flange.171819 Community preference is for units with green-painted splines/studs (зелёные шпильки), considered a marker of a preferred production batch; other versions are acceptable if the green-spline one is unavailable. One community supplier (Василий, contact 546273130) has stocked the green-spline version.656667686970717273

Not interchangeable. The bearing does not fit the X40.74 The Mazda 6 front wheel bearing/hub does not cross-fit the X80 either, unlike several other Mazda 6 suspension parts — do not attempt it.75767778 Despite the superficial similarity, the spindle fitment and ABS integration differ.5051525354555657123456789101112131415 The root cause is the design: the X80 hub bolts onto the knuckle, whereas on the Mazda 6 GG/GH the bearing is pressed into the knuckle. The CX-3, CX-5 and possibly the Mazda 6 GJ use a similar bolt-on design — unconfirmed.171819 (An early note mentioned a Mazda 6 cross-check, but it was never verified.74) Rear hubs from the Mazda 6 are a different story — see the rear card.

Cross-brand analogs. The Zekkert RL2434 (also written RL-2434) is a budget aftermarket front hub assembly proposed as an analog, about 6,000–8,000₽ (RU market, July 2026); nobody had confirmed fitting it when reported.7980 In Sep 2026 Zekkert had also appeared as a non-original alternative whose quality nobody knew yet.81 The ILJIN IJ123172 was mentioned as a possible match but is unverified by the poster. Standing advice: always compare the new part physically with the removed original before installing.82838485868788 The front upper ball joint C23034250 (from FAW Vita/B50) is a separate part that fits the X80.89

docs.title: Symptoms and diagnosis
docs.text:
Typical mileage. Reports differ. Play and noise typically develop at 70,000–100,000 km,90 and bearings commonly fail after 70,000–80,000 km of normal use.91 One owner's front bearing failed at 120,000 km (7 years of ownership) with a rattling/dribbling sound; KSN was recommended as a reliable replacement.90 Replacement is generally needed around 100,000–127,000 km,123456789101112131415 and the first front hub bearing typically needs replacing by about 127,000 km — one owner did a second replacement at that mileage.9293 Another report puts life at 20,000–70,000 km depending on driving conditions and rim/rotor quality: one owner's bearing failed roughly every 30,000 km until uneven/bent wheel rims were identified as the real cause; after the rims were trued, life extended to 50,000–60,000 km. Replace on symptoms and condition rather than a fixed interval, and check rim straightness before blaming the bearing.949596

What it sounds like. Wear shows as a periodic clicking or dribbling sound, most noticeable on turns and rough pavement. It is easily mistaken for a stabilizer-rod problem, and a visual inspection may not reveal early damage; replace promptly once symptoms appear to avoid safety issues.97 A detailed thread described the classic signature as whistling or humming that (1) starts around 50,000+ km, (2) intensifies while turning (which loads the bearing), (3) scales with vehicle speed and (4) worsens over speed bumps.9899100101102103104105106107108109110111112113114115116117118 Another case: tire/road noise audible only inside the cabin (not from outside) on only 2-season-old, lightly used tires, rising in pitch and volume with speed — this points to the hub bearing rather than the tires (Oct 2025).119120121122123124 To tell a bearing hum (гудит) from other noises in the steering area: a hum or grinding/scraping that changes or intensifies with the wheel turned to one side, plus a slight vibration through the steering wheel, indicates the hub bearing rather than the power-steering pump. Confirm on a lift by rotating the wheel by hand and listening for grinding; the fix is then the whole hub assembly.125126127128129130131132133134

Direction of the noise. Two independent reports agree that bearing noise is directional and worse on the outside of a turn. (1) For a dull noise from the left front, turn the wheel left: if the noise decreases or disappears, the left front bearing is the likely cause; if it persists, check the tie rods or other components. Left alone, the noise escalates to a loud hum comparable to an airplane taking off.135136 (2) More generally, a humming/grinding noise when turning right means the right (outer) bearing is the failing one. When replacing, fit the complete sealed unit rather than attempting a partial repair.137

Hand checks. With the wheel jacked up, engine off and the gearbox in neutral, spin it by hand: a healthy wheel spins freely with minimal resistance. A mechanic's first move on a lift is exactly this spin test, to separate bearing problems from caliper problems.138 A second method: a mechanic diagnosed a failed right front hub bearing (Aug 2026) by grabbing and turning the suspension/spring area by hand and feeling for excessive play or resistance, instead of listening on a lift. The right front hub was replaced and the symptom disappeared completely. The owner notes that diagnostic thoroughness varies between shops — one shop found "nothing wrong", a second physically manipulated the suspension and found the fault at once — so have the noise checked by hand or on a lift rather than relying on a single inspection.139140

Caliper or bearing? Symptoms that look like a bad wheel bearing — the car pulling to one side, heavier steering, uneven/rapid tire wear on one wheel — can also come from a sticking brake caliper, and the two overlap enough that they should be told apart before ordering parts. Poor or restricted spinning in the hand test points to a dragging brake pad or a binding caliper piston (see the brake caliper repair kits card for piston/guide-pin service) rather than the bearing. Other caliper-side causes of drag are a pad surface sitting out of plane and a loose caliper mounting bracket.138

Multi-symptom case at 73,000 km. One owner's front-end noise (rising with speed, worse in turns) was diagnosed as a combination of worn front hub bearings on both sides, worn brake pads, worn front suspension bushings (sway-bar links and longitudinal-arm bushings) and worn rear sway-bar bushings. See the suspension noise diagnostic checklist for the general approach.91

docs.title: Replacement procedure
docs.text:
Front hub replacement (2025-04 report, about 3–4 hours). Key steps: (1) turn the wheel fully inward to push the drive axle away from the hub; (2) unbolt the upper suspension arm — the shear pin here is the hardest access point; (3) remove the ABS sensor; (4) extract the CV joint (ШРУС); (5) reach and remove the hub bolts. The lower ball joint does not need removal. Alternatively, remove the steering wheel for better access to the hub bolts from inside the cabin. The tool needed is an old Soviet-style open-end wrench (17–19 mm); modern tool sets sometimes lack the right profile for this fastener.141142143144145146147148149150151

Another sequence (about 127,000 km report). Remove the wheel, suspend the brake caliper (do not disconnect the hydraulic line), disconnect the wheel-speed sensor, then unbolt the strut-to-knuckle attachment bolts to free the hub/knuckle assembly.9293 A detailed photo guide on Drive2.ru, "Замена передней ступицы (потом и кровью)" (front hub replacement, blood, sweat and tears), covers the whole job: https://www.drive2.ru/l/662909855111075430/152

Nut size. Undoing the front hub centre nut needs a 32 mm socket; Victor bought an Airline ATIS1247 head for about 300 RUB (RU market, Sep 2026) for the job.153154

Seized knuckle/driveshaft parts. Victor read that vinegar works better than WD-40 on rust and planned to soak a removed knuckle (кулак) with its driveshaft outdoors because of the smell.155 Василий Егоров says Coca-Cola removes rust within an hour and helped him after sea swims;156157 Victor replies that cola is not stronger than vinegar.158 The two positions differ and are recorded as such.

Ball joints and CV boots alongside. One owner replaced the front ball joints, front wheel hubs and outer CV boots at 5.5 years / 115,000 km — the first replacement at that mileage, considered normal wear. On this car the right-side ball joint was factory-welded to the control arm and could not be replaced separately; the whole arm had to be replaced (or modified).159160161162

docs.title: Sourcing, prices and brands
docs.text:
Sourcing channels. Front hubs are sold on Ozon and Avito,656667686970717273 on Wildberries (FAW-branded front hub with bearing),163 on Emex and zzap.ru, via AliExpress, and from direct suppliers and the KitZap/KitParts catalogs. Some owners suggest salvage yards when new-part prices rise.123456789101112131415 Several owners ordered 5CA033047B via AliExpress with a perfect fit ("подошли идеально"): a notably lower price than local suppliers, but about a month of shipping and the usual risk of an unverified overseas seller.164165166167

Price history (RU market).

  • June 2024: a new assembly cost 6,000–8,500₽;9899100101102103104105106107108109110111112113114115116117118 across ZZAP.ru, KitZap, KitParts and Ozon the range was 4,850–8,500₽, with unusually low prices flagged as likely refurbished rather than new.37383940414243444546474849
  • Sept 2024: AliExpress about 3,500 RUB with a ~1-month wait; chinaspare.ru (https://chinaspare.ru/c/faw/besturn-x80/tormoznaya-sistema/stupitsa-perednyaya-v-sbore-faw-besturn-x80) had acceptable pricing but no delivery time was available.21222324
  • March–May 2025: see the table below.
  • June 2026: 5CA033047B cost 10,019₽ at Emex.ru (an Ozon-affiliated seller, 4.3★, 27 units in stock, 14-day delivery at the time); also listed on Avito in the Moscow and Krasnodar regions. Confirm whether a listing is genuine OEM or aftermarket before buying.168169170171172173174
  • July 2026: Zekkert RL-2434 about 6,000–8,000₽; genuine FAW units via Emex/Wildberries about 3,990–4,000₽+.82838485868788
  • Sep 2026: Prosto Zuev bought the original for about 4,500 RUB (and one for about 3,500 RUB in July 2026);175176 Victor paid 4,580 RUB as a spare, when the only alternative was an unknown no-name Chinese part.177 Андрей pointed to zzap.ru at about 3,500 RUB;178 his screenshot of part SCA033047B shows about 16 sellers from roughly 3,340 up to 4,275 RUB, many on pre-order and the rest in stock with delivery in 1 to 7 days.179

Stock and the Sep–Oct 2026 listing. The front hub is listed under FAW number 5CA033047B. Victor said the original was not visible on Ozon at that moment;81 stock status was disputed — Victor said it was not on sale,180 while Prosto Zuev said it is available and linked the avz.ru catalogue entry.181182 Stock varies by seller — confirm before ordering.

Spread of prices and labor (community data, March–May 2025). The table mixes front-hub, rear-hub and bundled quotes and shows how wide the spread is.

Source/market Price Date Official FAW dealer (Commune, St. Petersburg), labor only 12,000 RUB (RU market) March 2025183184 DIY (self-performed, evening job at home) free (own labor) March 2025183184 Saint Petersburg, per hub 7,000 RUB (RU market) April 2025185186 Budget local market, per hub (installation) 3,000 RUB (RU market) April 2025185186 Kirov, bundled service (front hub + rear hub + rear brake discs + pads + rear longitudinal arm bushings) 5,800 RUB (RU market) April 2025185186 Krasnodar-city, Avito, per hub 5,800–11,000 RUB (RU market) 2025-05-20123456789101112131415 Moscow, FAW specialist (cooperative/non-certified shop) 5,500 RUB (RU market) 2025-05-20123456789101112131415 AliExpress 6,000+ RUB (RU market, ~1 month shipping) 2025-05-20123456789101112131415 Retail/authorized channel 10,000–15,000 RUB (RU market) 2025-05-20123456789101112131415

OEM-quality hubs versus cheap marketplace units. OEM-quality replacement front hubs (green-spline marking) cost about 9,500₽ each from a direct supplier (in stock; shipped via Sdek, Delovye Linii, Pek or Energiya; contact by private message for pricing/logistics). Conflict/warning: one buyer who bought a cheap hub on the Ozon marketplace had it fail after only 1,000 km. Another member explains the economics: marketplace listings carry ~50% platform commission plus logistics and taxes, leaving little margin for genuine OEM-quality parts at rock-bottom prices, so unusually cheap hubs are likely counterfeit or reconditioned. Physically inspecting stock before shipping, as the direct supplier offers, is the safer route.187188189190191192193194195196197198

Brands and counterfeits. FAG (German manufacturer) is considered a mark of quality: a FAG-branded hub priced around 5,000 RUB (RU market, March 2025) is likely counterfeit, since genuine FAG hubs cost significantly more. One owner reports 12,000+ km trouble-free on a genuine FAG hub. SKF and FAG are named among the best bearing brands for this application.199200

Bare bearing brands (2026-05 report, likely 6206/6206RS spec; applies to both axles). For the bare wheel bearing itself, as distinct from the sealed hub assembly: Lynx WB-1544 (Japanese) is recommended at around 500 RUB (RU market, May 2026), and Koyo (Japanese) is also considered acceptable at a similar price. SNR is considered overpriced. FAG/INA (marketed as European/German) have a good reputation but carry a high counterfeit risk on marketplaces such as Ozon — genuine SKF, Koyo, NTN and SNR bearings are not expected to sell below ~800 RUB (RU market, May 2026), so a suspiciously cheap "German quality" listing is a red flag. Buy from reputable sellers who can show original certificates.201202203204205 ILDJIN (a Korean Mazda OEM supplier) bearings were confirmed to work well and are endorsed by the community.20620720820978210

docs.title: Related parts
docs.text:
Wheel studs. Unlike the bearing, wheel studs (lug bolts) can be replaced individually without replacing the hub. Hammer or press the stud out from the outside toward the inside of the hub; identify the correct stud size before sourcing a replacement.211212213214

TPMS sensor. The tire pressure monitoring system (TPMS) sensor part number is BM133714XA. It may vary by production year, so verify it against the specific model year before buying.215216

Front ABS sensor location. One member stated that on the X80 the front ABS (anti-lock braking system) wheel-speed sensor is mounted on the front drive shaft (привод), not in the wheel hub (ступица). Single report, medium confidence.217

Noise when turning left. An owner with 40,000 km got a new noise when turning left after the wheels were rotated. Advice: remove the right front wheel and turn the hub by hand with the steering on full left lock to locate the source. Others suggest also checking the CV joint (ШРУС, slang "граната") and the tripod joint (трипоид), since either can make a noise as the car starts to move.218219220

docs.title: Lower control arm — brands and prices
docs.text:
Tags: #control-arm · #bushings · #price · #aftermarket

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

"Fork" (рычаг) assemblies from dismantlers: complete control-arm assemblies are available from vehicle dismantlers at reasonable cost (~500 RUB (RU market, September 2024) per part) and are reported to last 50,000+ km in normal use. FAW original cups, springs, and bushings are compatible as direct replacements after fitting a dismantler-sourced arm. After replacement, check suspension geometry 1.

Service pricing (Moscow, October 2024): lower control arm work with a new seal, plus pneumatic-spring replacement, plus silentblock installation totaled 5,200 RUB (RU market, October 2024). One shop separately charged 800 RUB (RU market, October 2024) just for removing and reinstalling the underbody protection plate — flagged by the community as a notable markup. Silentblocks are considered durable and worth replacing around 100,000 km as preventive maintenance 2.

Repeated lower control arm failures — silentblock bore mismatch: one owner reported replacing lower control arms 4 times over 256,000 km due to ball joint and silentblock failure (OEM pair first at 38,000 km, then a Volkswagen Jetta-sourced alternative at 20,000 km, a FAW alternative at 10,000 km, then a further swap at variable mileage). A critical fitment issue: the OEM silentblock bore is 40mm, but some aftermarket parts specify 42mm, causing fitment problems. The owner resolved this by sourcing polyurethane silentblocks for the Lynx/LinkS tie-rod attachment point. SH-brand lower control arms are noted as visually identical to the originals, with a matching silentblock fitment and the same nut design 3.

Rear suspension repair cost breakdown (Apr 2024, Russia): for a rear suspension job using all-new parts (alignment bolts were reusable): 2x bent rear control arms — 3,000 RUB; 2x rear longitudinal-arm bushings — 2,200 RUB; 2x rear cross-member bushings — 4,800 RUB. Springs were priced separately and not included in this total 4.

Rear bushings and dampers — no clear best brand (low confidence): one general discussion about which rear suspension bushing/damper brand is "best" concluded there is no single winner — quality varies significantly by supplier, and it's a cost-vs-quality tradeoff. Original (OEM) parts are considered the most reliable option but cost more 5.

Bent rear control arm — replacement cost (Oct 2025): a rear control arm bent after being hit from the side; replacement quoted at 2,000–2,500 RUB (RU market, October 2025) 678.

Used Mazda 6 GG front forks (control arms) — market prices: used Mazda 6 GG front forks/vanes (передние вилки), sold in good/restored condition, list for 1,700–2,000₽ per pair depending on seller and restoration work done (Avito/group marketplace, June 2026) 9101112.

Bushing brand reliability — CTR holds up, cheap Zekkert fails early, Sufix squeaks dry: CTR-brand suspension bushings tested to 20,000 km with no problems reported. Cheaper Zekkert bushings failed earlier (both ball-joint and bushing wear reported at lower mileage). Sufix bushings are available too but come with reports of squeaking in dry weather 131415.

Suspension component durability — Chinese analogs fail fast, OEM/Kayaba much better (long-term report): a detailed long-term comparison from one owner (Олег Белоусов): Chinese aftermarket brands referred to in the community as "Ситиер"/"Митиер" ("Sitier"/"Mitier") — covering ball joints, arm bushings, and related suspension bushings — are reported as poor quality across the board. His upper control arms: OEM lasted 190,000 km before the ball joints needed checking (ball joints outlived the bushings, which failed first); a Sitier-brand replacement arm failed at both ball joints after only ~1,000 km. His lower control arms: also fitted with "Mitier"/"Sitier"-brand arms, which lasted 70,000 km versus 160,000 km for the OEM arms. Tie-rod ends: OEM lasted 230,000+ km with only slight play developing by hand; a Sitier-brand pair felt suspiciously lighter than OEM on arrival and had not yet been road-tested at the time of reporting. Recommendation from this owner: avoid the cheap Chinese analog brands for suspension components generally and order OEM/original parts where possible 16. In a follow-up voice note, the same owner clarified specifically for the upper control arm ball joints: if the OEM arm is still fitted, it is usually the bushings that fail first while the ball joint stays serviceable — in that case replace only the bushings. If the ball joint itself has failed (developed play), look specifically for a Kayaba ball joint (sold separately) — reported as genuinely good quality — but Kayaba suspension parts for this application went out of production roughly a year prior to this report and are now hard to find 17.

Front lower control arm brand comparison — budget Zekkert fails fast, CTR holds up (Aug 2026): continuing the same 160,000 km durability conversation covered on the rear trailing arm bushing card (that card documents the rear-side half of this exchange), owner Arсhi 77 described his front lower control-arm history at that mileage: bushings only at first, then a full-arm replacement once the ball joint also started failing. A first, cheap complete arm assembly did not last long on his roads; a second, pricier arm has held up fine so far. Asked to identify the brands: the cheap one was Zekkert; the durable one, after checking, was CTR. In the same exchange, a full front lower control arm in assembly was quoted at roughly 3,000 RUB (RU market, August 2026) for the part alone, with labor to fit it around 1,500 RUB — a separate voice in the thread argued this is poor value compared to a bushing-only job at 700–1,000 RUB, calling the arm-replacement pricing a rip-off 18192021.

See also: Lower control arm bushings — sourcing (overview); Front lower arm bushings — numbers and sizes; Rear arm bushings — numbers and Mazda fit; Lower arm — Mazda 6 GG platform cross-fit; Lower arm bushings — pressing vs arm swap; Lower control arm — wear and aftermarket parts; Front upper arm — part numbers and ball joint.

docs.title: Lower arm bushings — pressing vs arm swap
docs.text:
Tags: #control-arm · #bushings · #diy

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Bushing-removal tool tip: for pressing sailentbloks (bushings) in and out, an impact perforator (industrial power drill fitted with a special tubular pusher, 20-100mm range) is reported as faster and more repeatable than the traditional manual-puller-plus-vise method. The tubular pusher set can be fabricated from standard pipe for DIY use 1.

Rear longitudinal-arm bushing replacement — DIY video guide: replacing the rear longitudinal control-arm bushing (see the SBX80PRODZK bushing on the rear bushing numbers card) is achievable DIY using heat plus a press. A YouTube guide (https://youtu.be/O3UCqnCH38M) documents the procedure; it requires a heat source, manual tools, and careful technique. For comparison, a commercial garage with a lift and hydraulic press completes the same job in roughly 15 minutes — DIY takes considerably longer 2.

Sealant-block (bushing) DIY press-out/press-in methods: bushings can be replaced without removing the entire control arm, using any of: (1) a heat-plus-drift method — heat the bushing, drive it out with a drift, then press the new one in; (2) a pneumatic hammer/perforator to assist pressing; (3) an improvised press made from a long bolt, stacked washers, and a wrench; (4) a rotary tool with a chisel to mill the old bushing out. Removing the full arm and using a shop press is the cleanest method, but all of the above DIY approaches are reported to work; if the ball joint is still serviceable, replacing just the bushings and keeping it is a valid option 3.

Rear longitudinal arm bushing — press-only, no simple swap (hardest part of a full suspension refresh): one owner replacing the rear longitudinal arm bushing alongside the front transverse arms and a lower right arm found every other part straightforward, but the rear longitudinal bushing "press-fit only" design made it far more difficult — no standard puller could reach it, with obstructions on all sides. The owner concludes they would rather pay a shop for this specific job next time. With two people working together it still took roughly 4 hours 4567.

Rear lower control-arm bushings — individually replaceable, retainer-ring type preferred, cost comparison (Nov 2025): confirming and extending the SBX80PRODZK bushing already documented on the rear bushing numbers card, the lower rear control arm's bushing (сайлентблок) can be replaced individually without swapping the whole arm 89. Buy only the bushing with a metal retainer ring, not the plain-rubber type — the ring type is harder to press in but performs better and is "the best of the silentblocks available" 1011. Mazda 6 GG-sourced bushings (and complete Mazda 6 GG arm assemblies) both fit the X80's rear 12131415. Cost comparison: a full rear control-arm assembly runs roughly 7,500–8,000 RUB (RU market, November 2025), versus individually replacing just the bushings, which one owner found considerably cheaper and did themselves 16.

Lower control arm bushings — Mazda 6 GG mixed-parts replacement: lower control arm bushings can be replaced using components from Mazda 6 GG (Mazda Atenza GG generation), typically as a mixed build — some factory-original components combined with aftermarket-compatible parts. New adjustment bolts are usually needed (2 pieces, for camber/toe adjustment) 17181920.

Oct 2026 update — removing the front lower arm with a puller. Сергей Елисеев says a puller (съёмник) makes lower-arm removal easy: tighten the puller, jack up the arm, and the joint releases with a click; raising two wheels simplifies the whole procedure 21. Victor could not remove the factory bushing without one, says a puller is definitely needed, and notes that his own puller is only for steering joints — arms need a heavier tool 22.

See also: Lower control arm bushings — sourcing (overview); Front lower arm bushings — numbers and sizes; Rear arm bushings — numbers and Mazda fit; Lower arm — Mazda 6 GG platform cross-fit; Lower control arm — brands and prices; Lower control arm — wear and aftermarket parts; Front upper arm — part numbers and ball joint.

docs.title: Lower control arm bushings — sourcing
docs.text:
Tags: #control-arm · #bushings · #mazda-6-compat · #part-number · #price

Overview. The front lower control arm (FAW part number FC0134J00) is sold only as a complete assembly; bushings can be pressed out and replaced with Mazda 6 GG or aftermarket units, but their bore dimensions must be matched, and the rear arms use similar bushings. The X80 chassis derives from the Mazda 6 GG, so many parts cross-fit. The detailed numbers, sizes, prices and procedures, each with its own sources, are in the cards listed at the end; this card keeps the symptom and diagnosis notes.

Lower ball joint squeak — same "replace the whole arm" rule applies: a loud squeak when turning the wheel to full lock (either direction) was diagnosed as worn lower ball joints on the front suspension — consistent with the sourcing cards linked below, the ball joint and its bushings are sold only as part of the complete lower control arm assembly, not separately; attempting to restore worn ball-joint rods is not considered economical 1.

Rear cross-member sideblock deterioration — how to assess severity: rear suspension sideblocks (silentblocks) commonly show some deterioration: slight peeling/separation at the edges is considered cosmetic and not urgent (it results from direct environmental/corrosion exposure, not structural failure). It becomes a real concern only if cracks appear near the center of the bushing, or if the separation reaches the main bonded area. At around 91,000 km, a full sideblock inspection is recommended as part of a general suspension refresh; Mazda sideblocks are sometimes used as a substitute but compatibility should be verified first 2.

Bent lower control arm causes steering non-return and alignment problems — replace and realign with X80 specs: a bent front lower control arm (передний нижний рычаг — the straight rod) causes the steering wheel not to return to center and throws off alignment. Diagnosis is by visual inspection from underneath or a video inspection. Fix: replace the bent arm with a new part, then perform a wheel alignment using X80-specific parameters — X80 alignment values differ from Mazda's and require a technician who actually knows this, not just a Mazda-6 alignment profile. (See the wheel alignment card for the broader steering-return/alignment symptom and parameter-source debate.) 34567.

Lower arm bushing wear at 210,000 km caused fender damage: at 210,000 km, lower control arm bushings showed significant wear with vertical play, letting the front-left wheel shift forward and damage the fender. Early warning sign: abnormal wear patterns in the wheel-well area — worth checking before it progresses to contact damage 89101112.

Caution — rough running/engine bucking after suspension work can be an air-intake leak, not an engine fault: if the engine starts pinning/bucking or running rough right after rear suspension work, don't assume it's an engine problem first — check for an air-intake leak caused incidentally during the suspension job (e.g. a disturbed hose/clamp near the intake). Locate and reseal any intake leaks before further diagnosis 1314.

See also: Front lower arm bushings — numbers and sizes; Rear arm bushings — numbers and Mazda fit; Lower arm — Mazda 6 GG platform cross-fit; Lower arm bushings — pressing vs arm swap; Lower control arm — brands and prices; Lower control arm — wear and aftermarket parts; Front upper arm — part numbers and ball joint.

docs.title: Front lower arm bushings — numbers and sizes
docs.text:
Tags: #control-arm · #bushings · #part-number · #mazda-6-compat · #silent-block

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Front lower ("longitudinal"/curved) control arm: FAW part number FC0134J00, sold only as a complete assembled unit — individual rubber bushings cannot be purchased separately from OEM suppliers. Bushings can be manually pressed out and replaced with aftermarket units, but sourcing loose bushings requires matching the exact dimensions 1. Aftermarket bushings are available via Chinaspare.ru (chinaspare.ru/c/saylentblok-perednego-nizhnego-krivogo-rychaga-faw), with catalog part numbers 61-04503-3X and 61-04504-3X, cross-checked against FAW and other Asian-manufacturer diagrams 2. Bushings for the front lower arm are also confirmed available for the facelifted (restyled) X80 via Kitzap.ru; the rear suspension uses similar bushings, and owners have successfully replaced the front set with rear work planned separately 3.

Cross-fit — Mazda 6 GG lower arm: FAW X80 lower control arms cross-reference to Mazda 6 (2002-2007 GG generation) and Mazda Atenza. Part number GJ6A34300 GG. Market price ~3,200 RUB (RU market, October 2024), available on M-Avto and other Russian automotive marketplaces 4.

Front control arms — detailed Mazda 6 GG compatibility: both the lower and upper front control arms are sourced from the Mazda 6 GG (first generation); measurements and silentblock dimensions match the Mazda GG parts per Sergey Elibeev. On bent/curved lower control arms, replacement can be attempted without full subframe removal — loosening (not removing) the subframe bolt on one side provides enough clearance. Quoted service labor was 8,000 RUB (RU market, May 2025) (2025-05-04). The Stellox brand part 57-71080a-sx is confirmed as a working lower-arm option 56.

Front lower-arm bushing brand comparison (Mazda 6 GG cross-fit, D-42mm): reinforcing the Mazda 6 GG cross-fit noted above (part GJ6A34300 GG) — the original X80 lower control-arm bushing bore is 42mm (D-42mm); Mazda 6 GG or first-generation Atenza (2002-2007) 40mm bushings are a direct fit and are generally preferred over buying a single loose bushing. An even better path is sourcing a complete Mazda control arm. Brand notes from the community: Lynx — decent rubber, standard quality; SH Parts — excellent quality, highly recommended; Suffix — poor-quality rubber; STR and 555 — unreliable/poor rubber. Cross-reference part GJ6A34300 GG on used-parts databases (e.g. Drom) for sourcing 7.

Lower control-arm restyle vs. pre-restyle compatibility — unverified, do not assume: whether the restyled (2018+) and pre-restyle lower control arms are interchangeable is not clearly established in the community; the recommendation is to verify part compatibility with a seller before ordering rather than assuming cross-fit between the two body styles (low confidence — no specific fitment difference was detailed) 8.

Conical bushing caution — lower ball joint to steering knuckle: when replacing front lower control arms, note there is a conical/tapered bushing installed between the lower ball joint and the steering knuckle. Handle it carefully during disassembly — improper technique can damage the bushing or the knuckle; taking photos before disassembly is recommended 9.

Front lower arm bushing — repeated failure and Mazda 6 GG cross-reference with dimensions: one owner asked where to source replacement bushings after having replaced the entire front lower control arm the previous year, only for the bushing to fail again 1011. Response: the front lower ("straight") control-arm bushing is available from any shop/marketplace, cross-referencing to the Mazda 6 GG (2002-2008) front lower control-arm bushing; dimension photos were shared for verification before ordering 1213.

Bushing maintenance at very high mileage — repress vs. full replacement, cost comparison (March 2026): at 260,000+ km, lower front control-arm bushings commonly need attention; the community lays out two paths with concrete March 2026 pricing: (1) repress the existing bushings (перепресовывать) — labor cost ~8,300 RUB (RU market, March 2026), preserves the original arms; or (2) replace the entire arm assembly — cheaper overall (~4,000–5,000 RUB per arm) and faster. Quality warning: budget Chinese arms (JD brand) were reported as poor quality, failing within 2–3 weeks of installation — separate bushing part numbers are hard to source on their own, making full-assembly replacement the more practical DIY route. Symptom: shaking/knocking when turning or over bumps indicates bushing failure 14151617181920.

Front lower control-arm anatomy — two arm variants, silentblock/ball-joint locations (March 2026): X80 front lower control arms come in two main variants: (1) a transverse short arm with a single silentblock and integrated ball joint, and (2) a longer transverse arm. Both variants have external and internal silentblock mounts, which is where bushing wear concentrates. At 260,000+ km, these silentblocks should be evaluated; professional testing involves inspecting the upper and lower arms with the vehicle on a lift. As with the maintenance-cost note above, complete arm replacement is generally more practical than bushing-only replacement for DIY work 162122232425.

Front lower control arm — two different-sized bushings, inner vs. outer: the front lower control arm (передний нижний рычаг) uses two differently-sized bushings that must not be confused: FC0134300-2 (inner/internal, сайлентблок внутренний) and FC0134300-1 (outer/external, сайлентблок внешний) — different diameters, different function, and both should be replaced together as a set when worn 262728.

Inner lower-arm bushing (sway-bar-link bolt point) — part FC0134300-2: the inner bushing at the front lower control arm's inner pivot (bolt position #22 on the exploded suspension diagram) is FAW part FC0134300-2, available from kitzapchasti.ru 2930.

Front lower control arm bushing — internal diameter mismatch (41mm needed, 40.3mm supplied): buying by part number alone is not reliable — one owner (Egor) ordered the lower control arm bushing and received a part with a 40.3mm internal (bore) diameter, when the X80 needs 41mm; checking other retailers' listings for the same nominal part turned up the same 40.3mm spec across multiple sites, suggesting the mismatch is widespread rather than a one-off packing error 313233. The same thread also covers upper front control-arm bushing wear and a dealer-vs-community sourcing dispute — see the dedicated upper control arm card for that part of the discussion.

See also: Lower control arm bushings — sourcing (overview); Rear arm bushings — numbers and Mazda fit; Lower arm — Mazda 6 GG platform cross-fit; Lower arm bushings — pressing vs arm swap; Lower control arm — brands and prices; Lower control arm — wear and aftermarket parts; Front upper arm — part numbers and ball joint.

docs.title: Lower arm — Mazda 6 GG platform cross-fit
docs.text:
Tags: #mazda-6-compat · #control-arm · #bushings

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Platform origin: the X80's suspension and chassis components are derived from the Mazda 6 (GG generation, 2003-2007), including struts, hubs, and control arms — which is the underlying reason so many Mazda 6 GG parts cross-fit throughout this card. The later Mazda 6 restyle (2008-2010) was never imported to Russia. The intake manifold and brake calipers are factory-modified for the X80 relative to the Mazda donor design 1.

B50 platform note: the FAW B50 shares the same suspension architecture as the X80, but silentblock (bushing) dimensions on the stock B50 control arms differ from the Mazda 6 GG equivalents despite an overall similar fit. One owner replaced a B50-style lower arm assembly outright rather than dealing with this complexity, even though the ball joint itself was still serviceable; silentblocks can be replaced separately (~1,000 RUB, RU market, May 2025) as a cheaper alternative to a full arm swap. Lesson: when sourcing cross-platform (Mazda-based) parts, always verify bushing dimensions even when overall fitment looks compatible 2.

Mazda 6 GG cross-fit (early confirmation): sway bar links, sway-bar bushings, and rear longitudinal-suspension-arm bushings from the Mazda 6 GG generation are reportedly direct-fit replacements on the X80 — search terms "chinaspare", "kitparts" for sourcing them; see also the stabilizer bar bushings card for the sway-bar side of this same report 3.

Mazda 6 GG suspension swap — comprehensive long-term case (262,000 km): reinforcing and extending the platform-origin note above — Mazda 6 GG (2002-2007) or first-generation Atenza (2002-2007) with the 2.0L engine is fully suspension-compatible with the X80, with the specific exception of the front hubs and brake calipers (the steering knuckle, control arms, brake discs, and brake calipers in this swap are all Mazda-sourced). Context: the X80 is roughly 200-250kg heavier than a Mazda 6, so component durability/stiffness expectations should account for that weight difference. One owner (Oleg) reports 262,000 km on a full Mazda suspension swap combined with pneumatic suspension add-ons, while still running the original X80 springs. Total swap cost was approximately 4,500 RUB (RU market, June 2025) for the suspension components plus 1,600 RUB for the pneumatic suspension add-ons 4.

Rear adjustment (control) lever — Mazda 6 fitment, support-bearing caveat (disputed): whether the Mazda 6 rear adjustment lever fits the X80 got a quick "yes, from 6GG" 56, but a follow-up question about whether the X80's own strut support bearings (опорные подшипники) would still work if Mazda forks and struts are fitted got only a tentative "probably yes" 78 — a separate community member recalls seeing elsewhere that the support bearings do differ from Mazda's, though this was not confirmed ("not 100% sure") 9. Conflict: treat support-bearing compatibility in a Mazda strut/fork swap as unverified until confirmed by a direct fitment check.

Mazda 6 GG control arms — fitment confirmed, durability highly variable (March 2026): reinforcing the Mazda 6 GG cross-fit already established on this card, both front and rear control arms from the Mazda 6 GG fit the X80 (a wheel alignment is required after installation, as with any control-arm swap). Durability, however, is reported as highly variable: cheap aftermarket GG-sourced arms failed at only 30,000 km for one owner, while genuine OEM lower arms on another vehicle lasted 187,000 km. Upper ball-joint seals are reported as a particular weak point. One owner needed a complete rear-suspension replacement after installed (non-OEM) arms failed at just 30,000 km 1011121314.

See also: Lower control arm bushings — sourcing (overview); Front lower arm bushings — numbers and sizes; Rear arm bushings — numbers and Mazda fit; Lower arm bushings — pressing vs arm swap; Lower control arm — brands and prices; Lower control arm — wear and aftermarket parts; Front upper arm — part numbers and ball joint.

docs.title: Rear arm bushings — numbers and Mazda fit
docs.text:
Tags: #control-arm · #bushings · #part-number · #mazda-6-compat · #rear-suspension

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Rear lower longitudinal arm bushing: part number SBX80PRODZK. Clarification from the community: this is the rear longitudinal arm bushing, not a front part — some service paperwork mislabels components. The X80 has two distinct lower-arm assemblies: the front lower wishbone (with 2 bushings plus a ball joint) and the rear longitudinal arm (with 1 bushing) 1.

Rear longitudinal arm bushing — Mazda fit confirmed long-term: rear longitudinal arm rubber bushings from Mazda fit the X80 1:1. One owner (Ayr) installed them and reports 40,000 km with no issues and good durability; cost is approximately 2,000 RUB (RU market, March 2025). Installation can be done using either KitParts-original or Mazda-sourced bushings (Masuma brand has been seen on the packaging in photos) 23.

Front upper ball joint — Vita/B50 cross-fit: the front upper ball joint C23034250, from the FAW Vita/B50, fits the X80. As noted on the hub-bearing card, the hub assembly itself is sold only as unit 5CA033047B and is not separable. Related part numbers reported in the same source: CV boots — outer B5DA122530, inner B5CA022540; rear upper arm bushing FC0128C10; rear cross-member bushing 5CA028430ZK (also written 5CA028430) 4.

Rear cross-member bushing 5CA028430ZK — aftermarket incompatibility confirmed: following up on the part number noted above, aftermarket copies of the rear cross-member bushing (5CA028430ZK) turned out to have a rubber outer shell, while the OEM part has a metal outer shell — making the aftermarket version physically incompatible. One community member spent 3,500 RUB (RU market, April 2024) on the wrong aftermarket parts before catching the mismatch via comparison photos. Recommendation from this experience: buy complete assembled rear arms rather than sourcing separate rear cross-member bushings, to avoid this kind of mismatch 5.

Rear longitudinal-arm bushing — sourcing question resolved to Mazda 6 GG: reinforcing the rear longitudinal-arm bushing cross-fit already documented on this card, a fresh sourcing question about which bushing fits the rear longitudinal arm was answered simply: "look at Mazda 6 GG" 67.

Rear control-arm bushings — Mazda source confirmed, described as simple: a fragment of a separate thread confirms Mazda-sourced bushings "will definitely fit" the rear control arms, with the poster noting they have only ever replaced the bushings (not the whole arm) in this way — describing the swap as "about as simple as it gets" 89.

Rear longitudinal-arm ("eared") bushing diameter — confirmed 60mm (Mazda 6 GG), not 70mm (GH): settling a diameter question about the rear longitudinal-rod bushing — is it the Mazda 6 GG 60mm size or the GH 70mm size? — multiple owners confirm the X80's rear longitudinal-arm bushing is 60mm, matching Mazda 6 GG (not GH). One owner recently replaced it and confirms the 60mm size directly; a shrink-tube/pressing reference of 60mm was also cited. The specific part shared in the community was Masuma-brand, sourced against the Mazda 6 GG part number 1011121314.

Rear longitudinal-arm bushing orientation — identical L/R, cone bolt-down (March 2026): the rear suspension's longitudinal control-arm bushings (silentblocks) are identical for the left and right sides — no separate L/R part numbers. Installation detail: the cone-shaped bushings must be positioned with their bolts pointing downward 1516.

Rear control-arm kit from Mazda 6 GG — initial uncertainty, then confirmed fitting: complete rear suspension control-arm kits from Mazda 6 GG (spanning GG/GH/GJ/GL generations, 2007–2023, bolts included) are sold on Ozon. An early report treated fitment to the X80 as unverified, since mounting geometry and attachment points could differ and would need manual checking. A follow-up in the same thread reports these Mazda 6 GG rear control-arm sets do fit the X80 without issues, available as a bolt-included kit on Ozon (https://ozon.ru/t/8qtbbkV) 171819.

Rear suspension bushings (silentblocks) from Mazda fit the X80: rear suspension bushings (сайлентблоки) sourced from Mazda fit FAW X80 models 202122232425262728.

Rear control arm bushings — Masuma MA-103 (Mazda 6 GG): another Mazda-6-GG cross-fit for the rear control-arm bushings/silentblocks: Masuma MA-103. Reported as indistinguishable from OEM sileblocks when bought new; this owner opted to buy a complete pre-bushed arm assembly rather than press old bushings out and rebuild 29.

Rear lower control arms — Mazda 6 GG, part numbers 5CA128300 / 5CA128350: rear suspension lower control arms (рычаги под пружину) for the X80 can be sourced from Mazda 6 GG under FAW part numbers 5CA128300 and 5CA128350 (left/right pair — note these are the FAW catalog numbers cross-referenced to the Mazda-sourced part, not raw Mazda numbers). Prices vary widely by brand: ~2,000₽ for budget brands up to ~4,000₽ for quality brands like KMK; KitZap pricing was considered unreliable/inconsistent by the community ("from kopecks to space" — always verify against multiple sources) 3031323334.

Rear suspension bushing part-number catalog (cross-brand from FAW B50): a fuller rear-bushing part-number set, several cross-referenced from the B50 platform: lower control arm bushing under the spring — 5CA028430; longitudinal control arm bushing (B50 cross-fit) — FA0128200-1; stabilizer link bushing — 5CA028156; upper control arm bushing — FC0128C10-1; rear suspension bolt — FQFD162866ZB; B50 lower control arm bushing alternative — FA0128500-1. Several of these are shared/interchangeable with the B50 35363738394041.

Rear bushing count and layout — 7 per side: the rear suspension uses 7 bushings per side total: 1 on the longitudinal control arm, and the rest split in pairs across the remaining control arms — useful as a checklist when doing a full rear-bushing refresh 4241.

Rear longitudinal-arm bushing — shared with B50, part FA0128250 / FA0128200: the rear longitudinal-arm silentblock is the same part on X80 and B50 — catalog number FA0128250 (also listed as FA0128200-1), available from multiple Chinese-parts suppliers 4344.

See also: Lower control arm bushings — sourcing (overview); Front lower arm bushings — numbers and sizes; Lower arm — Mazda 6 GG platform cross-fit; Lower arm bushings — pressing vs arm swap; Lower control arm — brands and prices; Lower control arm — wear and aftermarket parts; Front upper arm — part numbers and ball joint.

docs.title: Lower control arm — wear and aftermarket parts
docs.text:
Tags: #control-arm · #silent-block · #part-number · #price · #mazda-6-compat

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Arm layout and silent-block numbers. The front lower control arm has two silent blocks (сайлентблоки, rubber bushings), outer and inner, plus a ball joint; the rear longitudinal (trailing) arm has a single silent block with no front or rear label. A query that mixed the two arms received the unexplained code SBX80PRODZK.12 The inner silent block of the front lower arm is listed as FC0134300-2; the outer end, at the ball joint, is the other silent block, and a Stellox diagram circles the lower-arm bushing labelled 87-71050-SX.345 For the rear silent block of the front lower arm an owner gave GJ6A-34-460B (also found as GJ6A-34-460A) and the FEBEST equivalent MZAB-016.6 A Drom listing from M-Avto (Podolsk) offers the front lower arm GJ6A34300GG as fitting Mazda 6 / Atenza and FAW X80 / B50 at 2,800 RUB (RU market, May 2025); its 2002-2007 year range is the Mazda 6 range and is not verified for the X80.7

Wear and aftermarket experience. At about 160,000 km one owner replaced the lower arms because the silent blocks at the subframe had worn, noting that cheap parts wear quickly.8 Another owner puts the OEM lower arm (the one the strut mounts to) at around 10,000 RUB (RU market, June 2025) and calls SA Sparts (СА Шпарц, transliterated) aftermarket arms a good, original-quality alternative that lasted to about 250,000 km; cheap arms at about 3,000 RUB (RU market, June 2025) had silent blocks and ball joints that broke almost at once.9 A different owner had the tie rods and a lower arm replaced at a dealer, says cheap ball joints (шаровые) on these cars failed around 70,000 km, and fitted a Sufix-type aftermarket lower arm (the boot needs grease packed under it) that seems to work so far; he calls Japanese and Korean "imitation" parts junk.1011 On bushings alone, one owner reports about 7,000 km on Tenacity AAMMA1017 silent blocks while the original ones had failed by about 50,000 km (the bushing position is not stated); another member advised buying by exact dimensions, avoiding the cheapest option and buying several brands at once.121314

Service damage. In a 47-second video an owner shows a new lower arm that he says a service centre damaged while fitting it: the bolts were driven into the wrong hole, the arm was punched through and had to be pressed and refitted. He says the service admitted the fault, and attributes the repeated arm replacements partly to poor workmanship.1516

Wear points at 190,000 km. One owner's stock suspension lasted about 190,000 km before the whole chassis began to wear: struts, the three-link arms (two upper and one straight; the curved arm lasts longest), stabilizer bushings and links. A lower-arm bushing fell out of the subframe three days after a service refit. At the rear there are many rubber silent blocks, and two Mazda-type rear longitudinal arms did not fit, so he pressed their bushings out.171819

See also: Lower control arm bushings — sourcing, Control arm replacement cost, Rear trailing arm bushing, Steering tie rods.

docs.title: Power steering fluid — service procedure
docs.text:
Tags: #power-steering · #gur

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Confirmed-compatible fluid brand — ZIC. ZIC-brand power steering fluid (PSF) is confirmed suitable for the X80's power-steering system. One owner referred to "our" original fluid when discussing it, suggesting an FAW-branded OEM PSF may also exist/be available, though this wasn't independently confirmed in the thread.123

Level check and top-up. Power steering fluid level should be maintained at the proper mark on the dipstick/reservoir. If the level is at minimum but there's no visible leak, simply top up with the appropriate fluid — spec 3309 was cited for the correct fluid type.456789

Full flush procedure (optional, not urgent unless fluid looks degraded). A complete fluid flush can be performed via the return-hose method: run clean fluid through the system continuously until the fluid discharging from the return line comes out clean. This can extend the system's service life. It is not necessary to perform a full flush immediately just because the level was low — only prioritize it if the existing fluid visibly looks degraded (dark, cloudy, or contaminated).456789

Emergency repair for a ruptured return hose. If the low-pressure rubber return hose between the power-steering pump and the reservoir ruptures, all hydraulic fluid leaks out and the steering goes lock-solid immediately — this is a distinct failure from the level/topup guidance above and needs an emergency response, not a top-up. OEM replacement hose costs about 10,000 RUB (RU market, June 2026) with delivery and involves a wait; a faster/cheaper emergency option is a local RVD (hydraulic-hose repair) shop, which can re-crimp/reseal the old hose or fabricate a replacement for roughly 1,000–2,000 RUB, often same-day. One owner completed this repair for 2,000 RUB (RU market, June 2026) (re-crimp/reseal) and was back on the road the same day. Hose location: under the engine, connecting the hydraulic lines to the power-steering gear/rack.101112131415161718192021

Fluid spec — Mobil 3309 / Type IV, or a matching multigrade synthetic/mineral oil. Restating and confirming the 3309 spec already noted above: Mobil 3309 or Type IV fluid is permitted for the GUR (power-steering) system. A synthetic/mineral multigrade oil ("мультик") is also acceptable as long as it matches FAW's approval for the spec. The same fluid can be used interchangeably in both the GUR and the transmission.2223242526

Whining/howling noise from the engine bay — check GUR fluid first. A whining or howling noise from the engine bay, audible in the cabin at low RPM during acceleration and increasing during full wheel turns, has several possible causes, with GUR fluid level as the primary suspect: (1) low power-steering (GUR) fluid — check and top up first; (2) a worn bearing (alternator or another roller bearing); (3) a loose/slipping serpentine belt; (4) A/C-compressor-clutch engagement. First troubleshooting step: check and top up GUR fluid. If the noise continues afterward, inspect the GUR pump and steering rack for leaks. Reminder: the X80 uses hydraulic (not electronic) power steering, so this fluid-level check is a valid first diagnostic step for this noise pattern.27282930

GUR fluid specification restated — ATF 3309 or Type IV, interchangeable. The X80's hydraulic steering system uses ATF 3309 or Type IV fluid — an older (3309, "vintage") and a newer (Type IV) specification that are compatible and can be mixed. When replacing the fluid, changing the entire volume gives the best results rather than a partial top-up.313233

PSF = ATF confirmed, plus system pressure spec. Restating the ATF/PSF equivalence documented above with independent confirmation: power-steering fluid (PSF) is the same as the ATF used in the automatic transmission. System pressure spec, from a factory under-hood label: 127 kPa (18 psi).34353637
