Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Which aftermarket and Kayaba/KYB, Zekkert, Lynx, Narcin and other brands owners tried on the X80, and their verdicts. Overview: Shock absorbers — overview and platform baseline. See also front damper type and brand experience and fitment and quality issues.

Brand comparison: Kayaba shocks are considered overpriced relative to their performance. Lynx offers about a 3,000 RUB (RU market, September 2024) saving over Kayaba. Narcin is recommended by one owner as the best value alternative — cross-reference the Narcin part number against Kayaba's OEM number before buying 1. Disagreement: a separate, unidentified user instead recommends Masuma shocks, sourced from the DRIVE2 parts database 1.

Cosmetic variation: a purchased pair of shocks arrived with mismatched hardware finish — left unit had black-painted mounting bolts/brackets, right unit had unpainted/silver hardware. The parts were otherwise functionally identical; if the OEM part number and date code match, the cosmetic difference does not indicate a functional problem (likely different manufacturing batches/suppliers) 2.

Long-term rear "soft ride" fix: one owner replaced springs five times and added buffers/spacers without success (suspension kept settling immediately under load). Installing Zekkert-brand shocks (sourced via chinaavto, St. Petersburg) fully resolved the issue — the rear stayed soft with no bottoming-out even carrying ~200kg cargo plus 4 passengers. A KYB model 344363 had been tried first and failed (too short); universal Mazda 6 shocks were also ineffective. Conclusion from this owner's experience: rear ride softness depends primarily on shock absorber quality, not spring stiffness 3.

Rear shocks — Zekkert via Wildberries: an alternative rear shock absorber, Zekkert brand (described by one owner as "better than stock"), available on Wildberries. Model compatibility spans FAW B50/X80 and Mazda 6 — the same dampers are usable on both platforms. No left/right differentiation is needed; the same part number works on either side 45.

Brand comparison — Lynx preferred over Zekkert: Lynx-brand suspension components are reported to be universally preferred over Zekkert for X80 use, offering better performance and reliability; Zekkert is considered the lower-quality alternative in this comparison 67.

Rear shock option — Kayaba, factory-spec match: Kayaba-brand rear shock absorbers are available and were purchased by one owner as a factory-spec-matched replacement for rear suspension service 8.

Marshall brand — untested: Marshall-brand suspension shocks/struts are sold on the market (Ozon link shared), but as of the report no community member had reviews or hands-on experience with them yet 9.

Budget path — Stellox (Chinese) shocks, no fork swap required (April 2026): Stellox-brand shocks (Chinese, budget option) can be installed directly onto the standard Chinese-spec forks/struts already on the car, with no fork replacement needed. They are less expensive but lower quality than Japanese brands such as KYB or Monro 101112.

Rear shock upgrade — KYB 344363 vs KYB 349033, and stock-vs-KYB dimensions: KYB 344363 rear shocks reduce rear sway somewhat but not dramatically — adequate for street driving, not a major improvement over stock on rough terrain with passengers. KYB 349033 is about 1cm shorter and noticeably stiffer than the 344363 — a more aggressive setup that some find too extreme for daily driving. Dimensionally, the stock FAW rear shock measures 466/317mm inter-bushing spacing, 48.5mm body diameter, 62.4mm bushing length; the KYB NewSR NSF2065 alternative is 453/301mm inter-bushing, 45mm body (1cm shorter overall than stock, which reduces wheel-arch clearance slightly), same 62.4mm bushing length. By ~280,000 km stock rear shocks are typically worn out and due for replacement. Pricing: Kayaba 344363, ~8,900₽/pair via Emex (June 2026) 1314151617181920.

KYB NSF2065 — discontinued in Russia, and how it compares to stock: KYB NSF2065 rear shocks (Mazda GG-spec, already documented above) are reported as no longer available in the Russian Federation as of June 2026 (last units purchased the year prior). Compared directly against a worn stock shock: the stock unit is about 1.5× easier to compress by hand and rebounds about 1.5× faster; stock shocks at ~140,000 km are still functional but noticeably softer/worn. New KYB units are stiffer and pricier. One owner separately reports puncturing a KYB NSF2065 strut body on a pothole in winter, losing all its oil — "money down the drain... not made for our roads" 21222324.

Front shock upgrade path — Mazda Kayaba after 38,000 km, and a manual-vs-automatic spring/shock weight difference (Sept 2026): owner Андрей installed Mazda-sourced Kayaba front shocks after 38,000 km on the original setup, replacing the forks (вилки) at the same time as is standard for this swap (see the Mazda-fork notes in the Mazda GG fork swap card). Separately, owner Victor 🇷🇺 reported having bought a set of Kayaba shocks two months earlier but had not yet installed them, planning instead to run the original factory struts for roughly another 40,000 km before swapping. In the same exchange, discussing why rear springs seem inconsistent between cars, Victor noted that the automatic (АКПП) and manual (МКПП) versions of the X80 differ in curb weight by about 40kg, which he suggests means the rear springs themselves likely differ between the two: the automatic may use a thicker spring, while the manual is confirmed at 13mm wire diameter 252627.

docs.title: Damper types, cold behaviour and failure signs
docs.text:
Tags: #shock-absorbers · #cold-weather

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Oil versus gas dampers, cold-weather clunks, internal foaming, restoration services and the other failure symptoms owners report. Overview: Shock absorbers — overview and platform baseline. See also front damper type and brand experience.

Gas-oil dampers — general option overview: gas-oil (gas-filled) dampers improve handling and help prevent oil cavitation under load. 300+ variants are listed on Yandex Market, including recommended brands KYB, Sachs, Boge, Bilstein, Monroe (note: see the Sachs clunking warning in the damper-types paragraph below). Both front and rear variants are available; selection should be matched to the vehicle's model year 1.

Extreme cold (−20°C) failure — stock Tokico and new Stellox both affected: at −20°C, one owner's stock Tokico dampers failed to return fully after compression (the shaft got stuck); new Stellox (Chinese) dampers fitted as a replacement performed poorly in the frost as well. Conflict: a more experienced community member ("Master") warned in advance that switching to Stellox would have no effect on this symptom, and the owner's actual cold-weather experience with both stock and new dampers appears to bear that warning out — suggesting the issue may be inherent to the damper design/fluid at extreme cold rather than brand choice 234567.

Front shock rattling — internal foam/cavitation degradation, a systemic design issue (March 2026): X80 factory front shocks develop internal foaming/cavitation over time (typically 5–7 years), causing persistent metallic rattling and knocking from the front suspension. Symptoms intensify with vehicle age and load. This is reported as systemic — replacing with another OEM unit does not necessarily fix it, since new OEM shocks can exhibit the same noise again after only 2–3 weeks if the original design is retained. Recommended alternative: quality aftermarket shocks, with Mazda 6 GG shocks again reported as a superior option over continuing with stock-design OEM replacements 89101112.

Damper types and brand guidance — oil vs. gas, GG vs. GH generation notes (April 2026): almost all automotive shock absorbers are hydraulic (oil-based); the gas (nitrogen) charge is a pressure backup that prevents oil foaming, not a replacement for the oil damping itself. Oil-filled types with proportionally less gas give a softer ride. For the X80, Kayaba and Tokiko (non-FAW-branded Tokiko, i.e. the genuine Japanese brand rather than a rebadge) are the community-preferred brands. Avoid Sachs — reconfirms the clunking/clicking complaints already noted from multiple independent owners. The GG vs. GH suspension generations differ mechanically: GG has shorter damper strokes, GH has longer strokes and a different spring count per wheel side — relevant when cross-shopping Mazda-sourced dampers and springs together 1314151617181920212223242526272829.

Stiff ride and noisy front struts at 87,000–106,000 km — no failures yet: several owners report the suspension feels stiff and the front struts squeak around the upper mount area over bumps at this mileage range, without any outright failure. Mazda-strut replacement is suggested as a comfort upgrade, but some owners question whether it's worth the cost at this mileage if nothing has actually failed 3031323334.

Damper restoration service (gas-oil repressurization) — Moscow shops: some Moscow specialty shops offer damper (strut) restoration: pressure-testing and re-sealing on a dedicated bench followed by a fresh gas-oil charge, claimed to restore a damper to near-new condition for another ~100,000 km. This is different from a simple top-up and needs industrial equipment. Not recommended as a routine fix for safety-critical suspension parts — replacement is the safer default — but some owners report success with restored struts when new-part cost is prohibitive 35363738.

Front shock clunk/tap in cold weather — common, hard to pin down, often deemed within normal limits: a frequently reported cold-weather symptom (below ~0°C): clicking, tapping, or clunking from the front end over bumps, often asymmetric (louder on one side than the other). Multiple owners report the same thing, including cases at very low mileage (under 100,000 km). A shop technician who rode along and listened concluded it could simply be how the shock absorbers work in the cold and found no play or wear on inspection. Community consensus: described as a "frequent phenomenon, difficult to resolve completely" — no universal fix has been identified. Suggested underlying causes (unconfirmed): piston seal behavior changing in the cold, spring preload shifting with temperature, or normal manufacturing-tolerance stack-up that only becomes audible when parts contract in freezing weather. Worth cross-checking against the separate suspension noise diagnostic checklist, since caliper guide pins are a commonly confirmed alternate cause of a very similar cold-weather clunk 39404142434445.

docs.title: Shock absorbers — overview and platform baseline
docs.text:
Tags: #shock-absorbers · #mazda-6-compat

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

The X80 front and rear shock absorbers (амортизаторы) come from a Mazda 6 GG-derived suspension that owners describe as soft. The community knowledge is split into topic cards, each listed below; this page keeps the platform baseline and the overall brand consensus.

  • Mazda 6 GG shocks, forks and part numbers — part numbers, Mazda 6 GG/GH fitment and the fork swap
  • Shock absorber brands — owner verdicts — aftermarket brands (KYB, Zekkert, Lynx, Narcin, Stellox) and owner verdicts
  • Damper types, cold behaviour and failure signs — oil versus gas dampers, cold-weather clunks, rattling and restoration
  • Shock installation, bump stops and mounts — DIY replacement, spring compressors, bump stops, dust boots, mounts and bolts
  • Shock absorber prices and costs — dated prices and installation costs

Related existing cards: shock absorber replacement, fitment and quality issues, front damper type and brand experience, front strut dust boots sourcing.

Platform baseline — Mazda 6 GG architecture and cold-weather shock behavior (Feb 2026): the X80's suspension is architecturally based on the Mazda 6 GG — described by the community as inherently soft and prone to bottoming out on rough roads, though it rides smoothly at highway speeds. In cold weather (−15°C and below), shock absorbers commonly lose responsiveness and produce noise/clunking over bumps; this is temperature-dependent and does not necessarily mean the shock has failed. Given the platform's soft baseline, suspension maintenance is considered critical for regularly driving bumpy roads, and many owners prefer not to modify beyond necessary repairs given the limited proven alternatives 12345678910.

Why the ride feels soft — suspension is Mazda-derived, but the X80 is heavier: the X80's suspension design is sourced from the Mazda 6, but the X80's curb weight (~1.5 tonnes) is meaningfully heavier than the donor car. Community explanation for the car's generally soft, non-sporty ride feel: the extra mass naturally damps out dynamic driving response that a Mazda-spec suspension would otherwise deliver on a lighter chassis — i.e., the "softness" isn't necessarily worn components, it's an inherent mismatch between a lighter-car suspension tune and a heavier body 11.

Shock brand consensus — Kayaba best value, but counterfeits exist: for X80 rear shock replacement (OEM part 5CA028700A for the 2019+ facelift, aftermarket ~2,000–5,000₽ vs ~10,000₽ OEM), Kayaba remains the community's best-value consensus pick — but counterfeit Kayaba units are reportedly on the market, so buy only from reputable vendors and inspect for authenticity. Low-mileage used OEM shocks are another option but need careful vetting. General consensus: avoid no-name brands — "buy once, buy right" 12131415.

docs.title: Shock installation, bump stops and mounts
docs.text:
Tags: #shock-absorbers · #installation

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Replacing shocks at home, spring compressors, bump stops (отбойники), dust boots, strut support bearings, mounting bolts and other installation details. Overview: Shock absorbers — overview and platform baseline. See also shock absorber replacement and front strut dust boots sourcing.

Bump stops (отбойники) reduce knocking: the X80 uses soft dampers, with much of the spring load concentrated on the rubber bump stops rather than the shocks themselves. Rear knocking/clunking noise while driving was resolved by replacing the rear bump stops, with a bonus softer ride feel afterward. Front bump stops are recommended for replacement on the same schedule for consistent comfort 1. A separate report confirms the same fix: a dull, low-speed metallic clunk traced to worn shock-absorber bump stops was eliminated by replacing the rear units 2.

Front shock dust boot sourcing: front shock-absorber dust boots (пыльники) are available via Kitparts and Ozon catalogs. An attempted substitute — Lynx-brand boots intended for a Mazda CX-5 — did not fit (the seals were too short). A working alternative: a Lynx-brand set of two dust boots plus two bump stops (отбойники), sourced through KitZap with delivery 3.

Front strut support bearing (опорный подшипник) — pricing and sourcing: the front strut top support bearing is sold as two separate components — the housing/cup (чашка) and the bearing itself (подшипник). Factory pricing: cup 2,000 RUB (RU market, July 2025), bearing 1,200 RUB (3,200 RUB combined). One shop's retail price for the cup alone was 1,060 RUB (RU market, July 2025). Sourcing options: kitzapchasti.ru (sometimes doesn't list the bearing as a separate SKU), kitparts.ru (order-only, ~4-day wait), and zzap.ru (a parts aggregator that shows multiple store options by part number). Some retailers list only the cup, without the bearing as a separate purchasable item 4.

DIY rear shock replacement — needs a lift/pit, spring compressor essential (Sept 2025): rear shock replacement is not practical at home without a vehicle lift or service pit; even with an impact wrench and a helper, budget 2+ hours per side 567. The spring must be compressed for removal/installation — one owner's first pair of compressors failed (snapped) on the very first strut and again while releasing the last one, while a second, sturdier compressor set held up 8910. A recommended source: a 280mm double-hook spring compressor set (2 pcs) from Ozon, well lubricated before use; several owners report it holding up well, though a poor-quality compressor can snap and cause injury (numbed hands reported after one such failure) 11121314.

Front strut top mount ("опора") — also sourceable from FAW B50 (Feb 2026): a brief confirmation, separate from the SAM-4101/GJ6E strut mount bearing prices and sourcing in the prices and costs card — the front strut top mount itself can be sourced from the FAW B50 as a cross-fit part 15.

KYB shocks — longer stroke makes spring work much easier: KYB aftermarket shocks have a significantly longer stroke than the factory X80 units, so compressing the spring for install/removal is far easier and does not require a spring-compressor press — the stock shocks' very short stroke is what makes that job hard 1617.

Replacement front shock rod stub too long (38mm vs 35mm spec) — machine-shop fix: when replacing front shocks at high mileage (100,000+ km), a new unit can arrive with a longer rod stub than spec (38mm measured vs the correct ~35mm), throwing off suspension geometry and causing rattling/rubbing. Diagnosis: measure the rod stub length against the original (or with a ruler if the original isn't available). Fix: a machine shop shortens the stub by cutting ~2cm off, then the strut is reassembled. One owner discovered this at 130,000 km, after already replacing two front hub bearings, during a suspension service — always verify both old and new shock condition/dimensions before installing 1819202122.

Rear shock mounting bolts seized in rubber sleeves at 62,000 km: at 62,000 km, rear shock mounting bolts had corroded/bonded (galvanic action between the rubber sleeve and metal bolt) so badly they had to be cut out with an angle grinder. Prevention for future installs: coat the bolt with graphite lubricant or Lithol-type grease before assembly 232425.

Rear shock dust boots — Mazda 6 KYB kit, cheaper than some local sources: dust boots and rebound bump stops (пыльники + отбойники) for rear shocks are available as a Mazda 6 GG-fit KYB 910 107 kit (Mazda 6 '02+ fitment); found cheaper on Ozon than some alternative sources; one installer reports successful use 2627.

Factory assembly hooks on the shocks — safe to remove, plus a cheap angle-adjustment tool: stock X80 shocks have small hooks/brackets that look like manufacturing/assembly aids (likely used to hang the strut on the line before final bolting) — they serve no function after installation and tend to catch on things during removal/installation, especially off a lift. Many owners recommend simply removing them. A cheap (~100–1,000₽) fuse-box-style tool can help set the strut angle correctly during installation 28293031.

Metallic clank after rear shock replacement — likely bushings, not a loose fastener: if a metallic knocking sound appears specifically after replacing the rear shock absorbers, and a visual re-check finds everything properly torqued, the noise is more likely coming from worn suspension bushings (сайленты) than an actually loose fastener — inspect the bushings rather than continuing to re-check the shock mounting hardware 3233.

docs.title: Mazda 6 GG shocks, forks and part numbers
docs.text:
Tags: #shock-absorbers · #mazda-6-compat · #part-number

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Front and rear shock part numbers, what Mazda 6 GG (and GH) shocks fit, and the fork (вилка) swap that Mazda-sourced struts require. Overview: Shock absorbers — overview and platform baseline.

Front suspension rebuild — component-by-component recommendations: when refreshing the whole front suspension, community guidance is: (1) keep the OEM motor mounts (опоры) — no routine replacement needed; (2) source springs from a Mazda 626 GG (direct compatibility, see the front springs card for cross-fit detail); (3) use OEM suspension arms where available, or a quality aftermarket/used alternative otherwise; (4) keep the OEM top strut mounts unless actually worn; (5) consider aftermarket shocks if OEM units are unavailable 12.

Shock length/fitment caution on a full rebuild: when rebuilding the complete front suspension (springs + dampers together), check carefully — aftermarket shocks can be a different length than OEM (one case was 2cm shorter), which requires verifying spring protrusion before installation. OEM parts are rarely available, making a fully matched OEM set hard to source 3.

"Fork" fitment note: when fitting aftermarket suspension, the mounting fork (вилка) on some aftermarket parts is slightly thicker than the original, so Mazda-specification forks are needed rather than a direct OEM swap. This came up in the context of spring/shock selection during a suspension refresh 4.

Kayaba (Mazda 6 GG) shocks require donor control arms: Kayaba shock absorbers pulled from a Mazda 6 GG can be physically fitted to the X80 front suspension, but not into the OEM X80 mounting fork without modification — the original FAW control arm has a 46mm mounting hole, while the Kayaba shock mounts in a 42mm hole. Workaround: source the Mazda 6 control arms/forks together with the shocks so the hole size matches; installing a Mazda-generation shock into an unmodified X80 fork does not work 5.

Rear shocks — Mazda GG fitment, KYB premium option (Sept 2025): rear shock absorbers from Mazda 6 GG fit the X80 6. A premium alternative is KYB, reported to be higher quality but with long lead times (~25 days from Asia) and a steep price 78.

Front shock/strut sourcing — Mazda 6 GG fitment requires the Mazda fork too (Sept 2025): reinforcing the Kayaba/Mazda-fork note already on this card, KYB Kayaba shocks (KYB part numbers 341352 front-left, 341351 front-right, cross-referencing Mazda part numbers GJ6A34711A/GJ6A34911A for the matching fork/spindle) are widely recommended if sourced from a Mazda 6 GG — but installing a Mazda-generation front shock into the X80's own fork requires swapping in the Mazda fork as well; the two forks are not interchangeable 910111213141516.

Aftermarket shock diameter mismatch — thicker than OEM, plus a separate stripped-thread failure: a separate report describes a purchased aftermarket front strut with the fork's clamping thread stripped, causing a knock while turning; the same owner notes the replacement struts received were physically thicker in diameter than the original FAW units 17.

Mazda-fork swap — bolt specification and sourcing (Oct 2025): when swapping to Mazda front suspension forks, the X80's own bolts do not fit the Mazda fork holes. Required spec: M8 fine-thread, 5–6cm length. Retail sourcing (e.g. Avtopiter) runs about 300 RUB (RU market, October 2025) per bolt, but generic hardware-store bolts of this spec reportedly do not work and can mean a week's wait to source correctly — the community's practical recommendation is to buy complete fork assemblies from a dismantler (разборка), with their original bolts included, to avoid separately sourcing this hard-to-match bolt 18192021222324252627.

Front struts — Mazda 6 GG incompatible without a fork swap, OEM part numbers (Nov 2025): reinforcing and quantifying the "2mm thicker" incompatibility already noted on this card: X80 front struts are not directly compatible with Mazda 6 GG because the X80's strut body is 2mm thicker than the Mazda spec — a Mazda strut only works with a matching Mazda fork, not the X80's own fork. OEM X80 strut part numbers: 5CA034700 (right), 5CA034900 (left). Recommended sourcing: genuine FAW parts, or a complete used strut+fork assembly from a dismantler (cheap) rather than mixing components across platforms 28293031323334.

Front shock/Mazda 6 incompatibility — independently reconfirmed (Dec 2025): a separate thread independently reconfirms the same 2mm cup/strut-thickness mismatch between FAW and Mazda 6: Mazda front shock absorbers cannot be used without also swapping the fork/strut assembly; OEM FAW shocks are recommended as there are no true Mazda cross-fit alternatives for the shock alone 353637.

Premium path — KYB/Monro shocks require a fork swap (April 2026): KYB and Monro shocks (Japanese, higher quality) require replacing the forks with Mazda-spec forks (narrower rod diameter) — consistent with the fork/strut-thickness incompatibility already documented above on this card. The advantage of doing the fork swap is unlocking a wider selection of compatible springs; the tradeoff is the added cost of new forks 383940.

Kayaba shocks in Mazda forks — noticeably softer ride, upper-mount fit unconfirmed: one owner reports buying Mazda struts/forks (вилки) separately and fitting Kayaba shocks inside them — "the car became unrecognizable, soft like a Japanese car." Community reaction was mixed: some want to try the same swap, others warn that current Kayaba stock is inconsistent quality ("50/50 luck") and recommend genuine-Japanese or German Sachs units instead — though Sachs is flagged for clunking complaints (see the damper types card). Open question: whether the complete strut assembly (fork + Kayaba shock + upper mount/bearing) bolts on directly, or whether the upper strut mount/bearing needs separate sourcing, was not resolved in the thread 414243444546.

Mazda 6 GG vs GH struts — rod/stroke length mismatch with springs: Mazda 6 GG struts have a longer-stroke rod (~200mm) than GH struts (~180mm). GH-spec springs fit properly on GH struts, but leave roughly a 5mm gap when mounted on GG struts instead — a visual side-by-side comparison confirms the upper-eye and stroke-length differences that cause this mismatch. Match spring generation to strut generation (both GG or both GH) rather than mixing 474849.

Front strut has a welded, X80/GG/GH-specific mounting eye — generic shocks won't fit: the FAW X80 front suspension uses a welded-eye strut-tower mount unique to the X80/Mazda-6-GG/GH platform family. Aftermarket shocks with a different eye geometry will not fit, and Mazda GG/GH shocks with mismatched eye geometry can throw off suspension geometry if forced. Practically the only cross-fit options are Mazda GH-platform parts (including CX-5-sourced units, unconfirmed) or sticking with X80-spec replacement shocks 505152.

Complete Mazda 6 GG shock+fork swap — a 4-month, 18-cycle sourcing ordeal: one owner's account of converting to Mazda 6 GG-sourced shocks (with adapted mounting brackets/forks) took 4 months and 18 full suspension disassembly/reassembly cycles, with repeated alignment/vibration-stand sessions, before landing on a working combination — illustrating just how much trial-and-error the Mazda-fork swap (documented elsewhere on this card) can take in practice. Reinforced (усиленные) spring/shock variants are also available for this swap 535455565758596061.

Front forks + Kayaba shocks, one turn cut off the spring — "like a rocket": a simpler version of the same swap: installing Mazda 6 GG front forks (control arms) together with Japanese Kayaba shocks, cutting one coil off the front spring for clearance. Reported handling result: excellent — "just a rocket." The same owner planned to repeat the swap on the rear axle next 62636465.

docs.title: Shock absorber prices and costs
docs.text:
Tags: #shock-absorbers · #price · #part-number

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Dated prices for shock absorbers, strut assemblies, bearings and installation on the Russian market. Overview: Shock absorbers — overview and platform baseline.

Pricing (September 2024, Irkutsk, RU market): Narcin shocks ~1,700 RUB per unit; Belarusian-brand pneumatic air springs ~4,500 RUB per pair. Air-spring installation is often done at the same time as a shock swap to improve suspension travel 1.

Rear shocks for the facelift (restyled) X80: aftermarket set for ~1,300 RUB (RU market, December 2024), part marking LYKMC L-1003805 (also written C/H 1003805). Installation requires filing a small groove for the retaining plate (~2 minutes with a flat file); reported to fit well and perform fine after a week of driving 2.

Aftermarket bush-type shock/spring pricing: non-adjustable (bush-type) shock absorbers for a suspension upgrade run 800–1,500 RUB (RU market, February 2025) per pair; aftermarket spring options are plentiful 3.

Strut-assembly prices — Japanese import vs. Chinese Stellox (Feb 2026): complete Japanese strut assemblies (including springs and bearings), sourced via import companies on Avito, run 20,000–25,000 RUB (RU market, February 2026) per pair. New KYB units alone cost ~45,000 RUB (RU market, February 2026) per pair without backing plates or dust boots. Chinese Stellox struts are significantly cheaper but lower quality. Note: whether these prices are reasonable was itself debated by the community in the same thread 456.

Front suspension component replacement costs (March 2026, RU market): a consolidated price snapshot from the community — shock absorber support (strut mount) bearing SAM-4101 (Masuma, Mazda 6 02-07 spec): 3,500₽/pair; alternative bearing GJ6E-34-38X: 1,000₽/pair (fitment details for both are in the sources below); a complete used shock absorber assembly with mounting hardware (Mazda 6 GG, sourced from Avito, per pair): ~3,000₽; stabilizer bar links, NL308 polyurethane-reinforced (Mazda 6, pair): priced on Ozon (exact figure not given in this report — see the stabilizer bar bushings card). General recommendation reiterated here: OEM Mazda 6 shocks with correct fork type (вилки) are considered better quality than the stock X80 units 789101112.

Rear shocks — Kayaba 344 363, real-world install cost (June 2026): real-world purchase+install experience matching the KYB 344363 pricing already noted in the aftermarket brands card: parts ~4,450₽ (per unit) plus ~4,000₽ labor; the lower shock-mounting bolts came out easily without needing to be cut or drilled 13.

docs.title: Stabilizer bar bushing replacement
docs.text:
Tags: #bushing · #price

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Failure mode. Stabilizer bar bushings harden significantly over time (from ~5.5mm original thickness becoming rock-hard) — reported at around 48,000 km. Once hardened, they let the stabilizer bar shift sideways, causing it to contact the frame and suspension arms.123

Replacement without lift equipment or a pit. - Right side: removable through top access with a 14mm socket and extensions, working from under the hood — relatively easy. - Left side: more problematic. The front bolt removes with a 14mm key, but the upper bolts conflict with the steering rack, complicating access. The rear bolt is difficult to reach with standard tools without improvised/creative approaches.

Reassembly is harder than removal, given the same access constraints in reverse. Alignment verification is recommended afterward to confirm proper fitment/geometry.123

Shop labor pricing (2024-06 report). At a budget-tier service shop, stabilizer bar bushing replacement labor was priced at 1,000 RUB (RU market, June 2024) (1k) per bushing. The service was described as a difficult DIY task specifically because the bushings are press-fit and sometimes require burning out (heat) to remove, consistent with the stretched/stuck-bolt and access difficulties documented above — reinforcing that this job is a reasonable candidate for outsourcing to a shop rather than DIY for owners without the right tools/patience.456

Community-shared "hack" article (2025-12). A Drive2 article (referenced as "article #9" in the group) documents a workaround/improvised technique (referred to colloquially as "костылинг", literally "crutching it") for replacing stabilizer bar bushings without full disassembly access — multiple community members pointed to it as a known, worth-trying solution for the left-side access difficulty described above.78

Article numbers. The front stabilizer bushing (втулка стабилизатора переднего) is listed under 5CA034156 at kitzapchasti and kitzap, and a member says many shops stock it, so the article is the easiest way to search.910 The FAW X80 catalogue numbers are 5CA028156 (rear) and 5CA034156 (front); Masuma bushings fitting the Mazda 6 GG are rear centre MP-1036 (2002-2003) and front MP-1037 (GG/GY 2002-2007).111213

docs.title: Front stabilizer bar bushings
docs.text:
Tags: #bushings · #part-number · #price

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Wear pattern: front stabilizer bushings are a known high-wear item. Symptoms include the stabilizer bar sliding sideways (toward the right side in one report) inside its plastic retaining rings, and the bar striking/knocking against the frame as it shifts; wear is often asymmetric, worse on the left side 12. One owner replaced two complete bushing sets and had both squeak again quickly — the first set began squeaking after just 1 month, the second squeaked immediately after installation, suggesting the bushings themselves (or the installation) wear out fast 3.

Part number: 5CA034156 for the front stabilizer bushings 4.

Fix: replace the bushings ("резинки"/rubber rings) when slipping, knocking, or asymmetric wear is observed 14.

Replacement procedure and cost (Jan 2025): bushings-only replacement cost 1,440 RUB (RU market, January 2025) for parts. Removing the subframe to access the bushings adds about 1,800 RUB (RU market, January 2025) in labor. An alternative method avoids subframe removal entirely: jack up the vehicle, place a wooden block under the engine, and slightly lower the motor to open a clearance gap — this allows the bushings to be swapped without pulling the subframe. The left-side bushing is reported as noticeably harder to replace than the right, because the steering rack is in the way on that side. Some service shops will still opt for the subframe-removal route by default; the wood-block method is described as a DIY approach needing only slightly more labor time 56.

Curved vs. straight rod bushings: the front sway-bar rods come in two shapes with different-sized bushings — the curved (upper) rod's bushing is roughly 2x larger than the straight (lower) rod's bushing. Exact OEM dimensions were not found by the community, but bushings shared with the Mazda B50 platform work as cross-compatible parts; buying a single unit to test fitment before a bulk purchase is recommended 78. Sway-bar links and bushings from Mazda 6 GG (2002-2007) are separately reported to fit as direct replacements — search terms "chinaspare", "kitparts" for sourcing 9.

Part number cross-check and price (2025): 5CA034156 is repeatedly confirmed as the front stabilizer bushing part number, available via kitzapchasti.ru and kitzap.ru 10; a later report puts the OEM price at approximately 160 RUB each, noting Mazda-sourced alternatives fit but may need a larger-diameter variant — one owner ordered several options to test fitment and quality 11.

Bushing quality — VTR rejected, Emex works: VTR-brand front bushings were rejected as unsuitable: the rubber compound is much harder/stiffer than OEM, and the inner diameter measured 24mm versus the OEM 25mm (1mm undersized). An Emex-supplied part sourced under the OEM part number with a 0.8mm gap spec (matching a KAMAZ spec) was a better match — stock bushings are much softer than VTR's. For the rear position, VTR is reported as the only source available; no viable OEM alternative was found there 1213.

Front stabilizer bar diameter: measured at 26.30mm with a digital caliper, per Chinese-sourced documentation (FAW-CARS.RU) 14.

Rear stabilizer link cross-fit (unverified): a rear stabilizer link/stalk from Mazda 6 GG was proposed as a possible fit for the X80 rear suspension based on a comparison photo; the rubber-bushing receptacle diameter still needs verification against X80 specs — treat as low-confidence pending confirmation 15.

Replacement without subframe removal: several independent reports confirm stabilizer/sway-bar bushings can be replaced without removing the subframe, though the difficulty and exact technique vary by report: - One skilled mechanic replaced worn front bushings (96,000 km mileage) working carefully from underneath, without removing the subframe — most shops still recommend subframe removal for easier access, since this needs real mechanical skill 1617. - A left stabilizer link bushing was replaced in about an hour: remove the lower stabilizer tube (4 bolts, comes out with an upward motion), which exposes a bolt from below; remove the wheel; from the top, remove the stabilizer rod stud with a 14mm socket (the key can be bent slightly downward for access); remove the stud mount from the left side; reinstall in reverse 18. - For the front stabilizer bar end-link bushings specifically: cut/press the old rubber out from the bottom, along the flat plane of the mounting surface — never diagonally. Always install new bushings; misaligned orientation on reinstall has caused steering clicks/noise for some users. Rear bushings follow a similar procedure 19. - A more detailed procedure for the stabilizer link rod without subframe removal: (1) lower the engine/transmission as much as possible by loosening (not removing) the subframe bolts slightly; (2) note the clamp-bracket orientation arrow before removal — some sources suggest reversing it for easier bolt access on the left side; (3) the left side is difficult because the steering rack is in the way, leaving very tight clearance for bolt threading; (4) the left-side mounting screw needs a ratchet with a 14mm socket and a torque wrench; (5) estimated labor time is about 5 hours; the exact procedure is also documented on the Drive2.ru forum 2021.

Sourcing confirmation and typical retail: 5CA034156 confirmed again as the front stabilizer bushing part number; two pieces are needed per vehicle. Bushings can be found through general online retailers (Ozon, Wildberries) simply by searching the vehicle model rather than needing a specialty parts shop 22.

Subframe lowering required for DIY: separately from the wood-block workaround above, one report states the front stabilizer bushings cannot be replaced at all without lowering the subframe, and recommends taking the job to a service shop rather than attempting it DIY. These bushings are treated as a wear item that may need replacement every 1–2 years depending on driving conditions 23.

Stabilizer bar spacer — DIY anti-shift fix: to stop the stabilizer bar from shifting sideways after a bushing replacement, a custom spacer can be fabricated from polypropylene (PP) tubing, 25–25.5mm internal diameter and ~12mm width, for a snug fit between the bushing and the frame stop. Polypropylene may compress under lateral load over time, so copolymer tubing (~12mm thick) is suggested as a more durable alternative. The stabilizer bar itself has flattened sections at both ends (bushings cannot pass over the flattened part) 24.

End links — Ozon sourcing: stabilizer bar end links (стойки стабилизатора) confirmed available and fitting via Ozon.ru, with direct product links shared in the group 25.

Conflict — Mazda 6 GG/GH stabilizer bushings: one thread states stabilizer bushings must have upper and lower rings to keep water out at the joint angle, that Hover 3 bushings may work as a (slightly shorter but paired) substitute, and explicitly that Mazda 6 GG/GH bushings do NOT fit 26 — this contradicts the earlier report in this same card that Mazda 6 GG (2002-2007) sway-bar/stabilizer bushings fit as a direct replacement 91011. Treat Mazda 6 GG/GH bushing fitment as disputed until resolved; verify before buying.

Mazda Atenza polyurethane bushings — long-term durability report: one owner (Anton) installed Mazda 6 Atenza NL308 polyurethane stabilizer bushings (sourced via Ozon) and reports they lasted nearly 2 years — significantly longer than other aftermarket brands he had tried, which typically failed within 2–3 months. Considered a reliable upgrade option 27.

OEM polypropylene bushing — long-term durability check: an owner re-inspected the OEM polypropylene front stabilizer bushing after extended use and found it still structurally intact, with about 8mm of clearance remaining. He suggests a future fluoroplastic (PTFE) bushing would improve on this further, though no PTFE aftermarket option was available at the time 28.

Zeckert SS-1138 stabiliser link — Mazda 6 02+ fitment: a Zeckert-brand stabiliser (sway-bar end) link, part SS-1138, listed for Mazda 6 (2002+) applications, was purchased and installed on the front suspension via Ozon; the owner reported it fit on the same order where front springs were also replaced from Ozon-sourced parts. Treat as medium-confidence — the accompanying photos show Zeckert-branded packaging and an installed link, but the same message thread is primarily about a front-spring purchase, so independent confirmation of the SS-1138 stabiliser-link fitment is limited 29.

Front stabilizer end-link clunking — non-articulated (solid/"filled") links preferred, but not immune to defects (Oct 2025): extending the sway-bar-link durability notes already on this card, a fresh, extended thread confirms the front stabilizer bar produces a loud clunk when a link fails — loud enough to make the interior mirror vibrate on some cars 3031. Non-articulated (solid/"filled", залитые) links generally outlast the articulated (шарнирные) type, but can still develop an internal piston rattle from a manufacturing defect even when new — multiple owners report replacing links (including OEM) and getting the same knock, suggesting batch-quality issues rather than a design flaw 323334353637. One owner suspected the drive shafts (привода) instead, citing horizontal play, but this was not confirmed as the actual cause 3839. Bottom line from this thread: complete stabilizer-link replacement resolves the clunk in most reported cases, and the community treats it as a common, recurring complaint rather than a one-off 4041.

Mazda6 fork-swap bolts — same sourcing issue affects stabilizer-link installs: cross-referencing the Mazda-fork bolt-sourcing note on the shock absorbers card, the same M8 fine-thread, 5–6cm bolts (and the recommendation to source a complete fork assembly with its original bolts from a dismantler) come up in the context of this stabilizer-clunk troubleshooting thread as well 42.

Stabilizer bushings — polyurethane vs. rubber, front vs. rear squeak source (Oct 2025): a fresh round on PU vs. rubber rear stabilizer bushings. One owner had seen Russian-made PU bushings referenced for Mazda on Avtodoc, but without confirmed dimensions, and notes PU on the stabilizer specifically is prone to squeaking 434445. A second owner reports the front rubber bushings would not "settle in" and kept squeaking, and switching to PU up front made things somewhat better; a rear bushing separately came loose ("burped out") 4647. A third owner confirms PU is genuinely squeaky in cold weather and wears down no better than ordinary rubber over time, and — reinforcing the front-vs-stabilizer distinction already on this card — notes that front squeaks are usually from the upper control-arm bushings, not the stabilizer, so misdiagnosis is common 48.

Stabilizer bushing replacement without dropping the subframe — DIY shortcut (Oct 2025): a Drive2 write-up documents a shortcut method for replacing stabilizer bushings without lowering the subframe — normally the most time-consuming part of the job. See: https://www.drive2.ru/l/714769420546741487/ 49.

Correct installation and function — a diagram-backed baseline: the front stabilizer bar bushings should be mounted tight against the stabilizer rod, with no gap between the bushing and the metal limiters/collars on the rod. The bushings are held in place by clamp brackets and should not rattle or exhibit play. The metal limiters exist specifically to prevent excessive side-to-side travel of the rod. Bushings must be replaced when worn — not shimmed as a workaround. Replacement procedure: remove the clamp bracket (usually 2 bolts), slide the old bushing off, install the new rubber bushing, reinstall the clamp. Worn bushings cause rattling from the front suspension specifically during turning 5051525354555657.

Polyurethane vs. rubber bushings — general trade-off discussion (May 2024, earliest community round on this topic): prompted by a shared video ("Why is rubber stiffer than polyurethane?"), the community discussed the general trade-off between polyurethane and rubber bushings (applicable to stabilizer bushings and beyond): good-quality polyurethane outperforms rubber on stability and durability, but costs roughly 3× more than rubber and can squeak. Many repair shops stock only rubber because it's cheaper and readily available, even though it wears out faster and needs more frequent replacement — some shops recommend rubber specifically because it's softer and damps vibration differently. Polyurethane damps vibration faster (the car returns to a settled state quicker after a bump) but is somewhat stiffer; at the X80's curb weight (over 1.5 tonnes) this stiffness difference is not expected to be very noticeable. Rally/performance drivers prefer polyurethane specifically for this faster vibration recovery and greater durability. Bottom line from the thread: choose polyurethane (and replace all silentblocks/bushings together for consistent handling) if prioritizing handling and quick recovery after bumps; choose rubber if prioritizing ride comfort/softness 5859606162636465.

Polyurethane stabilizer bushing availability — direct follow-up question (May 2024): directly following the general PU-vs-rubber discussion above, HS Development asked whether polyurethane stabilizer bushings exist for the X80 specifically, noting the stock rubber ones on their car had only lasted about a year. Reply: a year is actually a normal-to-good lifespan for rubber stabilizer bushings — some fail even faster. Polyurethane stabilizer bushings were confirmed to be in stock/available at the time, though the responder had not personally tracked the exact part number/article, noting their own mechanic had previously discouraged them from bothering with the swap 6667.

Clamp/collar deterioration causing the bar to shift and hit the frame (March 2026): a related but distinct failure mode — the stabilizer bar itself (not just its bushing) can shift laterally and contact the frame due to aged/worn clamp insulators (стопора муфт), not just worn rubber bushings. This produces metal-on-metal rattling/clunking from the undercarriage, especially noticeable at idle or low speeds. Worn clamps were found to allow 1–2cm of lateral bar movement over time. Fix: replace the stabilizer bar clamp insulators and ensure proper torque specification on reassembly; the repair requires removing the bar and inspecting the mounting points 68697071727374.

Rear stabilizer bushings from Lada Kalina/Priora fit without modification (March 2026): this card's coverage above is front-stabilizer-focused; a separate report covers the rear stabilizer: aftermarket polyurethane rear stabilizer bushings sourced from a Lada Kalina (Priora-compatible parts) fit the X80 without any modification. One owner at 5 years / 32,000 km was considering replacement due to visible wear; no specific part number was given 7576.

Stabilizer link price — NL308 (polyurethane-reinforced, Mazda 6 cross-fit): as part of a broader March 2026 front-suspension pricing roundup (see the shock absorbers card for the bearing/shock prices from the same roundup), stabilizer bar links part NL308, polyurethane-reinforced, for Mazda 6, sold in pairs on Ozon, were listed alongside the other front-end component prices gathered in that thread 777879808182.

Front stabilizer bar links — VTR brand, 2-piece set: VTR-brand front stabilizer bar links (sold as a 2-piece set) fit the FAW Besturn X80. Available on Wildberries. Confirmed as a proper direct replacement by multiple community members 838485.

Stabilizer bushing replacement — access procedure and labor cost (May 2024): to replace the stabilizer bar bushings: (1) remove the engine under-tray/protection plate; (2) unscrew the 2 bolts per bushing clip; (3) remove the old rubber bushing and install the new one. Access is very tight — a vehicle lift is effectively required for proper access. For easier installation, the stabilizer end links (traction rods) can optionally be disconnected first. Reported labor cost: ~2,000–2,500₽ (as of May 2024). Note: aftermarket rubber bushings typically only last about 1 year before wearing out again 868788899091.

Stabilizer bushing squeak often accompanies (or precedes) upper control arm saiblock failure: stabilizer bushings frequently develop squeaking noises — a common wear issue on the X80. This symptom is typically accompanied or preceded by saiblock (rubber bushing) failures on the upper control arms; see the upper control arm card for the related ball-joint/bushing failure pattern 92.

Front stabilizer bushing sourcing — 26mm needed, 23mm (Mazda-spec) commonly shipped by mistake: multiple owners report ordering front stabilizer bushings and receiving the wrong diameter. The X80's front stabilizer bar is 26mm; the rear is reportedly ~20mm. A bushing listed as MZSB008 ("confirmed to fit" per online reviews) turned out to be 23mm and did not fit; a kitzapchasti.ru order placed by catalog part number 5CA034156 also arrived as a 23mm Mazda-spec part instead of the correct 26mm X80 part — the seller's own listing for that same part number is linked as the reference item to check against before ordering. One owner did have success ordering the correct 26mm bushing via Ozon. Practical takeaway: verify bushing diameter (26mm front) explicitly with the seller before buying — the catalog part number alone is not a reliable guarantee of correct fitment, since suppliers have shipped 23mm Mazda-spec parts against this same listed part number more than once 93949596979899100101102.

Rear stabilizer bushings/links — Mazda 6 GG cross-fit, part 5CA028156 (~90 RUB, RU market, February 2026): rear stabilizer bushings and links are compatible with Mazda 6 GG — reported as a direct bolt-in fit. The FAW-specific rear stabilizer bushing part number is 5CA028156, priced around 90 RUB (RU market, February 2026) via kitzapchasti.ru (in stock) 103104105.

Stabilizer bar link (front) — SUFIX SZ1303: a front stabilizer bar link (стойка стабилизатора) sourced under the SUFIX brand, part SZ1303, was linked via an Ozon listing 106107.

Creaking at 21,000 km — sway bar bushings suspected (low-mileage report): one owner reported front-suspension creaking at just 21,000 km and suspected the stabilizer-bar bushings as the likely cause, noting the car otherwise felt fine but that both front and rear suspension have some weak points and could use more give in city driving 108109110111112.

Front suspension wear order — upper control-arm bushings go first, then stabilizer bushings, before ball joints (Aug 2026): a fresh community exchange lays out the observed failure sequence on the front end: the upper control-arm bushings ("сайлентблоки" on the upper arm — see the upper control arm card for the dedicated failure pattern) tend to go first, followed by the stabilizer bar bushings covered on this card; ball joints typically outlast both. One shop quote for replacing only the stabilizer bushings (parts only) came in at 500–800 RUB (RU market, August 2026) per bushing in Moscow, though labor rates for the job vary widely by shop 113114115.

Rear stabilizer bar bushings are a separate part from the front — do not confuse the two: everything above on this card up to this point concerns the front stabilizer (anti-roll) bar. The rear stabilizer bar uses its own, differently sized bushing — do not assume the front part number or dimensions apply to the rear.

Rear stabilizer bushing dimensions (polyurethane, Aug 2026): for owners sourcing polyurethane bushings for the rear stabilizer bar: inner diameter 22mm (critical — do not substitute an 18mm-bore part, it will not fit), outer diameter 42–44mm, height/length 38–40mm. Polyurethane bushings run a slightly larger overall diameter than rubber because the material itself is firmer/harder than rubber. Before installation, lightly coat the mating metal surfaces (the stabilizer bar itself) with paraffin — an ordinary candle works — to prevent squeaking and extend service life. The rear stabilizer bar's own diameter was confirmed in the same thread at 20.3mm (consistent with the ~20mm figure already noted for the rear bar elsewhere on this card, versus 26mm at the front) 116117118119120121.

Oct 2026 tip — check the stabilizer bar offset. Victor shared a Drive2 post ("9. Лайфхак (костылинг) при замене втулок стабилизатора", a hack for replacing the stabilizer bushings): if the noise is loud after the job, check the offset of the stabilizer bar (стабилизатор), because when it shifts it can touch neighbouring parts. Link: https://www.drive2.ru/l/714769420546741487/ 122.

docs.title: Steering column lock type
docs.text:
The steering-column lock on the X80 is mechanical, not electronic — this holds true even on trims equipped with push-button start. The feature physically immobilizes the steering wheel when the engine is off, as a theft-deterrent measure 12.

Fix — stiff ignition lock in cold weather (silicone lubricant): the mechanical steering-column/ignition lock can become stiff and difficult to turn in cold weather. Fix: spray silicone lubricant into the lock mechanism, which resolves the stiffness. Some owners have gone as far as partially disassembling the steering column to clear the obstruction without replacing the lock outright, and continue driving with the column partially disassembled rather than deal with sourcing a replacement 345.

docs.title: Power steering pump fluid (ГУР)
docs.text:
Tags: #power-steering · #gur · #atf

Power-steering pump fluid specification: ATF-MV type (M-5 variant). Acceptable alternatives: fluids meeting the 3309 approval standard, Toyota Type 4 (T4), or multi-spec ATF fluids that meet the 3309 standard 12.

Hissing vs. whistling — telling a normal sound from an air-in-system problem. A hissing sound from the cabin during a full-lock steering turn is normal behavior for the X80's power-steering system — it is not a defect and shouldn't be diagnosed as one 345. A whistling sound, by contrast, is a different symptom and indicates air in the system: if you hear whistling (not just hissing), check fluid level and bleed the system by rotating the wheel lock-to-lock several times with the engine running 65. Merely loud hissing without whistling may instead point to dirty fluid rather than air — cycling the wheel lock-to-lock while topping up/replacing fluid can flush it: one owner reported doing this twice (removing the lower hose from the reservoir, turning the wheel, refilling) specifically to purge contaminated fluid, using the same fluid spec noted above (3309/Toyota Type 4-compatible) 7.

docs.title: Steering rack bushing wear and repair options
docs.text:
Tags: #bushings

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Steering rack bushings (втулка рулевой рейки) can develop play over time, and owners report difficulty finding the bushing sold as a separate part — it is unclear whether it is available loose at all. If the rack is not leaking, knocking, or sticking, community advice is that repair is optional rather than urgent 123.

Two repair paths if action is needed: (1) a specialized machine shop can turn/machine a new bushing surface onto the existing rod rather than sourcing a replacement part; or (2) replace the complete steering rack assembly outright. Which is more cost-effective depends heavily on local availability of a shop with the specialized machining capability — where none exists, full rack replacement may be the only practical option 23.

Hissing noise at full lock is normal: a hissing sound from the steering rack area when the wheel is turned fully lock-to-lock is documented as normal X80 behavior, per an official dealer statement — described as a "construction feature." It occurs on a warm engine when the power steering system is under load and is not indicative of a malfunction 4.

Taiwan-manufactured aftermarket racks and repair economics: Taiwan-manufactured aftermarket steering racks are reported to function adequately on Mazda-platform vehicles including the X80. Repair cost when seals fail runs 13,000+ RUB (RU market, April 2025); given labor cost and the lack of any warranty on a repair, full rack replacement is generally considered more economical than a repair. One owner's steering rack began leaking after extended use 5.

Steering rack dust boot — part number: the steering rack dust boot (пыльник рулевой рейки) part number is 5AA032122, available from kitzapchasti.ru 6.

OEM steering rack pricing and warranty (2025): a full OEM steering rack (sold as an assembly including tie rods/наконечники) costs approximately 24,000 RUB (RU market, July 2025). Supply is by factory order, typically arriving within about a month (sometimes faster); regional delivery via a courier service (e.g. Delovye Linii) adds roughly 1,000 RUB (RU market, July 2025). Aftermarket/Chinese racks run cheaper at 18,000-20,000 RUB (RU market, July 2025). Warranty terms are typically 1 year or 20,000 km per the service book (some components carry a shorter paint-coating warranty of around 10,000 km). Payment is generally 100% upfront, or a 50% deposit with the remaining 50% due on delivery to a local courier 7.

Steering feel/character — heavier than modern designs, but responsive: several owners describe the X80's steering as notably tight/heavy compared to modern electric power-steering designs, while still transmitting road feedback well. One owner compared it to a VW Touareg, which he described as extremely heavy but smooth; by comparison the X80's steering is somewhat firm for the vehicle's weight/size but considered acceptable — some owners view this as inherent to the design (likely the Mazda-derived hydraulic rack) rather than a fault, with the steering responding noticeably to road imperfections through the wheel 89.

Steering column vibration/dribble on cold start: the steering column shaft can vibrate or "dribble" at idle, especially noticeable on a cold winter start. Reported difficulty is low — accessing the shaft after removing the plastic shroud around the steering column takes about 15 minutes 10.

Heavy steering, worse in mornings/cold, with grinding on turns — power steering pump failure suspected (Nov 2025): a case of steering becoming hard to turn, especially difficult on cold mornings, with a grinding noise during turns — persisting even after the steering rack had already been replaced. This points away from the rack itself and toward the power-steering pump (ГУР насос) as the likely cause; one owner with the identical symptom confirms replacing the pump alongside the rack resolved it. Recommended checks: replace the power-steering pump, and/or verify the fluid level in the pump reservoir first before assuming a pump failure 11121314.

Heavy steering persists after rack AND pump replacement — break-in period, or inherent design heaviness (disputed, Nov 2025): extending the case above, one owner replaced both the steering rack and the hydraulic pump, yet steering remained heavy. Possible causes discussed: (1) new components may need a 100–200 km break-in period before feeling normal; (2) fittings/joints over-tightened during installation can restrict the rack's movement — on some designs (e.g. electric power steering) an over-tight bushing can nearly seize the rack and risk burning out the EPS motor, so installation torque matters; (3) the X80's design may simply be inherently heavier-steering than other cars due to the two lower control-arm geometry plus a comparatively weak hydraulic system — consistent with the "notably tight/heavy" characteristic already described elsewhere on this card. Recommendation: allow a break-in period before further diagnosis rather than immediately assuming a defective part 1516171819.

Full steering rack replace-vs-restore decision, with pricing (June 2024): a fuller pricing picture for the rack decision already touched on elsewhere on this card — restoration: ~15,000₽ including removal/reinstallation labor, but the rack comes back noticeably stiffer than before, so a restored rack may not fully solve a "heavy steering" complaint. New: 20,000₽+. Genuine FAW part 5CA03296 available through KitZap and similar suppliers at ~11,267₽. A cross-brand alternative: Mazda 6 I steering rack, Motorherz art. R22101NW. Caution: some restoration-service listings advertise suspiciously low prices — verify the seller is actually supplying new stock, not a refurbished unit at a new-part price 20212223242526272829.

Steering rack replacement cost — 17,000–17,340 RUB (RU market, April 2026), repair possible if only seals leak: another independent price data point: a full replacement rack costs 17,000–17,340 RUB via Ozon and Chinese suppliers ("Kitai.com"/kitzap-type sellers) — cheaper than the ~20,000₽+ new-rack figure quoted elsewhere on this card, suggesting price varies by supplier and should be shopped around. Repair may be worthwhile only if the fault is a seal/manifold leak with no play and no noise — in that case just the seals and piston would need replacing; finding a shop that actually does this specific repair (rather than just selling a swap rack) was reported as difficult. Conflict: one contributor considers a full replacement "safer" at similar total cost to a repair, given the difficulty of verifying repair quality, while also warning that sourcing a replacement rack itself is "a lottery" in terms of quality — so neither path is risk-free, and the choice may come down to whichever service is actually available locally 3031323334353637.

Steering rack dust boot — part 5AA032122, Mazda 6 GG as an unconfirmed alternative: the steering rack dust boot (пыльник рулевой рейки) part number is 5AA032122, sourced via an Ozon listing. When a different owner separately asked for the dust boot's dimensions (rather than the part number) to find a compatible generic replacement, the only suggestion offered was to try a Mazda 6 GG boot — but the suggester explicitly did not know the required dimensions and this cross-fit was not confirmed by anyone in the thread; treat it as an unverified lead, not a confirmed fitment 38394041.

Power steering pump noise/vibration at full steering lock — normal within limits, but don't hold it there (disputed in-thread): humming, vibration, and a slight increase in steering resistance when the wheel is turned to full lock and held is reported as normal — the pump is simply working at its maximum pressure limit, and the exact sound level varies between individual cars. Do not hold the wheel at full lock for an extended period — this can damage the pump over time even though the noise itself is expected. Conflict: one owner (Миша) called this "normal," while another (Василий) flatly disagreed ("this shouldn't happen, it's not normal") in the same thread. A third contributor clarified the distinction that resolves the disagreement: humming plus resistance at full lock is normal pump behavior, but grinding or crunching/clattering noises are not and indicate an actual problem needing service — so the two owners may have been describing different symptoms rather than genuinely disagreeing about the same noise 4243444546.

docs.title: Steering return vs. tire wear — diagnosis
docs.text:
Tags: #diagnostic

Diagnostic checklist — steering wheel not self-centering, combined with excessive tire wear: when the steering wheel does not return to center on its own and tires wear excessively (especially after a recent alignment), work through these checks in order rather than jumping straight to a rack or alignment shop: (1) steering rack — check for play, movement, or worn internal guides; (2) steering tie rods and their ball joints — check for play (see the steering tie rods card for part numbers and sourcing); (3) hub bearings — spin each wheel by hand and feel for resistance/ roughness (see the front and rear hub bearing cards); (4) brake calipers — check for sticking, which loads one side of the car constantly and both pulls the wheel and accelerates tire wear; (5) steering column bearing — condition affects return-to-center feel 123456.

Alignment-specific checks when pulling/non-return persists: if the checklist above doesn't resolve it, focus on alignment parameters specifically — (a) caster: critical for self-centering/return-to- zero behavior, and not adjustable on the X80 (unlike toe); if caster measures out of spec on the alignment rig, suspect a bent steering knuckle rather than a simple adjustment issue; (b) base/ wheelbase: check the frame distance between axles for impact/collision damage or subframe warping, which throws off caster indirectly; (c) tire inflation and wear-pattern uniformity — confirm before blaming mechanical parts 7.

If alignment checks out but the car still pulls — suspect the tires themselves: even with a technically correct alignment, a car can still pull to one side — the tire's own rubber/belt construction can have an inherent directional bias ("увод"/pull), something that specialized rigs can measure on supercars but that's rarely checked on a regular car. One owner chased this symptom through three full geometry checks with no result until swapping the front tires left-to-right (reversing their position) resolved the pull — worth trying as a low-cost diagnostic step before further part replacement, especially when alignment numbers come back clean 8910.

docs.title: Steering tie rods
docs.text:
Tags: #mazda-6-compat · #part-number · #price

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Mazda parts do NOT cross-fit: despite similar appearance, tie rods (наконечники) from Mazda are not compatible with the X80 — they differ in diameter and thread pitch. The same incompatibility applies to steering control arms from other vehicles. Recommendation: source X80-specific components only, even when a catalog photo looks identical — generic "looks the same" parts fail in practice 12.

Sourcing and lifespan: a left tie rod (наконечник рулевой левый) was listed on Avito as one sourcing option 3. Aftermarket analogs — brands like "555" and similar — are available in the 30,000–50,000 RUB (RU market, October 2024) range. Genuine OEM tie rods have shown strong durability in owner reports: one owner's original rods lasted 235,000 km before replacement was needed; another owner's lasted 190,000 km, after which the whole front suspension began showing wear (that owner made multiple unsuccessful service attempts to resolve rod-related issues before eventually replacing them) 45.

Conflicting later report — Mazda tie rods claimed as direct drop-in: a later thread (April 2025) reports the opposite conclusion from the one above: that Mazda 6 GG (2002-2007) and Mazda Atenza (2002-2007) steering tie rods are direct drop-in replacements for the X80, with identical mounting confirmed by photo comparison, priced at approximately 5,600 RUB (RU market, April 2025) each — the DROM parts database was used to cross-reference compatible parts. This directly contradicts the earlier (October 2024) consensus in this card that Mazda tie rods do not cross-fit due to diameter/thread-pitch differences. The wiki does not adjudicate between the two reports — treat Mazda-sourced tie rods as unverified until a specific spec comparison (diameter, thread pitch) resolves the contradiction, and prefer X80-specific parts where budget allows 678.

Further support for Mazda-sourced tie rods, plus the reason why: a later report explains the underlying reason Mazda tie rods keep coming up as a claimed fit: the X80's steering rack itself is sourced from a left-hand-drive Mazda 6 (first generation, 2002-2008 GG series) — so the steering rods (тяги) and tie-rod ends (наконечники) downstream of the rack are Mazda parts by design. No difference in this respect was reported between pre-facelift and facelift X80 models 9. Separately, tie rods were reported replaced using Mazda-sourced components with professional labor cost of approximately 1,000 RUB (RU market, June 2025), and dust boots/clamps were noted as single-use items that must be replaced whenever the tie rod is serviced 10. This reinforces the "Mazda parts fit" side of the conflict above — but the earlier caution about diameter/thread-pitch mismatches on lower control arm tie rods elsewhere in the community has not been retracted, so verify the specific rod/end being sourced.

Steering rod pricing (Aug 2025): steering rods (тяга) are available under order from parts suppliers for 1,450 RUB (RU market, August 2025). A Mazda OEM equivalent is reported at a much lower ~800 RUB (RU market, August 2025) — the FAW-specific ordering channel carries a significant markup over sourcing the Mazda-branded part directly 11.

Further confirmation — Mazda 6 GG tie rods installed and working (Sept 2025): adding to the "Mazda parts fit" side of the conflict above, a community member reports installing steering tie rods sourced from Mazda 6 GG and confirms fitment, with a plan to share the specific part number later 12.

Tie-rod ends and full tie rods — Mazda 6 GG, brand recommendations (Jan 2026): further reinforcing Mazda 6 GG compatibility, both tie-rod ends and complete tie rods sourced from Mazda 6 GG are confirmed working; recommended brands in order mentioned: CTR, Jikiu (a cheaper alternative reported as good quality), and TRW. At least one owner ordered a GMB-brand equivalent as a further alternative. Available through major online retailers 1314151617.

Suffix-brand tie rods — additional retail sourcing option (April 2026): steering tie rods are also available from Ozon and similar retailers under the Suffix brand, at moderate pricing (exact figure not specified in this thread). Drive2.ru is mentioned as a place to cross-check part numbers and fitment before buying — treat as a secondary confirmation source alongside the X80-specific sourcing already documented on this card 18192021.

CTR tie rods — part numbers CEMZ41 (right) / CEMZ-42 (left): specific part numbers for CTR-brand tie rods (brand already recommended above): right side CEMZ41, left side CEMZ-42. Recommended to replace both sides together for consistent handling even if only one has failed 22232425.

Tie-rod ball-joint fitment spec — 18mm inner / 14mm outer, and a B50 mismatch warning: the critical fitment dimensions at the tie-rod's ball-joint threaded end: 18mm inner diameter, 14mm outer diameter. This spec matters because at least one buyer ordered tie rods from KitZapchasti expecting X80 parts and received tie rods that turned out to be B50-spec (or otherwise mismatched) — they didn't match these dimensions and had to be returned. Always verify against this 18mm/14mm spec (not just the seller's "fits X80" claim) before accepting a delivery 26272829.

Ozon listing. A steering tie rod (тяга рулевая) for the FAW Besturn X80 is listed on Ozon under article C23032240K.30

docs.title: Steering wheel removal procedure
docs.text:
Tags: #steering-wheel

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Standard removal procedure: (1) remove the plastic clips under the spokes to access two 10mm bolts; (2) unscrew the bolts; (3) lift the wheel toward you carefully — note the airbag connector underneath and disconnect it before fully removing the wheel 12.

Stubborn-wheel removal — two documented methods: - Method A: apply pressure with your knees while pulling on the wheel, and tap the mounting nut (not the wheel itself) with a hammer to help break it loose. - Method B: loosen the mounting nut until it extends just beyond the threads (leaving it as a stop), then give the wheel a firm gentle shake — this typically works within about 15 seconds.

For especially stubborn wheels, a steering-wheel puller attachment can be used. In all cases, avoid excessive force to prevent damaging the splines on the steering shaft 345. ⚠️ Note: both removal methods are reported as valid — Method A/B and the puller approach appear suited to different situations (harder vs. more routine removals), not conflicting advice.

Airbag removal and battery-disconnect safety sequence (additional detail): before touching the airbag, fully disconnect the battery first. Under the steering column there are two plastic plugs to remove, then two bolts (10 or 12mm, confirming variation on the bolt size noted above); disconnect the wire harness directly at the airbag itself (this is described as the easier access point). To disconnect the wheel from the shaft, use a 22 or 24mm socket on the center mounting nut — ⚠️ do not turn the nut all the way off/loose before the wheel is free, since the wheel can suddenly swing and hit the dashboard (or, if not careful, the installer's face/hands). Gently pull the wheel toward you by hand once loosened; if it won't budge, use a steering-wheel puller tool (available on marketplaces, ~2,500 RUB (RU market, April 2026) on Ozon) 6789101112.

docs.title: Steering wheel spline realignment after removal
docs.text:
Tags: #steering-wheel

The steering wheel attaches to the steering column via a splined connection. When it has been removed for panel work (e.g. dashboard/airbag service), it can be repositioned on the splines if it comes back on misaligned. The wheel should be properly centered before final fastening. This is treated as part of the same overall process as wheel alignment — the alignment shop straightens the steering wheel first, then sets the alignment angles from the table relative to that centered position; if nothing was disturbed underneath the car, the wheel simply unscrews and can be reseated on the splines in the correct position 123.

docs.title: Subframe silent blocks (low confidence)
docs.text:
Tags: #silent-block · #low-confidence · #mazda-6-compat

⚠️ Low confidence / unconfirmed: the X80 may have subframe silent blocks (сайлентблоки подрамника) similar to the Mazda GH platform. Suspected function: vibration damping and compliance for the subframe's mounting to the chassis — a rubber-in-metal bushing assembly that absorbs shock and vibration during acceleration and braking, potentially contributing to ride quality and noise isolation. Neither the exact existence nor the specification of this component was confirmed by the community at the time of discussion 123.

docs.title: Front strut bearing noise in cold weather
docs.text:
Tags: #noise

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Symptom. The upper strut support bearing ("опорный подшипник") produces noise/clunking when driving in winter cold — reported as creaking that gets progressively louder.123456

Wear depends heavily on prior use, not just current mileage. One owner at only 28,000 km (with a previous owner known to have driven the car aggressively for the first ~26,000 km) experienced loud creaking and ended up replacing: control-arm assemblies, the serpentine (accessory) belt, tensioner, water pump, thermostat, and strut assemblies — a fairly extensive repair bill for a relatively low-mileage car. The owner's frustration was compounded by having invested significant repair money for only ~3,000 km of driving under their own ownership.123456

Community takeaway. Bearing/suspension wear correlates more with the previous owner's driving habits and road conditions than with mileage alone — some owners see few suspension issues past 100,000+ km, while others (like the case above) see extensive wear by 28,000 km if the car was driven hard or on poor roads early in its life. When buying used, ask about the prior owner's driving style, not just the odometer reading.123456

docs.title: Rear-end instability at ~110 km/h over a road wave
docs.text:
Near loss of control at 110 km/h over a road wave (July 2026): one owner (Victor 🇷🇺) reported an alarming highway incident: driving at about 110 km/h, the car hit a wave/dip in the road surface, and the rear end "squeezed down and then released," after which the car kept bouncing hard — he had to actively fight the steering wheel for an extended distance to bring it back under control. He suspected general suspension fatigue/wear as the underlying cause 1.

No such issue reported by another owner still on stock front suspension: replying in the same thread, a second owner (Che Guevara) said this had never happened to him. He specified that his own front suspension is still the original/stock setup, referencing an earlier, separate conversation in which he had told Victor he'd decided against replacing it — and that everything has been fine on his car so far 2.

Open question — stock vs. modified suspension: the thread does not establish whether Victor's suspension was stock or already modified at the time of the incident, nor whether any specific worn component (e.g. shocks, bushings, springs) was the cause. Treat this as a reported symptom rather than a diagnosed fault; cross-reference the suspension noise diagnostic checklist and the shock absorbers card for related failure modes (worn dampers, bump-stop wear, cold-weather shock behavior) that could plausibly produce this kind of rear-end instability over a bump at speed.

docs.title: Front suspension noise diagnostic checklist
docs.text:
Tags: #diagnostic · #squeak

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Two separate threads cover cases where the cause of a front suspension noise was not obvious and required systematic elimination. See also the dedicated cards on upper control arm squeak and stabilizer bar bushings for the most common specific causes.

Squeak appearing right after a tire shop visit: a front-left squeak heard when rocking the car up and down first appeared immediately after a tire-shop visit. Two candidate causes were suggested by the community: (1) a seized ball joint or worn lower front control arm — the shop suggested a dealership inspection to formally diagnose it; (2) stabilizer bar bushings — a common symptom of worn stabilizer bushings is the car rocking side-to-side over bumps. Recommendation: have the shop check both the upper control-arm play and the stabilizer bushing condition before leaving, since either can produce a similar-sounding squeak (unresolved conflict — the thread does not confirm which one it actually was) 1234.
