Persistent front-left knock, 2 years unresolved: one owner reported a small, persistent knock in the front-left wheel that had resisted multiple repair attempts over two years, including a power steering pump replacement and a full steering rack replacement — neither fixed it. Community-suggested checklist for this kind of hard-to-pin-down knock: - Check brake caliper guide-bushing play by grabbing the caliper by hand and shaking it — a felt play there is a strong lead. - Inspect the stabilizer bar bushings. - Verify the engine underbody protection plate is tightened (a loose plate can rattle/drum and be mistaken for a suspension knock). - Check subframe fastener tightness and front suspension arm silentblock tightness. - A similar-sounding knock on a Citroën was once traced to a small stone stuck in the spring cup — a reminder to check for foreign objects too.

Diagnostic approach recommended: isolate exactly when the noise occurs (over bumps, under braking, while steering) and then systematically check each suspension/brake component's play in turn, rather than replacing parts speculatively 5678.

Multi-cause noise at 73,000 km: one owner's front-end noise (increasing with speed, worse in turns) turned out to have several simultaneous causes once diagnosed: worn front hub bearings on both sides, brake pad wear, and worn front suspension bushings (sway bar links and longitudinal arm bushings), plus worn rear sway-bar bushings. See the dedicated front wheel hub bearing card for the hub bearing details of this case — a reminder that a single noise complaint can have more than one simultaneous root cause, so a full check rather than a single-part swap is often warranted 9.

Possibly the strut mount, not the arms: in another case, front suspension clicking/knocking that was first suspected to be the upper control arms or lower ball joints turned out not to be either — the owner resolved a similar-sounding noise by replacing the strut mount (опорник) instead. Even when visual inspection shows no damage or cracking, worn internal strut-mount components can still cause noise, and replacement is relatively inexpensive — worth trying before assuming the arms or ball joints are at fault 10.

Bump-stop replacement resolved rear knocking: the X80 uses relatively soft dampers, so spring load ends up concentrated on the bump stops (отбойники). One owner's rear knocking/clunking while driving was resolved by replacing the rear bump stops, with the side benefit of a noticeably softer ride; he recommends checking and replacing the front bump stops on the same schedule for consistent comfort 111213.

Metallic clunking over potholes — not always visible on inspection: some owners report metallic clunking/clicking specifically over potholes and uneven surfaces, which a dealer's visual diagnostic did not identify as damage. A possible cause raised by the community is loose/worn upper suspension-arm bolts 1415. A separate, confirmed fix for a similar symptom: disassembling both upper suspension arms and lubricating all bolts with SHRb-4 grease eliminated the clicking/squeaking over bumps — this can be done without fully removing the arms 1617 (see also the upper control arm card for the fuller writeup of this fix).

Dull clunk traced to the shock-absorber bump stops: a separate report describes a dull, metallic clunk at low speed, most noticeable on small suspension movements, traced specifically to the shock-absorber bump stops (rather than the spring-side bump stops above); replacing the rear shock-absorber bump stops eliminated this particular noise 1819.

Clunking/knocking radiating to the wheel or pedals — broader checklist: for knocking on small bumps or during turns that radiates to the steering wheel or the pedals, the community's broader list of possible causes (beyond the bump stops and upper-arm items above) includes: stabilizer bar bushings (still the most common single culprit), worn CV joints (both inner and outer ШРУС), steering-linkage wear, and even brake-pad issues — all should be checked in turn rather than assumed 202122.

Extended clicking/clunking discussion — comprehensive cause list at 7 years / 130,000 km: a long community discussion of clicking/clunking during acceleration or over bumps compiled a broader set of candidate causes than any single thread above: loose ball joints on the steering knuckles (шаровые опоры цапфы) not properly secured by cotter pins; worn stabilizer-link bushings and rods; hardened damper bump stops and protective boots; worn upper ball joints; and worn stabilizer-bar rubber mounts. A recurring point in the discussion: simply re-tightening fasteners does not fix clicking on its own — the root cause is wear and play at the joints themselves, so tightening alone is a temporary measure at best. At around 7 years / 130,000 km, a comprehensive suspension inspection and refresh (rather than chasing a single part) was the recommendation. Unresolved debate: contributors disagreed on whether stabilizer-rod noise or damper-rod noise better explained the symptom depending on exactly where on the road (which bump, which manoeuvre) the noise appeared — the thread does not settle this, so isolate the trigger conditions carefully before replacing parts 232425.

Long thread — worn upper-arm bushings causing grinding/creaking in turns, ~100k km: an extended troubleshooting thread (JÚLIA's car) started with a grinding/creaking noise during turns/cornering, initially suspected to be a broken spring. After inspection on a lift, the noise was traced to worn upper control-arm bushings (silentblocks) rather than the spring or brakes — at around 100,000 km these bushings can wear out completely. Replacing the bushings resolved the noise, and the suspension felt noticeably more responsive afterward. A brake-line routed against the body panel was separately flagged as capable of producing a similar-sounding noise, so it's worth ruling out too. Note on process: the thread includes a debate about whether a shop's diagnosis to replace "almost the entire suspension" from a lift inspection alone (without a clear description of the specific play found) can be a sales tactic — the community's advice is to ask for the specific worn component found, not just a general "replace everything" recommendation 262728.

General reminder — don't skip the OBD scanner: tangential to suspension noise specifically, but a recurring community reminder worth noting here: a check-engine warning light can indicate many different faults, and simple visual inspection of the dashboard alone is insufficient to diagnose it — always read the actual diagnostic trouble codes with an OBD scanner before attempting any repair 29.

Right-side dull knock that fades after driving a bit — strut suspected but unconfirmed (Oct 2025): a dull knock from the right side, disappearing after driving a short distance, was hunted extensively without a clear culprit; the owner suspected the strut/shock (стойка) as the most likely remaining source, even though the shaft moved smoothly by hand and no play was found by shaking the car. Community input: "plenty of things" in this dense suspension can make a dull sound, and the stock ride is very good at transmitting road noise generally — check stabilizer bar clearance from the frame as another possibility. This overlaps with, but was not conclusively resolved by, the OEM-shock-fork thread already on this card 303132.

Right-side "under the fender" knock persisting after a full front suspension refresh (Oct 2025): after replacing essentially the entire front suspension on one side — control arms, stabilizer links, lower links, strut, springs, bushings — a persistent right-side knock from under the fender area remained. Likely remaining sources discussed: steering-rack play over bumps, upper control-arm bushings, the steering knuckle, or a driveshaft/CV-boot area (bell-housing) issue. Systematic isolation (one component swapped at a time) was recommended rather than guessing 333435363738394041.

Cold-weather clunking — multi-cause dispute, no single fix confirmed (Dec 2025): an extensive, later thread specifically about clunking that appears (or worsens) in cold weather on small bumps and fades as the engine/car warms up. Diagnostic steps discussed: check CV-joint dust boots for tears, verify ball joints, inspect the stabilizer linkage and bushings (the stabilizer bar can shift right under load from worn bushings or geometry issues — one owner measured it sitting only ~1mm from the frame), check for play in the reactive/control arms, and examine the rear engine mount for cracks. One owner attempted a fix by loosening the subframe and reseating the reactive arm, suspecting a misaligned bolt on the left side near the body, but reported the tie rod/arm still drifted back out of position afterward — replacement parts alone did not resolve it for this owner, even with new OEM bushings installed and torqued with the car at ride height. Conflict: the thread does not converge on one cause — contributors variously blame stabilizer bushings, ball joints, or reactive-arm/frame geometry, and several report that replacing components didn't fully fix it; treat cold clunking as having multiple possible failure modes, some possibly design- or frame-tolerance-related, until proven otherwise on a specific car 42434445464748495051525354555657.

Rear engine mount — check for cracks as a specific cold-clunk source: as part of the cold-weather clunking diagnostic above, the rear engine mount (задняя опора ДВС) is called out specifically as worth checking for cracks or deterioration; see the engine mount card for full engine-mount diagnosis detail 42.

Cold "pok pok pok" wheel noise — separate report, same seasonal pattern: a related but separate report describes a knocking/tapping "pok pok pok" sound from the front and/or rear wheels specifically below freezing, likened to wooden parts or stiff rubber — audible at low speed, nearly silent once the car warms up. Likely cause discussed: suspension bushings (сайлентблоки) stiffening in the cold, or loose suspension fasteners expanding/contracting with temperature. Not urgent, but worth inspecting for sagging, bushing deterioration, or loose mounting bolts 58.

Right-side clicking with all-new suspension except the strut — amortisseur vs. ball joint (disputed, Dec 2025): a right-side clicking noise over bumps persisted despite every front suspension component being new except the strut; shaking the car by hand found no play except laterally. One owner leaned toward the strut or a ball joint as the cause; a second owner with genuinely new struts (sourced secondhand from Avito) still had the same noise, which weakens the "just replace the strut" theory. Conflict: the thread does not resolve which component is responsible — treat this specific right-side click as an open, recurring community complaint rather than a solved case, consistent with the cold-weather clunking conflict already on this card 596061626364656667.

Vibration at 100–140 km/h (chassis, not steering wheel) — wheel/rim/ brake-disc diagnosis path (Nov 2025): a chassis-only vibration (no steering-wheel input) appearing specifically in the 100–140 km/h range, with wheels rebalanced multiple times without resolving it and new engine mounts already ruled out, and the same vibration present on both summer and winter tire sets on the same rims — points away from tires/balance and toward a bent wheel rim or brake-disc runout. Suggested check: remove the wheel and manually rotate the hub/disc to feel for contact or wobble; no vibration under braking suggests the brake discs are internally OK, but radial runout (bent rim, or debris/rust inside) can still cause vibration unrelated to braking itself 68697071727374757677787980.

Cold-tire-change knock — seasonal tire swap onto different rims (Nov 2025, low confidence): a loud knock when turning right appeared immediately after switching from 215/60 summer tires to 215/55 winter tires on a separate set of rims (~40,000 km car); absent on the summer set, and wheel-lug tightness was double-checked. Suggested causes: tire-size/geometry mismatch, rim imbalance, or a CV-joint/drive-shaft issue coincidentally surfacing at the same time; recommended diagnostic: remove the affected wheel and manually rotate the hub while turning the wheel to the affected side to isolate the source 8182838485.

Front strut mount clunk on a restyle — rotating vs. non-rotating bearing type (March 2026): Маksim (restyle, 2018) reported a persistent clunk from the front shock/strut mounts and asked whether others had run into the same issue and what mounts should actually be fitted. He had previously had mounts with a rotating bearing ("подшипник поворотные") installed, which stopped the spring from turning with the wheel; per the parts catalog, the non-rotating ("не поворотные") type is listed as the correct original-spec part — but this non-rotating type clunked even brand-new. Shocks were replaced up to three times chasing the noise before the mounts themselves were identified as the actual cause; Маksim then re-ordered a second, different mount (matching the first photo he'd shared) after confirming the diagnosis. Сергей Крисман separately confirmed he'd go change his own the next day. This is the earlier stage of the same overall diagnostic saga that later used a specialized vibration bench, documented immediately below 86878889909192939495.

Vibration-bench diagnostics can isolate the exact suspension component: for cases like the ones above, a specialized vibration bench (вибро стенд) can diagnose suspension noise/vibration sources with much more precision than a road test or a visual check — the shop runs multiple scanner/sensor tools on the bench to isolate which specific component is at fault, distinguishing between shock-absorber failure, bushing wear, spring problems, and bearing issues. This service is available at some specialized repair shops and is worth seeking out for a noise that has resisted the usual part-by-part elimination process 969798.

Suspension bolts loosen after the first winter — preventive retightening: after a car's first winter season, suspension bolts (including shock-absorber fork/clevis mounts) can gradually loosen; ball joints may also loosen slightly from their factory torque. Recommended preventive maintenance: retighten all suspension bolts once after the first winter 99.

Rattle from the catalytic converter dust shield: a rattle/noise from the rear/underside of the engine can also originate from the catalytic converter's dust/heat shield (пыльник катализатора) — this sheet-metal shield can vibrate and produce noise at highway speed or in specific RPM ranges, and is worth checking alongside the engine-mount and exhaust-mount causes described on the engine mount card 100.

Metallic rattle from the rear — check for a partially broken spring coil: a distinct metallic rattling/clanging sound from the rear can indicate that a rear coil spring has partially broken, with the loose metal fragment striking the surrounding suspension component on every bump. This requires visual inspection of the rear springs and, if confirmed, spring replacement — see the rear springs card for sourcing 101102.

Stiff ride over parking-lot bumps is normal "stock tuning", not a fault: new owners frequently report that the X80 feels very stiff and transmits every small bump, especially at low speed in parking lots and over speed bumps. The community consensus is that this is normal for the platform's stock suspension tuning, not a defect. The only community-suggested remedy is to swap in softer Mazda-sourced suspension components for a more comfortable ride — at the cost of somewhat reduced handling precision; see the shock absorbers card and front springs card for the specific Mazda cross-fit parts 103104105106107.

Rear suspension bounce test — quick damper diagnosis: quick diagnostic for weak rear dampers: open the trunk and press down firmly on the rear of the car with your body weight, then release. Working dampers compress smoothly and return to rest position in a single motion without bouncing. Excessive bouncing (more than one oscillation) indicates worn/failing shock absorbers or weak springs. This symptom often shows up after speed bumps if the dampers are degraded 108109110111.

Rattle mistaken for suspension noise — loose exhaust heat shield: a loud rattling/ticking sound from underneath the car, especially under acceleration or in specific RPM ranges, is often not a suspension fault at all — it's commonly a loose exhaust heat shield (термозащита) whose mounting points have loosened from vibration. Diagnosis: locate the shield (typically over the catalytic converter or silencer area) and visually check for gaps or movement. Fix: tighten or re-seat all mounting fasteners; if the shield has fully detached and is resting against the exhaust, either reinstall it properly or remove it if it serves no remaining function. Self-tapping metal screws can serve as a temporary fix if the original bolts are missing. Worth ruling out before assuming a suspension component is the source of an underbody rattle 112113114115116.

Metal-on-metal clunk on takeoff — brake pads vs. suspension vs. engine mounts (undiagnosed): one owner reported a metal-on-metal clunk/click heard specifically when moving off from a stop (forward or reverse), intermittent rather than constant. A shop check (pry bars, shaking components) found "everything fine," but the clunk recurred at the next stoplight. Suggested causes from the community, in likely order: (1) Mazda-sourced brake pads that are physically shorter than spec and rattle inside the caliper bracket — especially noticeable moving off in reverse and braking; also check for stuck caliper guide pins or a sticky piston preventing the pads from retracting cleanly (lift the wheel, remove the caliper — if the pad has vertical play, that's very likely the cause); (2) worn suspension components — sheared ball joint or a cracked spring; (3) engine mount play. In this specific case the pads were confirmed genuine/non-Mazda and silent, and the noise was located at the front — the owner suspected engine mounts and, separately, found and suspected a spring crack (see the dedicated front springs card for that part of the same thread) — root cause was not conclusively confirmed in this thread 117118119.

Winter squeaking below -15°C — usually stabilizer bushings, resolves somewhat with driving: a recurring cold-weather complaint: suspension squeaking below about -15°C, typically on cold start and easing off after driving 1–2 km as things warm up. Most contributors point to the stabilizer bar bushings as the usual cause (see the dedicated stabilizer bushing card), though one owner who had already replaced the stabilizer bushings on service-shop advice still had squeaking afterward — just quieter, described as "creaking like a carriage" over bumps — suggesting strut top mounts or spring-seat spacers can also be squeak sources, not only the stabilizer. Separately, a distinct rattling (not squeaking) complaint in the same cold conditions, described as "sounding like a rattle from every direction at low speed," was attributed by one contributor to rubber bushings/mounts stiffening in the cold generally — a broader, less specific cold-weather symptom than the stabilizer-bushing squeak. One owner reported that replacing all bushings (сайленты) a year prior, at 100,000 km, had already improved things 120121122123124125126127128129130.

Front clicking on small bumps — caliper guide pins/pallets first, then links: front-suspension clicking/knocking over small bumps, with no play found on a vibration-stand ("вибростенд") check at two separate shops, both of which reported "everything is fine." Community diagnosis priority for this specific car: check the strut top mounts and caliper guide pins ("пальцы суппортов") first, then stabilizer links ("линки") if those check out. Field test: with the wheel off and cold, grab and shake the caliper by hand — if it moves freely side-to-side on its guide pins, that free play is what rattles when cold (grease resolves it once warm in summer, but the play returns in winter until serviced). This is described as an almost universal X80 symptom in cold weather — "like a rattle" — that quiets down as temperatures rise. A second diagnostic technique: drive over bumps while lightly braking — if the clunk disappears under light braking, that confirms the caliper as the source 131132133134135136137.

"Is the ride supposed to be this noisy/bouncy?" — yes, this is normal X80 character, not a defect: a new owner coming from a Ford Maverick asked whether the X80's noticeable shaking over every bump/speed bump was normal. Community answer: yes — "that's called suspension... it's noisy by nature," and the suspension is inexpensive to service if the bushings and springs are actually worn (see the suspension origin and weight note for why the Mazda-derived suspension feels soft/noisy on the heavier X80 body) 138139140.

Steering-wheel squeak while turning — reported, cause not identified (low confidence): a new owner separately asked about a squeak from the steering wheel specifically during turns. No diagnosis or fix was offered in this thread — flag as an open/unconfirmed report; possible causes by analogy with other steering-noise threads on this wiki include column trim contact or column lubrication (see the dashboard bezel squeak card for a related but distinct interior squeak) 141.

Oct 2026 — metallic knock over bumps after steering and arm work. Валерий replaced the steering rack with tie-rod ends, fitted an aftermarket straight lower control arm and had the alignment set, which cured the crooked steering wheel; a knock over speed bumps remained 142. The metallic knock is present even at low speed, and the right side became quieter after he replaced the right driveshaft, though play remains 142143. He suspects the right driveshaft or a rubber "donut" (бублик), because the noise fades as speed and engine rpm drop and starts at about 20-30 km/h 144. Arсhi 77 suggests crossing the bump slowly and smoothly should be quiet 145, and that loose brake pads moving back and forth a couple of millimetres will make noise anyway, and to listen to the stabilizer bar on potholes 146. The causes are unresolved; the positions (driveshaft vs pads/stabilizer/strut) are recorded as stated.

Recommended pressure. For standard-size tires on the FAW X80, the recommended pressure is 2.2 bar, with 2.3 bar cited as an acceptable alternative12.

docs.title: Tire size specifications and fitment
docs.text:
Tags: #tires · #fitment · #tire-pressure

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Standard X80 tire size: 215/60/17 1. Alternative sizes reported to fit: - 225/60/17 — common upgrade, good fitment 23. - 225/55/17 — lower profile; improves handling but the speedometer reads about 3 km/h slower 4. Recommended for winter use for better cornering 5. - 235/60/17 — slightly wider, ~12mm larger overall radius than 225/60 6. - 225/65/17 and larger — risk of light rubbing at full steering lock 7.

Tire pressure — official spec vs. practical use: the official owner's manual spec is 2.6 bar (solo driver) / 2.4 bar standard, per one owner's reading of the manual — though another owner's understanding was 2.3 bar standard, indicating some inconsistency in how owners recall the book values; check your own door-placard decal for the definitive figure 89101112. Practical usage reported by the community: city driving 2.2–2.3 bar for a softer ride and better pothole absorption (with 3 occupants, some run as low as 2.2); long highway/road trips 2.4 bar. Over-inflating to the full 2.6 bar spec creates a harsh ride where every small stone impact is felt — most owners find that too stiff for daily driving 131415.

Winter tire recommendation: Nokian Tyres Hakkapeliitta R5 SUV winter tires in size 215/60 R17 100R (matching the stock tire size) were confirmed by owners as a suitable winter fitment for the X80, shared via an Ozon marketplace listing 161718.

225/60/18 confirmed alongside 225/60/17: multiple owners confirm the X80 fits 225/60/18 wheels/tires without issues, in addition to the 225/60/17 size already noted above — both sizes are reported as 'normal' ('норм') fitment by owners 192021.

Additional confirmed sizes — 235/55, 225/65, and a 215/65 caution: further community reports on tire sizing: 235/55 R17 (same overall diameter as stock) fits without rubbing but increases fuel consumption and unsprung mass; 225/65 R17 fits without issues and is reported to "look good"; 215/65 R17, by contrast, sometimes rubs the fender liner during sharp turns — specifically noted as a winter-season issue (likely due to snow/ice buildup reducing clearance further) 22232425262728.

Offset (ET) and R18 visual-proportion note: reinforcing the sizing picture above — factory fitment is 215/60 R17 on 17-inch rims; 225/60 R17 is reported to improve appearance over stock. R18 wheels are possible but, even at 18-inch diameter, can look visually small relative to the body due to the X80's chassis proportions (body-to-wheel ratio). Offset (ET) is flagged as important: factory offset is approximately 40 mm — matching offset is called critical for suspension performance, and online wheel-fitment calculators are recommended for verification before buying 29303132.

docs.title: Tire sizing guide
docs.text:
Tags: #tires · #wheels

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Stock/OEM configuration: 215/60 R17 (also written 215/60/17R), on ET45 wheels, 7–7.5J rim width 12. Confirmed alternates that fit without rubbing: 225/60/17 (very common, most owners run this without issue) and 225/65/17 (confirmed by multiple owners, used year-round) 13.

Winter alternatives: 215/65 R16 (slightly lower profile than stock, cheaper, softer ride from the taller sidewall) or 225/60/16 (better snow performance, wider footprint) 42. Taller/higher-profile options such as 225/55/17, 225/60/17 or 235/60/17 are also used for winter — a taller sidewall improves comfort on rough roads 43. One unattributed post also mentions 215/65/17 as viable (~1.2cm lower than stock) per tire-size calculators, though not independently confirmed 5.

R20 wheels with 245/40 tires give a very low profile: stiff ride, limited tire selection, and expensive options — not recommended for most owners 4.

Fitment/appearance notes: 225/60/17 is the de-facto standard and works for most owners; 225/55/17 sits about 2cm lower and visibly changes the car's stance; 235/60/17 is used by some as a comfort-oriented upgrade 67. Rim guidance: keep ET around +45 (±2–3mm tolerance) to avoid stressing the suspension; minimum wheel center bore (DIA) 67.1mm for clearance; a 6.5J rim pairs well with 215mm-wide tires, 7–7.5J is better suited to 225mm-wide tires 2.

Disagreement on tire profile: some owners prefer the 55-series profile for sharper handling and agility; others prefer the 60-series for ride comfort and factory-look proportions. Both are reported to work well with no known downsides beyond personal preference 67.

Winter tire cost/performance comparison (Sept 2024, Irkutsk, RU market): Chinese-brand winter tires (225/55/17) performed adequately and cost about 6,900 RUB per tire; premium brands (Continental, Michelin) cost 23,000+ RUB per tire. Continental stayed flexible down to -40°C; a Bridgestone tire in the same test was less flexible in extreme cold. Budget-conscious owners reported Chinese tires as adequate for 1–2 seasons at a much lower cost, treating them as a rotation/replacement strategy rather than a long-term investment 8.

Speedometer accuracy vs. tire size: on stock tires the speedometer reads inaccurately fast — a real 130 km/h shows as roughly 137 km/h. Fitting the larger 225/65/17 tire improves accuracy but adds about 1.7cm of ride height. Recommended pressure across sizes is 2.2–2.6 bar, which also improves comfort. Unlike some other brands (e.g. Renault), the speedometer discrepancy on the X80 cannot be corrected via OBD. On 225/65 tires the speedometer reads more accurately; going to a lower 60-series profile reduces accuracy further 9.

Clearance gained by tire size — measured deltas vs. stock (Sept–Nov 2025): reinforcing and quantifying the fitment notes above, several owners report the actual clearance/diameter increase over the stock 215/60R17: 225/60R17 adds about +6mm; 215/65R17 adds about +11mm; 225/65R17 adds about +17mm and roughly +34mm to overall tire diameter. 225/60R17 was independently described as fitting well with no rubbing and being close to the practical maximum diameter for the stock arches; 225/65R17 fits without rubbing in normal driving but rides noticeably softer than 215/60R17 1011121314.

225/50R17 — too low-profile, not recommended: 225/50/17 was specifically flagged as too low a profile for the X80 (described as "electrical tape"-thin), unlike the 55–65 series options documented above 1516.

225/65R17 — light contact at full steering lock (multiple independent reports): several owners confirm 225/65R17 fits for normal driving but lightly scuffs/touches the wheel-arch liner at full steering lock in both directions; described consistently as minor/non-critical rather than a fitment failure. One owner running 225/65R17 as a winter tire plans to switch to 215/65R17 instead, feeling 225/65 is oversized for winter use 1718192021.

Speedometer error scales with tire size — additional data points: extending the speedometer-accuracy note above, one owner fitting 225/65R17 reports the stock speedometer's over-read (previously ~-6km/h error) is corrected; going the other direction, a smaller/different tire combination produced a +9 km/h over-read that could not be corrected via software on the stock ECU. General rule reported: the speedometer error grows with speed. Note the odometer and average-speed reading are not affected — they stay accurate regardless of tire size, only the speedometer needle itself over-reads on stock-size tires 2223242526.

18-inch wheel fitment: the X80 accepts 18-inch wheels; recommended size 225/60R18 fits without issues (confirmed on the restyle/facelift body). Trade-off: 18-inch wheels are more sensitive to road surface defects (potholes, cracks, small rocks) than the stock 17-inch setup 27282930.

215/65R17 front tire rubs inner fender — downsize front to 215/60R17: the OEM tire size 215/65R17 rubs against the plastic inner fender liner. Fix: downsize the front tires only to 215/60R17 (keep the rear at the original 215/65R17). This reduces tire diameter by roughly 5% per wheel and clears the fender without affecting rear suspension geometry 3132.

Perceived stiffness is often trim rattle and tire choice, not the suspension itself: the X80's ride can feel stiff mainly because of loose interior/plastic trim rattling and road noise, rather than actual suspension rigidity. To improve perceived comfort: fit 215/65 or 225/65 tires with a soft sidewall (look for "Comfort" branding rather than "Extra Load"/reinforced tires), and avoid over-inflating. Separately, removing/securing loose interior trim (door panels, sender covers) reduces rattling and noticeably improves the feel of the ride. Wheel/tire choice has more impact on perceived comfort than suspension stiffness itself 3334353637.

215/65/17 vs 225/65/18 — comfort trade-off, and rubbing risk at full lock: the X80 supports both stock 215/65/17 (more comfortable, absorbs bumps better) and 225/65/18 fitments; some owners also run a 60-profile alternative (225/65 -> lower profile trades comfort for a firmer feel). Larger-profile (higher sidewall) tires give a noticeably softer ride. Caution: slight rubbing against the fender liner at full steering lock can occur depending on suspension condition/load, regardless of size — always verify fitment before buying 383940414243.

Tested tire-size fitment results (June 2026): consolidated community fitment testing beyond stock 215/65R17 — (1) 235/65R17: rubs at full compression, too wide, avoid; (2) 225/65R17: fits well, comfortable, full turning radius normal; (3) 225/60R17: also fits; (4) 225/55R17: mathematically close in diameter to 235/50R17, marginal fit; (5) 235/55R17: fits per one report. Changing aspect ratio (e.g. 65→55) lowers ride height, and combining a lowered front (via spring modification) with 235-wide tires reduces ground clearance on rough terrain — one owner who lifted the front 20mm with springs and the rear with ~10mm (real) spacers still bottomed out on uneven ground. Larger wheels/tires generally improve handling but require a suspension-geometry check first. Regional tire supply varies — some areas stock only premium brands (AGC, FYG, XYG) 4445464748495051525354555657.

Larger wheels increase hub-bearing and CV-joint/driveshaft load — general engineering consideration: going up in wheel/tire size increases the rotational load and stress on the hub bearings and CV axles/drive joints, roughly proportional to the radius increase. This isn't a specific failure report but a standing engineering consideration when upgrading from stock sizes: larger wheels mean higher bearing wear rates over time and a higher chance of earlier component failure — worth weighing against the ride-height/clearance benefits documented elsewhere on this card, and relevant background for the hub bearing cards 58.

225/65 vs. stock 215/60 — one owner's no-rub experience at full lock: one additional data point on the already-documented 215/60 vs. 225/65 comparison: 225/65 (about 2cm larger overall than the factory 215/60) is reported by this owner to improve ground clearance for off-road use without fender rubbing at full steering lock — note this contradicts the "light contact at full lock" reports already on this card from other owners, so rubbing risk appears to depend on specific wheel offset/suspension condition rather than being universal. With the factory 215/60 size, this owner notes the tire doesn't reach the fender lip in the normal (non-turned) position 59606162636465.

225/60/17 confirmed again — replacement urgency, and mixed-tread-pattern question: another owner needed to replace a non-repairable flat and confirmed 225/60/17 as a safe, brand-agnostic replacement size for the stock 215/60/17 66. A separate question about whether mixing two different tire tread patterns on the same axle causes problems went unanswered in this thread — treat as an open question, not a confirmed safe practice 67. Matching wheels (rim/offset combination) shown by another owner were separately confirmed by the community as fitting the X80 6869.

Conflict — 215/65 R17 recommended as "standard," 225/65 R17 discouraged (contradicts other reports on this card): in a newer thread, one contributor recommended fitting the 215/60/17 factory size specifically to fix front-wheel rubbing on the inner plastic fender liner, and separately another owner stated 225/65/17 tires were "heavy and inconvenient," rubbed slightly at full steering lock, and hurt acceleration/fuel economy — switching to 215/65/17 "fit perfectly" by comparison 707172. This directly conflicts with the earlier, higher-confidence reports elsewhere on this card (sourced from a separate long thread) that 225/65/17 is a confirmed, rubbing-free fitment used year-round by multiple owners — treat 225/65/17 fitment as disputed and dependent on wheel offset/ alignment condition rather than settled either way 7374757677. Asked to confirm real-world experience with 235/55 R17 specifically, the same contributor who reported the rubbing/economy issues with 225/65/17 above replied that 235/55 R17 is "practically stock," just with a wider tread, and expected it to be fine 7872. Separately, one MT-gearbox owner running a staggered winter setup (215/60 rear, 215/55 front) reported noticeably livelier acceleration feel versus a matched-size setup — an anecdotal, single-owner data point, not a general recommendation 79.

Wheel/tire rubbing on inner plastic fender liner — check clips and offset before blaming tire size: when front wheels rub against the plastic inner fender liner (подкрылок) while turning, check two things before assuming the tire size is at fault: (1) wheel offset (ET) — verify it matches spec; (2) whether the plastic fender-liner clip has come loose, which alone can cause rubbing that looks like a tire-size problem. 215/65 R17 was described as the "ideal" tire for the X80 in this thread 7470768071.

Tire size vs. speedometer error — reference table: stock size 215/60/17 reads 8–9% high on the speedometer; the "optimal" size 215/65/17 reduces this to 4–5%; the maximum recommended size 225/65/17 further reduces error to 1–2% but may cause slight rubbing at full steering lock 81. A later, independent report gives consistent figures for two other sizes: both 235/55 R17 and 235/50 R18 measured 8–9% speedometer error — no rubbing was reported for either at these sizes. Switching to the 18" wheel size was said to improve handling/cornering, at the cost of roughly +1 L/100km fuel consumption from the added wheel weight and rolling resistance 82838485.

docs.title: TPMS sensor cloning when installing aftermarket wheels
docs.text:
Tags: #tpms · #wheels

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

When installing aftermarket wheels, the TPMS (tire pressure sensor) signals need to be cloned/reprogrammed to match the new wheel positions — otherwise the system will not correctly report pressure per position. This requires a specialized programming tool that ordinary shops do not have. Tire shops that offer sensor programming as a service (in addition to tire sales and installation) carry the needed equipment. The procedure is relatively quick — reported as typically under 1 hour 12.

Sensor part numbers, failure rate, and pricing: OEM TPMS sensor part numbers differ by body style — 5GA-prefix for pre-facelift, 5BA037973 for post-facelift (restyle) X80s; the two are not interchangeable, so confirm which generation your car is before ordering. OEM sensors reportedly fail frequently. Universal aftermarket TPMS sensors are a common alternative, but still require the same programming/registration step after installation, at roughly 200 RUB (RU market, August 2025) per sensor charged by service shops. Reported OEM sensor pricing is around 2,500 RUB (RU market, August 2025) each, with installation/programming adding about 200 RUB per wheel 3.

Battery swap doesn't always fix a dead sensor: replacing just the TPMS sensor's battery does not always restore function. If the sensor still fails to register after a battery change and a polarity check, the sensor's internal circuit itself has likely failed — the whole sensor needs replacing, not just the battery 4567.

Cross-platform part number and clone sensors: OEM sensor part number 5BA037973 was confirmed by an owner to fit not only the X80 but also the related FAW B50, B70, B90, and X40 models. Aftermarket clone/compatible sensors (e.g. Autel-brand) are an alternative but may require their sensor ID to be cloned from the original before they will register correctly 891011.

Persistent/inconsistent TPMS warning light — no confirmed fix: a recurring problem where the tire-pressure warning light appears and disappears inconsistently, with no clear specification found in the owner's documentation for the correct target pressure. Trial and error reported by one owner: 2.2 BAR gives a softer ride; different pressures still trigger intermittent warnings; resetting the warning via the menu does not resolve the underlying inconsistency. Likely cause is sensor calibration or an intermittent contact issue, but no owner in this thread found a definitive fix or the correct factory pressure spec for their car 1213.

docs.title: Front upper arm — part numbers and ball joint
docs.text:
Tags: #control-arm · #part-number · #mazda-6-compat · #price

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Arm numbers and cross-fits. The OEM number for the upper left front suspension arm is 5CA034250 (June 2025).1 A December 2025 listing gives SUFIX C23034250 for the upper left front arm of the FAW B50 and X80, and the sellers say it also fits the Mazda 6 GG.2 Other makers' listings for the X80: SH Auto Parts left SH31031 / right SH31030, and NK 5013231 (left) / 5013232 (right).3 A CTR CQ0253R front right upper arm (code 28736024) was shown on vseinstrumenti.ru at a last price of 4,437 RUB (RU market, May 2025), marked out of stock; X80 fitment is not stated in the image.4 The SUFIX SH-1365 upper left front arm appeared in a store screenshot at 1,720 RUB (4 in stock) and 1,950 RUB (2 and 6 in stock) (RU market, December 2025), posted by a Mazda 6 GG owner as a price comparison.5

Replacing the whole arm or only the bushings. One member replaced the whole arm and the silent blocks (сайлентблоки, rubber bushings) separately with Stellox parts and reports about 30,000 km without problems; he adds that the B50 arm is fine for the X80.6 For the front left upper arm (5CA034250) another member estimated two silent blocks at about 1,500 RUB plus about 1,000 RUB for pressing them in (RU market, March 2024), and noted that if the upper ball joint is worn, replacing the whole arm may make more sense.7 A commenter who replaced only the silent blocks later said the complete arm assembly would have been the better buy.8

Upper ball joint (шаровая опора). The upper front control-arm ball joint for the FAW Besturn X80 / X80 NEW has article C23034200-1, with analog C23034250; a kitzapchasti.ru listing showed it at 700 RUB (RU market, January 2026). Ball joints are sold either separately or with the arm, and the marketplaces only carry the assembly.91011 The B50 upper ball joint C23034250 was suggested as fitting the X80: one member said the joint is double-sided and fits either side, while another reported that the joint's code is registered as left-side and asked for the right-side code; fitment stays unconfirmed.121314 An owner states that only the FAW ball joint fits and that it is hard to find; a linked Kitz Zapchasti listing for C23034200-1 is titled for the Besturn B50, not the X80.158

See also: Front upper control arm — squeak and parts, Control arm replacement cost.

docs.title: Front upper control arm — squeak and parts
docs.text:
Tags: #control-arm · #mazda-6-compat · #squeak · #part-number

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Cross-fit: Mazda 6 GG/GJ/GL (2002-2007, generation 1) and Atenza (2002-2007, generation 1) upper control arms fit the X80. Critical detail: the arm's rod thickness must be ≥13.5mm for proper support — anything thinner is poor quality 1. A separate, low-confidence report says upper arms from Mazda 6 GG were investigated in general but no fitment was confirmed in that thread; treat as unverified pending an in-person dismantler check 2.

Squeak diagnosis: a squeak felt/heard through the steering column when hand pressure is applied to the upper arm indicates worn silentbloc bushings. Spraying silicone on the bushings and observing whether the sound disappears confirms the diagnosis 3. The squeak typically first appears around 80,000–86,000 km 4.

Repair options: - Bushings only: ~700–800 RUB (RU market, September 2024) each plus labor — cheaper but reported as having questionable longevity 3. - Full arm replacement: preferred by most contributors. Even a higher-quality arm's ball joint may fail after 35,000–40,000 km if it is not genuine OEM; investing in genuine OEM arms (7,000–8,000 RUB, RU market, September 2024) avoids repeating the replacement every ~35k km 3. - If the ball joint is still functional, replacing only the sileblock bushings is presented as far cheaper than a full arm — Mazda upper arms with integrated ball joints do not mount on the X80, but sileblocks (bushings) taken from other vehicles reportedly can fit; a diagnostic check is recommended before choosing between the two paths 5. - Silentblock-only replacement using Stellox 7701133SX bushings (fits both Besturn B50 and X80): two silentblocks per arm, can be pressed in by hand with no special tools; ~500 RUB (RU market, November 2024) per piece 6.

Part numbers: FAW OEM upper arms 5CA034250 (left) / 5CA034200 (right). Mazda 6 GG (2002-2007) cross-fit alternative: CQ0253R, ~4,500 RUB (RU market, October 2024) on Drom. AVT-brand alternative: SH31031 (left) / SH31030 (right), 2,107 RUB (RU market, October 2024) each. Genuine FAW parts derive from the licensed Mazda design; branded "Mazda"-labelled alternatives on the market are often actually Chinese-manufactured 78.

Recommended/avoided brands: Mazda-branded arms (durable seals) and FEBI (good reputation) are recommended. Avoid "JD Just Drive" — one owner had both the bushings and ball joint fail at only 15,000 km. Note Mazda 6's ball joint diameter differs from the X80's, so Mazda 6 ball-joint parts do not cross-fit even though the arm itself does. While replacing the upper arm, always inspect the front coil springs for cracks — spring failure can go unnoticed 9.

Disagreement on subframe removal: one owner (Сергей Арапкин) reports the arm could not be replaced without removing the subframe; others (e.g. Василий Егоров) report successful replacement without subframe removal when using the correct jacking technique 910.

Rubber vibration damper on the arm: some X80 upper control arms are fitted with a dynamic vibration damper (динамический виброгаситель) — a rubber-bushed sleeve mounted on the arm. It is not present on OEM/original arms but appears on some aftermarket units (e.g. Mazda-sourced arms), and points downward when correctly assembled. Function: dampens suspension vibration and impacts; it is not essential to operation and can be removed if desired. Community sources debate its exact purpose — some describe it as a bump stop, others as a pure vibration absorber 111213.

Detailed Mazda 6gg fitment and part numbers: upper control arm assemblies from the Mazda 6gg (generations GG/GH) fit the X80 front suspension. OEM is generally preferred over the Mazda part — one installer reported a Mazda analog "didn't work" for their case, though the specifics were unclear. A confirmed Mazda-compatible option is the Stellox brand 57-71079a-sx (right upper arm for Mazda 6 gg/gy, 2002+), available on Ozon for ~1,215 RUB (RU market, April 2025), installs in about 30 minutes, and is described as good quality by the installer. For the left arm, the part number differs only in the last digit (78 instead of 79), easy to identify in parts catalogs 1415.

Disagreement — does the upper arm affect toe-in? After replacing the upper control arm, one owner's toe-in angle shifted unexpectedly (a 48-minute change) even though the vehicle was rocked and re-checked during alignment. Community consensus is that upper ball joints/control arms should not theoretically affect toe-in (wheel convergence), but this owner's experience contradicts that — suggesting the shift may instead stem from prior impact/ accident history or a bent knuckle rather than the control arm replacement itself. Cross-reference: see the wheel alignment card for general alignment behavior and pricing 16.

Brand/price comparison (2025) — Stelox vs JD vs bushing-only: upper arm prices range 2,500–10,000 RUB (RU market, May 2025) depending on brand. Stelox held up well (5,000+ RUB (RU market, May 2025), verified past 5,000 km driven, durable construction) 17. JD was cheap (~2,500 RUB, RU market, May 2025) but failed at only 15,000 km, matching the earlier "JD Just Drive" warning above 18. If the shaft/ball joint is still good, some owners prefer replacing only the silentblock bushings (Masuma brand, ~1,000–1,200 RUB (RU market, May 2025) per piece) instead of the whole arm — this reportedly extends service life 50,000+ km. Once a silentblock fails badly, full-arm replacement is recommended over further bushing repair 1920.

Lubrication fix for clicking (not a bushing swap): metallic clicking from the front suspension over bumps can sometimes be resolved without replacing anything — by disassembling both upper control arms and lubricating all bolts with SHRb-4 grease. Owners who tried this reported the clicking/squeaking disappeared, and the arms did not need to be fully removed from the vehicle to do it 21.

Grinding/creaking distinguished from clicking — high-mileage bushing failure: a separate, distinct symptom — grinding or creaking noise specifically during turns/cornering (as opposed to the click/squeak covered above) — was traced to worn upper-arm silentblocks at around 100,000 km, not to broken springs or brake issues. The noise stopped after silentblock replacement, and the ride became noticeably more responsive. Note: brake-line routing rubbing against the body chassis can produce a similar sound and should be ruled out first 22.

Early creaking-over-speed-bump report — traced to upper arm silentblocks (May 2024): an early community report of a squeak/creak heard when driving over a speed bump on a pre-facelift car. Suggested first by the community as front-arm silentblocks, with silicone spray recommended as a first, temporary test 2324. The owner confirmed it sounded consistent with worn silentblocks 25; a separate contributor initially guessed stabilizer bushings instead, showing this symptom is commonly mixed up between the two sources 26. Resolution: another owner reports having the same issue and fixing it by replacing the upper front arm silentblocks — on the right side the old bushings had simply fallen out — after which the squeak disappeared 27.

Sourcing guidance — bushing-only vs. full arm, by cost (May 2024): when deciding whether to replace just the silentblock or the whole upper arm, the community's guidance is straightforward: base the decision on relative price, and if having the work done at an official/dealer service, clarify in advance whose part will be used and who performs the labor, since this affects both cost and warranty standing 2829.

Upper control-arm bushing — Tenacity AAMMA1017 (Nov 2025): a rubber upper control-arm (upper A-arm) bushing under part number Tenacity AAMMA1017 was purchased via Ozon; the buyer had not yet installed it due to cold weather at the time of reporting 30.

Upper control-arm bushings — Masuma RU496, dealer price comparison (Dec 2025): for the post-restyle X80, Masuma RU496 upper control-arm bushings (cross-compatible with other FAW models including the B50) are available via Ozon. For comparison, a dealer quoted 10,000 RUB (RU market, December 2025) in labor alone to replace 2 bushings, despite the car still being under manufacturer warranty (until 2028) 313233.

Upper control-arm silentblocks — received-parts photo verification: a community member who ordered silentblocks for the upper control arms shared photos of the received parts for a quick community fitment/spec sanity-check before installing 3435.

Ball joint failure timeline (Jan 2026): a separate owner reported an upper control-arm ball joint (described as "подкова"-shaped shear pins) failing again at only 25,000–27,000 km after a previous replacement — a much shorter interval than the 35,000+ km figures reported above. Linkx-brand replacement recommended, with 30,000+ km lifespan reported on that owner's vehicle 3637.

Squeak sounding "like a cart" (March 2026): a creaking/squeaking sound described as sounding like a horse-drawn cart (как телегу), especially over speed bumps and uneven surfaces, was again traced to worn upper control-arm ball joints. Two fix paths confirmed by this thread, matching the guidance above: (1) replace the entire upper control arm (complete rod with integrated ball joint), or (2) a more cost-effective route — buy a ball joint repair/press kit and press new ball joints into the existing arms. Replace both left and right as a pair 38394041.

Upper control arm sway-bar ball joints fell out of their bushings during a front spring job (62,000 km): during a front spring replacement at 62,000 km (spring broken on one side), the upper control arm's sway-bar ball joints simply fell out of their bushings when the arm was disturbed — they required re-pressing. The ball joints themselves were still serviceable at that point (rated to last to roughly 100,000 km), but the upper control arm showed rust. See the front springs card for the full spring-failure context; recommendation there was to replace dampers and ball joints together around 100,000 km, since re-pressed ball-joint boots may only last another 30,000–40,000 km 42434445464748.

Saiblocks on upper control arms fail early — one case at 50,000 km: rubber bushings ("saiblocks"/сайлентблоки) on the upper suspension control arms frequently fail, with one owner reporting failure as early as 50,000 km. Symptoms: squeaking noise and the bushing separating from its sleeve. This condition often requires replacement before 100,000 km — earlier than the general wear pattern might suggest. Often accompanied by stabilizer bushing squeak; see the stabilizer bushings card 4950.

Upper control arm bushings — Tenacity AAMMA1017: another cross-brand bushing option for the front upper control arm: Tenacity AAMMA1017. Install time reported at 10–30 minutes depending on skill and tooling; a press/orifice tool is needed, and one owner found one of the two bushings awkward to extract because of its mounting angle 51.

Upper control-arm assemblies and ball joints — SH vs. Miles, and a disagreement on SH longevity: complete upper control-arm assemblies (arm + ball joint) are commonly sourced under the SH brand, and Miles is used as an alternative. Disagreement: one owner's SH ball joints started knocking after roughly a year/~15,000 km, and they switched to Miles to see if it does better; another contributor pushes back, noting that Mazda owners running SH generally don't report complaints — so results may vary by batch/installer rather than being a blanket SH quality issue. If the original ball joint is still good, the cheaper fix is just re-pressing the bushings rather than buying a whole new arm assembly; the job can be done without removing the strut, in roughly the same 10–30 minute window as above 525354.

Upper control arm — no built-in travel limiters on X80, unlike some Mazda variants: the X80 upper control arm connects the strut to the frame via a ball joint with a limited range of motion, but — unlike some Mazda 6 variants — the X80's design has no built-in upper suspension-travel limiters/stops, which allows more compression/ extension travel than a Mazda-spec arm would. Practical consequence: when fitting wider springs (e.g. CX-5-sourced, see the rear springs card) or lift spacers, camber/ caster geometry shifts more than expected — always recheck alignment after this kind of modification 5556.

Upper front control arm — FAW part numbers: left upper front control arm is FAW part FC034250 (also listed as 5CA034250); right upper front control arm is FC034200 (also listed as 5CA034200). Both available from the kitzapchasti.ru catalog 5758.

Bushing replacement — dealer myth vs. community reality (71,000 km wear report): one owner (Денис З) reported the upper front control-arm bushings ("сайленты") worn out to nothing at 71,000 km; the official dealer told him bushings can only be replaced together with the whole arm assembly (2,500–5,000 RUB (RU market, August 2024) per arm + ~13,000 RUB labor per side, plus a wheel alignment). The community pushed back hard on this: bushings can be pressed out and replaced separately, and the ball joint is also sold separately — one contributor had done exactly this himself, replacing everything except the ball joint on his own arms 596061. A Masuma-brand replacement bushing was linked as one sourcing option 62. Separately, another owner (SKAtality) said no wheel alignment is required after an upper-arm bushing replacement — contradicting the dealer's claim that one is needed 6364.

Replacement procedure — no full suspension teardown needed: to replace the upper control arm (рычаг) itself, it is not necessary to remove the entire suspension: unscrew the stabilizer-bar link stud, the shock-absorber fork bolt, and the shock-absorber top mount, then remove and replace the arm and reassemble in reverse order. Jack the car up at the brake-disc rotor to get clearance for reinserting the bolt through the shock fork and arm. Reported total time, including breaks, about one hour in a simple driveway setting — no lift or special tools required 65.

Sealantblock (bushing) count — 4 total on the upper front arms: the front upper suspension control arms have 4 bushings total (2 per side), and community advice is to replace them as a full set rather than one at a time; check ball-joint condition at the same time, since a complete replacement kit can sometimes work out more economical than buying individual parts 666768.

Upper control arm alternatives — Mazda 6, thicker metal, ~2,700 RUB (RU market, as of November 2025): Mazda 6 upper control-arm assemblies (including bushings) fit the X80 and are widely available from multiple retailers. One owner who fitted a Mazda 6 arm reported its metal is noticeably thicker/more robust than the FAW-OEM arm. Reported cost: ~2,700 RUB (RU market, November 2025), ordered from Ozon 6970. A separate owner who bought a Mazda 6 arm assembly (Ozon, ~2,700 RUB, RU market, December 2025) confirmed direct fitment with no modification, alongside also sourcing Mazda-compatible stabilizer links that happened to be in stock locally 71.

Oct 2026 update — upper arm bushings: press, sizes and tightening; lifetime reports. Without a press, one owner noted it used to be cheaper to replace the whole upper arm assembly than to swap the bushings (silent blocks, сайлентблоки) 72. Arсhi 77 advises not to buy the cheapest and to make sure the sizes match exactly — a difference of a couple of millimetres in diameter means they will not fit, so order from several brands at once; he also stresses that the bolts should be tightened with the car standing on its wheels, i.e. with the bushings under working load, so they last 7374.

Lifetime reports differ widely. Arсhi 77 says his silent blocks are fine at about 170,000 km, that front-arm bushings seem to last longest in his view, and that he ignored a master's advice to replace them at 50,000 km ("pseudo-masters") 757677. Victor's upper silent blocks began to squeak from about 50,000 km and were later found torn 78.

docs.title: Wheel alignment: specs, shops and pricing
docs.text:
Tags: #mazda-6-compat · #price

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

Some advice here concerns sub-zero winters and is less relevant in a hot climate.

Official factory specification. Wheel alignment angles are documented in the factory manual (and the owner's manual), and some Russian aftermarket sources have also published alignment specs for the X80 123. The full table, unloaded, from the factory manual — front: camber −20′ ± 30′ (slight negative), caster 5.93° ± 1°, steering-axis inclination 6.53°, toe-in 0 ± 2mm, steering-wheel lock angles (inner 36.5° ± 3°, outer 30° ± 3°), vehicle height 435 ± 20mm; rear: camber −1°20′ ± 30′ (slight negative), toe-in 2 ± 2mm, vehicle height 462 ± 20mm. Height reference conditions noted in the manual: 12-liter fuel level, coolant at normal level 45. The same table was independently re-shared and re-confirmed in two further community threads, with no discrepancies from these figures 6789101112. Owners who had the alignment performed to X80-specific figures confirm the car handles correctly afterward 1314151617.

Early community reference (May 2024) — platform basis and fallback. An early card-founding thread established that the X80 is primarily based on the Mazda 6 (2002–2008 generation), though its automatic transmission (AKPP) is unique to FAW (modeled on Aisin principles); parts cross-reference across Mazda 6, Mazda CX-5, Ford, Volvo, and the FAW B50. Practical advice given at the time: ask the alignment shop whether they already have the X80 in their equipment software; if not, use Mazda 6 GG (not CX-5) parameters from the manual as the fallback reference. The same thread captured an early transcription of the factory figures: front wheel toe-in −20′ ± 30′, longitudinal (caster) inclination 5.93° ± 1°, rear wheel toe-in −1°20′ ± 30′, toe adjustment range 0 ± 2mm — consistent with the full table above, though with slightly different field labels 1819202122.

What can be adjusted: front versus rear. On the front suspension only toe-in (схождение) is adjustable — there are no camber adjustment bolts on the front wheels. On the rear suspension both camber (развал) and toe-in are adjustable. This asymmetry is a normal part of the X80's design, not a defect; keep it in mind after any suspension work (tie-rod replacement, ball-joint service) that requires resetting alignment 23. In October 2025 a professional alignment specialist confirmed again that no camber adjustment point exists at the front on this model; only toe/convergence can be adjusted there. Proper reassembly of suspension links and the integrity of the bushings (silentblocks) are critical for keeping the alignment: any looseness there causes misalignment that toe adjustment alone cannot fix 242526272829. Two cambering bolts (болт развальный) are used for suspension-geometry adjustment; at around 100,000 km service, a technician may recommend an aftermarket alternative to the OEM bolt rather than the original 30.

Shops refusing the service. Multiple service stations have refused to perform wheel alignment on the X80, claiming the car is not in their equipment's database; one owner was turned away by 3+ shops. This is a common complaint but not universal — it depends on the technician's willingness and how recently their alignment machine's database was updated. Workarounds reported: (1) use Mazda CX-5 alignment parameters as a substitute (risky — see below); (2) manually enter the X80 specs from the manual and calibrate by hand; (3) find a shop with a recently updated database that includes Chinese-market vehicles 313233. If a shop still claims it has no X80 specs, try the group's media uploads or consult the manual directly rather than substituting another vehicle's parameters 123. Availability has improved: in an April 2025 report, most alignment shops now carry the FAW X80's calibration parameters in their equipment, so owners can get alignment done at regular auto service centers, not just dealerships, with no special tooling or dealer visit required 3435. By January 2026 many shops had the X80 in their database; some had previously used Mazda 6 figures as a stand-in before X80-specific data was available 1314151617.

Why Mazda CX-5 parameters must not be substituted. One owner had the alignment done using Mazda CX-5 parameters in July before a long highway trip (Moscow–Voronezh) and found severe front inner-tire wear afterward — the front tire worn down to the cord/bald on the inner edge, especially on the left side, with the rear tires also excessively worn. Based on this, the owner recommends Mazda 6 GG parameters instead as a better match, though the exact parameter differences were not detailed in the thread 36. A second documented case reports inner tire wear appearing within roughly 400 km of driving on CX-5-sourced values before the discrepancy was caught; some shops may not know the CX-5 parameters are unsuitable for the X80, so if a shop's computer has no X80 entry, use the manual-input option with the official X80 figures above rather than accepting a CX-5 profile 37. The factory table is the community's authoritative reference on this point: the CX-5 has longer suspension arms and a different wheel offset (50mm vs the X80's 45mm), so CX-5 camber values cause accelerated inner-tire wear on an X80 45. Community consensus is to follow the owner's manual specifications rather than cross-platform parameters where possible 383940.

Problems after an alignment service. Steering wheel not returning after turns plus rapid tire wear: after a wheel alignment service, the steering wheel fails to return to center when turning (especially in one direction), and this correlates with unusually fast tire wear. Root causes: a bent lower control arm, or toe-in settings applied incorrectly by the shop. The fix requires physical inspection and a competent realignment using X80-specific parameters, not Mazda specs (see the lower control arm card for the bent-arm diagnosis/replacement procedure that resolved this in one case) 41424344. Vehicle pulling right (Dec 2025): a report of the car pulling right, especially noticeable on rutted or uneven roads and worse on winter tires, with the alignment done the previous autumn. Other owners confirmed the suspension is generally sensitive to road imperfections and that the hydraulic power steering is sensitive by design. Likely contributors discussed: alignment drift since the last service, worn suspension components, or road camber — but one mechanic's explanation is presented as a separate, non-fault possibility: on right-hand-drive-derived FWD layouts the inner driveshaft can be longer on one side, producing a slight pull under hard acceleration that is considered normal rather than a defect 4546.

Pricing. Moscow, October 2024: the FAW official dealership (Autogermés) charged 3,600–4,500 RUB (RU market, October 2024), with one owner noting 3,600 RUB was already a "discounted" price since the list price was 4,500 RUB; independent shops charged as little as 1,500 RUB. Some official-dealer shops are known to bundle unnecessary additional services into the alignment visit 383940. Other Moscow-area reports show the same spread by shop type: ~800 RUB at a budget garage (January 2023) and ~1,200 RUB (2024) 47, against ~4,000 RUB at the dealership-affiliated Autopilot chain in Odintsovo (RU market, October 2024) 48. Budget, non-dealership garages around Moscow are significantly cheaper than official dealership-affiliated service chains for this job 4748.

docs.title: Wheel bolt pattern and hub specifications
docs.text:
Tags: #wheels · #mazda-6-compat · #price

Prices and suppliers on this page are Russian-market (RUB, at the dates shown). Verify locally before relying on them in Syria.

FAW Besturn X80 wheel/hub specifications: bolt pattern (PCD) 114.3mm, center bore 67.1mm, offset (ET) +45mm 1. These match most standard lug nuts and wheel adapters 1. 19" wheels are also usable, with 235/50 tire size, ET +40, and hub diameter 73mm — this combination requires centering rings to take up the bore difference 2.

Hub retaining nut size (disputed, varies by year/restyle): front wheel hub nut size is 32mm (standard socket) on pre-restyled models. Rear hub nut size is reported inconsistently: one owner reports 34mm on a pre-restyled model, while another reports 32mm front-and-rear on a restyled model. Always verify which variant applies before ordering a tool or part — a special 34mm socket needed for some rear hubs costs roughly 400–1,100 RUB (RU market, April 2025) depending on source. Disagreement: the exact rule for which model years get which nut size was not resolved in the thread — treat as year/trim-dependent until confirmed for a specific VIN 3.

Replica wheels — Replay brand R18 experience: Replay-brand replica wheels (18", designed to match factory mounting) cost approximately 40,000 RUB (RU market, July 2025) per set, versus roughly 100,000 RUB for factory-brand alternative wheels. One owner tested a set on a different vehicle (a Honda Accord, 2021, 3 years of use) without issues, and reports the wheels appear visually well-made — thick rims, good paint finish. Weight is approximately 10.2 kg per wheel, described as normal for an 18" wheel. Caution: quality consistency across replica-wheel batches varies, so inspect paint coating and geometry carefully before installation 4.

Wheel-arch clips — Mazda cross-fit: the plastic clips/fasteners that secure trim on the wheel arches can be sourced from Mazda parts — a parts shop identified the correct clip as a Mazda CX-5-compatible item on sight. These are cosmetic fasteners for the wheel-arch trim area, not structural 5.

Wheel offset ET47 — fitment check (Feb 2026): an offset of ET47 (compared to the OEM ET+45 documented above) is reported as compatible with the X80. It sits roughly 2mm deeper than OEM wheels, but the difference is not visually apparent, and caliper clearance was confirmed adequate on the standard (non-modified) suspension 678910.

Wheel lug nut thread — M12x1.5mm (not 1.25mm), corrected (March 2026): FAW X80 wheel lug nuts are M12x1.5mm — not M12x1.25mm as some internet sources claim. The restyle (2018+) is confirmed to use the 1.5mm thread pitch specification. An incorrect 1.25mm-pitch nut will not thread properly. Do not confuse this with the hub retaining/stud thread below, which is a different fastener at a different pitch 11.

Front hub wheel studs — M12×1.25×45mm, and how to replace them without removing the hub (April 2026): this is a separate fastener from the wheel lug nuts above — the front hub's wheel studs (шпильки) are M12×1.25×45mm (metric thread pitch 1.25mm, length 45mm). Do not confuse with the M12×1.5 stud/nut spec used on the Mazda 6. Approximate cost: ~159 RUB per stud (RU market, 2026); available from autotc.ru and other suppliers 12131415161718. Replacement procedure — no hub removal needed: to replace a front wheel stud, position it at the edge of the protective cover (защитный кожух), pull it out slightly, and it comes out and goes back in easily; the cover can be pulled back far enough to access the studs without pulling the hub, and brake calipers do not need to be removed if working carefully 192021222324. See also the Drive2.ru front hub replacement write-up ("Замена передней ступицы (потом и кровью)") linked from the front wheel hub bearing card for the full hub-out procedure when a stud job isn't enough.

Front hub retaining nut — thread spec and part number FQGJ2133042B (2024): a separate fastener again from both the wheel lug nuts and the wheel studs above — the front hub retaining/axle nut thread is M20, 1.5mm pitch, left-hand thread (резьба левая — note the reverse-thread direction when loosening). Part number FQGJ2133042B ("Гайка передней ступицы FAW Besturn X80"), listed around 400 RUB (RU market, May 2024), is available from kitzapchasti.ru and similar retailers. (In the same conversation thread, an unrelated parts question came up about the air-filter intake resonator box — FC011319X is the main/primary article number, with 5CA21319X as an alternate reference for the same restyle-spec resonator; see stock and sourcing links at kitzap.ru, kitparts.ru, and kitzapchasti.ru — this is noted here only because it shares the same source thread, not because it's a hub/wheel part.) 2526272829303132333435.

Compatible aftermarket wheel specification range — R17/7.0-7.5J/5x114.3/ ET40-45/DIA67.1: for choosing aftermarket wheels generally (not tied to one donor car), search by these X80 parameters: R17, 7.0–7.5" width, 5x114.3 bolt pattern, ET45–50, hub bore (DIA) 67.1mm. Practical advice on offset: prefer ET40–45 over ET50 — ET50 sits noticeably recessed into the fender ("утопленные"); tire width can be used to partly compensate for offset choice, but ET is the primary lever — the lower the ET number, the further the wheel sits outward 36. Wheels from Mazda, Kia, or Hyundai were named as compatible donor brands meeting this spec 36. One owner fitted Mazda 6 wheels but got the offset wrong and had to add spacers to compensate 37. Another owner runs Mazda CX-5 wheels directly, paired with 225/60 tires, with no spacer mentioned 3839.

Wheel nut socket size. Victor answered that the wheel bolt/nut head is 21 mm (not 19 mm) 40.
